title: Monitoring of Sweat Calcium Using Skin Patches
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Bone loss can occur during bed rest due to lack of limb use, and exercise has been researched as a potential countermeasure. Calcium loss in sweat from this normal exercise program has been a concern, especially if the exercise occurs at normal room temperature. In previous bed rest studies, early changes in bone mass have been detected by measuring calcium. Past subjects have undergone a negative calcium balance due to a rapid increase in calcium excretion through the urine and feces. Most studies did not measure calcium loss in sweat, because researchers assumed that the loss had a negligible effect on calcium balance. This assumption was not tested often, partly because an accurate measurement of sweat calcium was difficult. However, one previous study showed that calcium loss through sweat was much greater during one hour of running on a treadmill at room temperature than for the entire remainder of the day. The mean value of the calcium loss was 47 mg per hour while running and 0.8 mg per hour for the rest of the day. Another earlier study also supported the conclusion that sweat calcium loss was greater during strenuous exercise than for sedentary activities. Thus, loss of calcium in sweat could indeed prove to be a significant factor in total body calcium loss, especially when the countermeasures for bone density loss are applied. Since bone density and calcium balance are important factors in health, countermeasures against their degradation need to be optimized and a simple, reliable method of calcium sweat detection should be determined. This bed rest study had two main purposes. First, researchers tested a non-invasive sweat collection method for its ability to monitor sweat calcium loss. Second, changes in skin calcium loss were measured with and without a resistive exercise countermeasure performed at a lower environmental temperature.
approach: The subjects of this bed rest study consisted of six females (five white and 1 black) and ten males (nine white and one black). The subjects ages ranged from 22 to 48 years, and weight ranged from 60 to 97 kg. Heights ranged from 157 to 185 cm. Subjects were divided into three groups. One group was assigned resistive exercise with a workload that increased progressively throughout the bed rest study. A second group did not exercise, but ingested a drug called alendronate (brand name of Fosamax®), which is used to strengthen bone. The third group did not exercise or ingest a drug; these subjects served as controls. To collect sweat from the subjects, skin patches (Osteopatch®), were attached to the skin on the back, lower chest, and upper part of the arm. Initial studies involved placing two patches, one on each side of the body, on each area for a total of six patches. Later the number was reduced from two patches to one per body region. Data from the patches were collected from four different time periods: a baseline ambulatory time before bed rest and at 6, 12 and 17 weeks of bed rest. Patches were worn for 24 hours on two consecutive days. The subjects that were assigned resistive exercise performed the exercise six days a week with no exercise performed on Sunday. The two consecutive days for exercise sweat collection occurred within this six-day period so that both days contained exercise. For this group of subjects, sweat was collected on rest days, as well as exercise days. Since there were not two consecutive days without exercise, this sweat collection occurred on two successive Sundays. The bed rest room temperature was 23 to 26°C. The room temperature during exercise was 18°C or less to minimize sweat loss. The skin patch used to collect sweat had an absorbing area of 14 cm 2 and absorbed the solid components of sweat while the fluid evaporated out. The skin was cleaned with an alcohol swab and allowed to dry before the patch was applied. After 24 hours of wear, the patch was removed and the absorption pad portion was refrigerated until analysis. During elution, the pad was placed at the top of a tube and dried for 30 minutes to remove all fluid. One milliliter of distilled water was then added to the pad. After an hour, the tube was centrifuged for ten minutes at 3000 rpm to collect the liquid at the bottom of the tube while the patch remained secured at the top. Calcium concentration was determined from the collected liquid.
results: Baseline data, which were taken from 12 subjects, each with six different patches duplicating the three body areas, show no differences between the duplicate body measurements. Significant differences in calcium excretion were found between back versus arm sweat and back versus chest sweat. However no significant differences were found between chest versus arm calcium excretion in sweat. No significant differences were found between the two different but consecutive days. In addition, no interaction or change in the relationships between the three regions was found over the consecutive days. The most variability in the results, 58%, was attributed to body region site with only 0.3% variability attributed to the day and 10% to site by day interaction. The range of inter-individual variability during the baseline collection varied from 18 to 32% for the three regions, with arms at 20% variability, chest at 18% variability and back at 24% variability combined over the days. The inter-individual variability for the two days combined over sites was 20% and 29%. For seven subjects who did not exercise, data collection occurred over the four time periods. No significant differences were observed between their baseline and the other collections, which occurred at 6, 12 and 17 weeks of bed rest. Some of these subjects ingested the alendronate and others were in the control group. During the bed rest timeframe, data from five exercise subjects were taken on exercise days and on rest days. No significant differences were observed between the rest days and the exercise days or between the two consecutive exercise days for the same subject. Total body sweat calcium for the twelve subjects during baseline data collection was averaged for the three sites and was 35 ± 4 mg/day. The mean value for the arm was 33 mg/day. The chest mean value was 35 mg/day and the back was 37 mg/day. The patch collection method was shown to be reliable for the measurement of sweat calcium loss. This conclusion was supported by the lack of large variations among repeated measurements by day and by site. The small difference between the back calcium excretion and the arm and chest excretion agreed with another published study that found a higher evaporation rate from the back. In this investigation, dermal calcium excretion was not studied during profuse sweating, so no conclusions could be drawn about the use of the skin patch in that circumstance. No significant differences were found between exercise and rest day values of sweat calcium loss for bed rest subjects that performed resistive exercise with a lower room temperature. In addition, no significant differences were found between baseline and bed rest calcium loss values; this room temperature was also controlled, but was not kept as low as it was during the exercise condition. Calcium excretion in sweat has been shown in other studies to increase significantly when aerobic exercise was performed at standard room temperature. In this study, no effect was observed on sweat calcium due to exercise. This observation was due to the cool environment in which the exercise was performed and also, possibly, to the fact that the exercise in this study was resistive rather than aerobic. This bed rest study showed that the skin patch could be used to determine the amount of calcium excreted in human sweat for up to 24 hours in normal sweating conditions. Any changes in sweat calcium from bed rest, with or without exercise in a cool environment, did not significantly affect total body calcium balance.

title: Osteoblast Adhesion and Phenotype in Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The purpose of this experiment was to investigate: 1) whether microgravity induces changes in osteoblastic cells similar to those caused by bone resorption-stimulating agents like parathyroid hormone (PTH), and 2) whether those phenotypic changes are associated with alterations in cell shape and/or adhesive interactions with the extracellular matrix.
approach: A permanent cell line derived from a rat osteosarcoma and stably exhibiting an osteoblast-like phenotype (ROS 17/2.8) was cultured on microcarrier beads and inoculated into 24 STL cartridges. At times ranging from 6 hrs to 10 days post-launch, samples of conditioned medium were collected from pairs of cartridges from the 12 flight and 12 ground control groups, and the cartridges were perfused with fixative. Upon recovery after landing, the medium was assayed for lactate (an indicator of metabolic activity and cell viability), alkaline phosphatase (an osteoblast marker enzyme), cyclic AMP (produced by osteoblastic cells in response to PTH) and prostaglandin E2 (a locally produced mediator of bone turnover). The cells were examined by phase contrast and fluorescence microscopy to assess shape changes, cytoskeletal organization and interactions with their substrata.
results: Measurements of lactate, alkaline phosphatase, cAMP and PGE2 indicated the presence of viable cells expressing an osteoblastic phenotype; however, no differences were found in any of these parameters between the flight and ground samples. Microscopic examination of the beads indicated that a loss of cells occurred early after inoculation into cartridges in flight and ground samples alike, followed apparently by slow recovery and growth. No gross differences were found in cell shape between flight and ground samples.

title: Dosimetric Mapping
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Radiation constitutes one of the most important hazards for humans in long-duration space missions. Leaving the earth's surface, humans are exposed to a wide spectrum of particles and energies of galactic and solar origin. The intensity, energy, and elemental composition of the radiation field changes considerably with orbital parameters, shielding thickness and solar activity. Results from numerous space probes demonstrate heightened radiation levels compared to the earth's surface and a change in the nature of the radiation field, particularly the heavy ion component. Although considerable data has been accumulated from several spaceflights, it is not yet possible to provide a quantitative description of the radiation field, especially at the edge of the radiation belt, because of its highly complex composition regarding the particles present and their energy spectra. Data comparison is hampered by uncertain angular distribution of the single radiation components, by missing knowledge on the angular response of instruments and missing information about shielding distributions at the instrument locations. Current models either under- or overestimate the contribution of different radiation components. Due to the variety of particles and energies present in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), no single detector system is capable of providing sufficient information. Therefore, the DOSMAP (Dosimetric Mapping) dosimetry package consisted of several types of detectors to allow for measurement of different particle types and energies. The DOSMAP dosimetry package was further supplemented with instruments contributed by NASA (Phantom Torso) and NASDA (Bonner Ball). The different systems allowed for the first time inflight cross-calibration of measurements at the same shielding configurations. This is absolute necessary when recognizing that the comparison of currently available data is often not possible due to not well known angular response of the detector systems combined with unknown angular incidence of radiations and only approximate knowledge of shielding distributions.
approach: Several components of the DOSMAP dosimetry package (dosimetry telescopes [DOSTELS], computer interface unit [CIU], and the thermoluminescent dosimeter [TLD] reader and bulbs) were brought to the International Space Station (ISS) aboard A Shuttle flight. These components were unstowed and set-up in the Retention Net of the Human Research Facility (HRF). Another shuttle brought the remaining DOSMAP hardware (mobile dosimetry units [MDUs] and nuclear track detector packages [NTDP] to the ISS. The MDUs were charged, and an initial read-out was performed for the MDUs and the TLD bulbs prior to their installation throughout the U.S. Lab and Node 1. The NTDPs were also placed at the required locations. All placements were photo documented. Data collected from the TLD bulbs by the TLD Reader were downloaded to the HRF PC every 7-10 days, and data collected from the MDUs were downloaded through the CIU to the HRF PC every 5 days. During the same time intervals the MDUs were recharged. The DOSTELs were activated and data downloads to the HRF PC were performed every 10 days. All data of the active instruments were downlinked during the mission. All of the dosimetry hardware was returned to Earth on A shuttle flight.
results: All data received by the investigators was of good quality. Several hardware issues resulted in small amounts of data loss. Due to the retirement of Prof. W. Heinrich the evaluation of the CR39 NTDP detectors by the group of the University of Siegen could not be completed. The science return may be roughly quoted at about 95%. TLD Based on the characterization of the different detector systems, the following can be concluded. The data for all the different applied TLD systems agree very well taking into account the different Linear Energy Transfer (LET) efficiency of the detector types used as well as the different neutron sensitivity of 6Li doped and 7Li doped TLD materials. The higher dose values for TLD600 and TLD700 dosimeters are due to the higher LET efficiency of these dosimeter materials compared to Cu, P doped LiF crystals. Neutron Dose The determination of neutron dose equivalent using chiefly recoil protons can give too high of a dose value depending on the amount of primary protons contributing to the signal. For this reason, two methods of neutron dose equivalent determination were used. However, both methods still have their limitations and uncertainties. On the other hand, the neutron dose values determined by the two different methods are almost comparable within the standard deviations determined by uncertainty propagation, which indicates that the assumptions made are not too wrong. Measurements with converters with even higher sensitivity to thermal neutrons may improve the standard deviation and better spectral knowledge of the neutron spectra in space may improve the uncertainty of the calibration factor for Albedo dosimeters. Passive Dosimetry System (PDS) The use of the Pille reader in automatic mode permitted dose to be measured as a function of orbit number by TLD A0101. Orbits that passed through the SAA received doses of 30 to >50 µGy/orbit. During these particular orbits, the spacecraft received a substantially larger exposure to trapped protons than during orbits that did not pass through the SAA. For orbits that did not traverse the SAA, the absorbed dose was ~10 µGy/orbit. All orbits that passed through the SAA do not receive the same dose because each orbit passed through only a fraction of the SAA and the size of this fraction changed as the ISS orbit precessed around the Earth. Generally, the ISS passed through the SAA twice during each twenty-four hour period. Following exposure and return to the laboratory, each PDS detector was disassembled and the individual CR-39 PNTD layers were selected for chemical processing (etching). The combined LET spectrum for the x-, y- and z-oriented short-etch CR-39 PNTDs was generated following readout of the 3 detectors. Similarly, the combined LET spectrum was generated for the x-, y- and z-oriented long-etch detectors. There is fairly close agreement between the three mutually orthogonal spectra measured in the long-etch detectors. Similarly, for LET <100 keV/µm, there is fairly close agreement between the 3 mutually orthogonal detectors measured in the short-etch detectors. Only above 100 keV/µm is there a difference in the 3 spectra, where the curve measured in the short-etch x-oriented detector lies significantly above those measured in the short-etch y and z detectors. This is likely due to greater shielding in the x direction relative to the other two directions. The relative contribution to the LET spectrum from neutron- and proton-induced target fragments tend to increase with increasing LET. The reduced efficiency with which tracks are detected in the short-etch detectors below ~30 keV/µm is apparent, as is the increased signal due to target fragmentation in the LET region above 100 keV/µm in the short-etch detectors. There is fairly close agreement between the detectors for the 2 etch regimes in the LET interval between 30 and 100 keV/µm. The crossover point of the short-etch and long-etch spectra, 35 keV/µm for PDS A0103, was located in the plot differential LET fluence spectra and used in combining the short-etch and long-etch curves into one total LET spectrum. During the DOSMAP experiment, mean total dose rate measured in the PDS dosimeters ranged from 6.88 ± 0.42 µGy/hr in Node 1, above the forward hatch leading to the FGB module, to 10.36 ± 0.54 µGy/hr above the aft hatch of Node 1. The mean total dose equivalent rate varied from 14.06 ± 0.93 µSv/hr to 18.81 ± 1.11 µSv/hr at these same respective locations. The average quality factor varied from 1.82 ± 0.13 above the aft hatch of Node 1 to 2.11 ± 0.16 on the starboard side of the US Lab near the aft hatch. DOSTEL By chance a significant solar particle event occurred during the active phase of DOSTEL on April 15, 2001. Thanks to the action of the crew, DOSTEL 1 was switched into a special mode while DOSTEL 2 remained in the mode for article and dose rate measurement. In the special mode, the 2 detector signals of DOSTEL 1 were stored for each individual particle. Stopping protons impinging from the top and bottom of the telescope were clearly seen, along with some stopping He-particles that were also identified. A plot of dose rates during the mission clearly shows the dependence of dose rates from the altitude, which ranged from 404 km to 386 km. Based on the mean quality factor derived from the LET spectra by applying the LET dependence of the quality factor as defined in ICRP Report No. 60 equivalent doses can be calculated. Mobile Dosimetry Unit (MDU) Approximately 4.5 MB of rough compressed information was received by each MDU. After decompression, the volume of data increases by an approximate factor of 30. The values of the mean doses per day was 180.7, 189.9, 166.1, 126.3 µGy/day in MDU#1 to MDU#4, respectively. When graphed these doses lie on the AP8MAX prediction line. Comparison of fluxes by 4 different MDUs shows that large differences are produced by the differences in the position of MDU and shielding distributions for them. In the time span 27 June-4 July 2001 four MDUs were placed at fixed locations: one unit (MDU#4) in the ISS "Unity" Node-1 and three (MDU #1-3) units were located at different locations in the US Laboratory module. MDU #2 results showed that the spectra inside the ISS has a maximum energy of 300 MeV and that the place of the maximum of the spectra moves from about 100 MeV at low L values toward 50-60 MeV at higher L values. The agreement of the data received by active and passive detectors is in the range of ±10%. Comparisons of the passive devices yield even a smaller range, when corrected by the efficiency function of the different materials. Dose equivalents were calculated from the measurements using the quality factor (Q) as defined in ICRP Report No. 60. In comparison to other spaceflight missions, the lower dose equivalents seen for ISS are due to less solar activity during the measurement period and due to higher shielding of the ISS. The dose equivalents received by the combination of nuclear track detectors with TLDs show values close to the DOSTEL dose equivalents. The error in the determination of the dose equivalent from passive detectors is about 6%. The combined CR39 NTDP/TLD dose equivalent appears too low compared to the DOSTEL dose equivalents. Since the low let measurements of the TLDs are in good agreement with DOSTEL and the CR39 NTDP LET spectra as well, further investigations are needed to close this gap of knowledge. Adding the neutron dose from the personal dosimeter would increase the dose equivalent measurements by about 33 µSv/day. The DOSMAP experiment was the first effort to map dose and dose equivalent as function of the location in the US lab and in Node 1 of the ISS. Having a fully developed 3-D ray tracing model the obtained data can be used to validate the Model. A quite impressive set of data has been produced by the "Dosimetric Mapping" experiment from which only a part could be presented in this summary. Since the radiation field is both complex and dynamic, measurements across the ISS need to be continued in future missions to study the radiation field and its modification by mass shielding, leading to attenuation, build up and/or activation. There is a continuous need for information on absorbed dose, particle and linear energy transfer spectra in real time.

title: The Evaluation of Concentric and Eccentric Skeletal Muscle Contractions Following Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Loss of muscle strength and endurance after long exposure to microgravity can interfere with the safe completion of critical tasks during space flight, emergency or routine landing, or during egress. Decreases in leg strength have been documented after Skylab missions as well as after Russian space flights. The objectives of this study were to assess pre flight-to-postflight changes in muscle strength and endurance and to evaluate the effect of in flight exercise on these changes. Changes in muscle performance after missions of shorter or longer duration were compared.
approach: Muscle performance was tested before and after space flight in 19 astronauts (3 women, 16 men), 10 from 5-day missions and 9 from missions lasting 9 to 11 days. LIDO isokinetic dynamometers were used to measure muscle performance in the back and abdomen and at the knee, ankle, shoulder, and elbow. These dynamometers provide variable resistance so that movements will continue at the same speed (i.e., they are isokinetic) regardless of the force applied. Both concentric and eccentric strength were measured. Concentric strength is the strength of a muscle as it contracts to move a body part, while eccentric strength is the strength of the muscle as it is gradually lengthened while resisting the motion of a body part. Endurance was tested during 25 repetitions of concentric knee flexion and extension. The eccentric torque maximum was 400 foot pounds. Subjects abstained from food for 2 hours before testing, from caffeine 4 hours before, and from exercise 12 hours before. The dynamometers were calibrated externally and internally (electronically) before each test session. Joint configurations and ranges of motion were recorded for each subject and reproduced for each test session. Testing of the limbs was unilateral with the dominant limb, unless contraindicated. Verbal instructions were consistent and given before each joint test. No verbal encouragement was given during the tests. Mean results from tests conducted approximately 1, 2, and 3 weeks before launch were compared to results from landing day and from 7 days after landing. Only 17 subjects were tested on landing day. Losses greater than about 9% were considered to be operationally relevant. Four of the astronauts also performed in flight exercise as part of DSO 476, using a treadmill with a tether system to simulate gravity. They followed continuous or interval exercise protocols with target heart rates intended to correspond to 60% to 85% of preflight maximum oxygen consumption. The percentages of change in their strength and endurance test results were compared with those of 5 astronauts who did not exercise during the flight.
results: From before the flight to landing day, large decreases in the strength of the back and abdomen occurred. Strength had decreased by 23% in the concentric tests of the back, 14% in the eccentric tests of the back, and 10% in the concentric tests of the abdomen. The loss in back strength was greater after flights of 9 to 11 days (concentric, 28%; eccentric, 17%) than after flights of 5 days (concentric, 18%; eccentric, 11%). Eccentric abdominal and concentric back strength had recovered significantly 7 days after landing. A significant (12%) decrease in concentric strength of the quadriceps muscle of the thigh was also seen on landing day. No significant loss of strength was seen in the hamstring muscles or in the tests at the ankle, shoulder or elbow, except for a few minor losses that were not considered operationally relevant. The four astronauts who exercised during flight actually gained eccentric strength of the gastrocnemius muscle of the calf. Although the exercising astronauts lost concentric strength in the quadriceps, the percent change was significantly less than for the four nonexercising astronauts. For the other results of the knee and ankle tests, decreases in strength were generally smaller in those who exercised; although, the differences between exercisers and nonexercisers were not statistically significant. Treadmill exercise did not prevent losses of strength in the back or abdomen. Decrements exhibited by muscles of the five astronauts who did not exercise during flight indicated that muscles are less able to maintain endurance and resist fatigue after space flight. The astronauts who exercised had no loss of endurance. There was no change in endurance after 5-day flights, but the endurance of the quadriceps decreased after flights of 9 to 11 days. Endurance recovered within 7 days of landing. These results showed that space flight results in losses of skeletal muscle strength and endurance, and that the losses are greater after flights of longer duration. Strength was lost primarily in the antigravity muscles of the legs and torso. Exercise may prevent losses of muscle strength and endurance.

title: Characterization of Respirable Airborne Particulate Matter in Shuttle Atmosphere
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Shuttle crewmembers have reported eye and respiratory irritation they attributed to visible debris in the air. Some cases of equipment failure can be attributed to airborne debris. Large amounts of particulate matter have been found in microbial air samplers and on filters and vacuum bags after flights. However, airborne particulate matter in the Shuttle had never been systematically collected. The objectives of this study were to assess the concentration, size distribution, composition, and potential sources of airborne particles on the Shuttle flight deck and middeck.
approach: Two Shuttle Particle Samplers (SPSs) and one Shuttle Particle Monitor (SPM) were carried on each of two Shuttle missions. One particle sampler was activated early in the flight, and another, late in the flight. The particle sampler trapped particles during a 24 hour period and separated them according to their aerodynamic size into four fractions: 100 µm. Particles larger than 100 µm were trapped on a screen with 100 µm openings, in the inlet cap. The other particles were collected on Teflon filters. The particle sampler had two virtual impactor stages, each with six nozzles. After a flight, the SPSs were returned to the laboratory, where the largest particles were vacuumed from the filter onto another filter and weighed, and the other particles were weighed on the filters that had trapped them. The filters had been weighed when empty. The elemental composition was determined by X-ray fluorescence for the smaller particles and by energy-dispersive spectroscopy for the larger particles. Some larger particles were also examined by scanning electron microscopy. The SPM measured particle concentrations by photometric detection of light scatter. It automatically recorded the minimum, maximum, and average particle concentrations over 15-minute intervals throughout the flight. It was set to zero by running it in clean air and was calibrated by running it alongside the particle sampler. The particle monitor was useful for following changes in particle concentration over time; however, it recorded only particles that were smaller than 100 µm.
results: The particle concentration averaged 56 µg/m3 on one flight and 35 µg/m3 on the other. The particle concentration did not increase over time. Judging by the elemental composition, most of the particles were probably of organic origin. These results should be useful for evaluating the effectiveness of modifications to cabin air filtration systems.

title: In-flight Radiation Detection
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Observation of light flashes in the eyes of Apollo astronauts, which were determined to be caused by radioactive cosmic rays, renewed concern about potential radiobiological effects of high linear energy transfer (LET) particles in space flight. The documentation of high-LET particles in a variety of space flight conditions is an important factor in assessing potential hazards to humans in space.
approach: The 9-day ASTP mission was flown between July 15 and July 25, 1975, at an altitude of 220 km and an inclination of 51.6 degrees. High-LET particle radiation was recorded in passive dosimeters worn by the three U.S. Apollo-Soyuz Test Project astronauts. The dosimeters consisted of thin films of plastic nuclear track detectors and a silver chloride (Gal) crystal. The radiation is measured by counting the tracks made as the radioactive particles impact the crystal and scar its surface. After each dosimeter was returned to Earth, the plastics were removed and processed in temperature controlled, mechanically stirred etching tanks. Scanning and measurement of the tracks made in the plastics was done with an optical microscope at 430x magnification. The AgCl crystals were removed, in a darkroom, from each dosimeter and immediately stabilized with yellow light for 30 seconds and placed in a light-tight box for storage. Tracks were developed by decorating each crystal with ultraviolet (UV) light for 17.5 minutes. The crystals were then scanned in red light at 650x magnification in a darkroom. Only tracks which intersected both surfaces (i.e. spanning tracks) of a crystal were counted.
results: Generally, near-Earth missions with high inclination orbits (versus low inclination orbits) receive a higher flux of high-LET particles because of the decreased absorption of particles in the atmosphere at higher inclinations. Lunar missions normally receive higher radiation exposures than near-Earth missions due to the absence of shielding of radioactive particles by the Earth's atmosphere. A total of 48 events were located in a 0.192 square centimeter area of the crystal, giving the fluence value of 250 tracks/cm2. The flux recorded in the plastics and AgCl crystal was, respectively, 1.15 and 27.5 particles/cm2 per day. Thus, there was higher particle registration sensitivity in the AgCl than in the plastics. Comparison of results showed that the high-LET particle flux incident on Skylab astronauts was a factor 2.9 larger than ASTP, due to both the lower altitude orbit of ASTP (220 km compared with 435 km for Skylab) and the greater spacecraft shielding that ASTP had. The main feature of the ASTP measurements was a sharp decrease in particle flux toward large LET values. Radiobiological damage expected from particles with long range and large LET values can be expected to be quite severe.

research_area: Toxicology; Environmental monitoring; Life support systems
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: With long-term space habitation quickly becoming a reality, the need for development of more advanced life support systems has become a priority. One drawback of current life support systems is the lack of real-time, on-site monitoring of the changing concentrations of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) present in the living environment. Applications of this technology extend far beyond life support systems; they have a number of ground-based uses as well. These include engine exhaust analysis, human breath analysis, stack monitoring, and fence-post monitoring. Technological advances in this field are vital to ensure human health and will have to be thoroughly researched before long-term space habitation is possible. The Mir station environment is one example where this type of real-time, on-site, monitoring of VOCs would be very useful. The types and concentrations of VOCs in the Mir station atmosphere are not well characterized. Detailed information regarding the types and concentrations of VOCs present in the Mir environment would be very useful in assessing the long term health risks associated with living in such an environment. Present methods of monitoring VOCs using cartridge and grab methods of sampling and GC/MS for analysis are both proven and cost-effective, but have several drawbacks including the lack of on-site, real-time monitoring. Newly developed direct sampling ion trap mass spectrometry (DSITMS) shows excellent promise in both real-time monitoring of VOCs and space portability. The following were objectives of this experiment: Characterize the Mir station environment using proven sampling and analysis methods Demonstrate the use DSITMS for direct monitoring of VOCs in air samples collected from Mir station Document the types and concentrations of VOCs present on the Mir station analyze the results in collaboration with other investigators in order to further the goals of the NASA research announcement.
approach: During the NASA (2-6)/ Mir (21-24) missions, air samples were taken from various locations on the Mir space station. Twenty-four hour time averaged air samples were obtained using Solid Sorbent Air Samplers (SSASs) and instantaneous air samples were obtained using Grab Sample Canisters (GSCs). The air samples collected from the Mir station were returned to the JSC toxicology lab; a subset of these was transferred to Dr. Belisle's lab for analysis (the 1st subset of Mir-21 samples were analyzed at Dr. Palmer's laboratory). Both GSC and SSAS samples were analyzed by gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) and direct sampling ion trap mass spectrometry (DSITMS). Samples were analyzed via GC/MS using a modified version of the EPA TO-14 method. The VOCs were first concentrated and then isolated from the bulk of the air sample. A GC/MS data system was then used to separate and detect individual VOCs. Once separated from one another, both retention time matches and library searching of mass spectral data were used to identify individual VOCs. Calculating the actual concentrations of the VOCs was very complex due to the fact that the Mir samples had been repressurized, and therefore diluted, during analysis at the JSC toxicology lab. Taking this into account, many correction factors and proportional relationships between intensities of samples and standards were used when calculating actual concentrations of VOCs present in the Mir environment. DSITMS analysis was performed on samples from Mir 22, 23, and 24. Air samples from Mir-24 were reserved for DSITMS analyses only. Air samples were introduced into an ion trap mass spectrometer (ITMS) by a prototype sample introduction system known as a Real-Time Air Monitor (RTAM). The ITMS then analyzed the samples in MS scan mode in order to detect as many VOCs as possible in a single pass. MS/MS analysis would have provided better selective deduction of individual VOCs but due to limited sample volume this was not a viable option. VOCs were tentatively identified by the presence of characteristic ions. This data was then compared to intermediate and working gas standards prepared on the same day.
results: Analysis of air samples taken from the Mir station showed the air to be nominal, if not better, than that of most indoor environments on earth. Space maximum allowable concentrations (SMACs) were not available for all VOCs identified, but most fell between 0.1 and 1000 mg/m3. Nearly all VOCs measured were less than 1mg/m3 and were well within SMACs. The target compounds for the GC/MS analysis included VOCs in the TO-14 standard plus additional VOCs identified in samples from prior Mir missions. Several fluorocarbons and chlorofluorocarbons were identified in Mir samples. These compounds are highly volatile and were shown to be not very well trapped by the SSAS devices. Several aromatic hydrocarbons were identified, including benzene, which is thought to have been a product of incomplete combustion from the solid fuel oxygen generator fire (SFOG). Biogenic hydrocarbons identified on Mir most likely came from plant growth experiments. Similar to the fluorocarbons, these compounds were better identified by the GSCs. Two siloxane compounds were identified in Mir samples and are thought to have come from either silicone-based sealants or anti-perspirants, both of which are common on Mir. Although the DSITMS analysis was more qualitative than quantitative, it was proven effective and reliable. The DSITMS analysis was effective because it identified all VOCs present above the 10-50 ppb detection limit. The DSITMS was proven reliable in that it did not indicate any false positive (identifying a VOC that was not present in GC/MS analysis). Although DSITMS is still under development it's selectivity, speed, and simplicity make it a viable option for future earth and space applications.

title: Nutritional Status Assessment during Phases IIa and III of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Nutrition is a critical concern for extended-duration space missions. Loss of body weight is a primary consequence of altered nutrition and is frequently observed during space flight. Other existing dietary concerns for space flight include excessive intakes of sodium and iron and insufficient intakes of water and vitamin D. Furthermore, dependence on closed or semi-closed food systems increases the likelihood of inadequate intakes of key nutrients. This is a significant concern for extended-duration space missions. Space nutrition research often necessitates detailed recording of all food consumption. While this yields extremely accurate data, it requires considerable time and effort, and thus is not suitable for routine medical monitoring during space flight. To alleviate this problem, a food frequency questionnaire (FFQ) was designed to provide a quick and easy, yet reasonably accurate, method for crewmembers to provide dietary intake information to the ground support crew. This study was designed to assess nutritional status before, during, and after the 60-day and 91-day chamber stays. An additional goal of the study was to validate a food frequency questionnaire designed specifically for use with space flight food systems.
approach: The subjects completed a standard food frequency questionnaire, prior to entering the chamber to assess usual diet over the past year. During the chamber stay, a specialized food frequency questionnaire was completed to assess intake either over 24-hour (FFQ 24-h) or seven-day (FFQ 7-d) periods. Five-day weighed food records were completed on weeks 2 and 5 of the 60-day study and on weeks 3, 7, and 11 of the 91-day study. During the weighed record sessions, subjects were provided a digital scale and log book and were instructed to weigh and record all food, fluids, vitamin/mineral supplements, and medicines consumed. A research dietitian met with the subjects before the prechamber data collection session to provide training for all diet intake assessment methods. A complete biochemical nutritional assessment profile was developed for use with flight crews on extended-duration space missions. This assessment profile was used in these ground-based studies to determine the impact of the semi-closed, space-like food system on crew nutritional status. Bone densitometry and body composition were determined using dual energy X-ray absorptiometry techniques. Total body water (TBW) was determined using isotope (18O) dilution, as described previously. Sodium bromide was used to measure extracellular fluid volume (ECF). Body weight was determined weekly using a standard scale. Blood samples were collected before and after both chamber studies, as well as two times during the 90-day test. For the 60-day chamber study, a total of 52 mL of blood were collected over approximately 70 days. For the 91-day chamber study, a total of 98 mL of blood were collected over approximately 100 days. Urine was collected for two 24-hour periods before, every day during, and two 24-hour periods after the chamber studies; pre- and postchamber urine collections began on the day of blood collection. Complete urine analysis was conducted once during the 60-day study and three times during the 91-day chamber study.
results: Energy and protein intakes were similar for the three intake assessment techniques during both studies. Caloric intakes were 94 ± 16% and 85 ± 16% of the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations for the subjects in the 60-day and 91-day tests, respectively. Subjects in both tests maintained their body weights within 3% of their pretest values on exit from the chamber. During the 60-day study, questionnaire estimates of calcium and iron intakes were lower than those of the weighed diet records. Subsequent analysis revealed that these differences were related to differences in the nutrient content data used for two foods (milk and cereal), specifically between the nutrient databases used to analyze the weighed diet records and the food frequency questionnaire. When the databases were synchronized for nutrient content of these food items, no differences were observed. Sodium intake assessment yielded similar results for the three techniques during the 60-day chamber study. However, the FFQ 24-h sodium intakes were higher than those for FFQ 7-d questionnaires during the 91-day study. Water intake assessment during the 60-day study was different for all three assessment techniques. Conversely, no differences were observed during the 91-day study. Body weight did not change during the chamber studies. No changes in total body water were observed in either chamber study. Markers of lean body mass, urinary creatinine and 3-methylhistidine were unchanged during the chamber studies. Extracellular fluid volume (ECFV) was measured using a 1.2 g dose of sodium bromide in capsule form for the 60-day study. One subject experienced gastric distress and subsequently did not receive the bromide dose after the chamber. ECFV did not change in the other three subjects. Modifications to the ECFV protocol resulted in administration of 1.5 g of sodium bromide as a ~50 mL liquid solution for the 91-day study. This form of the dose was better tolerated, and ECFV was similarly unaffected during the longer chamber study. Iron status tended to be negatively influenced throughout both studies, despite high dietary iron intake. Serum ferritin decreased by 21 ± 13 µg/L (p = 0.054) after the 60-day test, and by 29 ± 22 µg/L p The study described here provided a valuable opportunity to test a nutritional assessment profile and a unique food frequency questionnaire in an environment similar to that found on a space station, without the constraints of an actual space mission. The results indicate that a specially designed food frequency questionnaire can be used to reliably estimate individual dietary intake. These studies confirm that a semi-closed food system can support nutritional requirements over a short period of time (i.e., two to three months). The comprehensive nutritional status assessment profile described here (with minor modifications) has been implemented by NASA as a medical requirement for extended-duration (i.e., International Space Station) space travelers. The anthropometric, biochemical, clinical, and dietary assessment components each contributes valuable information to the total picture of nutritional status. The intent is to provide a preflight assessment of crew nutritional status to assure optimal status prior to flight, a real-time means of monitoring dietary intake during flight, and a nutritional component for the postflight rehabilitation program. Although nutritional status was generally adequate in the 60-day and 91-day tests, micronutrient status is of concern in a semi-closed food system. Three subjects in the 91-day test had inadequate folate intakes, and three subjects in each test had inadequate vitamin D intakes. However, 10 days of the vegetarian BIO-Plex diet did not affect any of the biochemical indices examined during the 90-day test.

title: Anticipatory Postural Activity (POSA)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Gravity supplies a frame of reference for the human sensory-motor response. In the absence of gravity, such as during space flight, several systems are hindered. These disturbances are compensated for by the brain, and ultimately, the body adapts to the weightless environment. Balance and locomotion functions are temporarily disturbed after return to Earth, but eventually return to preflight levels. Postural problems reported by crewmembers include increased sway while standing, difficulty in rounding corners and increased body movement during locomotion. This investigation assessed the impact of microgravity on neuromuscular anticipatory postural activity and examined the changes, intending to provide a better understanding of balance and locomotion in humans and to design countermeasures which could reduce the time course of readaptation to 1-g. The five objectives examined during this study were: (1) Determine how long-duration space flight altered the anticipatory neuromuscular activity associated with arm movement. (2) Perform proof-of-concept research to determine whether foot sensory input modified neuromuscular responses during space flight. (3) Determine the time course of adaptation during long-duration space flight to foot sensory input as measured by patterns of neuromuscular activation. (4) Determine whether long-duration space flight modified anticipatory neuromuscular postural activity in the immediate postflight period. (5) Determine whether modifications in anticipatory neuromuscular postural activity associated with long-duration space flight were correlated with postural instability immediately after landing and during the recovery period.
approach: During all ground-based data collection, subjects wore shorts, t-shirts and stocking feet with electrodes and accelerometer leads attached to the body with adhesive tape (Belt Pack Amplification System (BPAS) vest assembly). The accelerometer was attached to a wrist splint worn by the subject. The subject stepped onto a force plate, assumed an upright position with feet shoulder-width apart and arms resting comfortably at the sides. With eyes closed, the subject performed 15 rapid, 90 degree shoulder flexions, keeping the arm and wrist locked throughout the movement. The movements were self-initiated and the subject regained stability before performing the next movement. The Flock of Birds motion analysis system was used during this testing to obtain measures of segmental body motion. The BPAS vest assembly was used inflight to collect electromyogram (EMG) and acceleration data during a series of arm raises. EMG signals were obtained by placing an electrode on a muscle, and flexing the muscle. Acceleration data were obtained by placing the accelerometer wrist assembly on the right wrist, and then raising and lowering the arm. Voice data was obtained by speaking into the TEAC data recorder microphone. All data were stored in the TEAC data recorder for ground-based analysis. Four test conditions were utilized inflight: 1) 15 arm raises while free floating, 2) 15 arm raises while free floating with the addition of foot pressure, 3) 15 arm raises while attached to the Mir support surface, and 4) 15 arm raises while bungeed to the Mir treadmill. Foot pressure boots were worn during test conditions 2 and 3. Force plate and motion analysis data were not obtained inflight. This integrative approach helped determine whether returning crewmembers were able to perform the appropriate coordination patterns required for complex movements as efficiently as before flight.
results: All subjects demonstrated decrements in postural control associated with voluntary arm movements. Center of pressure (COP) measures indicated that two postural control strategies were evident after space flight. Some subjects increased the magnitude of COP motion despite a decrease in arm acceleration features. This increased COP motion brought these subjects closer to the limits of their base of support, thus jeopardizing their stability. Other subjects displayed compression of the COP motion after space flight. This fact, combined with decreased arm acceleration suggested that these subjects chose to minimize their COP motion to stay clear of their base of support boundary. For all subjects, data indicated that the precise neuromuscular activation patterns necessary for optimal arm movements were not produced after space flight. Inflight data indicated that the addition of foot sensory input (i.e. provided by pressure to the feet) resulted in neuromuscular activation, which was not normally present without foot pressure. These results strongly suggested that inflight foot pressure may be used as a countermeasure to retard muscle atrophy and maintain the health of neuromuscular reflex loops. Muscle activation patterns associated with the "bungeed to treadmill condition" were dissimilar to those observed during arm movements made in 1-g. This finding was important because the bungee cords were calibrated to create a load equivalent to the subject's body weight (i.e. 1-g loading), but the altered activation patterns suggest that bungee loading was not biomechanically equivalent to a 1-g condition. Thus, for movement tasks, it would be inappropriate to compare responses observed during inflight bungee loading with those observed on Earth. Additionally, adaptations in neuromuscular activation patterns associated with different inflight support conditions indicated that the sensory-motor system maintained it’s response flexibility even after 130 days in microgravity. In conclusion, the evidence suggested a wide response range of the movement control system to space flight, and the ground-based Posa test could be utilized to characterize this response range. The ability to generate the neuromuscular activation patterns characteristic of preflight movement was compromised after space flight. In addition, evidence from the application of inflight foot pressure confirmed previous findings that neuromuscular activation was enhanced during free-floating arm movements.

title: The Response of Single Human Cells to Zero Gravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Studies with centrifuges demonstrated that gravitational acceleration has a significant influence on cell biology systems. The purpose of this experiment was to determine the effects of zero-gravity on living human cells during and subsequent to the Skylab 3 mission. A strain of diploid human embryonic lung cells, WI-38, was chosen for this purpose. In general, this experiment was designed to detect the effects of zero-gravity on cell growth rates and on cell structure as observed by light microscopy, transmission electron microscopy and scanning electron microscopy, and histochemistry. Studies of the effects of zero-gravity on the cell function and the cell cycle were performed by time lapse motion picture photography and microspectrophotometry. Subsequent study of the returned living cells included karotyping, G- and C- banding, and analyses of the culture media. Some of the living cells returned were stored by deep freeze techniques for possible future experiments.
approach: The Woodlawn Wanderer 9 was used inflight to support the growth of human embryonic lung cells. Cell cultures were maintained with the proper replacement of media with new fresh media. The cells were kept at a constant temperature of 36 degrees Celsius and at a constant pressure of one atmosphere in a hermetically sealed compartment. Two phase-contrast time-lapse motion pictures of living cells for 28 days was used to collect data on the cell cycle and mitosis. An automated system fixed the cells at predetermined intervals for postflight examination under the light microscope, scanning electron microscope, and transmission electron microscope. Cultures were maintained at approximately 22 degrees Celsius after the first 12 days of the mission for the return of intact cells for subsequent subculture. The cell cultures brought back to ground for subculture were analyzed for chromosomal aberrations, and the cell culture media was analyzed to determine chemical composition. Cellular growth rates were determined by cell counting procedures accomplished with the aid of a phase-contrast contrast microscope using a grid reticle in a 10X magnification eyepiece. Postflight, cell counting was performed with the 15X eyepiece due to the fact that the high density of the cell population made it difficult to determine single cells. Time lapse films were analyzed with a projector which permitted projection 1-8, 16, and 24 frames/second. Cells were counted every 3 hours. Cell multiplication was determined by adding the number of observed mitoses and mitotic activity, which was calculated from the average cell density. The rate of cell migration was determined by covering the projection screen with paper and tracing the location of the nucleus of individual cells every hour. Whole coverslips with attached cell monolayers in 4 percent glutaraldehyde fixative with cacodylate buffer were processed for transmission electron microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, and phase contrast microscopy. Scanning microspectrophotometry was performed on selected areas of the nuclei using a scanning microscope photometer having a 1-micron measuring at 1 micron intervals at 540 nanometers. Subcultures were incubated overnight with fresh growth medium, then harvested with standard colchimid arrest and hypotonic treatment procedures. Banding analysis was performed on air dried slides. Five cells from control cultures were analyzed for G-band pattern and 10 cells were analyzed for C-band pattern. At least 10 cells of the flight culture were analyzed for G-band pattern and 20 cells were analyzed for C-band pattern.
results: Ten cultures were fixed during the first 12 days of flight. Growth curves, DNA microspectrophometery, phase microscopy, and ultrastructural studies of the fixed cells revealed no effects of a zero-gravity environment on the ten cultures. Two cultures were photographed by means of phase time-lapse cinematography during the first 27 days of the flight. Analysis of the films revealed no differences in mitotic index, cell cycle, and migration between the flight and control cells. No differences between the flight and control cell cultures were observed in the karotype and chromosome banding. Minor unexplained differences have been found in the biochemical constituents of the used flight and control media.

title: Cardiovascular Responses to Lower Body Negative Pressure Following Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Orthostatic intolerance is a significant safety concern for Shuttle crew members during return to a 1-g environment and in cases of emergency egress. Orthostatic intolerance may result from decreased body hydration, increased leg compliance, or impaired cardiac or vascular compensatory response. Lower body negative pressure (LBNP) introduces a simulated orthostatic stress in a gradual and graded manner and it was used to test the orthostatic function of crew members before and after flight.
approach: Twelve crew members on 6- to 14-day Shuttle flights completed this protocol, but data from 2 were excluded, so that the number of participants was 10. Two different protocols of LBNP were used: pre-syncopal limit (PSL) and ramp. In the PSL protocol, which was used to assess the orthostatic tolerance and presyncopal symptoms of crew members, LBNP was applied continuously in 3-minute stages of 10 to 20 millimeters of mercury (mm Hg). The ramp protocol was more gradual and consisted of consecutive 5-minute stages at -0, -10, -20, -30, -40, -50, and -60 mm Hg. Measurements were made before, during and after ramp and PSL LBNP. Heart rate (HR) was measured with Lifepak and blood pressure with a sphygmomanometer. Total peripheral resistance (TPR), cardiac output, and stroke volume were measured by echocardiography. Blood samples were drawn before, during and after LBNP to estimate changes in body hydration (hematocrit, hemoglobin, and plasma total solids) and cardiovascular autonomic response (plasma catecholamines). Leg compliance during LBNP was measured by a mercury-in-silastic strain gauge placed around the calf. At least 2 months before flight, each subject performed 2 or 3 PSL LBNP protocols. In the 4 months before flight, each crew member performed 2 or 3 ramp protocols. The postflight LBNP ramp test was done within 4 to 6 hours of landing (R+0), and at 3 other times between R+1 and R+8.
results: Before flight, all crew members completed the LBNP ramp test. On day R+0, 5 of 10 were unable to complete the test due to presyncopal symptoms; HR remained elevated during all recovery tests. TPR was greater after landing than before flight. Blood analysis on R+0 revealed slight hemoconcentration and augmented catecholamine levels. Catecholamine levels were also increased by LBNP between R+1 and R+8. Leg circumference decreased dramatically after space flight and the decrease persisted for 6 to 8 days after landing. This may represent an acute decrease in muscle mass, not due solely due to dehydration because blood results indicated rapid recovery of body fluids within 48 hours. In comparing postflight response to LBNP and the stand test, LBNP gave no evidence of depressed orthostatic peripheral vascular response, which may be due to the difference between these two types of orthostatic stressors.

title: Noninvasive Estimation of Central Venous Pressure During Space Flight
research_area: Renal, fluid and electrolyte physiology; Cardiovascular physiology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Evidence suggests that cephalad fluid shifts during weightlessness stimulate arterial and cardiopulmonary baroreceptors, leading to cardiovascular readaptation syndrome. Central venous pressure (CVP) is one variable used to monitor fluid shifts. A noninvasive Doppler technique was used to document CVP during weightlessness.
approach: The subjects' jugular flow was monitored via a pocket Doppler device, which provided an audio Doppler signal. The character of the jugular flow was assessed, and after a verification trial, the target pressure was accepted as the CVP estimate. A total of 9 astronauts, 4 women and 5 men, were subjects for this investigation. They flew on 4 Shuttle flights with flight durations of 5, 5, 6, and 8 days. Preflight data were collected one or more times from all 9 subjects while they were supine, and inflight data were collected as often as possible.
results: For the 9 subjects, absolute data, as well as data normalized using the preflight average, showed a significant decrease in CVP from early in the mission (day 1) to late in the mission (day 6). After inspection of the data, subjects were grouped according to whether or not the last in-flight data point was greater than their preflight average. The 2 groups (n=4 and n=5) were compared with respect to the relationship between CVP response and the subjects' sex, age, severity of motion sickness, body weight, and changes in body weight. The results for these factors were equivocal because of the small number of cases. The decrease in CVP agrees with earlier studies, but this study showed a different time course for the changes.

title: Chromosome Analyses of Gemini Astronauts
research_area: Cell and molecular biology; Radiation biology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Exposure to ionizing radiation was a known hazard during the Gemini program. Although the U.S. Mercury and Gemini crews, as well as Soviet crews, received only small doses of radiation during their missions, scientists were certain that future high altitude orbital flights and ultimately the lunar missions would subject crews to appreciable exposures. In the 1960s, relatively little was known about the radiation response of man, and therefore much less was known about flight crews and what their responses would be if exposed to various doses under various circumstances. It was assumed that radiation responses on the ground would be identical to radiation exposure in spaceflight. In earlier suborbital and orbital flights, biological materials were flown, and had results of radiation exposure several magnitudes higher than expected, given the relatively low doses they were exposed to during flight. This led to the hypotheses that (1) a synergism might exist between radiation and some other parameter of spaceflight, such as weightlessness or vibration, or (2) that weightlessness itself might induce effects more commonly associated with radiation exposure. In an attempt to answer these hypotheses, several inflight experiments were carried out during the Gemini program. Chromosomal aberration production in human peripheral leukocytes irradiated in vitro during the flights was studied. This measurement had been demonstrated to be a sensitive method of biological radiation dose estimation, and had been successfully used in a number of cases of accidental whold body irradiation.
approach: This study was first conducted on Gemini 3. Preflight and postflight peripheral leukocyte chromosome analyses were made of blood samples obtained from the Gemini 3 crew. These measurements had two purposes: first, to serve as a control of the experiment entitled "Synergistic Effect of Zero-g and Radiation on White Blood Cells" (experiment ID S004), and secondly, to examine the effect of spaceflight on human chromosomes. Subsequently, preflight and postflight chromosome analyses were made on all other Gemini flight crews (except Gemini 8, where postflight samples could not be taken because of the mission''s early termination). Leukocyte samples were obtained from blood drawn during the last preflight medical exam and the first postflight medical exam. For most flights, postflight samples were flown to and processed at Cape Kennedy; the samples for Gemini 3 and 11 were processed aboard the recovery vessel along with the samples for the S004 experiment. Short term leukocyte cultures were prepared, and the leukocytes were then separated from the heparinized blood by centrifugation. The cells were then placed in culture medium: 10 ml of Medium 199 with 30% AB+ inactivated human serum, 5000 units penicillin, 5mg streptomycin, and 0.5 ml phytohemagglutinin M (Difco) per culture. The cultures were then incubated at approximately 36 degrees Celsius in an atmosphere of 5% CO2 in air. Colchicine was added after 60 hours of incubation to a final concentration of 10 to the -4 M, and cells were fixed after 66 hours. Cells then suitable for chromosome analysis were scored for chromatid- and chromosome-type aberrations. It should be mentioned that on the Gemini 4, 5 and 7 flights, small quantities of various radioisotopes were injected into the crewmen preflight and postflight for other studies of plasma volume and red cell mass: RISA (125I-iodinated human serum albumin) was used on Gemini 4 and 5 51Cr-labeled red cells were used on Gemini 5 and 7 DFP (tritiated di-isopropyl fluorophosphonate) was used on Gemini 7. Preflight and postflight blood samples for this chromosome study were obtained before any of these isotopes were injected; on Gemini 4, however, one postflight sample from one crewman did not produce satisfactory cultures, so a second sample had to be obtained 1 week after recovery (after postflight isotopes had been injected.) While the estimated total-body radiation doses from the decay of these isotopes was very small (less than 88 mrem per man for the Gemini 5 flight, for instance), even minute radiation doses like these could cause some chromosome breakage. More complete details can be found in the experiment "Bioassay of Body Fluid" (experiment ID M005). Furthermore, for the missions where RISA was used, a control subject was injected with 2.5 micro-c of RISA and blood samples were taken for chromosomal analysis at times corresponding to the flight crew sampling times. No controls were done for the 51 chromium or DFP procedures.
results: No large chromosomal effects of spaceflight were demonstrated. Postflight effects of the magnitude seen in biological materials flown on pre-Gemini flights were not seen on any of the Gemini flights. Some classes of aberrations did show a slight increase after some of the flights, but could not be correlated with flight duration, isotope injection or extravehicular activity (EVA). In particular, postflight increases of chromatid- and chromosome-type deletions are significant by a simple Chi-square test. The results were quite puzzling, in that chromatid-type aberrations occurred; these aberrations are only induced in cells that have already started DNA synthesis. However, the researchers used phytohemagglutinin-stimulated cultures, which were in the pre-DNA-synthesis stage. Only chromosome-type aberrations can be induced in such cells. The investigators offered a possible explanation for the origin of the chromatid-types: either the cells or the serum, some of which is always carried over into the culture with the cells, contain some chemical substance capable of breaking chromosomes during or after DNA synthesis. This, however, does not explain why only some crewmembers showed the increases. These experiments correlated with the results of the Gemini 3 and 11 in vitro experiments, in that investigators were unable to demonstrate any dramatic spaceflight effects on chromosome aberrations. None of the observations with the leukocyte chromosome system suggested any special genetic hazards associated with spaceflight. The leukocyte system was recommended to be a feasible biological dosimeter for future missions.

title: Environmental Radiation Measurements on Mir Station
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: This experiment attempted to expand the knowledge of environmental radiation at the 51.6 degree orbit, the location of the Mir station and future location of the International Space Station. Information on the shielding effects of the station and different methods of radiation dosimetry was also gathered. The data and associated analysis contributed to the establishment of a reliable database for the radiation environment in space.
approach: Two types of spectra were measured and compared: linear energy transfer (LET) and absorbed dose. The measurements for both spectra occurred inside six area passive dosimeters (APDs) that were flown to Mir via Shuttle mission STS-76 and placed at six different locations on Mir. LET spectra was measured using CR-39 PNTDs that were placed on the APDs. The CR-39 plates were etched with a NaOH solution and read out on an image digitizer system and analyzed. The absorbed spectra was measured using thermoluminescent detectors (TLDs) attached to the APDs. The flight data was compared with data read from background and calibration TLDs.
results: By using identical APDs in the exact locations on Mir, changes in radiation levels over time were recorded and analyzed. The measured dose rates in the APDs ranged from 268 to 422 mGy/d, yielding an average of 324 mGy/d. The differences in the high and low values were most likely caused by shielding differences due to the individual APD placements on Mir. Also, secondary target fragments, generated by inelastic scattering of protons and alpha particles within the detector medium, contributed to the spread of values. The dose and dose equivalent rates were used to calculate the effective quality factor, which was determined to be about 9 for LETs 25 keV/mm. This value shows the significance of short-range high LET target fragments to dose equivalent. The shielding data is currently being used to model the APD measurements made in the Mir Core.

title: Biostereometric Analysis of Body Form
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Biostereometrics is the science of measuring, and describing in mathematical terms, the three-dimensional form of biological objects. Exposure to weightlessness results in a dramatic change in the patterns of muscular activity in the human body insofar as they control posture and are responsible for locomotion. These changes in muscular activity might be expected to result in changes in the bulk of particular muscle groups, and in the overall energy consumption of the body, which, unless accompanied by a compensating change in food intake, would cause a change in body fat. Biostereometric analysis of the Skylab crewmembers enabled changes in muscle bulk to be measured, and by examining those areas of the body containing fat deposits enabled general conclusions to be drawn about changes in each Skylab crewmember's body fat.
approach: The biostereometric measurements of the Skylab crewmen were made using four-camera stereophotogrammetry, during the immediate preflight and postflight periods of Skylab 2, 3, and 4. The subjects were weighed within a few minutes of taking the photographs. Each subject was instructed to stand between two control stands, which provided dimensional information in the three orthogonal axes. Two cameras in front, and two cameras behind then simultaneously photographed the subject. The subject was nude except for an athletic supporter, and a skullcap to press his hair down. To minimize variations in chest volume, photographs were taken in maximal forced exhalation. Between each pair of cameras was a strobe-projector, which through a focusing lens projects a pattern of lines onto the subject's skin, making it easier to visualize during the subsequent plotting process. The stereophotgrammetry cameras were modified to accept fine-grain glass plates, for dimensional stability of the image. Duplicate sets of plates were exposed to insure against breakage or camera malfunction. The equipment was portable, and photographs were taken at Johnson Space Center (JSC), Kennedy Space Center (KSC), and on the recovery ships. After development the plates were analyzed on a stereoplotter, which derived the three-dimensional coordinates of thousands of points on the body surface, punching them on IBM cards for subsequent computer analysis. The computer program derived area, shape, and perimeter of between 80 to 100 sections of different parts of the body, the volume of any segment of the body, and of the body as a whole.
results: Measurements of leg circumference derived from stereometric analysis were compared to tape measure circumferences obtained on the same day. A pattern typical of all comparisons made between the two methods, resulted in the stereometric techniques exceeding the tape measurements by 10 to 20 millimeters. There are two probable causes for this difference. Firstly, the stereoscopic photographs were made with the subject standing, whereas the tape measurements were made with the subject supine; the leg volume standing would exceed that supine by the volume of blood and interstitial fluid brought into the leg under the influence of gravity. Secondly, stereometric analysis, being a noncontact method, did not involve the compression of tissues, however small, which resulted from the use of a tape measure. The 10 to 20 millimeter discrepancy between the methods represents a difference in limb volume of 250 to 500 milliliters, which is entirely reasonable for the increased volume of blood and tissue fluid in the leg after transferring from the supine to the standing position. Next, a comparison was made between the mean preflight weight and volume of the nine Skylab crewmembers and the first postflight determination. Density for all measurements was within the range 0.98 to 1.04 g/cm 2 . This is less than the normal range of density (1.02 to 1.10 g/cm 2 ) derived from hydrostatic weighing or gas displacement, because the volume figure includes the residual lung volume, the volume of air enmeshed in the hair, and the volume of those areas which cannot be visualized by the cameras (axillae and perineum). These additional volumes should be reasonably reproducible from one measurement to another on the same subject, except for the hair volume, which is probably the largest single source of error. It is unrealistic to calculate the density of the tissue lost during the course of the flight, as small errors in the volume determination would lead to impossible values for tissue density. Two of the Skylab 4 crewmembers showed little or no weight change, although a redistribution of body volume did occur. Generally speaking, the changes in weight and total body volume were of similar magnitude, and the apparent changes in density were probably not significant. Differences between the mean preflight and first postflight measurements of regional and total body volume, and body weight were also analyzed.
