title: Crewmember and Crew-Ground Interactions During NASA-Mir
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: During future long duration missions, international crews will be engaged in complicated activities over long periods of time. A number of interpersonal issues likely to impact these missions must be addressed to ensure healthy crewmember interactions and optimal performance. The objectives of this study were to measure and characterize changes over time in a number of important interpersonal factors, such as tension, cohesion, leadership role, and the relationship between space crews and ground support personnel during the NASA/Mir missions. The formal hypotheses addressed a number of aspects related to crew and ground control tension, cohesion, and leadership role. Over the course of long-term space missions, tension in the crew environment and crew cohesiveness were expected to change. Researchers expected an association between the level of tension in the crewmembers and their relationship with people on the ground, and between tension in mission control personnel and their relationship with management. Also, it was hypothesized that the perception of both the leadership role and outside monitoring support would change over time. Although specific stressors that occur during the mission, there is evidence, can influence these issues, that time alone may be a factor. One approach, the biphasic model, proposes that significant psychological and interpersonal difficulties may occur after the halfway point of a mission. Hence, a sense of relief that half of the mission is over is outweighed by the realization that another half is yet to come, and this results in decrements in mood and interpersonal functioning of the crew. The triphasic model describes three phases of reaction for people working in isolating and confined conditions for long periods. The initial anxiety in the first few weeks are mainly due to the novelty of the situation; depression during the long middle period of the mission are mainly due to monotony and homesickness; and euphoria and adolescent behavior during the last few weeks due to anticipation of returning home. When crews are composed of people from different countries or different ethnic backgrounds, language and cultural differences are important since they may lead to intra-crew tensions and disruptions in cohesion, and this in turn may negatively affect morale and interfere with the performance of mission tasks. Issues related to language and cultural differences have been reported in both simulation and space environments. Language and cultural issues also may adversely affect the interactions of mission control personnel on the ground, although these individuals have not been studied previously. The relationship between the crewmembers and their mission control support personnel is important, since miscommunication or insensitivity between these two groups may lead to misaligned work schedules or inappropriate responses during times of danger. A phenomenon that may negatively influence crew ground communication is displacement, which occurs when tension and distressful dysphoric emotions (e.g., anger, depression) that arise within the crewmembers during the mission cannot be expressed openly and are instead transferred outside to ground personnel, who are perceived as unsupportive and negative. Interactions suggestive of displacement have been reported during space missions and during space simulation studies on Earth. In simulations, crewmember anger directed to outside monitors has been especially observed when overt anger and tension were not seen between the confined subjects, and vice versa. Earlier work explored several of the above psychosocial issues in confined groups and included a questionnaire study of 54 astronauts and cosmonauts who had flown in space and a study of three male Russian subjects who were secluded in the Mir space station simulator in Moscow for 135 days. The study described in this paper involved a series of space missions in which two Russian cosmonauts and one American astronaut worked together on board the Mir space station for periods of four to seven months. The objectives of the study were to determine how tension, cohesion, and leader support affected the space crewmembers and mission control personnel on the ground and to determine how these factors changed over time. Several of the hypotheses predicted decreases in crew behavior during the second half of the missions in accordance with the biphasic model. The value of the triphasic model was also explored and other time effects that might be present while the crewmembers were on orbit. As stated in the hypothesis, displacement of tension and dysphoria would occur from crewmembers to mission control personnel and from mission control personnel to management; differences in response between Russians and Americans and between crewmembers and mission control personnel, were explored. We made no predictions concerning these differences since little empirical evidence existed that would allow us to form hypotheses related to these socio-cultural factors.
approach: American astronauts, Russian cosmonauts, and American and Russian mission control personnel who were involved with the Shuttle/Mir space program were asked to participate in our study. The number of subjects who volunteered, gave informed consent, and participated in the study during the on orbit periods included 5 astronauts (in 5 U.S. missions), 8 cosmonauts (in 4 Russian missions), and 42 American and 16 Russian mission control personnel, who included flight surgeons, operations leads, engineers, mission scientists, spacecraft communicators, and psychological support staff. To measure mood state and group interpersonal climate, standardized measures were used which have been shown to be valid and reliable in a number of studies on Earth. To assess emotions, we utilized the Profile of Mood States, or POMS, which consisted of 65 adjectives describing various affective states, such as "tense" and "cheerful", and were rated on a weekly basis by the subjects on 5 point Likert scales: 0 = Not at all 1 = A little 2 = Moderately 3 = Quite a bit 4 = Extremely To assess the interpersonal climate in the crew and mission control groups, subscales from two well-known instruments: the Group Environment Scale, or GES, and the Work Environment Scale, or WES. Both of these instruments measured dimensions of a group's interpersonal environment through subject endorsements of statements as being either "true" or "false" of their particular group during the previous week. An example of a question is: "There is a feeling of unity and cohesion in this group". Subscale scores were determined by summing the scores from related POMS, GES, or WES items. Examples of subscales were Tension-Anxiety (from the POMS), Cohesion (from the GES), and Supervisor Support (from the WES). Changes in subscale scores over time were regarded as alterations in the subjects' perception of mood and group climate. Descriptive analyses of the data suggested that the subjects considered the full range of responses when completing the measures. For example, on 63 of the 65 items from the Profile of Mood States, subjects gave all possible responses from 0-4 with exceptions for: "spiteful" and "forgetful", and on all 126 items from the GES and WES, subjects answered both true and false responses. For most items, however, the distributions were skewed in the direction of adaptive functioning (i.e., low values on negative subscales and high values on positive subscales). The above measures comprised our study questionnaire, which was available in both English and Russian computerized and hard copy formats. The questions took 15-20 minutes to complete. Both crew and ground subjects completed the questionnaire with reference to the preceding seven days Overall, 82% of the expected questionnaires were received from subjects participating during the on-orbit periods (70% from crewmembers and 85% from mission control personnel). This totaled 212 from crew subjects and 1,088 from ground subjects. Data analysis strategies One analyses examined the data for differences between U.S. and Russian subjects and between crewmembers and personnel in mission control personnel. Mean scores were calculated for each subject on each of the POMS, GES, and WES subscales. Subsequently, the number of observations that contributed to it weighted each mean, and a two-way repeated measure analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed. The model included main effects for country (American, Russian), group (crewmember, mission control personnel), and their interactions. A second set of previous analyses dealt with hypotheses related to the displacement of negative emotions for both crew and ground subjects. Displacement was operationalized as the negative association between measures of tension and dysphoria with WES Supervisor Support over the course of a mission. For the crewmembers, supervisors were defined as members of the outside monitoring staff in mission control, and for the mission control subjects, supervisors were defined as members of the American or Russian space agency management staff. A mixed model analysis was used to test the effects for each measure of tension or dysphoria. During weeks that there was high tension and dysphoria in the "in-group" (i.e., the crew or ground), we hypothesized that there would be a tendency to displace these feelings outwardly to the respective mission control or management "out-group" and to perceive these supervisors as not being supportive. A third set of analyses examined hypotheses related to the biphasic model, which predicted decrements in crewmember emotional state and interactions during the second half of the missions. Before analysis, the distribution of the raw data was examined for normality. Several subscales (dependent variables) had scores that were normally distributed. Others were successfully normalized using a logarithmic transformation. Still others had greatly skewed distributions and needed to be dichotomized. Cutoffs were made as close as possible to include 50% of the scores in the "high" category and 50% in the "low" category. These dichotomous variables were analyzed using Generalized Estimating Equation (GEE) fixed effect models with logit link functions and binomial variance. All other variables were analyzed using a mixed model approach that modeled random intercepts and slopes and assumed a decreasing correlation as the lag interval increased. Both the GEE and the mixed model approaches accounted for the effects of autocorrelation and were not handicapped by missing values in our longitudinal data caused by random events that prevented the subjects from completing the measures during a given week. The bi-phasic analysis used a piecewise linear regression approach. The weekly subscale scores for each subject for each mission were arrayed around the midpoint of the mission (counted as week = 0) because the launches and mission periods of Americans and Russians were staggered in calendar time and were of differing lengths. The missions varied from 16 weeks (an American astronaut) to 28 weeks (two Russian cosmonauts). From the actual weekly subscale scores, overall estimates of the average slope in the first half and in the second half of the missions were calculated, with these slopes intercepting at the midpoint. Another analyses also tested for the effects of time during the on-orbit period but modeled the effects of triphasic rather than biphasic changes. A regression approach with a quadratic function was selected to test for a pattern indicative of the presence of three phases in all crewmembers and in the Americans and Russians taken separately. For example, the literatures have suggested that crew tension levels would be high initially, and then drop during the middle phase of the mission. Tension would then rise again at the end as the termination approaches. Since quadratic functions describe curves with one bend, this analytic procedure was a reasonable way for us to test for U-shaped patterns among the variables in the data. However, since other curvilinear patterns may give a significant quadratic result as well, we had to visually inspect the data to see if a U-shape or some other curve best defined it. Since the regression models with a quadratic function included tests for linear functions in the analysis, a comparison of the quadratic pattern with a linear pattern was explored for the subscales throughout the course of the mission. If both of these tests for a given subscale are significant, then it is appropriate to present only the quadratic results. It is important to realize that the pattern of change in the actual data for a given subscale variable may not in itself be linear. For example, for variables that were dichotomized and subject to a GEE analysis, what was being evaluated was the presence of a linear pattern in the logit transformed values, not in the actual data. The most one could infer from such a case was that there was an overall tendency for a variable to increase or decrease versus showing no change over time (e.g., the tension level rose or fell during the course of the total mission versus staying pretty much the same). Therefore, one needs to visually examine the plot to deduce what kind of pattern is evident. A second set of new analyses was conducted to determine whether crewmember subjects differed from normative samples on Earth. T-tests were used to compare mission means with normative scores from other groups on Earth, both in terms of all subjects pooled and in terms of American and Russian subjects taken separately. A third set of new analyses tested for differences in the subscale variables during the missions compared to pre- and post-mission. Mean scores were calculated for each subject on each of the POMS, GES, and WES subscales for the mission itself and for the pre- and post-mission periods. Subsequently, each mean was weighted by the number of observations that contributed to it, and a one-way repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed that compared crewmember subscale mean scores during the missions with pre- and post-mission means. Again, we looked at all crewmembers pooled and at Americans and Russians taken separately. All of the previously conducted and new regression analyses were performed using a SAS macro based to execute the GEE analysis and the SAS MIXED procedure for the mixed models. The t-tests were conducted using the SAS t-test procedure, and the ANOVAs were conducted using the SAS GLM procedure. To control for a possible inflated Type I error rate associated with multiple significance tests, the false discovery rate procedure was utilized to determine an adjusted significance threshold. This procedure controls the expected proportion of falsely rejected hypotheses (i.e., the false discovery rate). For each effect being evaluated, the actual p-values from each of the total number of N subscales being tested were rank ordered from smallest to largest. Multiplying .05 by the rank number of each subscale result and then dividing by N calculated a cutoff significance threshold. The p-value from each subscale result then was compared against the threshold p-value until a comparison was found that did not exceed the threshold. This p-value became the significance level threshold for that particular effect. The results reported below have been interpreted with reference to the appropriate calculated Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold.
results: Interpersonal and cultural results To examine the potential impact of interpersonal and cultural factors, we used an analysis of variance to explore differences between Americans and Russians and between crew and ground subjects. Seven of the total of 21 subscale comparisons gave p-values lower than the adjusted significance threshold for the country main effect: Americans scored higher than Russians on POMS Vigor-Activity and WES Work Pressure, and lower on WES Managerial Control, GES Task Orientation, GES Self Discovery, WES Physical Comfort, and GES Leader Support. For the group main effect, four comparisons were significant, with mission control subjects scoring higher than crewmembers on four POMS measures of dysphoria (Tension-Anxiety, Fatigue-Inertia, Confusion-Bewilderment, and Total Mood Disturbance). There were significant country by group interactions for three GES subscales: Leader Support, Expressiveness, and Independence. American crewmembers scored lower than any other group on all three measures. Taken together, these findings suggested that Americans (especially U.S. crewmembers) experienced more emotional and work related problems than Russians, and that mission control personnel were more dysphoric than crewmembers. Displacement results Strong support was found in favor that displacement would occur for both crewmembers and mission control personnel using a mixed model analysis. Six subscales were picked to evaluate displacement (POMS: Tension-Anxiety, Depression-Dejection, Anger-Hostility, Total Mood Disturbance; GES Anger & Aggression; WES Work Pressure), and the phenomenon was indicated operationally when there was a significant negative association of each of these subscales with a measure of outside support (WES Supervisor Support). All six predicted associations were significant for the crewmembers, and five of the six were significant for the mission control subjects with the exception of WES Work Pressure. These results strongly suggested that crewmembers displaced tension and negative emotions to mission control personnel and that mission control personnel displaced tension and negative emotions to management. Biphasic model results According to the biphasic model, as hypothesized, there would be a significant rise in measures of crew tension, a drop in measures of crew cohesion and leader support, and a drop in measures of mission control leader support during the second half of the missions. The cohesion hypothesis was tested by examining six subscale variables: GES Cohesion, GES Task Orientation, GES Order and Organization, POMS Depression-Dejection, POMS Fatigue-Inertia, and POMS Vigor-Activity. We tested our tension hypothesis in terms of four variables: POMS Tension-Anxiety, POMS Anger-Hostility, GES Anger & Aggression, and WES Work Pressure. Finally, leader support was examined for both the crewmembers and the mission control personnel by exploring two variables: GES Leader Support and WES Supervisor Support. Using a piecewise linear regression approach with the appropriate mixed model or GEE analyses, only one of the, variables was significant when the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold was applied: there was a significant drop in GES Leader Support for crewmembers in the second half. Overall, the results did not indicate the presence of a moderate to strong biphasic time effect. The findings reported below deal with triphasic and linear time effects and with emotional and group climate responses reported by the crewmembers during their time on-orbit (the mission period). Unlike mission control personnel, the crewmembers were confined in space during the missions in an environment quite different from that on Earth. This isolation made them especially vulnerable to group and time pressures. Consequently, the results will have special relevance for the crew subjects. Quadratic (triphasic) model results The triphasic model was evaluated in terms of a regression approach with a quadratic function, since this gives a reasonable test of the U-shaped pattern one would expect to see in the subscales over the course of the missions if this pattern was in operation. However, since quadratic functions also describe non U-shaped curves, it is important to inspect the data visually to see just what kind of curve is depicted. A significant quadratic component in the model indicates that the quadratic function is a better representation of the data than a linear function. For the crewmembers, all of the 21 subscale variables from the POMS, GES, and WES were tested. After applying the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, the results indicated that none of tests for the quadratic function in these subscales met the adjusted significance threshold (p = .0024). Additional evaluations were made of the quadratic function in the 21 subscales for Russian and American crewmembers taken separately. For the Russians, none of the tests resulted in significant findings. For the American crewmembers, three of the subscales were significant for quadratic functions, with the p-value being less than the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold of p =.0024. These were: GES Order & Organization (beta = .007, p = .000); GES Task Orientation (beta = -.007, p = .000); and GES Self Discovery (beta = -.099, p = .000). Since all three of these variables had a skewed distribution and were dichotomized, they ~ere analyzed using a GEE model. Linear model results For all the crewmembers and for the Russians taken separately, regression analyses for the linear model were made on all 21 subscales. In both cases, none of the subscales resulted in p-values that were less than the Benjamini and Hochberg adjusted significance threshold (p = .0024). For the American crewmembers taken separately, only one subscale variable (other than GES Self Discovery) had a p-value that was less than the Benjamini and Hochberg threshold of p = .0048: GES Cohesion. A GEE analysis had been performed on GES Cohesion since the data were skewed and needed to be dichotomized, and this resulted in findings of beta = -.144 and p = .003. The negative beta meant that the probability of achieving a high score decreased in some manner from the beginning to the end of the mission. Although the shape of the logit curve was better described by a linear than a quadratic function, this did not imply that the actual data necessarily would plot as a straight line. Crewmember results versus scores from normative samples on Earth For nearly every subscale, the crewmember means were in the positive half of the subscale range. That is, where a high score defined a negative outcome (e.g., POMS Tension-Anxiety), the crew mean was below the scale midpoint (18 for this subscale), whereas where a high score defined a positive outcome (e.g., GES Cohesion), the crew mean was above the scale midpoint (4.5 for this subscale). This suggested that the crewmembers generally endorsed positive adaptive responses, especially for the POMS emotion variables. The normative means and standard deviations were determined from several thousand people participating in non-patient work and task groups. The POMS sample consisted of 1,130 adult males who participated in a smoking cessation program; the GES sample consisted of individuals who participated in 101 task-oriented groups in health care, correctional, and educational settings [41]; and the WES sample consisted of 8,146 individuals who participated in 116 general and health care work groups [42]. Using t-tests and the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, a total of 13 subscales resulted in p-values that were below the adjusted significance threshold of p = .033. For all six significant POMS variables, the crewmembers endorsed significantly less dysphoria than the POMS normative sample. They also scored lower on GES and WES measures of group expressiveness, independence, anger & aggression, and innovation; and higher on measures of cohesion, leader control, and managerial control. The subscale means and standard deviations for Russian and American crewmembers were taken separately, along with their respective comparisons with the normative samples; a given difference did not always reach significance (probably due to the smaller sample sizes). One notable new finding is GES Self Discovery, where the Russian mean is significantly greater than the norm, and the American mean is significantly smaller. Mission versus pre-and post-mission results Crewmember subjects were asked to complete the POMS, GES, and WES questions each week during the time they were on the Mir. They also were asked to complete these measures for four consecutive weeks pre-mission, ending at one month before launch (i.e., baseline data collection period), and for two consecutive weeks after they returned to Earth. However, it was discovered that during the post-mission period the American and Russian subjects were separated from each other, so there was no group environment to evaluate using the GES and WES items. Consequently, only POMS data were collected. To look for differences in subscale scores before, during, and after the missions, mean scores were calculated and compared using a repeated measures ANOVA (pre-mission versus on-orbit versus post-mission for the POMS subscales, and pre-mission versus on-orbit for the GES and WES subscales). After applying the Benjamini and Hochberg procedure, none of these comparisons were significant in terms of all crewmembers, Russians alone, or Americans alone. CONCLUSION There was no support for the triphasic or linear models for all crewmembers or for Russian cosmonauts alone when the Benjamini and Hochberg criteria were applied to contol for Type I errors. Although there were three significant quadratic findings for American astronauts, only one variable, GES Order & Organization, showed a U-shaped pattern consistent with the triphasic model. This finding suggested that Americans in space felt that their interpersonal environment was comparatively more organized at the beginning and end of the on-orbit period than during the middle. This makes some sense because the new astronauts were formally oriented to the Mir shortly after arriving by the departing astronauts and by the continuing cosmonauts, and because the preparation for the return to Earth required the astronauts to undergo a number of specific procedures during the end of their on-orbit period. The other two significant quadratic functions for the Americans, GES Task Orientation and GES Self Discovery, gave a different pattern, with the probability of a high score being greater during the beginning weeks of the missions, then declining as time progressed. This pattem also was evident for the significant linear function finding for GES Cohesion. Taken together, the results from these three subscales suggested that the American crewmembers might have been impacted by the novelty of the situation during the first few weeks of their missions. They perceived the crew environment to be one where orientation to tasks was high, where they could grow individually, and where there was a strong bond among the crewmembers. Over time, there was a significant decrease in these areas. Perhaps the novelty of the situation simply disappeared. Alternatively, the decreases may have reflected an emotional change in the Americans due to homesickness or asthenia, although one would have expected to find some POMS changes as well if this explanation was valid. The above results were found only for American astronauts. The Russian estimated probabilities for high scores were in the .4 to .8 ranges for all four of the subscales shown in the figures, and they did not vary significantly over time. Thus, the cosmonauts were much more likely to endorse higher scores throughout the mission than their American counterparts. This difference may have reflected actual cultural differences or differences based on interpretations of the English and Russian versions of our measures. But it also might have reflected the specific interpersonal characteristics of the Shuttle/Mir missions, where there usually were two Russians and one American on-board, where the leader was always a Russian, where the Mir and its operation was in Russian control, and where the predominate language being spoken was Russian. Thus, an American astronaut was psychosocially isolated during these missions, and the U.S./Russian differences may have been more a reflection of the crew composition and operational situation than of characteristic cultural differences. First, although the estimated curves were significant, an inspection of the figures suggests that the estimates are not idea fits of the actual proportion data. The smooth estimated probability curves contradict the variation that is occurring in the mean weekly responses. Only biphasic, quadratic, and linear functions were tested, and perhaps some other function would give a better fit to the data. Second, for GES Order & Organization, GES Task Orientation, and GES Cohesion, the high/low splits were at 9/8. This means that about half of the total responses were the highest possible value of nine, and about half were eight and below. Therefore, in many cases, the indicated drop in scores was from a high of nine to a low of eight or seven, still in the upper part of the subscale range. In contrast, the high/low split for GES Self Discovery was 5/4, which gave more room at the top and bottom of the subscale range for the subjects to score. Little support was found for the presence of moderate to strong time effects in the crewmembers during the Shuttle/Mir missions. In comparison with other work and task groups on Earth, the crewmembers were significantly less dysphoric and perceived more cohesion and direction from their leaders and managers. They also felt that their group environment allowed them less opportunity to express themselves and to be independent and innovative, and they reported lower levels of group anger and aggression. American and Russian subjects taken separately generally echoed these overall findings. In addition, unlike many work environments on Earth, the Shuttle/Mir missions were busy and highly structured, with many timelines, procedures, and directions from the ground that needed to be followed. One interesting difference between Russian and American crewmembers pertained to GES Self Discovery, with the former scoring significantly higher than the normative sample and the latter Scoring significantly lower. Although the Russian crewmembers perceived their interpersonal environment as conducive to such discussion (compared with the normative group on Earth), the American crewmembers had an opposite perspective. Perhaps language differences and a sense of psychosocial isolation handicapped the latter and prevented them from learning about themselves through such informal group interactions. No significant differences were establish in crew response before, during, or after the missions in terms of all crewmembers or Americans and Russians taken separately. Significant pre/post seclusion differences using the same measures were found in our 135-day Mir simulator study, and we expected to replicate some of the findings. For example, POMS Tension-Anxiety levels were significantly lower, and GES Leader Support, Expressiveness, and Self Discovery levels were significantly higher during the Mir simulation seclusion period than before. However, the psychological meaning of this simulation was much different from the Shuttle/Mir missions in terms of anxiety and perceived danger, and one must be cautious in extrapolating the findings from earth-bound psychosocial simulation research into space. Crewmembers may be more comfortable with their work environment in space than mission control personnel are with their work environment on Earth, and it is possible that for astronauts and cosmonauts, the excitement of being in space offsets any negatives from living and working on earth. Thus, crewmembers perceived their work environment differently form people on Earth, and they demonstrated equanimity in mood and group perceptions, both in space and on the ground.

title: Bioassays of Body Fluids
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Orthostatic hypotension and weight loss were observed in the crewmembers of Gemini 3, 4, 5, and 6 immediately after flight. Scientists were concerned that space flight might affect the balance of body fluid and electrolytes since fluid losses can contribute to both of these symptoms. This led to a series of ground-based studies to simulate some of the conditions of space flight. An attempt was made to define the physiological parameters that would be affected by the condition of microgravity. These studies utilized bed rest and water immersion as a means of simulating microgravity. Both the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems experienced changes during the ground-based studies. Changes in body fluid chemistry were found to be reflective of the status of these systems. This experiment was designed to obtain objective data concerning the effects of space flight on the human body by examining alterations in the body fluid chemistry.
approach: Preflight plasma samples were collected from all crewmembers of Gemini 7, Gemini 8, and Gemini 9 approximately 10 days and 3 days before launch. Plasma samples were not collected in flight. Gemini 7 postflight plasma samples were collected immediately after recovery, and 6 hours, 24 hours and 72 hours after flight. Gemini 9 postflight plasma specimens were collected after recovery, and 6 hours and 72 hours after flight. The Gemini 8 mission was terminated after 11 hours and no postflight data was collected for this experiment. Urine sampling was scheduled preflight, inflight, and postflight for Gemini 7, 8, and 9. Preflight, two 48-hour urine samples were collected approximately 10 days and 3 days before launch. Inflight urine collection on Gemini 7 and 9 was accomplished by utilizing a specially designed urine transport system. The urine transport system permitted researchers to calculate the total urine volume for each void by means of tritium dilution. A 75 ml aliquot of each void was collected into a plastic sample bag and stored for return to Earth. No refrigeration was used, but benzoic acid was added as a preservative. Urine was collected continuously for 48 hours after landing. Inflight and postflight urine samples were not collected for the Gemini 8 crewmembers. Water and fluid electrolytes were examined to determine the mechanisms associated with weight loss during flight. The concentrations of plasma sodium, potassium, and chloride ions were measured preflight and postflight, and the rates of urinary excretion of these electrolytes were determined pre-, in-, and postflight. Total plasma protein concentrations, measured preflight and postflight, were used to indicate dehydration. Fluid intake and output were measured to determine whether weight loss was caused by sweat and insensible losses or by changes in renal function. Fluid intake was ad lib, but the quantities ingested during the pre- and postflight phases were recorded. The majority of the fluid intake was obtained with the diet. Inflight intake was estimated from a water dispensing device on board the space craft. The information was not sufficiently precise to perform calculation of fluid balance data. To complement the water measurements and electrolyte-balance measurements, both urinary antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and aldosterone were measured. The production of ADH is responsive to thoracic blood volume changes, and it was postulated that microgravity would decrease ADH secretion and result in an increase in urinary volume. Aldosterone was measured to study the mechanisms associated with sodium excretion. Increases in aldosterone secretion would result in decreased urinary excretion of sodium, and vice versa. Researchers hypothesized that aldosterone secretion would be decreased in space flight, resulting in an increased urinary excretion of sodium. To measure the effects of stress in space, two groups of hormones were assayed. The first group assayed, 17-hydroxycorticosteroids, was indicative of long-term stress responses. The second group assayed, catecholamines, was indicative of short-term or emergency responses. These parameters provided an objective, long-term evaluation of the physiologic cost of space flight. Bone demineralization was evaluated by measuring calcium, magnesium, phosphate, and hydroxyproline in plasma and urine both preflight and postflight and in urine collected in flight. Changes in bone mineralization were studied by calculating the ratio of bound to unbound calcium in the plasma. This ratio was approximated from an estimate of plasma protein and calcium. Hydroxyproline, an amino acid unique to collagen, was measured in urine to study bone and collagen breakdown. It was presumed that an increased excretion of hydroxyproline accompanying bone demineralization resulted from dissolution of bone matrix. Urinary urea concentration was measured to study protein intake and tissue metabolism. Creatinine excretion was measured to study muscle protein metabolism. Decreases of creatinine excretion are associated with loss of muscle tone and activity.
results: When the preflight and postflight plasma samples were analyzed for Gemini 7, by far the longest Gemini flight, electrophoretic patterns were normal. All values were in the normal range, except for an anticipated increase in 17-hydroxycorticosteroids in the first sample taken after recovery. These values decreased to preflight values within 6 hours following recovery. Hydroxyproline did not change significantly. Plasma uric acid was reduced. The cause of the reduction was unknown, but presumed to be dietary. Plasma ADH was significantly elevated in the first postflight plasma sample of one subject of Gemini 7, but returned within normal range as urine output returned to normal. It was concluded that 14 days of orbital space flight did not result in any gross aberrations of plasma electrolytes. During the first 24-hours after Gemini 7, there was marked water retention for both subjects. The output for each subject was approximately 1 liter less than the preflight 24-hour volume. In addition, there was marked retention of chloride, sodium, and potassium. The water retention and the rapid weight gain after flight were consistent with the hypothesis that weight loss during flight was the result of fluid loss. Electrolyte and water retentions observed immediately postflight in the Gemini 7 subjects were consistent with bed rest studies that showed an increased ADH secretion contributed to decreased urinary volume. During Gemini 9, inflight urine volumes based on the tritium dilution were as great as 12 liters per urination. This great variation in urine volumes was indicative of an anomaly. Therefore, no further attempt was made to analyze or interpret the urine samples collected in flight. The Gemini 9 subjects experienced significant postflight retention of water. This was accompanied by retention of sodium, potassium, and chloride. Urinary calcium decreased slightly immediately postflight. The excretion of 17-hydroxycorticosteroids was increased immediately postflight. This was probably caused by the stress of re-entry. Postflight, the increase of plasma protein and a slightly smaller increase of plasma electrolytes were consistent with an inflight water and electrolyte loss that resulted in dehydration followed by the retention of water and electrolytes. It was not known whether the losses resulted from diuresis during flight or from sweat.

title: Nutritional Studies
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The importance of nutrition in the adaptation of man to weightlessness was recognized early in the United States manned space flight program. Investigators were concerned with the possibility that exposure to microgravity would impose high demands on micronutrients and would therefore lead to nutritional deficiencies. Experiments conducted during the Gemini program led space life scientists to believe that some physiological changes associated with space flight were related to nutritional imbalances. It was noted that the musculoskeletal system is one of the primary physiological systems affected by microgravity-induced nutritional alterations. Numerous studies documented that imbalances between bone formation and resorption can lead to clinical disorders such as increased calcium in the blood and urine and osteoporosis. Bed rest investigations lasting from 30 to 36 weeks provided evidence that mineral losses associated with bone resorption were likely to continue unabated during prolonged space flight. In addition, the physical data on astronauts from the Mercury and Gemini programs showed a consistent pattern of postmission weight loss. The weight reduction was believed to have resulted from water and muscle tissue losses. Scientists also considered the possibility that the weight loss was due to insufficient caloric intake. Therefore, the issue of inflight caloric requirements was investigated thoroughly during the Apollo missions. Apollo scientists were also concerned with the fact that food systems having minimum weight and volume are required for space flight. The food consumed during the Apollo missions was generally dehydrated and specially formulated to occupy minimal volume. Therefore, the effects of the specialized food packaging methods on the nutritional content of the food was investigated. Thus, the objective of the Apollo nutritional investigation was to conduct a comprehensive metabolic balance study in order to correlate nutrient intake and excretion data to specific inflight physiological changes. The study helped scientists acquire an accurate knowledge of inflight human nutrition requirements which was essential for the development of more advanced space food systems.
approach: Food analysis: All foods were analyzed for nitrogen, fat, carbohydrates, crude fiber, phosphorus, iron, sodium, potassium, and magnesium content. Some composite Apollo menus were analyzed for water- and fat-soluble vitamins. Dietetics: The menus used by the Apollo astronauts were formulated from flight-qualified Apollo foods in combinations that complied with the personal preferences of the crewmen and that met the Recommended Daily Allowance (RDA) requirement. The menus were primarily composed of dehydrated foods that were reconstituted before eating. The foods were consumed in a prearranged sequence, but could be supplemented by additional items. Nutrient intake measurements: Each meal was composed of a predetermined number of food items. Records were kept on any foods omitted or incompletely consumed. Snack items consumed that were not part of the programmed meals were also recorded in the flight logs. All food residue and unopened food packages were returned from the missions. Residue was weighed to provide more precise information on inflight nutrient intake. For the Apollo 17 mission, a five-day metabolic balance study was performed approximately two months before the mission by using the flight menus and collecting urine and fecal wastes. Fecal measurements: Fecal samples were returned from all Apollo flights and analyzed for a variety of constituents either by nuclear activation analysis or by wet chemistry techniques. Metabolic balance: A partial metabolic balance study was performed on the Apollo 16 crew. Urine and fecal samples were returned for analysis and the data was compared to the inflight nutrient intake data. For a more detailed metabolic balance study in conjunction with Apollo 17, accurate measurements of fluid intake and output were performed approximately two months before the mission. A five-day food compatibility / metabolic study was performed in which three Apollo 17 prime and backup crewmembers consumed their flight foods and participated in metabolic collections. The study was designed to obtain baseline data on the excretory levels of electrolytes and nitrogen in response to the Apollo 17 flight menu. Beginning 64 hours before Apollo 17 lift-off and continuing throughout the mission until 44 hours following recovery, all food and fluid intake was measured. During the preflight and postflight periods, conventional meals were prepared in duplicate for each astronaut. One duplicate of each meal was analyzed in addition to the residue from the meal that was consumed in order to measure nutrient intake and output. Every food item consumed inflight was derived from a group of foods that had been analyzed for nutritional content. All deviations from programmed food intake were logged and reported. Inflight water consumption was measured using a beverage dispenser. All urine was collected, measured, sampled and returned for analysis. Inflight urine samples were collected by means of a biomedical urine sampling system (BUSS). Each BUSS was marked with the name of the crewmember and the time of collection. Following each collection period, the urine pool was thoroughly mixed before a sample was taken. The urine samples represented a 24-hour void and were subsequently analyzed for electrolytes, nitrogen, and creatine. Complete stool collections were also performed. Body volume measurements: For the Apollo 16 crewmembers, three preflight and three postflight body volume measurements were made by stereophotogrammetry. Body density was calculated from body volume and weight. Density was used to calculate the percentage of fat. Changes in calculated lean body mass and total body fat were converted into caloric equivalents. Total body water was measured using a potassium-42 dilution technique.
results: Food analysis: The overall nutritional analysis indicated that the typical Apollo diet was composed of protein, fat, carbohydrates, fiber, and minerals in the following percentages (percent of dry weight): 18.0, 17.0, 61.0, 1.0, and 3.0, respectively. The results of the vitamin analysis indicated that the Apollo diet provided an excess of some vitamins (A, E, C, B12, B6, and riboflavin) and marginal amounts of others (nicotinate, pantothenate, thiamine, and folic acid). Nutrient intake measurements: The daily intake (grams) of protein, fat, carbohydrates, and fiber averaged over all Apollo missions was 76, 61, 269, and 5.4, respectively. The daily intake (milligrams) of calcium, phosphorus, sodium, and potassium averaged over all Apollo missions was 773.0, 1121.0, 3666.0, 2183.0, respectively. Metabolic balance: A detailed assessment of energy metabolism was conducted for the Apollo 16 metabolic balance study and special emphasis was placed on potassium intake and excretion. The average energy intake (kcal/day) for the Commander (CDR), Command Module Pilot (CMP), and Lunar Module Pilot (LMP) was 2403, 1565, and 2366, respectively. The average daily inflight potassium intake for the CMD was 113.6 milliequivalents (mEq). In flight, the CMD lost potassium by the fecal route at a rate of 6.4 mEq/day, whereas 18.8 mEq/day were lost preflight and 20.5 mEq/day postflight. For the LMP, the average daily pre-, in-, and postflight potassium intake was 110.5, 114.7, and 97.5 mEq, respectively. During the pre-, in-, and postflight phases, the average daily potassium fecal losses for the LMP were 33.5, 11.1, and 31.0 mEq, respectively. For the CMP, average daily pre-, in-, and postflight dietary potassium intakes were 94.3, 79.9, and 82.4 mEq, respectively. CMP fecal samples for the same periods indicated that potassium levels were 27.6, 6.3, and 26.2 mEq, respectively. The metabolic data from the Apollo 17 mission was compared to the five-day control study data, however, the duration of the pre- and postflight measurement periods was not sufficient to establish reliable metabolic baselines. Inflight urine outputs were proportionately lower for all three crewmembers compared to control study values. Inflight estimates of water loss for all crewmembers indicated that 900 to 1200 ml/day were lost. Total body water measurements did not indicate a negative water balance for the crew. Calcium, phosphorus, and nitrogen balance results indicated that all crewmembers were in negative balance for these elements during the inflight period. Intake and output measurements for sodium indicated a positive balance for this element during the flight for all crewmembers. Anthropometric measurements: The average inflight weight loss for all crewmen in the Apollo program was 3.53 kg. Body volume (liters) measurements for the Apollo 16 crew indicated that the CDR, CMP, and LMP had preflight volumes of 75.5, 62.1, and 73.2, respectively. Postflight data on body volume showed that the CDR, CMP, and LMP had body volume measurements of 74.8, 57.8, and 71.4 liters, respectively.

title: Joint U.S./Russian Investigations: Sensory-Motor Investigations (SMI)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: During space flight, space motion sickness (SMS) and perceptual disturbances have led to reductions in performance efficiency and sense of well-being. During entry and immediately after landing, such disturbances could have a serious impact on the ability of the commander to land the Orbiter, as well as on the abilities of all crewmembers to egress from the Orbiter, particularly in a non-nominal condition or following extended stays in microgravity. An understanding of spatial orientation and motion perception is essential for developing countermeasures for SMS and perceptual disturbances during space flight and upon return to Earth. Countermeasures for optimal performance in-flight and a successful return to Earth require the development of preflight and in-flight training to help astronauts acquire and maintain a dual adaptive state. This study was intended to enhance the understanding of adaptation to space flight and readaptation after flight on various aspects of human spatial orientation, neurosensory, sensory-motor, physiological, and perceptual functions and on autonomic gastric functions associated with space motion sickness (SMS). This experiment correlated the postflight recovery of postural equilibrium control, head and gaze stability, readaptation changes in vestibular function, and examined the relationship between voluntary oculomotor performance and passive vestibulo-ocular responses following space flight. Changes in stomach nerve response to food consumption over the first few days of flight were to be observed and analyzed, and evaluated when SMS symptoms occurred. The investigators were also interested in how nerve activity correlated with the symptoms before, during, and after their occurrence.
approach: Protocol A Voluntary Head Movement (VHM) Standard electro-oculography (EOG) techniques recorded horizontal and vertical eye position. A head mounted tri-axial rate sensor measured head velocity in the pitch, yaw and roll planes. The BOG and rate sensor signals were collected with the Superpocket physiological monitoring system and recorded on a TEAC cassette recorder. A goggle assembly controlled visual conditions via an electronic shutter, changing instantly from a clear state to an opaque state according to the experiment protocol. A cruciform target and four additional visual targets were mounted on the middeck locker for on-orbit data collection and on a screen during baseline data collection. A microcassette recorder delivered a sinusoidally-modulated audio tone during one portion of the VHM protocol. Tasks performed in-flight were tested pre- and postflight as well. Subjects were asked to report perceptual sensations associated with each stimulus. VHM Inflight - Four of the six inflight experiments were designed to investigate voluntary oculomotor function. Two additional experiments were performed pre- and postflight only investigated this function. The protocols involved a combination of eye and/or head movements to acquire targets along a visual display. Calibrations of eye and head signals were performed. Each task was repeated three times in both the horizontal and vertical planes. The tasks are described below: Head Calibration - the subject directed a head-mounted laser spot to the central target and moved their head to pre-selected targets in both the horizontal and vertical planes. Eye Calibration - with head fixed, subject acquired a successive sequence of target positions in the horizontal and vertical planes, visually fixating on each target for two seconds. Target Acquisition - a cruciform target arrangement, located 34 inches from the subject's eyes was used to display a series of targets in both the horizontal and vertical planes. Subjects acquired each target with both a head and eye movement. Gaze Stabilization - the subject first visually fixated on a wall-fixed target with the head in a central position. When the goggles became opaque and vision was occluded the subject rotated the head while maintaining ocular fixation on the just-seen wall-fixed target. When the goggles became clear the subject refixated the target with the eyes only. The subject then rotated the head back to center, keeping eyes on the target. Spontaneous/Gaze Nystagmus - was measured with the crewmember fixating on a wall target, and then imagining the same wall-fixed target with vision occluded, and then with the eyes closed. Gaze nystagmus, or the effect of a change in eye position was evaluated by having the crewmember fixate on imaginary 40 degree targets (vision occluded) in both the vertical and horizontal planes for 20 seconds per imaginary target. Measurement of eye movements continued for an additional 20 seconds when the eye position was returned to straight ahead gaze. Sinusoidal Head Oscillations - With Vision: Subjects attempted to maintain visual fixation on a wall-fixed target while smoothly oscillating his/her head in yaw or pitch in cadence with an audio tone that is sinusoidally modulated to sweep over the bandwidth of interest (chirp). Without Vision: Subject repeated the chirp with vision occluded while attempting to maintain ocular fixation on the remembered location of the target. The subject repeated this entire procedure in each plane for each condition. VHM Pre/Postflight Non-Predictable Target Tracking - for these trials, the target was initially stationary in the center of the field of view. At an unpredictable time, the target began to move at constant velocity, either rightward, leftward, upward, or downward. The onset time of target motion, direction of motion, target velocity, and final target displacement was randomized. Predictable Target Tracking - the target oscillated at 0.3 Hz. For each trial, tracking was performed for at least six cycles. Positional Nystagmus - spontaneous eye movements were collected with the crewmember in seven different static positions: 1. Seated upright 2. Supine 3. Supine with head turned to the right 4. Supine with head turned to the left 5. Supine with head and neck extended over the edge of the examination table (head and neck will be supported by test operator) 6. Body and head turned to the right side 7. Body and head turned to the left side Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN) A binocular Optokinetic Stimulator provided a full visual field optokinetic stimulus during the OKN protocol. Standard electro-oculography (EOG) techniques recorded horizontal and vertical eye position. The EOG signals were collected with the Superpocket physiological monitoring system and recorded on a TEAC cassette recorder. Tasks performed inflight were tested pre and postflight as well. Subjects were asked to report perceptual sensations associated with each stimulus. Postural Equilibrium (pre/postflight) Measurements pertaining to postural equilibrium were collected using standard electromyography (EMG) techniques on the upper thigh and lower calf segments of the subject's left leg, sway-bars situated at the shoulders and hips, and force transducers situated in the foot plate of the posture platform. In addition, overhead and full field video was recorded through the entire test session. The subject's primary task was to maintain a normal upright stance. Head and Gaze Stability During Locomotion (pre/postflight) Whole body movement during locomotion on a treadmill and during a jump task was videotaped and the locations of retroreflective markers placed on specific locations on the body were analyzed with the aid of a computerized motion analysis system. In addition, eye movement and leg muscle activity during these tasks were recorded using standard electro-oculography (EOG) and electromyography (EMG), respectively. Path Integration ((pre/postflight) To examine the cognitive processing of spatial orientation information, whole body movement during locomotion along a previously memorized path (parallelogram or square) were videotaped and the locations of retroreflective markers placed on specific locations on the body were analyzed with the aid of a computerized motion analysis system. Protocol B This experiment marked the first attempt to obtain measurements of the stomach muscle activity in humans during space flight. In this study, myoelectric activity of the stomach was examined following a meal. Gastric activity associated with space motion sickness was measured using EGG in which electrical impulses associated with stomach secretion and movements were recorded. To perform this EGG, three electrodes were situated on the abdomen. Each subject participated in two preflight training sessions which occurred at 12 months prior to launch (L-12) and at 10 months prior to launch (L-10). To compare subject inflight EGG data that were associated with eating to eating under normal ground conditions, there were two baseline data collection sessions. These sessions occurred after both preflight training sessions. During one baseline data collection session, subjects were given fluids and during the other session, they were given a small meal. Subjects fasted for 6.5 hours before a data collection session. When the small meal was consumed, data collection began 20 minutes before the 5 to 10-minute meal and continued for three hours following the meal. To ensure proper and consistent placement of EGG electrodes on the abdomen inflight, a permanent marker was used to mark the correct locations after a meal had been consumed within eight days prior to flight. The EGG data were collected using a portable recording instrument designed for space flight. The electrodes amplified the signal at its source and the main part of the recording instrument amplified it further. A one Mb RAM card held twenty-four hours of data. The hardware was lightweight and worn on a belt. It was capable of registering input from the crewmember regarding food or water consumption and SMS symptoms. There were five events that were coded by number: eating, drinking, stomach awareness/discomfort, nausea and vomiting. When a crewmember experienced one of these events, he pressed the event marker with the correct code number and the event with its corresponding Mission Elapsed Time (MET) was recorded. Insertion of event markers did not disrupt data collection or logging. The EGG equipment was donned as early as possible in the flight. Continuous data collection occurred for at least the first three flight days. The electrodes, RAM card and battery were replaced every 24 hours.
results: Protocol A Results for this portion of the experiment aren’t available at this time. Protocol B Crewmembers responded normally to ingestion of a meal preflight, showing an increase in the amplitude and power of the normal three gastric cycles per minute. An abnormal decrease in the dominant power occurred on Flight Day (FD) 1 for all subjects but the response returned to normal on FD3. Individual differences were observed and one crewmember actually showed a slight abnormal preflight response to the meal. All three crewmembers experienced moderate to severe loss of appetite on FD1 and two of them showed mild loss of appetite on FD3. When appetite returned and SMS symptoms resolved, the gastric responses after a meal returned to normal. Two nausea events were recorded by one crewmember and one vomiting event was recorded by another crewmember. Percent spectral power was assessed to determine the regularity of normal gastric slow waves. The percent of time that normal waves are recorded by the EGG and the percent of time that abnormal (faster or slower) waves are recorded is the percent spectral power. EGG data showed that in the first episode of nausea 60% of spectral power was associated with deviations in normal contraction cycles before nausea was reported. Forty percent of the power was associated with fewer contractions per minute and 20% was associated with higher contractions per minute. The percent of spectral power associated with these alterations of rhythmic contractions increased to approximately 75% for 15 minutes following the report of nausea, then decreased to about 45%, which was noted at 45 minutes following the nausea report. In the second report of nausea, the percent spectral power associated with altered stomach contractions was high (75-80%) throughout the entire period of EGG recording. The researchers speculated that the data indicated that this second report of nausea lasted longer than the first. Also of note was that the first nausea report data corresponded to slower gastric contractions two to three times more than faster ones throughout the entire recording period. In the second episode, data was associated with faster frequency contractions during the time following the nausea report. Other studies have shown that faster frequency contractions are associated with motion sickness as compared to slower frequency contractions. Similar to the nausea, the EGG data showed altered stomach contraction rhythms before and up to 30 minutes following the vomiting episode. For this entire time, 75 to 80% of the spectral power was associated with abnormal rhythms. Forty-five minutes after the report the gastric activity was normal. One interesting point is that this crewmember specifically stated that he had no symptoms prior to vomiting, which is a fairly common characteristic of SMS. For both nausea and the vomiting episodes, crewmembers had altered rhythmic gastric contractions at least 30 minutes prior to reporting the symptom. The abnormally fast neural myoelectric waves that are detected by EGG have been associated in other studies with decreased spontaneous movement of the stomach and the absence of stomach contractions. Findings in this study indicate that spontaneous stomach movement may be decreased during both mild and severe symptoms of SMS, which occur during the first few days of space flight. The perturbations of this movement may affect absorption of nutrients and oral medications for both astronauts and motion sickness victims on Earth. Since astronauts must treat several physiologic abnormalities that occur in space, it is important that drug absorption and bioavailability be preserved for pharmaceutical effectiveness. Also, crewmembers must maintain adequate nutrition for physically and mentally demanding work, much of which is critical to safety of the crew or the vehicle. This investigation utilized a noninvasive technique to successfully record human stomach myoelectric activity in space over a long period. Future work should involve confirmation of these findings and further characterization of the altered stomach rhythms in relation to the presence of nausea and vomiting, especially in regards to the precise timing of the EGG data and the subjective reports of the SMS symptoms. This technique could potentially be utilized for monitoring stomach muscle and nerve conditions as an early warning before SMS symptoms appear. It could also potentially assist flight surgeons in making decisions regarding medication administration and timing. However, in order to function in such a manner, the data would have to be available real-time or near real-time.

title: Direct Measurement of the Initial Bone Response to Space Flight in Humans
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The human skeleton undergoes a continuous renewing process. Under normal conditions a balance exists between breakdown and reformation of the bone material. There is evidence that space flight upsets the system and causes an imbalance, even during short-duration missions. Furthermore, the cumulative effect of multiple short-term flights may be similar to that of extended exposure to microgravity. This is a major concern for the health of astronauts. Scientists believe that reduced mechanical work loads on the body in space induce the skeleton to discard bone it no longer needs. It is believed that the process of bone resorption begins almost immediately upon reaching microgravity. Researchers feel that the temporal relationships in calcium/bone homeostatic and endocrine responses will serve to prove or disprove this hypothesis. The purpose of this investigation is to define the response of the human calcium/bone homeostatic system to microgravity and gather data that will allow prediction of consequences for the health of astronauts. Previous investigations flown on the Spacelab Life Sciences 1 and 2 (SLS-1 and SLS-2) missions (see experiment titled Pathophysiology of Mineral Loss During Space Flight) verified that the human calcium regulatory hormone system functions normally in space. The increased calcium levels in the bloodstream, from increased bone breakdown, cause higher excretion of calcium in urine and a decrease in calcium absorption in the intestines. A higher calcium intake - the therapy for osteoporosis on Earth - is expected to cause further urinary calcium excretion and increases the risk of kidney stones for space travelers.
approach: From 10 days before launch until 7 days after landing, each participating astronaut ingested a nonradioactive, stable isotope of calcium (48Ca) with each meal. The labeling was done to distinguish between calcium coming from the diet and calcium being resorbed from bone material. Samples of blood, urine and feces were collected. The samples collected during the space flight were frozen at -20° Celsius. The ratios of calcium isotopes (48Ca/40Ca) were measured after landing. In addition, the astronauts kept a log book, tracking their food and drug intake as well as exercise sessions.
results: Bone resorption increases relatively early in space flight (3-5 days). Serum ionized calcium is increased as a result and remains elevated throughout the duration of the flight. The normal adaptive responses of a decrease in serum PTH as ionized calcium is increased occur. The effect of a short term exposure to space flight is still manifest two months postflight with increased bone turnover and possibly elevated serum calcium.

title: Evaluation of Skeletal Muscle Performance and Characteristics
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Traditional muscle deconditioning is characterized by atrophy and decreases in metabolic enzymes. Previous studies have demonstrated post-flight or post-bed rest decreases in muscle tone and other alterations in neuromuscular functions. Different degrees of altered performance (strength, endurance, and coordination) appear in different muscle groups and may be related to these changes after exposure to real or simulated microgravity. Altered integrated muscle performances (walking, running, standing, etc.) have been noted after exposure to real or simulated microgravity. All changes have been reported from a series of separate flight and simulation studies on different subjects and species over "flights" of different duration using a variety of in-flight exercise countermeasures. Muscle deconditioning may be better understood by examining multiple individuals doing the same countermeasures and tests during a single space flight. The objective of this experiment was to increase the understanding of muscle deconditioning and to evaluate the effects of the inflight countermeasures on muscle performance and characteristics. Based upon previous research, the investigators evaluated the following hypotheses. Muscle performance will change in a non uniform manner during flight and will slowly readapt to before flight levels upon return to 1-g. These non uniform changes include: Legs, arms, back and neck muscles will decondition to different levels Extensors muscle characteristics will have greater changes than flexors Different types of contractions will have disproportionate changes after flight The major mechanisms for muscle deconditioning will be neural and changes in other muscle characteristics. These changes will slowly readapt to before flight levels upon return to 1-g. There will be a significant decreases in integrated muscle performance (treadmill and cycle exercise) during the flight and will slowly readapt to before flight levels upon return to 1-g. The decreases in integrated muscle performance will be due to the changes in the individual muscle performance and their underlying mechanisms.
approach: Skeletal muscle characteristics and performance were measured before and after flight on the three Mir 18 crewmembers. Muscle tone was the reflex muscle stiffness measured with a reflex myotonometer on the gastrocnemius. Strength velocities characteristics were assessed with the LIDO (LIDO Active Multi-Joint Isokinetic Dynamometer). Subjects contracted muscles of the ankle, knee, and back at maximal levels against a lever arm that is moving in the same direction as the muscle contraction (concentric contraction), and in the opposite direction as the muscle contraction (eccentric). No back data was collected at the flight surgeons' request. Voluntary Isometric contractions were assessed with the LIDO. Subjects contracted muscles of the ankle, knee, and neck on LIDO at maximal levels against a stationary lever arm. EMGs were recorded on select muscle groups. Fatiguability was assessed with a hand dynamometer (hand). Hand endurance was assessed at current and relative strength levels. The crewmember will be asked to hold a 50% of current strength for as long as possible. The absolute endurance was assessed with a series of contractions (3 s contraction, 2 s relaxation) at 75% of preflight strength. The test stopped when the target force was not met. Evoked isometric contractions (tendometria) assessed the single, double and tetanic twitches of the soleus/gastroc muscles in one subject. Sport (treadmill) testing was done using the Russian protocol. Metabolic and physical (running speed) parameters were recorded. EMG data of select muscles were recorded.
results: Although time constraints canceled 50% of data collection sessions (SPORT had 75% canceled) and sample size was too small to make general inferences for all long duration space flights, valuable results were still obtained. Results showed that subjects who completed a greater percentage of the prescribed exercise were closer to before flight levels of performance for postural muscles (Quadriceps, Tricep Surae, Hamstrings, Neck Extensors), than those who completed less of the prescribed countermeasure program. Muscles used to maintain position during flight (tibialis anterior) maintained isometric but not isokinetic strength. The magnitude of the decreases in isokinetic strength, appear to be related to joint speed. Regardless of maintenance or loss of strength all muscles lost efficiency (more electrical activity needed to produce force after flight). The decrease in efficiency may be a function of contraction speed. Relative endurance (relative to 50% current level of strength) increased or was maintained after long duration flight. However, the absolute endurance (same work rate before and after flight) decreased dramatically. This decrease in absolute endurance may impact future EVAs. Evoked (tetanic) Contractions of Subject C. The decrease in the maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) was 4 times greater than that observed from the tetanic (evoked) contraction. This suggests that muscle potential for force developement was a small reason for the decrease in performance. Decreases in neural factors probably account for this difference. The large decrease in the single twitch force is thought to be related to decreased muscle tone (stiffness). Twenty-five percent of the large decrease in ankle strength (MVC) in subject C was due to the muscles inability to produce force (tetanic). Slower rates of force development and relaxation and the larger IEMG activity suggests that the remaining (75%) decrease in force in this subject had a strong neural component. The treadmill (SPORT) results showed decreases in peak running speed while maintaining metabolic demand, which suggests a decrease in running economy that may be linked to the decrease in muscle performance and vestibular problems. The larger decreases in NME at the high joint speeds may also be a contributing factor.

title: Osteoblast Adhesion and Phenotype in Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The objectives of this experiment are to determine if space flight causes changes in the osteoblast consistent with a reduction in bone formation and increase in bone resorption by analyzing the biochemistry of the cells, the histochemistry of mineral, matrix and cells, and adhesion plaque properties. The level of integration (cell vs. whole specimen) required for gravitational effects on bone will also be determined.
approach: A permanent cell line derived from a rat osteosarcoma and stably exhibiting an osteoblast-like phenotype (ROS 17/2.8) was cultured on microcarrier beads and inoculated into 24 STL cartridges. During flight, fraction collection from the 12 flight and 12 ground control cartridges, followed by fixation with paraformaldehyde or Histochoice, occurred at L+3 hr, L+1d, L+2d, L+4d, L+7d, and L+10d. Post flight, cultures were assayed for lactate, an indicator of metabolic activity and cell viability.
results: Upon examination, all cartridges showed a yellow color in the extra-fibril space occupied by cells and beads. This discoloration had not been observed in any previous experiments using the Cellmax culture systems. Analysis of lactate production in conditioned media samples showed considerable variation in lactate levels among replicates. Several samples from later time points showed a decline in lactate levels to near zero. These declines are presumably due to active degradation: control studies indicated that lactate levels in conditioned medium from ROS 17/2.8 cells remained essentially constant at 37 degrees C for over 2 weeks. The yellow color was most likely caused by microbial contamination, which could account for variations in lactate levels in the conditioned media. The likely presence of contaminants in the samples unfortunately compromises any experimental findings.
