title: Effects of Exposure to Heavy Particles
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Future missions in space may involve long-term travel beyond the magnetic field of the earth, subjecting astronauts to radiation hazards posed by solar flares and galactic cosmic rays. The objectives of this research project were to describe and characterize heavy particle-induced behavioral and neurochemical deficits, determine their underlying causes, and develop approaches to minimize such deficits. To achieve these objectives, behavioral and neurochemical models were used that have been previously shown to be sensitive to radiation exposure, and which may provide a basis for defining the risks of exposure to heavy particles on brain functioning and related behavior. An understanding of this risk may be vital to the effective performance and possibly the survival of astronauts during future missions in space. Project Aims The general objectives of the experiments reviewed in this report were to determine the effects of exposure to heavy particles on dopaminergic neurons in the brain, the neurochemical processes that mediate the effects of exposure, and on the behaviors that depend upon the integrity of the dopaminergic system. More specifically, the aims of the research program were to: 1. Further characterize the neurochemical effects and the mechanisms that mediate the effects of exposure to 56Fe particles. 2. Further characterize both acute and late behavioral/cognitive effects of exposure to 56Fe and other particles. 3. Characterize organismic variables, such as age, as mediators of the effects of exposure to HZE particles. 4. Further characterize the effects of exposure to high-energy protons on neurochemical and behavioral functioning. 5. Evaluate the effects of diet on the neurochemical and behavioral effects of exposure to 56Fe particles.
approach: Behavioral Measures Measurement of behaviors within 3-7 days following exposure to heavy particles or protons utilized the facilities available at the site of irradiation. For the measurement of behaviors that require specialized equipment, or which can take repeated trials for the acquisition (e.g., conditioned place preference, water maze performance or operant conditioning procedures) the animals were shipped to University of Maryland Baltimore County (UMBC) or Human Nutrition Research Center on Aging at Tufts University (HNRCA) for testing. In each case, both irradiated and non-irradiated controls were shipped to provide a control for any possible effects of the shipping. The basis for the selection of the behavioral tests is: (a) the behaviors are dopamine mediated (CPP, amphetamine-induced CTA, variable interval operant responding, upper body strength); and (b) they are behaviors that show deterioration as a function of age (water maze, radial arm maze). Conditioned Taste Aversions: The conditioned taste aversion (CTA) is a procedure by which rats are placed on a 23.5-hr water deprivation schedule for 7 days. On the conditioning day, they are presented with a calibrated drinking tube containing 10% sucrose solution instead of water, and intake recorded. Immediately following the drinking period, the rats are presented with the unconditioned stimulus (amphetamine, 3 mg/kg, ip). On the test day the rats are again given the 10% sucrose solution for 30 min. The acquisition of a CTA is shown by reduced sucrose intake on the test day compared to the conditioning day. Conditioned Place Preference: This procedure, which is used to evaluate the reinforcing qualities of a specific stimulus, utilizes an apparatus with three distinct compartments (black and white compartments which are separated by a gray compartment). The rat is given a reinforcing stimulus (e.g., amphetamine, 2 mg/kg) in one compartment and, on alternate days, a neutral stimulus (e.g., saline) in the other. An “unbiased” procedure is used, in which the compartment associated with injection of amphetamine is randomly assigned - some rats are given the amphetamine in the black compartment and some in the white compartment. After three pairings of each compound with a specific compartment, the rat is allowed to move freely about the apparatus and the amount of time spent in each compartment is measured. A Conditioned Place Preference (CPP) is shown when the organism spends significantly more time in the compartment paired with the presumptive reinforcing stimulus (amphetamine) than in the compartment paired with the neutral stimulus. Operant Conditioning: The proposed procedure is a standard one in which rats are rewarded for making an instrumental response on a fixed ratio schedule. In a fixed-ratio design, the animal is rewarded after n number of responses, such that on an FR-5 schedule, the rat is rewarded after 5 responses (bar presses) and on an FR-10 schedule, after 10 responses. Rats are first trained to press a lever using an FR1 schedule by placing them in an operant chamber for 12 hrs. After the response has been learned, the rats are trained to respond on a fixed-ratio schedule by providing several trials using an FR-5 schedule. During testing the rats are then given 30-min sessions in which they are rewarded using FR-1, FR-5, FR-10, FR-15, FR-20, FR- 25, FR-30 and FR-35 reinforcement schedules. If exposure to 56Fe particles disrupts operant performance, then the irradiated animals should make fewer responses than the sham-irradiated controls and the discrepancy between the irradiated and control rats should increase as the number of responses required for the delivery of a food pellet increases. Water Maze and Radial-Arm Maze: These procedures are the standard ones used to evaluate changes in spatial learning and memory. Performance on these tasks were sensitive to hippocampal damage and show decreased performance in aged organisms. Morris water maze: The Morris water maze consists of a circular black fiberglass pool (134 cm in diameter x 50 cm in height), filled to a depth of 30 cm with water maintained at 23oC. The pool is divided into four equal-size quadrants. A circular escape platform (10 cm in diameter) is colored black and therefore hidden from sight. The platform is submerged 2 cm below the surface of the water in the center of one of the quadrants; its location is changed to a different quadrant for each session of testing. The maze is placed in a room with the lights dimmed, and there are numerous extramaze cues on the walls. Performance on each test is videotaped and analyzed with image tracking software (HVS Image, Hampton, England). The task requires an animal to use spatial learning and memory to find a hidden platform just below the surface of the water, and to remember its location from the previous trial. The rat must acquire a cognitive representation of location in space and have the ability to effectively navigate the environment; therefore, the animal must use distal cues to effectively locate the hidden platform. Accurate navigation is rewarded by escape from the pool. Several dependent measures are used to estimate the efficiency of the rat's performance: directionality, latency of finding the hidden platform on each trial, length of swim path as well as the distribution of swimming time and swim path in the four quadrants of the pool during transfer or probe trials (in which the platform is removed from the pool) or during reversal trials (in which the platform is moved to another quadrant of the pool), number of crossings and latency to cross a previous platform location, and swim speed. Several experimental procedures have been developed to measure different aspects of cognitive performance, including reference (long-term) and working (short-term) memory. Radial Arm Maze: The radial arm maze consists of eight equally spaced plexiglass arms (70 cm long, 12 cm wide) radiating from an octagonal central area 30 cm in diameter. Various extra-maze cues are present in the testing room. Each maze arm contains a small dish at its end that can be baited with 0.25 ml of 0.30% saccharine solution or a small food pellet (45 mg pellet). The task involves the successive selection of arms, radiating from the center of the maze, in order to obtain a water or food reward. Rats are water or food deprived to 85% of their body weight to ensure motivation. An optimal strategy involves using spatial memory to visit each arm only once, since the arms are not rebaited. Working memory is required while the rat is selecting the next arm to visit, apparently "keeping track of" which arms were previously selected. Various control experiments strongly suggest that the rat performs the radial arm maze test by utilizing extra-maze cues. One possibility is that the rat builds a cognitive map of the environment to learn the maze, and utilizes its working memory to monitor which arms have been visited. Motor Behavior Motor behavior is assessed using a wire suspension task. Each rat's forepaws are placed on a taut horizontal wire placed 10 cm above a foam cushion. The length of time that the animal can remain suspended is measured. This test measures muscle strength and prehensile reflex of the forepaws. Each animal serves as its control, with suspension time measured before, and following irradiation. Neurochemical Measures Dopamine Release: Dopamine release was determined by preparing 300: m slices of striata using a McIlwain tissue chopper. Slices of one caudate nucleus from each animal were placed in glass vials containing a modified Krebs-Ringer buffer that has been bubbled for 30 min with 95% O2/5% CO2. The buffer consists of 21 mM NaHCO3, 3.4 mM glucose, 1.3 mM NaH2PO4, 1 mM EGTA, 0.93 mM MgCl2, 127 mM NaCl and 2.5 mM KCl (pH 7.4). The slices were washed in this medium and 150: l aliquots are placed into two chambers of a superfusion apparatus containing 16 chambers, the perfusion of the slices from eight animals in the same experimental "run". The tissue and buffer media are maintained at 37oC throughout the course of the experiment. The tissue is then allowed to equilibrate for 30 min while being perfused with the oxygenated basal release medium at the rate of 124: l/min. After equilibration, a 5 min baseline fraction is collected and the medium is switched to one containing (in mM) KCl 30, CaCl2.H2O 1.26, (in place of EGTA) and NaCl 57, as well as the other components listed above. Following the switch, 5-min fractions continue to be collected for 30 min into vials containing 0.4 perchloric acid (to prevent the autoxidation of the dopamine). To assess cholinergic effects on dopamine release, oxotremorine (500: M) is added to the release medium perfusing alternate chambers. Dopamine release is assessed by HPLC coupled to electrochemical detection. Oxidative Stress Aliquots of tissue were prepared the same as the dopamine release. To evaluate oxidative stress the aliquots of tissue were loaded with 2',7'-dichlorofluorescin diacetate which oxidizes to 2',7'-dichlorofluorescein in the presence of reactive oxygen species. The level of brain-associated fluorescence was monitored using a Cyto Fluor Multi-Well Plate Reader (perSeptive Biosystem, Framingham, MA). Neurogenesis Assessment of neurogenesis in the rat brains is determined by bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation into the nuclei of dividing cells. BrdU is a thymidine analog used as a mutagen in genetic research, which is selectively incorporated into cellular DNA during the S-phase of cell division. Each rat receives 1 daily intraperitoneal injection of BrdU (50mg/kg) for 6 consecutive days. Rats are sacrificed and perfused one day after the last BrdU injection in order to study the proliferation of newly divided cells. Additional rats are sacrificed 28 days following the last injection to study the differentiation into cell types. Every sixth section of a series through the hippocampus (approx. 240um apart) will be selected and BrdU-positive cells were counted using a modified version of the optical fractionator method. Stereological estimates are made of the total number of BrdUpositive cells located throughout the entire extent of the granular cell layer, subgranular zone and the hilus.
results: Neurochemical Mechanisms Oxidative Stress: Different brain regions (striatum, hippocampus, frontal cortex) were evaluated for oxidative stress using 2',7'- dichlorofluorescin diacetate 1-2 months following exposure to 1.5 Gy 56Fe particles. In the presence of reactive oxygen species, the compound oxidizes and becomes highly fluorescent. Results indicated that there were significant increases in reactive oxygen species in the hippocampus and frontal cortex, but not in the striatum of rats exposed to 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles. These results suggest that exposure to 56Fe particles cause oxidative stress, although irradiation may not produce equivalent effects throughout the entire brain. Cellular Signaling in the Brain: Calcium homeostasis and calcium-dependent signaling (e.g. calcium dependent protein kinases (PKs) and calcium-mediated neurotransmitter release) are essential for memory formation, particularly spatial memory. Changes in calcium-dependent PKC, PKA, were observed during the experiment, suggesting altered cellular signaling. Furthermore, these changes in brain responses significantly correlated with reference and working memory errors in the radial arm maze. These results show differential brain-region-specific sensitivity induced by exposure to 56Fe particles. Neurogenesis: Recent research has indicated that, neurogenesis occurs in mature, as well as developing organisms. One way of determining whether or not neurogenesis is occurring is to evaluate cells in specific brain regions for bromo-deoxy-uridine (BrdU) staining. Preliminary combined counts of the subgranular zone and granular cell layer of the hippocampus suggest that the subjects irradiated with 2.5Gy of 56Fe radiation have significantly less BrDU-stained cells in this region than do control subjects. Behavioral Studies of Exposure to 56Fe and Other HZE Particles Conditioned Taste Aversion Learning: Previous research had shown that the motor deficits in dopaminergic function were still observed up to 180 days following exposure to 1 Gy of 600 MeV/n 56Fe particles. The amphetamine-induced CTA, which depends upon the integrity of the dopaminergic system was utilized to evaluate whether or not there is recovery of behavioral function 4 months following exposure to 1 Gy of 56Fe particles (1 GeV/n). These results compared to the control animals revealed that radiated animals showed a significantly greater decrease in sucrose intake, indicating an enhanced aversion to the normally preferred sucrose solution. Although more research is needed to evaluate the mechanisms that may have been responsible for this change in behavior, it is possible that the loss of dopamine may have resulted in the up regulation of these receptors. Morris Water Maze: The effects of exposure to 56Fe particles on cognitive performance were analyzed by using the Morris water maze to evaluate possible heavy particle induced deficits in spatial learning and memory. Rats exposed to 1.5 Gy of 1 GeV/n 56Fe particles demonstrated cognitive impairment compared to a control group, as shown by increased latency to find the hidden platform, particularly when the location of the platform was moved 180° from its previous location or when the platform was removed from the pool to test for the use of spatial strategies. These results provided the first indication that exposure to non-lethal levels of 56Fe particles could affect the cognitive ability of an organism. Radial Arm Maze: The radial arm maze consists of 8 arms radiating from a central area. The arms can be baited with food and the rat enters each arm to obtain food. The most efficient procedure is to enter each arm once, and only once, to obtain the food. When all arms are baited, rats exposed to 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles show somewhat better performance than control rats by entering each arm in turn. However, when only half the arms contain food, the performance of the radiated rats is poorer than that of controls. It appears that under these conditions, the radiated rats are not able to use spatial cues to guide their behavior, so they repeatedly enter the unbaited arms or arms which they have previously entered. These results support previous research, which indicates deficits in spatial learning and memory following exposure to 56Fe particles. Operant Responding: Groups of rats were exposed to 0, 1.0, 1.5, or 2.0 Gy of 56Fe particles and trained to press a lever in order to obtain food reinforcement. Once the response was acquired the rats were placed on an ascending fixed-ratio (FR) schedule starting with FR-1 (every lever press rewarded with a food pellet) and extending to FR-35 (35 lever presses are required to produce 1 food pellet). In general, as the ratio increases, rats increase their rate of responding. However, the results showed that at ratios greater than FR-20, rats exposed to 2.0 Gy failed to increase their rate responding. These results indicate that rats exposed to 2.0 Gy of 56Fe particles cannot respond appropriately to increasing work requirements. The rats that had been trained on the operant response tested on the ascending fixed ratio reinforcement schedule at 7, 10 and 15 months following irradiation. The results showed that the rats exposed to 1.0 or 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles and which showed no differences from control animals (0 Gy) when tested at 3 months post-irradiation, showed significant decreases in performance compared to the control rats when tested at these later time intervals. In addition, the rats exposed to 2.0 Gy continued to show a significant reduction in performance. These results indicate that, not only is there no recovery of function over time following exposure to heavy particles, there is a further decrease in performance which may be related to the increased age of the rats at the time of testing. Conditioned Place Preference (CPP): CPP, a standard procedure for evaluating the capacity of a stimulus to reinforce behavior, is produced by pairing a rewarding stimulus (e.g., amphetamine) with specific environmental cues. The first experiment in this series showed that 2-4 weeks following exposure to 1.0 Gy of 56Fe particles, radiated rats fail to acquire an amphetamine-induced place preference. This indicates a disruption of the dopaminergic mechanisms that mediate reinforcement. Follow-up experiments evaluated place preference learning 2 months and 4 months following irradiation to determine if there was any recovery of function. The results showed that the irradiated rats failed to acquire an amphetamine-induced place preference when trained 2 or 4 months following exposure to 56Fe particles. These results indicate that the effects of irradiation on reinforcement show no recovery as a function of time following exposure to 1.0 Gy of 56Fe particles. Because the results of the initial experiment showed a high degree of variability in terms of the amount of time spent in the amphetamine-paired compartment, it was decided to use a higher dose of 56Fe particles (1.5 Gy) to determine if the higher dose could eliminate the variability in the behavioral effects of exposure. Although the higher dose did eliminate the variability, it also eliminated the effect of irradiation on behavior: there was no effect of exposure on the acquisition of an amphetamine-induced place preference. Currently available data do not permit a determination of the factors that might be responsible for the dose-dependent effects of exposure to 56Fe particles on behavior. Environmental Responsiveness: As shown with operant responding, rats exposed to 56Fe particles have difficulty in responding to changes in environmental contingencies, including adjusting work requirements to reinforcement contingencies. An alternate approach determining the effects of irradiation on the responsiveness of the organism to the environment is to evaluate the open field activity of irradiated rats and their reaction to spatial and non-spatial changes. Animals irradiated with 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles took longer to enter, visited less and spent significantly less time in the middle and the center portions of the open-field than did controls independently of total frequency and duration of activity of both groups. Likewise, irradiated subjects reacted significantly more to novel objects placed in the open-field than did controls. However, irradiated subjects did not vary from controls in their exploration patterns when objects in the open-field were spatially rearranged. Thus, irradiation with a dose of 1.5 Gy of 56Fe high-energy particle radiation elicited age-like effects during the spatial and non-spatial rearrangement tasks. Taste Aversion Learning 28Si: Because astronauts will be exposed to other types of heavy particles in addition to 56Fe on long-duration missions outside the magnetosphere, it is necessary to evaluate the neurochemical and behavioral toxicity of other types of heavy particles. The initial experiments evaluated the effects of exposure to 28Si particles on amphetamine-induced CTA learning. This endpoint was selected because it has been shown to be very sensitive to irradiation with 56Fe particles and because there is a significant amount of data from 56Fe experiments to provide comparisons. Rats were exposed to 2.0, 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of silicon particles. These doses were selected to take into account the lower LET of 600 MeV 28Si compared to that of 1GeV and 600 MeV 56Fe particles which have thresholds for behavioral and neurochemical effects of .8 and .1 Gy, respectively. Doses of 28Si particles produced an enhanced aversion compared to the non-irradiated controls. Because similar results have been observed following exposure to higher doses of 56Fe particles, these results suggest that the tested doses were too high, despite the lower LET of 600 MeV/n 28Si particles. Operant Responding Following Exposure to 5 GeV/n 56Fe: Most of the research reviewed in this report has utilized 1 GeV/n 56Fe, which has an LET = 148keV/?m. For one run we had access to 5 GeV/n 56Fe, which has an LET = 142keV/?m. Rats were exposed to doses ranging between 1.5 to 2.5 Gy. When tested on an ascending fixed-ratio task 3 months following exposure, there were no significant differences between any irradiated group and the non-irradiated controls. Organismic Variables (Aging) Two approaches have been utilized to evaluate the effects of age on neurochemical and behavioral endpoints following exposure to HZE particles. First, rats have been maintained up to 1 year post irradiation and performance on specific tasks measured at intervals during the is time period. This approach using operant responding on a fixed-ratio reinforcement schedule shows that performance decreases as age increases: doses of 56Fe particles that were ineffective in altering performance in young animals had deleterious effects on aged animals. The second approach studied the effects of exposure to HZE particles in older organisms. Exposure to HZE particles produces a series of neurochemical changes and motor deficits that are similar, but not identical, to those seen in older animals. To begin an evaluation of the possibility of an interaction between age and heavy particle irradiation, a preliminary experiment was run to determine oxotremorine-enhanced dopamine release in young and middle-aged F-344 rats following exposure to 1 Gy of 56Fe particles. The results showed a greater deficit in dopaminergic function in the older animals than in the younger animals. Statistical analysis of the results showed that there was a significant decrease in dopamine released in the aged, non-irradaiated rats. The difference between the middle-aged control rats and the irradiated young animals was not significant. These results suggest that dopamine release in a young rat exposed to 1 Gy of 56Fe particles is similar to that in old rats that have not been irradiated. Neurochemistry: Exposing rats to 1.5, 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of 250 MeV protons produced no significant alterations in dopamine release. Comparted to control animals, all groups of irradiated animals, particularly those exposed to 1.5 and 3.0 Gy, showed a slight increase in dopamine release, but this was not significant. These results indicate that exposure to up to 4.0 Gy of high energy protons does not affect the functioning of the dopaminergic system. Conditioned Place Preference: Rats were tested for the acquisition of a CPP following exposure to 4 Gy of protons or following control procedures. Both the irradiated and the control rats showed a similar preference for the amphetamine-paired compartment. The amount of time spent in each compartment was not significantly different for the proton-exposed and control rats. Spatial Learning and Memory: Exposing rats to protons produced no consistent alteration in water maze performance. Rats irradiated with 4.0 Gy showed increase latency to find the hidden platform on Day 1, but by Day 2 were identical to controls. Rats irradiated with 1.5 Gy demonstrated impairments in re-learning compared to the control group as shown by increased latencies on the reversal day (Day 4), when the platform was moved to the opposite quadrant. However, spatial memory and learning were not disrupted as all groups performed equally well on the probe trials, showing that all groups utilized spatial strategies to find the platform. CTA Learning: Two sets of experiments were conducted. In the first experiment, rats were exposed to 1.5, 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of protons. There were no significant differences between the irradiated or the control rats; both groups of rats showed equivalent test day sucrose intakes following injection of amphetamine. In contrast to the results obtained with rats exposed to 56Fe particles, exposing rats to up to 4.0 Gy of 250 MeV protons did not disrupt the acquisition of the dopamine-mediated CTA produced by injection of amphetamine. In the second experiment, the rats were placed behind 6 gm/cm2 aluminum to see whether the fragmentation characteristics produced by protons passing through aluminum shielding would affect the behavioral response to administration of a dopamine agonist. The acquisition of a CTA following exposure to 3.0 or 4.0 Gy of protons was not affected by shielding. There were no differences in the intensity of the amphetamine-induced CTA between the control rats and the radiated rats. Operant Responding: Proton-irradiated and control animals were trained to press a lever for food reinforcement using a fixed-ratio schedule. In contrast to the results obtained following exposure to 56Fe particles exposure to 4 Gy of high-energy protons had no effect on fixed-ratio responding for food reinforcement. Both irradiated and control animals showed increased levels of responding as the ratio was increased from FR-1 to FR-35. Exposing rats to high-energy protons does not affect the capacity of the organism to respond appropriately to changes in reinforcement contingencies. Effects of Antioxidant Diets Dopamine Release: Previous research had shown that exposing rats to 1.5 Gy 56Fe particles produces a significant decrease in potassium-enhanced striatal dopamine release. Because similar effects are observed in aged animals, and because diets rich in antioxidant phytochemicals can prevent the neurochemical change, the first experiment in this series was designed to evaluate whether or not these diets are equally effective in preventing heavy particle-induced neurochemical changes. Rats maintained on the control diet continued to show a 56Fe-induced reduction in dopamine release. In contrast, the rats maintained on either the strawberry or blueberry diets did not show the radiation-induced reduction in dopamine release. Compared to their respective controls, the radiated animals maintained on the antioxidant diets apparently showed an enhanced dopamine release. Dopamine-Mediated Taste Aversion Learning: Rats were maintained on the control diet or on the diets containing 2% blueberry of strawberry extract. Two days following irradiation with 1.5 Gy of articles failed to develop a CTA to amphetamine. The rats fed either the blueberry or strawberry diet did show an amphetamine-induced CTA. These results indicate that antioxidant diets that have been shown to ameliorate the effects of normal aging are equally effective in preventing the disruption of amphetamine-induced CTA learning by exposure to 6Fe particles. Tumorigenesis: Among other effects on the health and functioning of the organism, oxidative stress and the production of reactive oxygen species have been linked to carcinogenesis. As part of another study, rats that had been given either antioxidant or control diets prior to 56Fe exposure were evaluated for tumor development for 1 year after irradiation. Rats were sacrificed when a tumor developed or when there was some obvious health problem. The rats that were maintained on the blueberry or strawberry diets prior to irradiation with 56Fe particles showed a significantly greater survival time and developed significantly fewer tumors than rats maintained on the control diet. Effects of Diet on Operant Responding: Rats were maintained on control or antioxidant diets for 2 months prior to exposure to 1.5 Gy of 56Fe particles. When tested on an ascending fixed-ratio schedule 7 months post-irradiation, there were no significant differences in response rate as a function of irradiation status or diet. When tested 12 months post-irradiation, the irradiated rats fed control or blueberry diets showed significantly poorer performance than the non-irradiated rats or the radiated rats fed the strawberry diet.

title: Overweight and Obesity in the LSAH Population
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The rising prevalence of overweight and obese Americans has been the frequent topic of recent media articles. Various national surveys show that the majority of Americans are overweight. According to data obtained from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), the percentage of overweight adults (ages 20-74) in the general population has increased from 45% in 1960-1962, to 64% in 1999-2000. The percentage of obese individuals has increased from 13% to 31% within the same time period. The terms overweight and obesity are defined using the Body Mass Index (BMI), a measure that expresses the relationship of weight to height. BMI is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by the squared height in meters. This study compared the BMI of the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) participants with that of the general population.
approach: Data for astronaut participants and a group of comparison participants were obtained from the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) database. The BMI calculations for LSAH participants used weight and height data obtained from annual physical exams. Data for the general population were obtained from the NHANES database.
results: When compared to the general population, LSAH participants showed a similar trend of rising overweight and obesity over time (1967-2003). A graph of the data showed that a smaller percentage of astronauts and comparison participants were likely to be overweight, as compared to the general population. Astronauts were the least likely of the groups studied to be overweight. Over time however, a higher percentage of astronauts and comparison participants were likely to become overweight than the general population. Some of this rising trend may have been a function of the small sample sizes of LSAH participants, and may have reflected their propensity to gain weight as they age. As indicated by their R-squared value, all trend lines showed good representation of their respective data points and their trend over time (compared to an R-squared maximum value of one.) The obesity comparison showed both astronauts and comparison participants maintaining much lower obesity prevalence as compared to the general population. The trend lines suggested that LSAH participants become obese at a lower rate than the general population, with astronauts maintaining lower obesity than the comparison participants. However, R-squared values for the astronauts’ and comparison participants’ obesity trend lines indicated a higher variability for their obesity data than their overweight data. Taken together, these comparisons suggest that although LSAH participants maintain much lower obesity as compared to the general population, their overweight trends show a rapid rise that may result in prevalences similar to that of the general population. Aging is certainly a factor in the rapid rise of their overweight prevalence. However, they may do well to take action to decrease their overweight prevalences for the sake of their health.

title: Development of the Fish Medaka in Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The goal of these experiments was to determine the effect of microgravity on the early development of the fish Medaka. There were two objectives for this flight series. The primary objective was to assess the effects of microgravity on different stages of development and to ascertain whether the relevant developmental questions can be addressed at the gross morphological level or if the issues involve more subtle questions about regulation at the molecular and cellular levels. The secondary objective was the assessment of the utility of flight hardware with the capabilities to perform embryological studies.
approach: In this experiment, thirty-six Medaka embryos were used to examine the effects of microgravity on embryogenesis. One advantage of fish Medaka embryos was their clear appearance, because it allowed direct observation by video-microscopy. Video sequences, video tape, and digital images were all utilized to monitor development of the embryos. All of the embryos have been embedded and sectioned. Some embryos were fixed and returned to Earth for further analysis. However, two groups of embryos were returned to Earth unfixed in order to investigate their postflight development and reproductive abilities.
results: In comparison to the ground controls, the flight group did not display any gross morphological abnormalities. An important observation from the experiment was the overall normal development of the flight animals. Data from the study also indicated that animals exposed to microgravity during embryogenesis retain their ability to reproduce. Furthermore, it was determined that the flight groupï¿½s progeny was fertile as well.

title: Medical Microbiological Analysis of U.S. Crew Members
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) was a unique space flight in which spacecrafts from America and the Soviet Union docked together in space. This presented an opportunity to study cross-contamination of one crew with the medically important microorganisms carried by the other crew. Accordingly, the objectives of this study were to identify and trace all microorganisms of potential medical importance. Medical microbiological analysis of U.S. crewmembers was performed as a part of a larger study, the Microbial Exchange Experiment (AR-002), conducted during the historic ASTP space flight.
approach: Microbial samples were collected from the three Apollo crewmembers and two Soyuz crewmembers on L-45 days, L-30, L-15, L-7, L-0 (launch day), once during flight, and on recovery days R+0, R+15 and R+30. Backup crewmembers served as experimental controls. Sample collection sites included: 1) A 20 square centimeters area of hair (and scalp) on the top of the head 2) Right and left external auditory canals 3) 20 square centimeters area below hairline at base of neck 4) Internal area of both nostrils 5) The tonsils and posterior pharyngeal vault 6) 20 square centimeters area on right and left palms 7) 20 square centimeters area below the hairline of each axilla 8) 5 centimeter strip from rear to front on right and left inguinal area between legs 9) Area between the two smallest toes of each foot 10) The throat and mouth Preflight and post flight, microbial specimens were collected from each crewmember using calcium alginate swabs wet with 0.3 millimolar phosphate buffer. Dry calcium alginate swabs were used to sample the tonsils and pharyngeal vault prior to the collection of the gargle specimen. In-flight samples, consisting of the first six areas outlined above, were obtained from all five flight crewmembers on flight day 3. A specially developed microbial sample collection device was used to collect in-flight samples. This device consisted of a cotton-tipped Teflon swab on a capillary tube containing a conservative fluid, which kept the microorganisms alive. Each swab was housed within an airtight case to prevent desiccation. Each sample was serially diluted under aseptic conditions and inoculated onto nutrient media. The variety of media, number of plates inoculated and dilution range were selected on the basis of what was required to isolate and quantitate the autoflora present in each sample area. Sabauraud's Dextrose Agar (SAB) plates were incubated at 30 degrees Celsius for five days. Cornmeal, malt-extract, yeast extract (CMMY) agar plates were incubated at 25 degrees Celsius for 7 days and all others were incubated at 37 degrees Celsius for 48 hours. Following incubation, the resulting aerobic bacterial colonies were categorized and counted with one sample of each morphologically different colony type transferred to nutrient media and stained with Gram's stain. Apollo sample analysis was conducted at the NASA Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center (JSC) in Houston, Texas.
results: Gram-negative Rods: Escherichia coli, Enterobacter aerogenes and Proteus mirabilis , members of the enteric bacilli group, were found on the ASTP crewmembers at sites other than the lower intestinal tract. Bacilli species are generally considered of potential medical importance when they are recovered repeatedly, or in large numbers, from sites other than the lower digestive tract. Escherichia coli is generally accepted as the most reliable evidence of fecal contamination. Outside the intestinal tract it can cause urinary tract infections, peritonitis, gall bladder infections, wound infections, septicemia and enteritis. E. coli was repeatedly recovered from the groin of ASTP subject B and occasionally from the upper respiratory tract of the other two prime crewmembers. In all cases, no medical significance was indicated by the occurrence or quantities of E. coli. Enterobacter aerogenes is found in the large intestine of man. Its pathogenic significance is similar to that of E. coli . This species was always carried in the nasal and buccal cavities of ASTP subjects B and C and was frequently isolated from two backup crewmembers. E. aerogenes was not spread to ASTP subject A or to other sites on the carrier subject during the flight. In addition, E. aerogenes quantities were not increased postflight. Proteus mirabilis can cause urinary tract infections, abscesses and gastroenteritis. More often, they cause secondary infections of the middle ear, mastoid process, meninges and urinary tract, as well as in existing wounds. P. mirabilis was carried in low numbers in the nasal passage of ASTP subject A. This species and E. aerogenes provided a good model system for analyzing the response of Gram negative rods to space flight conditions. It has previously been reported that the Gram-negative rod component of the autoflora could change during or following confinement in a closed environment and that this change could result in "dysobacteriosis," such as flooding of an area with a particular species. The ASTP mission had no such effect on the qualitative or quantitative presence of these microorganisms. Moraxella species are parasites found in the mucous membranes of man that can cause diseases such as conjunctivitis. Although carried in the mouth of ASTP subject C for 45 days preflight, no discernible microbial alteration was demonstrated following the mission. Acinetobacter calcoaceticus , of minor medical importance, was isolated from multiple sites on ASTP subject B. It did not contribute significantly to the microbial load of Gram-negative rods recovered from ASTP crewmembers. Four species of Haemophilus were isolated from the oral cavity of each ASTP astronaut. These were H. influenzae, H. haemolyticus, H. parahaemolyticus and H. parainfluenzae . Although each of these species is a common inhabitant of the human mouth, each is a strict parasite, requiring certain growth factors present in blood. H. influenzae is found in lesions and in the upper respiratory tract of carriers. It may be either a primary or a secondary invader. This microorganism is responsible for meningitis, septicemia, conjunctivitis and upper respiratory tract infections, and as a secondary invader in influenza and pertussis cases. H. influenzae was isolated from each crewmember preflight in quantities from 10,000 to 600,000 viable cells/ml of gargle. The post flight loss from two crewmembers and quantitative reduction in contamination of ASTP subject A was contraindicative of a space flight mediated increase in infective potential. H. haemolyticus and H. parahaemolyticus are often associated with acute pharyngitis when present in high numbers. As with the H. influenzae , the overall incidence and quantitation of H. haemolyticus and H. parahaemolyticus decreased following the ASTP flight. H. parainfluenzae is the least harmful of the four species recovered and is used largely as a marker organism due to its universal appearance. Candida albicans Candida albicans has been recovered from astronauts throughout the Apollo and Skylab missions. Because this species can cause serious oral cavity diseases, its presence was carefully monitored. C. albicans was isolated from ASTP subjects B and C at all sampling periods. Data analysis indicates the inflight transfer of C. albicans to ASTP subject A. No such transfer occurred in the backup crew, although C. albicans was carried by one crewman. All of these events demonstrate the importance of this species in space flight. The importance could increase during the in-flight use of antibiotics, because this could cause a loss of competing bacterial species and eventual overgrowth of C. albicans. Staphylococcus aureus Although Staphylococcus aureus is a common skin and nasal contaminant, all strains are potential pathogens. S. aureus can cause boils, abscesses, meningitis, furunculosis, pyemia, osteomyelitis, suppuration of wounds and food poisoning. Several studies have indicated increases in the toxigenic activity, virulence and pathogenicity of this species with stressful confinement of the human host. Lesions caused by S. aureus in space flight were important because of their interference with close contact surfaces, such as the tight fitting and abrasive pressure suits. Accordingly, the presence and activity of this species was monitored before and after each space flight. Data from Apollo 13, 14 and 15 missions, and from the Skylab missions confirm in-flight cross contamination with S. aureus. Data show that each crewmember (flight and backup) carried a different strain of S. aureus . Different strains are expressed as bacteriophage types. One type (52,52A,80,81), carried by ASTP subject C, was transferred to ASTP subject A during flight. Apparently colonization did not ensue, as this strain was not recovered from subject A post flight. During the ASTP mission, a post flight increase of S. aureus did not occur among the astronaut population, as reported during previous missions, and disease events did not result from its presence. Total Load of Potential Pathogens One idea that resulted from previous space flight microbial studies was that crewmembers could suffer "microbial shock" upon return to Earth, and therefore, respond negatively to renewed contact with the potentially pathogenic microorganisms absent in the space flight environment. This was based on the assumption that contact with potential pathogens during space flight would be very limited, resulting in a reduction of immunocompetence. However, there was no demonstrable decrease in the incidence of medically important microorganisms recovered from the astronauts on R+0, a finding which supports earlier results. Therefore, if a reduction in total immunocompetence occurred during the ASTP mission, it was not in response to decreased contact with medically important components of the resident microflora. Although several potential pathogens were recovered from each of the flight and backup crewmembers before and after flight, no disease events were reported. C. albicans and S. aureus were transferred from one crewmember to another in-flight, but no other medically significant changes in the microbial population were observed.

title: Adaptation in Artificial Gravity Environments
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The objective of this study was to provide a technical base for evaluating the feasibility of a rotating "artificial gravity" environment for long-duration space missions. The investigators previously demonstrated that Coriolis forces generated during rotation at 10 rpm disrupt head and arm movements but adaptation is possible. Specific goals were to study 1) the rotation rates up to which adaptation is possible, 2) whether measurements of disruptions caused by rotation and subsequent adaptation in 1-G underestimate or overestimate the effects to be expected during rotation in environments with a background force level less than 1-G, and 3) how the magnitude and orientation of the background force affect retention and transfer of adaptation to rotation.
approach: Twelve subjects stood in a heel-to-toe stance in the rotating room. Each test session involved three phases: 1) pre-rotation, 2) per-rotation, and 3) post-rotation. In each phase, subjects were tested in both eyes open and eyes closed conditions. Four measures were used to characterize center of mass movement and head movement: mean sway amplitude, total power, mean power frequency, and frequency of maximum power. Each measure was computed for anterior-posterior and medial-lateral sway.
results: Both anterior-posterior and medial-lateral head and center of mass sway during rotation had significantly greater mean sway amplitude and total power compared with pre- and post-rotation values. Mean power frequency and frequency of maximum power were little affected. Eyes open conditions were significantly more stable in all test phases than eyes-closed, but vision did not completely suppress the effects of rotation. The greatest effect of rotation was in the eyes-closed condition with mean sway amplitude and total power increasing more than twofold. Inverted pendulum sway was maintained in all phases of both test conditions. No aftereffects of rotation were present after the four 25-s exposures each subject received.

title: The Effects of Micro-Gravity on In Vitro Calcification
archive_status: No data from this study was submitted to LSDA. Please contact LSDA if you know of available data.
objectives: Earlier observations of animals flown in microgravity have produced conflicting information about the nature and amount of the mineral formed in bone during flight in microgravity. One cause for these differences was that much of the mineral had been formed on Earth, and there was no way of knowing how much new mineral formed in microgravity. Since crystals formed in vitro in microgravity are generally larger and more perfect than those formed under similar conditions on Earth, it was hypothesized that the initial mineral crystals formed under physiologic control in microgravity would also be larger. The purpose of this experiment was to evaluate the initial mineral formed in flight, and compare it to mineral formed in ground based controls. Since biologic mineralization is mediated both by the cells and the extracellular matrix, the second goal was to evaluate the effects of microgravity on the cells and matrix formed in this culture system.
approach: Cartilage cells were grown as micromass cultures and flown for 11 days; total time in culture was 16 or 19 days. All cells were fixed in 2 percent paraformaldehyde plus 0.5 percent glutaraldehyde in 0.05M cacodylate buffer, pH 7.4 for electron microscopy, histochemistry and immunocytochemistry.
results: No mineral was formed in either ground controls or flight experiment. There was increased cell proliferation inflight.

title: Microbial Interaction in the Mir Space Station Environment
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Transfer of infectious agents between crewmembers became problematic early in both the Soviet and U.S. space programs. During Apollo missions 7, 8 and 9, microbial associated illnesses were frequently observed. In later missions (Apollo 10, 11 and 12), although no microbe related illnesses were reported, changes in microbial flora of crewmembers were seen in postflight samples. As a result, preflight quarantine procedures were implemented beginning with the Apollo 14 mission. This approach was effective, and no microbial associated problems were reported with subsequent flights. Nevertheless, microbes with pathogenic potential (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus , Pseudomonas aeruginosa , Candida albicans ) were isolated from astronauts in these later Apollo missions. With the advent of the U.S. Space Shuttle program, since preflight quarantine practices continue and flights are of shorter duration, less emphasis is placed on microbial associated problems. These problems are likely to become more severe in the longer, more complex missions contemplated for the future. The long-term goal of this project was to understand the nature of microbial behavior in closed, long-duration space flight systems. The main objectives were: 1) To use pulsed field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) as a genomic fingerprinting technique and Staphylococcus as a target organism to: a. Measure the degree of microbial transfer between crewmembers b. Determine the origin of microorganisms isolated from the spacecraft environment (e.g. which crewmember did the organism come from or was it preflight contamination) c. Determine to what extent endogenous or acquired microbes of crewmembers increase or persist after landing. 2) Using a set of previously characterized Staphylococcus samples, assess the limits of simpler and faster fingerprinting methods using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and develop a strategy for using a primary assay. 3) To extend these results to other microorganisms of interest in long-duration missions. 4) To evaluate these assays in ground-based systems where additional monitoring was possible. 5) To determine the nature of the DNA variation being measured by the fingerprinting method.
approach: Samples of microbial flora were taken by the Microbiology Department at Johnson Space Center (JSC) during preflight training (starting approximately 5 months before launch), postflight (up to two weeks after landing), and by the crew during the mission. Samples were taken from several body locations on the crew and from environmental locations on board the Mir and Space Shuttle. These samples were processed by the JSC Microbiology Department to isolate and identify microorganisms that were present. Individual microbial isolates were then archived. Staphylococcus aureus isolates from several missions, as well as previously characterized control isolates from local hospitals, were subjected to DNA fingerprinting procedures. The two procedures used were restriction fragment length polymorphism mapping by pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (RFLP-PFGE) and PCR analysis using repeated sequence primers (REP-PCR). These methods were compared using both control and experimental samples. In addition, REP-PCR was performed on a well-characterized strain of Escherichia coli (whose chromosomal DNA sequence has been completely determined) and amplified fragments were cloned and sequenced. The sequences were analyzed to determine their origin in the genome. All samples were processed multiple times for DNA fingerprinting to ensure high quality and reproducibility of results.
results: A sufficiently large number of isolates of Staphylococcus aureus were obtained to allow conclusive testing of the methods and observation of microbial transfer. However, it is believed that sampling of each individual was not exhaustive enough to determine if there might be other strains of S. aureus that were not recovered. Such thorough sampling was not practicable under the sampling constraints, but does not seriously detract from the study. Method Development: The REP-PCR technology was found to be nearly as sensitive as RFLP-PFGE. At the same time, REP-PCR was less demanding and faster. The REP-PCR technology was determined to be an excellent alternative to RFLP-PFGE. Since REP-PCR was less demanding and faster, it should be used as the initial screen in the analysis of large numbers of samples. Samples that are different can readily be distinguished by this approach. Samples that cannot be distinguished by REP-PCR can then be analyzed by RFLP-PFGE analysis, which offers increased sensitivity. Although this is more laborious, this is not a limitation when only a small number of samples are being evaluated. Microbial Transfer: Clear examples of S. aureus transfer between crewmembers were found during the 9-12 month periods of interaction between crewmembers. This was qualitatively a higher incidence than found previously on short-term Shuttle missions. Some crewmembers were found to carry multiple strains of S. aureus , others did not carry detectable S. aureus . Some crewmembers seemed more susceptible to colonization by S. aureus than others. The greater prevalence of microbial transfer during the Mir missions as compared to the shorter term Shuttle missions argues that this phenomenon should be considered in designing other long-term missions. Differences between crewmembers as carriers could be determined ahead of time and appropriate steps could be taken to reduce individual microbial loads, possibly minimizing microbial transfer. Candidate Strains: Analysis of the total isolates of microorganisms from STS-71, Mir 18, Mir 19 and NASA 3/Mir 22 demonstrated a number of other microbes, both bacteria and fungi, that could be transferred between crewmembers or between the crew and environment. REP-PCR methodology was shown to be applicable to several of these strains ( E. coli , Corynebacteria spp., Bacillus pumilis and Enterococcus spp.). The presence of other possible candidates for microbial transfer suggests the issue may go beyond the behavior of S. aureus . The applicability of REP-PCR to the analysis of these strains suggests that further studies could readily clarify how often transfer occurs. Molecular Basis of REP-PCR: Sequence analysis of E. coli DNA fragments generated by REP-PCR showed that in over 90% of the cases, the fragments were generated by simple PCR. Rarely was the fragment generated by crossover PCR following binding of primers at non-continuous sites. The fact that the fragments generated by REP-PCR were primarily accurate reflections of the underlying genome structure indicated that no overly sensitive steps were involved (such as would be the case in crossover PCR) and that this method was most likely to be very reliable. Therefore, REP-PCR would be a possible target for the modification of instrumentation and assay conditions for use in flight, especially on long missions where returning samples to Earth would not be possible. Overall, this study demonstrated that microbial transfer is likely to be more of an issue for long-term exposure situations than for most current NASA missions. Moreover, a reliable and convenient method for tracking microbes by DNA fingerprinting was developed and implemented.

title: Microbial Analysis of International Space Station (ISS) Air, Surfaces and Water
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: NASA scientists have continuously performed routine environmental monitoring of the air, surfaces, and water systems of the International Space Station (ISS). Surface sample collection began in 2000 (Expedition 1), air sample collection began in 2001 (Expedition 2) and water monitoring of the U.S. potable water system has occurred since the installation of the potable water dispenser (PWD) in 2009 (Expedition 20). The specific objectives of the air, water, and surface sampling are: 1. To ensure that the air quality is microbiologically safe for crewmembers and to ensure compliance with existing acceptability limits established for microbial air sampling. 2. To ensure a microbiologically safe environment for crewmembers and to ensure compliance with existing acceptability limits established for microbial surface sampling. 3. To check for the presence of microbial contaminants in the potable water provided for crew use on the ISS and verify compliance with established water quality requirements.
approach: Samples were collected and enumerated during space flight operations. Identification of these isolates occurs on samples returned to the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Microbiology Laboratory. The organisms have been identified as either being collected from air and surfaces or the potable water dispenser. Samples were collected in the following U.S. ISS Modules: Node 1, Node 2, Node 3, U.S. Laboratory, and the Permanent Multipurpose Module (PMM). Bacteria from surface and air samples are isolated on Tryptic Soy Agar for identification. Bacteria were isolated from water samples on the ISS using a filtration unit, the Microbial Capture Device (MCD) which contains an R3A medium. Bacteria are also isolated from water samples returned from the ISS to JSC in an archive water bag. Samples are processed using an R2A medium. Identification of bacteria was performed using either a VITEK Identification System (bioMérieux) or 16S genetic analysis.
results: The JSC Microbiology Laboratory has several isolates collected and identified during the microbial monitoring efforts available for research evaluation. Several types of microorganisms have been identified multiple times during sampling and are available for evaluation as a time course indicated as early, mid, and late in the life of the ISS. It is important to note that microbial identifications were performed during ground processing of samples returned from space flight. Further characterization was not performed. A partial list of microbial isolates collected can be downloaded for review and requested for further research.

title: The Effect of Microgravity on Mycobacteria
research_area: Cell and molecular biology; Radiation biology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The aim of this work is to determine whether mycobacteria have enhanced virulence during space travel and what mechanisms they use to adapt to microgravity. We will use M. marinum as a model mycobacterium species, as its optimal growth is at 30-33°C and it is less problematic in terms of causing serious human infections. M. marinum also infects fish, and this provides a future small animal model for both ground-based studies and possible experiments on the International Space Station. We therefore hypothesize that M. marinum grown under conditions of microgravity will be more infectious in terms of entry and survival inside macrophage cells, and that this will be achieved by altering gene expression to promote survival under stressful conditions. Oxygen has been found to play a role in altering gene expression in Pseudomonas aeruginosa grown during space flight, and Salmonella enterica are more resistance to oxidative stress when grown under microgravity. We hypothesize that genes involved in surviving oxidative stress will be induced in M. marinum grown under microgravity. M. marinum grown under microgravity and normal gravity will be tested for their ability to infect and survive in macrophage, for resistance to hydrogen peroxide and for gene expression changes stimulated by microgravity. Specific mutant strains defective in detoxification processes, damage repair or biofilm formation will also be generated and if time allows will also be tested for survival in macrophage after growth under microgravity. This will further extend our understanding of mycobacteria pathogenicity during space travel and potentially reveal mechanisms to target mycobacterium infections in space and on Earth.
approach: The liquid culture medium for M. marinum was Middlebrook 7H9 liquid medium supplemented with 0.2% tween 80, 100 µg/ ml cycloheximide, 0.5% glycerol and 10 % ADS (albumin, dextrose, saline solution). M. marinum were grown from colonies until the optical density at 600 nm (OD600) was 0.8-1 in 3-5 mls of liquid medium in a bacterial incubator at 30°C and 120 rpm. This takes between 4-6 days. The culture was then diluted either to OD600= 0.002 for early gene expression and growth studies or OD600= 0.0005 for long term gene expression studiesand cytotoxicity studies. The diluted culture was then put into two 10 ml or 50 ml high aspect ratio vessels (HARV) and attached to a rotary cell culture system (RCCS) in a water-jacketed humidified incubator at 30°C. One disk was orientated to be subjected to normal gravity and one disk was subjected to low shear simulated microgravity. The disks were rotated at 25 rpm in all the experiments. All methods are described in Abshire et al NPJ Microgravity (2016) 2, 16038; doi: 10.1038/npjmgrav.2016.38. 1. Growth analysis – Two types of M. marinum were used for this study: the parental 1218R strain and a derivative of this strain (LHM4) carrying a plasmid integrated into the genome that expresses resistance to kanamycin and encodes for expression of red fluorescent protein (RFP). 2. Gene expression – The M. marinum 1218R strain were used for these studies. The effect of growth in the HARV subjected to normal or simulated microgravity on gene expression was studied. 3. Resistance to hydrogen peroxide, acid and gamma radiation - These studies used M. marinum LHM4 grown and treated as described in Abshire et al NPJ Microgravity (2016) 2, 16038; doi: 10.1038/npjmgrav.2016.38..
results: The objective of this proposal was to determine whether waterborne pathogenic mycobacteria alter gene expression, become resistant to stress, and hence could be more infectious when grown under low shear simulated microgravity (MG). Mycobacterium marinum was the model organism used in this study. This is a bacterium that naturally infects fish and amphibians to produce a tuberculosis-like disease in a variety of organs. In humans, M. marinum can cause a disease known as swimming pool granuloma, which is restricted to the skin due to the lower temperature of body extremities. The pathology is similar to dermal Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection and the infection route is through cuts or abrasions. Infection is usually limited to the skin in humans since M. marinum grows at 28-35°C. M. marinum infects and survives inside immune cells called macrophage by the same mechanisms as M. tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium. M. tuberculosis and M. avium cause serious lung infections in humans. M. marinum is therefore a good model to understand how these pathogenic mycobacteria survive and adapt to the hostile environment inside macrophage. Since M. marinum and M. avium exist in the environment on Earth and can form biofilms in water systems, it is important to understand the effect of microgravity on these pathogenic mycobacteria as they could exist in the water systems on space vehicles. M. marinum strain 1218R and LHM4 (a derivative of M. marinum carrying a plasmid encoding kanamycin resistance and red fluorescent protein) were grown in high aspect ratio vessels (HARV) in a rotary cell culture system (RCCS) under normal gravity (NG) or MG. By following the optical density of the culture as well as the colony forming units per milliliter we determined that the growth of both strains was altered by growth under MG once the culture was in exponential phase. There was no difference in the growth for ~40 hrs (early exponential phase) but the growth of the MG culture was significantly slower after 40 hrs. The doubling time during early exponential was ~6 hrs and after 40 hrs this increased to ~10-11 hrs for the NG cultures and to ~15.5-16 hrs for the MG cultures. We hypothesized that the slowing of growth may have been due to an oxidative stress in the bacteria. Hydrogen peroxide can cross membranes and so we repeated the growth studies adding catalase to the culture. Any hydrogen peroxide exiting the bacteria and existing in the medium would be detoxified by the catalase. This did not however improve the growth of the M. marinum under MG. To determine the effect of MG on the stress responses activated by the growth conditions, we used RNAseq to examine what genes were expressed. For RNAseq, the bacteria were harvested, RNA isolated and converted DNA (cDNA), and the cDNA sequenced using the MiSeq benchtop sequencer. Using bioinformatics, the amount of expression of the different M. marinum genes were compared between the NG and MG samples. To make sure that we were examining only gene expression changes due to MG, only bacteria in early exponential growth were used in the RNAseq studies. Triplicate NG and MG cultures were used to generate samples of bacteria grown for ~40 hrs. We also grew triplicate cultures for 4 days and then diluted them again and grew them for another ~40 hrs so we could examine gene expression from bacteria exposed for a longer time. From these studies it was obvious that stress response pathways were activated in the MG cultures and the stress responses were at a higher expression level the longer they were exposed to MG. Expression seemed to change to be similar to responses of M. tuberculosis inside macrophage. This suggests that the MG stress was similar to that of mycobacteria inside immune cells. Using the MG growth conditions may be useful in the future to test drugs designed to kill mycobacteria during infection. We are in the process of identifying regulator proteins that may be involved in aiding mycobacteria survival under MG. Published studies indicate that other species of bacteria show altered resistance to hydrogen peroxide and acid (pH 3.5) once grown under MG. We tested our LHM4 strain and determined that as found for other bacteria M. marinum were more sensitive to killing by hydrogen peroxide but did not alter their resistance to acid conditions once grown under MG. M. marinum sensitivity to gamma radiation did not change also. This type of study may aid in designing disinfection techniques for future space travel. In summary, growth of M. marinum under MG results in changes in growth, gene expression and sensitivity to stress conditions. SigH is a stress response protein that increases transcription at specific operons and this work suggests SigH may be involved in the response to growth under MG. We are in the process of generating an M. marinum sigH mutant that can be used in future studies to determine whether SigH is an important factor in the adaptation of M. marinum to the stress of growth under MG.

title: Effects of Microgravity on Growth Hormone Concentration and Distribution in Plants
archive_status: No data from this study was submitted to LSDA. Please contact LSDA if you know of available data.
objectives: The absence of a well defined neuronal system in plants should simplify the detection of gravity effects at the cellular and molecular level. Plants grown in microgravity may be used to detect the adaptations that have occurred during growth in Earth gravity, allowing the potential isolation of the genes which control the plant's responses and structures produced because of gravity. This experiment was to study the effect of gravity on the concentration and distribution of the plant growth hormone, indole-3-acetic acid (IAA or auxin), as a possible indicator of microgravity effects on plant growth.
approach: Zea mays seeds (soaked) were maintained in special filter paper inside plant canisters, in total darkness throughout the mission. After four days of flight, two of the four canisters were placed inside gaseous nitrogen freezers to arrest growth and preserve IAA inside the plant. The two remaining canisters remained untouched for postflight analysis of continued growth. After landing, measurements were made of the fresh weight, dry weight, dry/fresh weight ratio, free and conjugated IAA, and free and conjugated weight of ascorbic acid. The IAA assays employed IAA labeled in the benzenoid ring with six atoms of 13C.
results: Postflight examination revealed 100% germination and extensive growth. The plant material had an abnormal growth pattern. Tissues of flight plants appeared normal and seedlings differed only in the lack of orientation of roots and shoots. In many cases, the roots and coleoptiles (shoots) grew in parallel, or the shoots were twisted and appeared knotted. Many adventitious roots were produced along the primary root below the seed. Weights and hormone content of flight seedlings, with minor exceptions, did not statistically differ from seedlings grown in similar conditions on the ground. No serious chemical perturbations appear to have occurred in the seedlings during 5.5 days of growth in microgravity. It was concluded that results suggest that the major problem of growing plants in space may lie in providing a substitute vector for orientation of the growth of plant roots in space.

title: Water Quality Monitor
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Water supplies on Earth are constantly monitored for any characteristics that could prove harmful to humans, animals and plants. This is no different in space. Water used in space must meet various standards (set by NASA, the Russian Space Agency and other government agencies), which are imposed to ensure the health of the crew. Therefore, the water supplies, whether originating from recycled humidity condensate or supplied from the ground via a Russian or U.S. spacecraft, need to be regularly monitored and analyzed. The purpose of this investigation was to demonstrate functionality of the Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Analyzer in microgravity and to determine whether the design met analytical requirements for monitoring the quality of International Space Station (ISS) reclaimed water supplies. The experiment hardware was expected to provide real-time or near real-time feedback on the quality of the water available to the crew, instead of having to return samples to Earth for analysis.
approach: The Water Quality Monitor experiment was flown on STS-81 and operated on board the Shuttle only (not on Mir). Six water test samples of known composition were analyzed for total carbon, total organic carbon (TOC), total inorganic carbon (TIC), pH, and conductivity on flight days 2, 3, and 7. In addition, one Mir SVO-ZV (ground-supplied) water sample and one Mir hot water sample were analyzed on flight day 7. In addition, six duplicate water test samples of known composition, as well as aliquots from the two Mir water samples were archived for analysis on Earth. Results were compared to on-orbit data, which helped to evaluate performance of the Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Analyzer in microgravity. These test samples were analyzed using commercial instruments, including the Sievers Model 800 for carbon, Orion Model SA720 for pH, and YSI Model 32 for conductivity. The difference between on-orbit and ground results was computed with percent errors, and the results were compared to accuracy specifications. The Water Quality Monitor experiment hardware consisted of a Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Supply Kit and the Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Analyzer. The TOC Supply Kit contained water sample syringes (for two Mir water samples plus a spare), the ground prepared test sample syringes (six different test samples plus spares), spare fuses, RAM data card and other miscellaneous items. The Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Analyzer was a portable electronic box. Samples were inserted into a sample access door using a water sample syringe. The analysis took place automatically within the analyzer by pushing a button on the instrumen's front panel.
results: All eight planned analyses were successfully completed on STS-81. Inflight test sample results met accuracy specifications with the exception of a few pH values and the Mir hot water TOC value. Inflight Mir sample results agreed with postflight archive sample results. The experiment was successful in demonstrating the technology, and the hardware seemed to operate nominally on-orbit. However, after the hardware was disassembled upon return to Earth, several leaks were found inside the containment structure. The leakage problem will be corrected and minor packaging modifications will be made before utilization on the International Space Station (ISS). Several inflight anomalies were encountered during the experiment. On flight day 3, a test sample analysis was prematurely halted due to a low-pressure error. The cause was determined to be insufficient tightening of the syringe connection. A backup test syringe was installed and analyzed without any loss of science. A locking syringe connector will be added to the hardware to prevent this from occurring during analysis on board the ISS. On flight day 7, the first test sample syringe was initially analyzed without removing the syringe plunger spacer, causing a decrease in pressure within the system. An alarm should have sounded, indicating the low-pressure situation, and analysis shut down should have occurred. The plunger was subsequently removed, and the analysis was repeated successfully on a duplicate sample syringe. A device will be added to the hardware to prevent installation of the syringe with the spacer in place before use on the ISS. Hardware changes for the International Space Station will include upgrading the pressure sensor to 200 PSIA instead of 100 PSIA, the waste container will be modified to eliminate leakage from the bags and housing, and the top of the housing will be designed to be removable with screws and an O-ring seal. Additional modifications will be made to enhance analytical performance, reliability, and reduce on-orbit crew time. In conclusion, operation of the Total Organic Carbon (TOC) Analyzer in microgravity was demonstrated, and the technology was verified for use on the ISS. Hardware design changes for use on the ISS are in work based upon the STS-81 experience.

title: Crew Height Measurement
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Gross effects of zero-g on man's anthropometry were observed during and after extended orbital flights of the Skylab missions. In weightlessness, crewmen "grew taller" and the one-g erect posture was altered at several skeletal joints, namely the neck, shoulder, elbow, hip, knee and ankle. Quantification of these effects was important for optimizing the physical interfaces between the crewman and his workstation and flight clothing, particularly the space suit. The Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) provided an opportunity to quantify the effects of zero-g on crewman height and to determine the change as a function of time over mission length.
approach: Data on ASTP crewmen were obtained during routine physical examinations conducted on L-45 (45 days before flight), L-30, L-15 and R+0 (day of recovery). Data requirements for all height measurements consisted of maximum stature, seated height, and eye-level height. Inflight data requirements were completed during three mission phases: 1. In the Command Module (CM), before docking module (DM) transfer, seated height and eye-level height were measured immediately after weightlessness was attained. 2. In the DM, stature and eye-level heights were measured periodically. 3. In the CM after DM jettison, seated height and eye-level height were measured immediately prior to reentry. Measurements in the CM were made with the crewman on the center couch. Seated height was measured with the seat in the 90-degree seat-to-backpan position. Eye-level height was measured with the seat in the 180-degree (flat) position. The crewman relaxed to the neutral, zero-g posture, his back parallel to the couch back and his feet touching the lower equipment bay (LEB) bulkhead. Measurements were made from the top of the couch support frame, parallel to the back of the couch, down to the top of the head and then to eye-level height. The measuring tape from the Leg Volume Measuring Kit was used for these measurements. Stature measurements were made as the crewman assumed a fully extended posture on the control and display (C&D) panel with his feet touching the DM hatch (Soyuz end). For eye-level height, the crewman assumed the neutral, zero-g posture, with his back to the C&D panel and feet touching the hatch. Measurements were read from a measuring tape decal affixed to the C&D panel.
results: Because of scheduling problems and the limited number of data points completed, only the stature measurements were quantified. In addition, only R+0 measurements were obtained due to crew health concerns. An increase in stature was noted for each ASTP crewman. This increase was attributed to the absence of g-loading on the spine, which resulted in loss of normal spinal curvature and an expansion of the intervertebral discs. A slight increase (less than 1.3 cm (0.5 in)) occurred between launch and mission day 6, which was the first measurement opportunity in the DM. The next larger increase, as much as 6.6 cm (2.6 in), occurred between mission days 6 and 9. This data, in conjunction with Skylab height data, indicated a two-step height increase. The smaller initial change may result from removing g-loads on the body and thus permitting loss of thoracolumbar curvature. A similar expansion is observed on Earth when stature is compared between standing and supine body positions. The second larger change may be accounted for from the expansion of the now unloaded intervertebral discs. When the muscles relax in weightlessness, the vertebral discs are unloaded and absorb water from the vertebral bodies. This expansion may be further affected by the headward fluid shifts in zero-g. Application of this data was used to develop workstation interface designs for future missions.
