title: Microgravity Effects on Bone Cell Gene Expression
research_area: Cell and molecular biology; Skeletal physiology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Astronauts on long-term missions suffer continuous calcium loss and degradation of skeletal weight-bearing bone mass. Bone loss has been attributed to a decrease in the rate of bone formation, which is possibly caused by both direct and indirect effects of microgravity. Systemic or hormonal changes in body chemistry or the cellular response to a lack of stress due to gravity could contribute to this condition. Osteoblastic cells must properly attach to the extracellular matrix (ECM) in order to grow normally. Fibronectin (FN), a cell surface adhesion protein, mediates the attachment of various cell types to other components of the ECM and is a known factor in cell shape and growth regulation. This experiment addressed whether the FN message, protein synthesis, and matrix organization affect bone formation.
approach: About 120,000 to 200,000 cells of an osteoblast cell line, clonally derived from embryonic mouse calvaria (MC3T3-E1), were plated for flight experiments. These plates were grown in 10% serum containing alpha minimal essential medium (a-MEM) and then the plunger units were held in the shuttle middeck for 17 hours before launch. A modified guanidinium thicyanate method was used to extract the cultured osteoblast cells. Agarose gel electrophoresis was used to identify polymerase chain reaction bands. The bands were then photographed and scanned at 400 dpi (dots per inch) for quantification.
results: Analysis of transcriptional and translational control of FN (fibronectin) suggest that aberrations in the FN portion of the ECM (extracellular matrix) due to microgravity do not cause cell morphology changes. Further extrapolation indicates that loss of osteoblast growth in space flight is not due to changes in FN. However, other alterations may be related to FN binding and receptor-mediated signaling changes in microgravity. Samples fixed for immunofluorescence localization studies showed that microgravity did not affect FN synthesis, that FN protein had been exported out of the cell, and that the cell matrix was organized normally. Furthermore, 1-G on-controls, ground controls, and samples activated in microgravity had indistinguishable regulation of FN. Overall, these data suggest that changes in FN regulation do not directly changes in cell shape, bone matrix formation, and loss of bone growth in microgravity.

title: The Effects of Hypogravity on Osteoblast Differentiation
archive_status: No data from this study was submitted to LSDA. Please contact LSDA if you know of available data.
objectives: Weightbearing is essential for normal skeletal function. Without weightbearing, the rate of bone formation by osteoblasts decreases in the growing rat. The fundamental question of whether the defects in osteoblast function due to weightlessness are mediated by localized skeletal unloading or by systemic physiologic adaptation such as fluid shifts has not been answered. This study proposes to examine whether exposure of cultured rat osteoblasts to spaceflight inhibits cellular differentiation and impairs mineralization when isolated from the influence of both systemic factors and other skeletal cells.
approach: Osteoblasts were purified by collagenase digestion, plated on microcarrier beads in Petri dishes, then loaded after five days into polypropylene fiber cartridges. Cells were maintained for two days on continuous flow CellCo Units, then transferred to the STL hardware and maintained on the unit for four days prior to launch. The flight duration was 11 days. Within four hours after landing flight cartridges were recovered. Differentiation was assessed by histological analysis with light and electron microscopy and by the measurement steady-state expression of mRNA genes (alkaline, phosphatase, osteopontin and osteocalcin) that mark progressive osteoblast differentiation. In order to measure metabolism of the cultures, glucose and lactate concentrations were measured eight hours before the flight, during the time the cartridges were in the STL unit, and after the cartridges were recovered.
results: Analysis under light microscopy revealed that the flight cultures had less cells per section, but were otherwise indistinguishable from the control cultures. In addition, ultrastructural analysis by electron microscopy showed that osteoblasts exposed to spaceflight possessed less well-organized rough endoplasmic reticulum/Golgi apparatus than ground controls. These results indicate that osteoblasts exposed to microgravity are less differentiated than control cells. After the omission of suspected defective culture from the statistical pool, glucose utilization and concomitant lactate production was significantly lower for flight cultures. These results indicate that spaceflight may inhibit energy metabolism and the protein-synthetic activity of osteoblasts.

title: Stability of Pharmacotherapeutic Compounds
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Analysis of certain medications returned from the Space Shuttle and the International Space Station (ISS) have indicated that some pharmaceuticals are significantly degraded in space, and this may compromise treatments and the health of crews on future exploration missions. Data gathered from past Space Shuttle missions suggest that some of the medications packed in the Shuttle's medical pack degrade even after relatively brief periods (less than 20 days) of space flight. The observed degradation included both physical and chemical characteristics of medicine formulations. Physical and chemical instability of medications could render treatments ineffective for assurance of optimal crew health during long duration space exploration missions. An evaluation of subjective data on medications used by crewmembers during space flight indicated that 8% of all treatments administered in the Space Shuttle program were reported ineffective. Pharmaceutical instability may modify effectiveness and safety, and is one possible cause of the ineffectiveness of treatments. The objective of this project was to identify the pharmaceuticals that degrade in space by collecting data on the magnitude and time course of degradation of select pharmaceuticals. This investigation studied the effects of radiation in space on complex organic molecules, such as vitamins and other compounds in food and medicine. This could help researchers develop more stable and reliable pharmaceutical and nutritional countermeasures suitable for future long-duration missions to the moon and Mars.
approach: The pharmaceutical kits contained 35 types of pharmaceutical drugs, including tablets, ointments, suppositories, and injectable solutions. In addition to the food and drug items, the kits were equipped with two temperature loggers and a dosimeter to measure radiation.
results: There was no crew interaction with the contents of the kits, which were configured to prevent them from being inadvertently opened. One of the kits was immediately returned on STS-122 after 13 days, while the other three remained aboard ISS for 353, 596, and 880 days of spaceflight. Each kit was returned on subsequent Shuttle flights. The flight kits were analyzed in parallel with the eight ground control kits, identical to those flown. Results from this investigation designed to examine changes in chemical content and physical attributes of dosage forms stored aboard space missions suggest that there may be differences with respect to potency and rate of degradation of formulations stored in space compared to those on the ground. Some APIs and formulations may be more sensitive than others, and specific chemical and formulation characteristics may influence the stability of medications in space. Cumulative low dose radiation and dispensers used for solid dosages in space appear to influence stability of pharmaceuticals in space.

title: Evaluation of Portable Ultrasound in Remote Environments: NEEMO
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: As space missions become longer and venture farther into space, the risk of a serious medical event occurring increases. Because the medical capabilities on a spacecraft or at any remote landing site are quite limited, there is the need for a tool that can be used to diagnose a variety of conditions by a person with a minimal medical background. Ultrasound technology gives a person the ability to diagnose several conditions that are likely to occur during an exploration-class mission, such as renal stones, appendicitis, and fractures. While many ultrasound machines are large, bulky, and difficult to operate by anyone but a trained ultrasonographer, newer portable devices have been developed that are easier to use. The objective of this experiment was to test a portable ultrasound device during a simulated medical event in the space flight analog provided by NEEMO.
approach: Prior to the mission, two crewmembers received training on how to operate the ultrasound device using one or more of the following imaging procedures. Focused Assessment by Sonography in Trauma (FAST) with the Thoracic Module for Microgravity (Expanded FAST) - imaging in standard locations of the abdomen and chest for signs of organ injury, including pneumothorax General Abdominal Protocol for Microgravity (liver, gallbladder, spleen, pancreas) Renal/Pelvic Protocol for Microgravity (kidneys, urinary bladder) Representative Musculoskeletal Protocol (wrist and forearm - bones, tendons, muscles, joints, nerves) At an undesignated time during the mission, one crewmember was green-carded with symptoms indicative of a medical condition. At that point, a trained crewmember, following the instructions of the crew surgeon in the Exploration Planning and Operations Control (ExPOC), attempted to manipulate the ultrasound probe in such a manner that allowed the surgeon to diagnose the condition. Standard ultrasound gel (Aquasonic or similar) was used to maintain acoustical contact of the probe with the subject’s skin. All activities were video taped by a third crewmember. The resulting video was used to evaluate the quality of training received, the ease-of-use of the ultrasound device and its procedures, and the ability to communicate successfully with the crew surgeon from the remote environment.
results: One data session was planned and completed. Additional data was captured during the session by using two different operators to capture the images. Although some visible degradation of the images was noticeable, the pixel resolution, grayscale resolution, and frame rate were all acceptable for both remote guidance and real-time focused diagnostic assessment. There was some fluctuation in the bandwidth available for video conferencing, which caused slower frame rate of the video for short (2-5 seconds) periods of time. The remote guidance expert waited until the connection improved and continued the guidance. Although not ideal this was tolerable and expected. No other hardware anomalies were encountered. Data Analysis and Findings Subjective perception of the data quality was such that gross pathology would not be overlooked. Fine detail (such as minute non-obstructing calculi (stones) in the renal collecting system) could potentially be overlooked, and in case of suspicion would be ruled out through post-event image transfers. The approach to quality, in the opinion of the investigators, should be conservative, and in the absence of scientifically proven metrics, the interpretation of data should consist of phases. 1. Preliminary Real-Time Imaging Interpretation : most conservative and preliminary, focusing on the imaging representation of anatomical and functional situation in the patient's organism potentially causing signs and symptoms or threatening safety or life. This preliminary real-time assessment (in the process of the imaging session) Confirms, modifies, or changes the Crew Surgeon's and/or Consultant's concept of the diagnosis, prognosis, and management Allows changing the course of the imaging session, expand, or focus the imaging session through additional inputs / orders from the Crew Surgeon Is expected to make the most difference in the decision-making process and the outcome of the most severe and time-critical medical contingencies If the remotely guiding ultrasound expert is an RDMS/RVT/RDCS but not a physician, this phase still retains its legitimacy [such preliminary assessments are common in terrestrial environment, and the responsible physicians use the diagnostic imaging input upon their discretion and responsibility] 2. Preliminary Post-Imaging Interpretation : takes place in less demanding conditions, after the remote guidance session is completed, and has some additional features Is normally performed by a qualified interpreting physician (normally radiologist or cardiologist for cardiac imaging), (jointly with the remote guidance expert if different) Allows sufficient time for review of the audio / video recording of the session Is the first formal (written or dictated) imaging report Is the closest to a terrestrial imaging report, and includes recommendations to the Crew Surgeon regarding follow-up imaging or clinical / diagnostic correlations as necessary Includes assessments of data quality and emphasizes any aspects of quality degradation or deficiency of the imaging data caused by the fact of data transmission through non-digital imaging and communications in medicine (DICOM)-compliant media remote guidance an inexperienced operator time delay limited time and other factors that may have resulted in spurious or incomplete data, compared to average similar examination in common terrestrial setting 3. Final Imaging Report : includes results of the above phases of interpretation, and any new information derived from additional data reviews, lossless downloaded still image or cine-loop files, takes into account technical image quality analysis. Clinical Outcome and Contribution of Imaging During this simulation, ultrasound allowed ruling out major urinary obstruction. Thus, it contributed objective data for diagnosis and management. The Crew Surgeon accepted the results in both real-time and immediate post-imaging phases, and prescribed monitoring instead of considering emergency evacuation. While the diagnosis of kidney stones, urolithiasis, in this simulated patient remained unchanged, the following evidence: ureteral patency (by power Doppler method) normal sizes and shapes of both kidneys no signs of dilatation of collecting systems and ureters no asymmetry of the structure and imaging features of the two kidneys explicitly symmetrical ureteral orifices in the urinary bladder trigone absence of signs of calculi, within the overall sensitivity of the system absence of signs of any other condition with a clinical presentation similar to urolithiasis This allowed medical personnel to postpone the consideration of immediate medical evacuation, and distribute the available treatment resources (including the limited amount of analgesics and antibiotics) according to best available prognosis of the further course and outcome.

title: Development of a Flash X-ray Radiography and Tomography System to Measure Bone Mineral Density
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: This project addressed NASA's need for a relatively compact and portable x-ray system to perform bone mineral density studies on the International Space Station. The use of a 60 ns x-ray pulse to image biological specimens has been successfully demonstrated. With the dual-energy flash source, there is no need to change the anode-cathode (AK) voltage since the applied voltage across the AK gap is effectively swept during operation. The x-ray energy is high early in the pulse and lower later in the pulse. Utilizing the dual energy properties of the x-ray source to perform x-ray absorptometry without changing the applied voltage across the AK gap or changing filters simplifies the implementation of the source. A computer simulation model was developed for the x-ray source, which permitted the distribution of radiated energy in a plane normal to the symmetry axis of the x-ray anode to be determined as well as its spectrum. The use of two amorphous silicon (aSi) imaging panels stacked in tandem with a metal x-ray filter yielded both hard and soft x-ray images. X-ray assays of bone mineral density (BMD) to accuracies of 2% percent are possible when the attenuation of the soft tissue is removed by means of a subtraction algorithm and by using a calibration phantom. The dual-energy x-ray absorptometry (DEXA) project implemented a complete system that integrates the dual energy pulsed x-ray source with the aSi digital imaging panels. Experiments were performed to determine the distribution of radiation over the image plane and the sensitivity or modulation transfer function of the imaging panels. Based on the imaging experiments and the ability of the software to generate computed tomographic (CT) images, a decision was made to add CT capability to DEXA imaging so that a 3-D map of the site bone mineral density could be obtained. The addition of the CT capability increases the patient radiation dose; so image-based reconstruction was planned for the purpose of reducing the dose. In this process a limited number (3 to 5) images of a target site are processed using a priori knowledge of the site architecture to construct a CT image. The following questions were examined and answered during this project. Is the fluence, forward distribution, repeatability, and energy spectrum of the pulsed x-ray source sufficient? Will the sensitivity of the aSi digital imaging panels and the choice of conversion phosphor produce an image suitable for DEXA analysis? Will the DEXA software operate correctly, and is it capable of generating a 3D map of bone mineral density?
approach: System tests were run to evaluate the CT image capability of the software. The DEXA system was configured to examine a Lamb femur. The specimen was frozen to prevent motion during the periods between image collection. The images were recorded on two stacked aSi digital panels and processed. The front panel was designed to be sensitive to 25-45 keV photons. Each image was processed using pixels located within a slice equivalent to a fan-beam. The set of all slices was processed to generate a volume view of the object capable of full 360 degree rotation about the x,y,z axis. Since hard and soft x-ray CT image data were available, the DEXA could be used to extract both the density and composition of the scanned object. Specifically, the DEXA software used a plastic-aluminum calibration phantom to create a raster of all possible values scanned, then correlated this data to the correct attenuation value, generated a surface polynomial to approximate the surface, and used the surface to correct a complete dataset by simulating a monochromatic source. When the corrected dataset was passed through a CT 3D reconstruction, the resulting reconstruction contained calibrated data that could be used to determine the volumetric density. To further evaluate the DEXA's imaging capabilities, the denser bone-mineral was extracted from the surrounding tissue by applying a cubic volume opacity filter followed by an isosurface reconstruction of the digitized x-ray image. By using both soft (25-45 keV) and hard (67-150 keV) images, the bone mineral density in the CT volume reconstruction could be determined.
results: Understanding the process of charge flow in Marx-driven x-ray tubes was one of the goals of this research. The SCL flow in x-ray tubes with conical anodes and coaxial cathodes was successfully modeled using Langmuir's analytic solution for charge flow between coaxial cylinders, provided that the width of the plasma cathode was treated as a free parameter and that magnetic field effects were neglected. The use of simulated cathode current and AK voltage in a calculation of the x-ray emission spectrum confirmed that the x-ray tube was operating as a SCL diode and that the model could accurately simulate the emission spectrum and total radiated energy in the x-ray pulse. Moreover it was shown that when the filtered hard x-ray pulse was subtracted from the unfiltered x-ray pulse, the residual pulse was the expected soft x-ray pulse with the correct temporal shape. title: Chronic Recording of Otolith Nerves in Microgravity
archive_status: No data from this study was submitted to LSDA. Please contact LSDA if you know of available data.
objectives: The main goals of this study were to record the responses of primary afferents of the otolithic organs to document otolithic organ response dynamics in normal gravity and in microgravity. According to the Otolith Asymmetry Theory, structural asymmetries between the bilateral otolithic organs develop during growth and maturation. However, in 1 G, Central Nervous System efferent neural impulses compensate for the asymmetries by adjusting primary afferent discharge to be equivalent bilaterally. When the organism is exposed to an altered gravitational environment, the existing structural otolithic asymmetries become evident as the efferent compensation is now inadequate. Thus, unbalanced signals are transmitted to the brain. Studies of these aspects of the vestibular system and its efferent control can add to our knowledge of its function and may suggest future therapies for control of Earth-bound motion sickness.
approach: Experimental difficulties precluded obtaining useful in-flight data as originally planned. However, fish were received within eight hours of the Shuttle return to Earth and utricular nerve afferents recorded sequentially for five days postflight. For this, anesthetized, paralyzed toadfish underwent a small craniotomy to allow the implantation of glass micro-electrodes (2 M LiCl2), in the nerves innervating the utricle. Records of primary afferents in response to linear acceleration were taken. Position and motion of the fish were documented by linear and rotary potentiometers.
results: Results from Neurolab were combined with those from STS-95, for a total of four experimental subjects. Control responses were obtained from three fish that did not fly. For flight subjects, the magnitude of response to an applied linear acceleration was on average three times greater than for controls within the first day postflight. By 30 hours post flight, responses had returned to normal and were statistically similar to controls. Directional selectivity appeared unaffected by exposure to microgravity. To examine for possible recording bias, all measured parameters were compared between control and post flight afferents; no statistical difference was found in the range and mean of afferent discharge rate and regularity of discharge between postflight and control fish. Thus the reduced gravitational vector and linear acceleration in orbit apparently resulted in an up-regulation of the sensitivity of utricular afferents. More tests must be done to determine whether a specific population of afferents demonstrated increased sensitivity or whether this finding is a general feature of all classes of cells. The original plan called for the implementation and perfection of a sieve electrode to allow for continuous recording of afferents during flight. For this the sieve was placed in the path of a severed utricular nerve and the nerve allowed to regenerate through the sieve. Previous work from our laboratory documented the time course and completeness of nerve regeneration in the species employed. Presently although experimental difficulties precluded the completion of the entire original plan, the perfection and utilization of the sieve electrode was achieved. High fidelity records of primary otolithic nerve single afferents were recorded chronically. This sieve technology might have future application to the human condition in conjunction with the utilization of prosthetic devices or other prostheses that require an interface with the nervous system.

title: Recovery of Neurological Function in Long Duration Crewmembers
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Neurological adaptation to microgravity is driven by the stimulus rearrangement associated with loss of gravitational loading of the vestibular otolith organs, the proprioceptive organs (muscle spindle, golgi tendon and joint pressure) and the exteroceptive organs (pacinian corpuscles, etc.). It is also driven by altered biomechanical constraints on body stabilization in space and locomotion through space. The neurological adaptive response to microgravity is characterized by alterations in CNS integration of sensory information, perceptions of spatial orientation, and motor coordination strategies. Upon return to gravity following extended stay in microgravity, the lost sensory stimuli and biomechanical contraints return, and a period of readaptation occurs. During readaptation, crews cannot perform duties and activities requiring keen sensorimotor control or spatial orientation skills on a par with their preflight abilities. The amplitudes and time constants associated with recovery of preflight performance capabilities are much greater for a long duration flight (>60 days) than for a short duration flight (<20 days).
approach: Evaluation of fitness to return to affected duties was assessed quantitatively using performance measures obtained from the following standardized test batteries: Balance Control (Posture): this test battery provided a quantitative assessment of the ability of crewmembers to fully utilize vestibular, proprioceptive and visual information to estimate spatial orientation (balance status) and to maintain stable control of upright stance. At each test session, the subject completed a standard clinical battery of sensory organization tests (SOT) on the Equitest dynamic posturography system. Each test lasted for 20 seconds, during which the subject maintained a quiet, upright posture with normal, absent, and or mechanically altered visual add proprioceptive sensory inputs. Test conditions were: standard eyes open Romberg test with support surface fixed; standard eyes open Romberg test with visual surround and support surface fixed; sway-referenced visual surround with fixed support surface; sway-referenced support surface with fixed visual surround; sway-referenced support surface with eyes closed; sway-referenced support surface with sway-referenced visual surround. Performance assessment was based on the peak body sway during each condition. Locomotor Control (Locomotion): tests of dynamic visual acuity (DVA) and impaired modulation of shock wave transmission during locomotion served as global indicators of sensorimotor dysfunction. This test was a two-part test in which subjects first walked along a short overground track and then on a treadmill. During overground locomotion, the subject gripped a bitebar in the teeth while walking 6-8 meters at a freely chosen pace across a walkway with a built in force plate. The task was repeated 4-6 times to ensure clean right foot contact with the force plate. Performance assessment was based on the relative amplitude of the shock wave transmitted from the heel to the head. During the treadmill locomotion, the subject walked t 6.4 km/hr and focused gaze on a laptop computer screen placed 2 meters in front of the treadmill at eye level. While walking, the subject read aloud a series of numbers of varying sizes that flashed across the screen. Performance assessment was based on the number of correct responses to the dynamic visual acuity task. Eccentric Gaze-Holding: this task provided a quantitative assessment of stability (state) of the brainstem neural integrator function, and indirectly, of the eye movement control system following space flight. This test was only performed on NASA 7. The study was conducted preflight and postflight. Preflight baseline data collection was performed at 60, 30 and 10 days before flight, and postflight collection occurred on landing day (2-3 hours after landing) and on days 1, 2, 4, 8, 12 after landing. Sessions at 16, 32 and 64 days after landing were conducted if the investigator did not see a return to preflight responses in the preceding sessions.

title: Epidemiologic Analyses of Risk Factors for Bone Loss and Recovery Related to Long Duration Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Bone loss is estimated to occur at a rate of one percent per month in space, particularly in weight-bearing bones in the legs and spine. This rate of loss is equivalent to what a human might lose in a year with advancing age on Earth. It remains unknown what this loss signifies for future fracture risk in crewmembers. While unloading of the skeleton in the weightless environment of space is considered the key factor contributing to bone loss, there are likely other factors that also play a role. Current prevention strategies have not been effective at preventing this bone loss. Improved understanding on the risk for fracture following long-duration space flight, as well as the factors contributing to bone loss in microgravity, and its recovery, are needed in order to develop better prevention strategies for the benefit of crew health, both during and after long-duration space exploration, and mission success. This study had the following specific aims: Investigate the risk of microgravity exposure on long-term changes in bone health and fracture risk. Provide a summary of the current evidence available on potential risk factors for bone loss, recovery and fracture following long-duration space exploration.
approach: Data assembly at NASA-Johnson Space Center (JSC) on risk factors known to be related to bone loss and fracture risk was completed in early 2012. The investigators performed analyses on these available data to help better understand the variability in hip bone mineral density (BMD) loss and recovery, postflight. Risk factor data included, medication use, bone turnover markers, and surrogates of exercise status inflight, such as changes in strength measures, and lean muscle mass. Data assembly and data cleaning were completed. The investigators noted that there were limited data on risk factors available beyond the initial return post long-duration flights, so analyses were restricted to the immediate post-flight period.
results: Following review of all the different measures available for analyses, the investigators identified several different risk factors which may help identify those at greatest risk for bone loss during long-duration missions. These included pre-flight measures of elevated bone resorption, as well as surrogate markers of better muscle strength and greater aerobic capacity preflight. Results suggest that individuals with high bone resorption markers preflight may benefit most from anti-resorptive therapy before a long-duration mission. Findings also suggest that those who are the most physically fit preflight may have bones that have adapted to greater than average loading stimuli and therefore may be more susceptible to enhanced bone resorption once unloaded in microgravity, reinforcing the importance of maintaining adequate physical conditioning during long-duration space flight. Of note, the results are from data largely prior to US crewmembers having access to the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED), which may have helped overcome this important risk factor. The data from this study is medical and thus is housed with the Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH). A final report was archived in the LSDA.

title: Hearing Loss Among LSAH Participants
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Noise is one of the most common causes of hearing loss, and noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) is the most common occupational illness in the United States. The effects of noise on hearing are often underestimated because the damage takes place so gradually, without pain, and cannot be visibly detected because the delicate inner ear is buried deep in the skull. Audiometric testing, using pure tone stimuli, has been the traditional method of monitoring hearing loss. Hearing tests have always been part of NASA’s hearing conservation program for personnel exposed to hazardous noise from aircraft and other equipment. Audiometric data from the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) database was reviewed in order to assess trends and compare data with other population studies.
approach: Audiometric data of LSAH astronaut participants, a group of comparison participants, and Air Force subjects (during 1975-1976) were reviewed. The mean of the audiometric hearing thresholds at 3000, 4000, and 6000 Hz were compared for the LSAH participants and other populations.
results: Formal hearing conservation efforts (e.g., training in hearing protection and effects of noise, enforcement of hearing protection use) have been aimed at all astronauts, but only those comparison participants who worked in noise-hazardous jobs at the NASA Johnson Space Center (JSC). Consequently, it would be logical to assume that the astronauts, as the target population of the conservation efforts, were more at risk for and would show more NIHL as compared to the comparison participants. However, the analysis of the data yielded surprising results. A hearing threshold is the lowest sound level that is detected from a specific percentage of presentations during a hearing test, so a higher value indicates less acute hearing. While hearing loss data in the comparison participants closely matched the average high frequency hearing loss for similar age groups reported for the general population (International Organization for Standardization, 1999), astronauts showed less hearing loss (in the 50 and 60 year-old age groups) than the comparison participants. When compared to a study of Air Force personnel for the years 1975-1976, astronauts also had better hearing sensitivity, suggesting that close vigilance and high motivation in NASA hearing conservation programs among astronauts may have yielded more effective hearing loss prevention. In the 70 and 80 year-old age groups, astronauts had more hearing loss than the comparison participants. One possible explanation is that hearing conservation programs did not exist or were very primitive prior to 1970. As a result, the current hearing losses among these individuals may have been accelerated by early NIHL, when hearing conservation efforts, now more rigidly enforced, were not effective. Whatever the basis for the audiometric results, it is clear that hearing loss prevention is vital to protecting remaining hearing function.

title: Integration of Neural Cardiovascular Control in Space
archive_status: No data from this study was submitted to LSDA. Please contact LSDA if you know of available data.
objectives: The Integration of Neural Cardiovascular Control in Space experiment was one of four autonomic nervous system experiments performed during the 1998 Neurolab mission. This experiment focused on how the autonomic nervous system and circulatory system are integrated. During previous missions, alterations in cardiovascular control have been noted inflight. With the key role that this system plays in survival, it is important that it be better understood for the safety and health of the astronauts. One of the goals of this experiment is to do just that - contribute countermeasures for improved crew health in space. Through the study of cardiopulmonary receptors, information will be collected on the mechanisms mediating cardiovascular adaption to microgravity and quantitative aspects on general human cardiovascular regulatory mechanisms. Medically, this experiment will provide useful reference material for both the evaluation of patients with autonomic dysfunction, and for future life sciences research in cardiovascular and regulatory physiology. Together, this comprehensive set of measurements should help solve the puzzle of why astronauts have problems with blood pressure control after space flight. The answer is important not only for helping astronauts to re-enter gravity safely after being in space, but also for helping patients who suffer with diseases of blood pressure control systems.
approach: Throughout the autonomic team's experiment sequence, cardiovascular parameters were measured, including blood pressure and heart rate. An estimation of blood flow to the brain was also estimated via the non-invasive transcranial Doppler (TCD) technique. The TCD emits high-frequency sound waves used to show how blood flow to the brain is regulated. This assessment is important because not all people who have orthostatic intolerance after space flight experience a drop in blood pressure. Instead, an astronaut may have a problem with brain blood flow control which Doppler measurements can reveal. While these measurements were taken, tests were conducted to activate the body's blood pressure control system and raise blood pressure. A standard test was to place a subject’s hand in ice water to elicit a response, but in space the astronaut’s hand was placed in an insulated glove at about -12.5 degrees Celsius. Called the cold pressor glove, it is used in conjunction with cuff blood pressure during its two minute use and recovery period. Another test had the subject squeeze a handgrip to 40% of his/her maximal voluntary contraction (MVC) force. As soon as the handgrip force dropped below 32% of MVC (i.e., 80% of target force) for more than a second, the cuff was inflated to a suprasystolic pressure to occlude circulation and the subject was prompted to release the handgrip. Occlusion continued for two minutes, and then the cuff was deflated during a two-minute recovery period.
results: All three nominally scheduled sessions were performed, one session early (Flight Day 2), the second session mid (Flight Days 7 and 8), and the third session late (Flight Days 12 and 13) in flight. The protocol was repeated for two subjects on Flight Day 10, due to a signal loss that occurred in the mid-mission session. Additional sessions were performed on Flight Days 2 and 8 by one subject on the early mission session. In this study, the hypothesis that space flight impairs cerebral autoregulation was studied in six astronauts approximately 72 and 23 days before, after 1 and 2 weeks in space (n = 4), on landing day, and 1 day after the 16-day Neurolab space shuttle mission. Beat-by-beat changes of photoplethysmographic mean arterial pressure and transcranial Doppler middle cerebral artery blood flow velocity were measured during 5 minutes of spontaneous breathing, 30 mmHg lower body suction to simulate standing in space, and 10 minutes of 60 degree passive upright tilt on Earth. Dynamic cerebral autoregulation was quantified by analysis of the transfer function between spontaneous changes of mean arterial pressure and cerebral artery blood flow velocity, in the very low- (0.02-0.07 Hz), low- (0.07-0.20 Hz) and high-frequency (0.20-0.35 Hz) ranges. Resting middle cerebral artery blood flow velocity did not change significantly from preflight values during or after space flight. Reductions of cerebral blood flow velocity during lower body suction were significant before space flight (P < 0.05, repeated measures ANOVA), but not during or after space flight. Absolute and percentage reductions of mean (+/- s.e.m.) cerebral blood flow velocity after 10 minutes upright tilt were smaller after than before space flight (absolute, -4 +/- 3 cm per sec after versus -14 +/- 3 cm per sec before, P = 0.001; and percentage, -8.0 +/- 4.8% after versus -24.8 +/- 4.4% before, P < 0.05), consistent with improved rather than impaired cerebral blood flow regulation. Low-frequency gain decreased significantly (P < 0.05) by 26, 23 and 27% after 1 and 2 weeks in space and on landing day, respectively, compared with preflight values, which is also consistent with improved autoregulation. It can be concluded that human cerebral autoregulation is preserved, and possibly even improved, by short-duration space flight.

title: Body Mass Changes in NASA/Mir Astronauts
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: International Space Station (ISS) Phase I, more commonly known as Phase I, served as a precursor to the ISS experience. In this program, the existing resources of the US Shuttle orbiters and the Russian Space Station Mir were used to test the challenges facing the international partners in the areas of cooperation, data gathering, and logistics. As part of Phase I, seven NASA astronauts served as Mir crewmembers between March 1995 and June 1998. Physiological data gathered on these NASA astronauts can give insight on the effects of long-term weightlessness on individuals, which in turn is important for future ISS considerations.
approach: Changes in body weight during periods of prolonged weightlessness were examined for six of the seven US astronauts who have flown on Mir. The data present mean body weight and standard deviations (SD) at four intervals: the annual examination in the year prior to flight (Preflight Annual), inflight on approximately Flight Day 90 (FD 90), the third day after return to Earth (R+3), and the annual examination in the year after flight (Postflight Annual).
results: Mean weight was 77.2 kg at the preflight annual examination, 73.8 kg at FD 90, 77.3 kg at R+3, and 78.1 kg at the postflight annual examination. There was a downward shift in mean weight inflight, with return to preflight mean weight occurring by R+3. However, inflight mean weight was not statistically significantly different from the preflight and postflight mean weights. Another way to look at this type of data is to calculate and examine the percent change between preflight and inflight values. Data are inflight data, comparing weight on FD 30, FD 60, and FD 90 to weight at preflight annual examination. Percent of change is calculated by the difference between the preflight annual examination weight and the inflight weight divided by the preflight weight multiplied by 100. The resulting negative value indicates that weight decreased early in the mission (-3.5% by FD 30) and then remained relatively constant at the next two inflight intervals (-4.0% by FD 60 and -4.25% by FD 90). The method of measurement is different for inflight and on ground, which may contribute to the differences in weight reported here. These results suggest that during periods of prolonged weightlessness, astronauts may experience weight loss early in the mission. Inflight weight appears to stabilize at the new level, and return to preflight levels after return to Earth. Further research into nutritional status during long duration spaceflight may reveal the causes and consequences of this temporal weight loss.

title: The Relationship of Space Adaptation Syndrome to Middle Cerebral Artery Blood Velocity Measured in Flight by Doppler
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Space Adaptation Syndrome (SAS) has an incidence of approximately 73 percent in first-time flyers, typically occurs during the first three days of space flight, and can include many symptoms ranging from malaise to repeated bouts of vomiting. The pathophysiology of SAS has not been determined, but one etiology may be related to the head ward fluid shifts that occur during this adaptation period. These fluid shifts may cause changes in cerebral blood flow as well as intracranial pressure (ICP). Symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, lethargy, and malaise may be manifested by those with increased ICP as well as by astronauts with SAS. To study these phenomena as they relate to SAS during space flight, a noninvasive method of measurement was sought. Transcranial Doppler (TCD) uses Doppler technology to noninvasively measure intracranial blood flow velocity through a window in the temporal bone of the skull, where the bone is thin enough to permit insonation. From this window, the middle cerebral artery (MCA) is typically the only artery found at depth between 25 and 50 millimeters, making it relatively easy to locate. Since it carries approximately 80 percent of the blood flow to the hemisphere and does not exhibit acute changes in diameter, the MCA is often chosen as the optimal vessel to study for indications of cerebral blood flow.
approach: Crewmembers on three Space Shuttle missions volunteered to be subjects for TCD MCA measurements preflight and in-flight. Each subject was studied a minimum of four times preflight and two times inflight. Preflight data were collected in both the supine and sitting postures. Three of the subjects were trained as operators and assigned subjects on whom they collected all data. At the beginning of each data collection session, the operator measured the subject's pulse rate (at the radial artery) and blood pressure (by ascultative sphygmomanometry at the brachial artery). The operator then obtained the MCA flow velocity in a reproducible sample volume using a plastic template. These templates were developed to locate the optimal temporal window and sample depth previously determined for each subject by an experienced operator. Space motion sickness symptoms were reported for each day in flight on a symptom response sheet. This sheet included the following symptoms: headache, malaise, sluggishness, impaired concentration, disorientation, decreased appetite, stomach awareness, nausea, vomiting, and a space to indicate other symptoms. Each subject's symptoms were evaluated by the investigators and each subject was assigned a general score from 0 (no symptoms) to 3 (severely ill) for each flight day. Doppler data were analyzed postflight using a system developed by Micco and Dietrich at the University of Colorado. The tape recording of each session was divided into 30-second segments. After the 30-second segments of data were analyzed, the segment with the greatest number of cardiac cycles having the highest velocities was analyzed in greater detail. Systolic and diastolic blood pressure data were also compared, and systolic resistance (systolic blood pressure/maximum velocity), mean resistance (mean blood pressure/mean velocity), and diastolic resistance (diastolic blood pressure/minimum velocity) were calculated for comparison. Preflight and in-flight data were also divided into post-sleep (morning) and pre-sleep (afternoon and evening) groups to study diurnal variations. The terms post-sleep and pre-sleep are used because morning and night do not apply in the same context while in Earth orbit. Thus, one preflight post-sleep data set and one preflight pre-sleep data set were established for each subject. In-flight data were also diurnally grouped by flight day (FD). The only in-flight pre-sleep data collection occurred on FD 1; all other in-flight data collection occurred in the post-sleep period.
results: Preflight Trends When general comparisons were made between all preflight data, there were no significant differences between TCD or any related parameter. When viewed with respect to diurnal (post-sleep vs. pre-sleep) variation, there were significant increases in mean velocity, maximum velocity, pulsatility index, and blood flow acceleration. Diastolic blood pressure decreased significantly from 68.9 to 65.25 mmHg, as did systolic resistance from 1.87 to 1.51 mmHg/cm/s, mean resistance from 2.21 to 1.79 mmHg/cm/s, and diastolic resistance from 2.58 to 3.22 mmHg/cm/s. Preflight to Inflight Changes Preflight and in-flight general data were grouped according to SAS scores: subjects with a score of 0 or 1 (well) and subjects with a score of 2 or 3 (sick). Using the SAS groups from FD 1 (five sick, three well), there were no significant SAS main effects and no significant day main effects between the preflight general average and FD 1. However, there was a significant SAS-by-day interaction between the preflight average and FD 1 for mean velocity and mean resistance. For the preflight averages only, the two SAS groups did not have different mean velocities or different mean resistances, but on FD 1 only the SAS groups did have significantly different mean velocities and mean resistances approaching significance. These changes in significance of the SAS main effect across days explain the SAS-by-day interaction. In-flight Trends There was a significant general in-flight decrease from 5.56 to 4.16 mls/s in blood flow acceleration between FD 2 and FD 5. No in-flight diurnal effects could be determined from FD 3 or FD 5 data. SAS in-flight effects were not calculated due to the fact that different subjects were sick on different days, so there was no uniform way to group subjects for multivariate analysis.

title: Electrophoresis Experiment
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Cell membranes are the site of many important biological phenomena. To understand specific cell functions and membrane systems, protein characterization and separation must be examined. Electrophoresis is a highly efficient method used to separate cells or other biological particles, and it can be applied without producing damage or loss of viability. Because of this, electrophoresis was considered an essential tool for investigation in space. Separation capability was expected to be increased under weightless conditions, resulting in new applications that depended on improved resolution. The objective of the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) electrophoresis experiment was to investigate and evaluate sample resolution and flow rates achievable in space for future Spacelab applications.
approach: The concept was based on a principle known as free-flow electrophoresis. By this method, the sample is introduced continuously into a 5 ± 3 degree Celsius separation chamber, in which a buffer solution flows in a layer (laminar flow). An electric field is generated perpendicular to the direction of flow. Particles having different surface charge densities are deflected from the buffer flow direction at an angle, which is determined by the sample flow rate and electrophoretic mobility of the particles. Samples of rat bone marrow cells, rat spleen cells, rat lymph node cells (mixed with human erythrocytes) and a mixture of human and rabbit erythrocytes were studied. With the exception of the human/rabbit erythrocyte mixture, all samples were freshly prepared 15 to 20 hours prior to liftoff. All samples were stored at 4 degrees Celsius for approximately 45 hours before the start of the experiment. The erythrocyte mixture was prepared 2 weeks before liftoff, and the cells were preserved by fixation in 2% glutaraldehyde. Bone marrow cells of rats were flushed out of the bone using a syringe containing a Puck TC solution combined with 2.5% bovine serum albumin. A single-cell suspension was prepared by passing the cells several times through a plastic syringe without a needle. The cells were then washed twice and resuspended in ampholine buffer. Spleen and lymph node cells were prepared by teasing the organs in Puck TC solution at 4 degrees Celsius with injection needles. These cells were washed twice with the same solution, filtered through cotton wool, and resuspended in ampholine buffer. For sterile tests, the buffer solution and cell suspensions were inoculated onto blood agar and incubated for 5 hours at 28 degrees Celsius. This test, as well as light microscopy, showed no bacterial contamination of the cell suspensions or buffer solutions. Cell viability (tested with trypan blue exclusion test) was more than 90% in each sample. All containers were sterilized with formaldehyde and washed 5 times with 20 ml of sterile ampholine buffer. Four days prior to liftoff, the deep freezing container was filled with a 0.8 ml mixture of rat lymph node cells (25XE6 cells/ml) and human erythrocytes (30XE6 cells/ml) and kept in liquid nitrogen. Fourteen hours prior to liftoff, the other three sample containers were filled with 1.4 ml each of the fixed human (30XE6 cells/ml) and rabbit (50XE6 cells/ml) erythrocytes mixture, rat bone marrow cells (80XE6 cells/ml) and rat spleen cells (80XE6 cells/ml). The experiment began on July 16, 1975, and lasted for one Earth orbit (1.85 hours). Sample containers were stored at 0 to 5 degrees Celsius. For experiment operation, they were removed from the freezer and inserted into the electrophoresis apparatus so that the sample flow entered the buffer flow. Flow was directed by a peristaltic pump. The equipment was designed for successive runs of four 1.6 ml samples. Each sample was subjected to the following sequence: 1) During prerun, the sample circuit was refilled with sample fluid and any remainder of the previous sample was removed from the separation chamber. 2) The following settings were established: Electric field: 60 V/cm Buffer flow rate: 0.275 cm3/s Sample flow rate: 5 cm3/h 3) The sample flow rate was decreased from 5 to 1 cm3/h, maintaining the two other conditions. 4) Finally, the electric field intensity and the buffer flow rate were reduced to two-thirds of their original values, keeping the flow rate constant (1 ml/h). Sample separation was evaluated by an optoelectronic method, in which a narrow slit across the downstream end of the separation chamber, parallel to the electric field, is illuminated. Light passes through the quartz plates of the separation chamber and is expressed as a function of biomaterial distribution density. Light intensity, which is related to cell density, is measured on the other side of the chamber with a photodiode array, and is recorded in digital form on a magnetic tape. After passing through the separation chamber, the sample buffer and chamber buffer mixture enter the waste container, which is combined with the storage container but separated by a membrane. Two flow rates were included for each sample to study the influence of buffer velocity. Data acquisition, evaluation and processing, as well as flow rates and temperatures were performed by electronic units of the electrophoresis apparatus.
results: During the separation process, a "true" cell distribution curve was not obtained, because baseline values were above the maximum peak absorption. The optical system had produced a light too bright to discern true cell distributions. Experiment analysis appeared to be impossible. However, during the stationary phase of separation (i.e., during the 90 second separation time) irregularly occurring pulses, called events, were recorded. Event patterns reflected the expected course of the separation curves. Pulses were caused by cell aggregations in the region of the separated bands. To confirm this assumption, an aliquot of the sample used aboard ASTP was separated under the same conditions at Kennedy Space Center in an identical apparatus under one-g conditions (electrophoresis engineering model (EM) with a 0.7 mm buffer film thickness). In addition to the expected cell distribution curves, stray pulses were shown to be caused by cell aggregation, which had a greater absorption. Event accumulation at the same location during a separation time of approximately 2 minutes yielded distribution curves similar to normal separation curves. To check this finding and obtain a reliable interpretation, such separations were repeated many times with the EM apparatus. Each experiment was performed and evaluated with normal and increased lighting. It was clearly established that the cell aggregations were representative of actual cell distributions. These studies allow assertions to be made regarding all electrophoresis samples. Bone marrow cells tend not to aggregate, and although only a few events could be analyzed, excellent separation was indicated by the distribution curve. Insufficient human and rabbit erythrocyte data were available to determine a distribution curve for this sample, because these cells have a weak tendency to form aggregations. The best results were obtained for spleen cells; 358 events were recorded, which were sufficient to identify fine details of separation. Good separation, similar to that of spleen samples,was inferred under one-g and zero-g conditions for lymph node cells with added human erythrocytes. Postflight examination of the flight unit indicated all housekeeping data (i.e., electrophoresis sequences, voltages, temperatures, electrical fields, etc. ) were within the tolerance range. Buffer and sample amounts corresponded to the required specification according to volume measurements. Buffer samples revealed no bacterial contamination despite the long storage period, and cell particles were present in the separation buffer (collection container). The expected remainder of cell suspension, more than 3 months old, was found in the sample containers. However, the gold-plated containers were unexpectedly corroded. All buffer tube systems were intact and penetrable, and the pump systems were fully operational. This information reveals accurate operation of the buffer and sample courses and the electronic system. Surprisingly, the error in the optical detection system shown by the tape (saturation of photodiodes) was at first not identifiable. Both the current and the voltage of the lamp were normal. By contrast, the light intensity measured by the diode array was, as expected, too low because of turbidity. This phenomenon was caused either by a fault in the electrical contact, which arose during the flight, or an increase in lamp helix temperature attributed to zero-g conditions. The latter could be explained by the absence of thermal convection in the gas-filled tube. In conclusion, applicability of free-flow electrophoresis under zero-g conditions was confirmed. The technical problems arising from the special environmental conditions in a Spacelab were controlled. This observation applies to the technical concept of the electrophoresis apparatus as well as the manual operation by crewmembers. Buffer flow systems operated despite the difficult conditions imposed by a closed system. Effective gas removal from the electrode buffer was a necessary part of the experiment. Under zero-g conditions, cells were separated with viability maintained, and cell aggregations did not correspond to a decrease in viability.

title: In-flight Urine Collection Absorber Evaluation (IUCAs)
research_area: Metabolism and nutrition; Renal, fluid and electrolyte physiology; Technology development
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Urine collection devices used in Space Shuttle missions have taken up too much space, have tended to leak, and have been cumbersome for men and impossible for women to use. The in-flight urine collection absorber (IUCA) was developed for the collection of small volumes of urine for metabolic studies involving stable (nonradioactive) isotopes such as deuterium (2H) and "heavy oxygen" (18O), which are used to study energy expenditure, water metabolism and body composition. The objectives of this hardware study were to evaluate potential effects of the absorbent filter on the analysis of these isotopes and to evaluate the ease of use of the IUCA by men and women in flight.
approach: The IUCA is a small, conical piece of highly absorbent filter paper that can be placed in the Shuttles' urine-collection funnels. It is removed after a void and stored inside 2 resealable plastic bags. It weighs approximately 20 grams (g) empty and 35 g full. In evaluations on the ground, tap water spiked with known amounts of 2H and 18O was placed in IUCAs or in other urine-collection devices (UCDs). The samples were stored and weighed periodically to monitor evaporative losses. In addition, urine samples from 3 study subjects who had ingested water labeled with 2H and 18O were collected and stored in standard containers, urine collection bags, UCDs or IUCAs. The isotopes were analyzed by mass spectrometry. The IUCAs were also tested in flight by 5 astronauts (3 men and 2 women).
results: In the tests on the ground, evaporative losses from the IUCA were minimal and far less than from the UCD. Results of the isotope analyses were similar for the IUCA and the UCD. Collection of the urine with an IUCA rather than by one of the other methods made little difference in determinations of total energy expenditure and total body water. During flight the IUCA was able to collect samples of 11 to 13 milliliters, with no difference by gender. The results show that the IUCA is acceptable for collecting urine samples during flight for experiments involving stable isotopes, when urine volume measurements are not required. It can be used by men and women, even in constrained areas like the Shuttle middeck. It could also be used on the International Space Station.

title: Development of Vestibular Organs in Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Many species sense gravity, and therefore linear acceleration, by way of otoliths (dense calcium carbonate crystals attached to hair cells and associated nerve fibers). As the mass moves with acceleration, a signal is sent through each hair cell to the central nervous system. The knowledge of the factors that control development of these otoliths (and their analogs in some species) is limited. Previous studies suggest that altered gravity does not substantially affect the volume of the otoliths or their analogs in adult animals. This study was designed to test the hypothesis that during development the mass of the otolith is regulated to achieve a desired weight; as such, one would expect to reference larger-than-normal otoliths in animals reared in microgravity.
approach: The statoconia (analogous to otoliths) of the pond snail, Biomphalaria glabrata, and the otoliths of the swordtail fish, Xiphophorus helleri, were the focus of this study. Thirty-five adult snails, four pre-mated adult female swordtail fish, and 50 to 200 juvenile swordtail fish were flown in the Closed Equilibrated Biological Aquatic System (CEBAS), which contained seven liters of water and 50 grams of the hornweed, Ceratophylum. The specimen container was videotaped for later analysis. Many of the snails mated in flight, and produced the juvenile snails used in the experimental analysis. The pregnant adult swordtail fish were selected at a stage that they would produce developing fry but not have any hatch by the end of the mission. On landing day, approximately half the juvenile snails were fixed; the other half were fixed five days postflight. Adult fish ovaries and juvenile fish were fixed in alcohol on landing day. Fixed snails were removed from their shell and sectioned at 1-2 micrometer; serial sections were examined by transmission electron microscopy.
results: Results were obtained from both the Neurolab flight (16-day) and a similar experiment of nine days duration, using the same organisms, flown on STS-89. Total statoconia volume in the snails varied considerably within both the flight and ground control groups. However, the difference in mean values for the two groups was significant at p < 0.05, with the average total volume greater in the flight group. In most of the groups of flight snails (divided into groups by shell diameter), the increase in statoconia volume increased as the animals developed another five days on Earth. Overall, the flight-reared snails had approximately 50 percent more statoconia than the ground controls. This indicated that rearing in microgravity causes the supporting cells to produce more statoconia, of approximately the same size as in ground-reared animals. Otoliths of the embryonic fish from STS-90 (Neurolab) exhibited a greater growth, with increased body length in the flight-reared animals, compared to ground controls. Although there was a trend for larger otoliths in the flight-reared juvenile swordtails, this difference did not reach statistical significance. The embryos from STS-89 were much smaller that those retrieved after STS-90, since this was a shorter mission. In this case, the growth of otoliths of the ground-reared fish embryos was actually larger than that of the flight-reared animals. These results suggest a critical period, in the late embryonic stages, where rearing in microgravity produces larger otoliths.

title: The Effects of Prolonged Space Flight on Head and Gaze Stability During Locomotion
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Newly returned astronauts have shown instability in walking and in making jump landings and have experienced oscillopsia (apparent bouncing of viewed objects). The mechanisms of these abnormalities are not known, although changes in muscle tone, muscle activation patterns and vestibular function could contribute. Instability of gaze could result from changes in the coordination of head and body movements. The objectives of this study were to investigate space flight-induced changes in locomotor control, including changes in the coordination of movements of the head, trunk and legs during walking, and the relation of those changes to the ability to maintain a stable gaze; changes in the ability to maintain spatial orientation while walking; and changes in motor strategies for absorbing impact during jump landings.
approach: Locomotor control was studied in 5 protocols. For 4 of the protocols, reflective markers affixed to appropriate places on the astronaut's head, spine, and limb joints were tracked by 4 video cameras. The position of each marker in space was determined with the aid of a video-based motion analysis system. In some of the studies, some subjects also wore shoes with foot switches beneath the heel and great toe. In 3 of the protocols, the astronauts walked on a motorized treadmill at 6.4 km/h (4 mph) while wearing a safety harness attached to an overhead frame. (The protocol using the treadmill was denoted as DSO 614A and was performed on the following missions: STS-43, 44, 45, 46, 47, 48, 49, 50, 53, 57, 58, 63, and 65). The treadmill tests were performed under 3 conditions: with the astronauts fixating on a visual target either 30 cm or 2 m in front of them, or alternating open eyes and closed eyes for 5 seconds at a time while trying to keep the eyes directed at the target. Eye closures were confirmed by electro-oculography. Data from about 10 days before flight and from 2 to 4 hours after landing were used for comparisons. Head-trunk coordination was studied in 23 astronauts (19 male, 4 female) who flew on 8- to 15-day missions. Fifteen were veterans of previous space flights. Recordings were made of the vertical movements of the trunk and the pitch movements of the head. Lower limb movements were studied in 7 astronauts (6 male, 1 female) on 8- or 9-day missions. Five were veterans of previous space flights. The angular displacement and angular velocity of the hip, knee and ankle in the front-to-back and vertical directions were determined from the video recordings, and the times of heel strike and toe off were determined from foot switch data or from toe velocity. Plots of angular velocity versus angular displacement were used to represent the periodic motion of each joint. Neuromuscular activation patterns were studied in 10 astronauts (7 male, 3 female) who flew on 8- to 15-day missions. Six were veterans of previous space flights. This protocol did not make use of the reflective markers and cameras; instead, electromyographic (EMG) recordings were made from electrodes placed on the skin over selected muscles of the lower limb. Foot switch data were also collected. The EMG recordings were normalized with regard to the level of activation and the temporal relation to heel strike, yielding reduced waveforms that represented the activity of each muscle throughout the gait cycle. Spatial orientation while walking a path was studied in 7 astronauts (5 male, 2 female) who flew on 8- to 14-day missions (STS-64, 66, 67, 68); this protocol was referred to as DSO 614B. The astronauts walked clockwise and counterclockwise around a triangular path, either with their eyes open or with their vision blocked after they had looked at the path. The astronauts wore a helmet equipped with blackened goggles to block vision and headphones that played white noise to mask auditory spatial cues. Three reflective markers extended above the helmet, and their positions were used to compute the astronauts' walking direction and velocity. Data from 15 days before flight and from 2 hours after landing were used for comparisons. Movements of the lower limb and the center of mass during jump landings were studied in 9 astronauts (8 male, 1 female) who flew on 7- to 14-day missions. The tests were performed 2 to 6 months and 9 to 15 days before launch and within 4 hours of landing. While wearing a safety harness and reflective markers, an astronaut jumped from a platform 30 cm (1 ft) high and landed on both feet. Jumps made with eyes open and fixated on a target were alternated with jumps made with eyes closed and directed toward the remembered target. The angles and angular velocities of the ankle, knee and hip joints were computed from the positions of the markers. The time of impact was determined from foot switch data or from toe velocity. The position of the astronaut's center of mass was estimated from the marker positions, and the velocity of the center of mass was calculated. A simple mathematical model for the vertical motion of the center of mass, in which a spring and a parallel damping mechanism represented the legs, was used to evaluate the stiffness and damping functions of the legs.
results: In the preflight treadmill tests of head-trunk coordination, pitch head movements were smoothly coordinated to oppose the vertical movements of the trunk, thereby helping to maintain a stable gaze. The coherence between these wavelike movements decreased significantly after space flight, and the decrement in coherence was greater with the far visual target than with the near target. Both before and after space flight, the amplitude of the pitch head movements was greater with the near visual target, which would have larger apparent motion and would provide stronger feedback. After space flight, with near (or far) visual targets, the amplitude of pitch head movements was reduced in 6 (8) astronauts, unchanged in 13 (11), and increased in 4 (4) astronauts. The reductions occurred in novice astronauts, but not in veterans. Both before and after flight, when the eyes were closed the head was tilted forward and the amplitude of pitch head movements was reduced. The amplitude was restored almost immediately when the eyes were again opened. In the treadmill studies of lower limb movement, variability in the gait cycle increased after space flight. Variability increased for the knee at the time of heel strike, for the ankle during the swing phase and for the hip at the moment of toe off. However, the increased variability in the motion of individual joints did not interfere with the basic pattern of lower limb coordination, and the stability of the system as a whole was retained. The basic temporal characteristics of the gait cycle were also retained: the stride time and the proportion of time spent standing during each step varied less than the variability of the treadmill speed. It was surprising that so little change was detected in the overall gait pattern, considering the wide-based, cautious, shuffling gait of several astronauts when they entered the testing room after flight. Use of the treadmill may have limited the gait abnormalities that could be detected by requiring a subject to keep the pace and restricting the width of the gait. Also, some astronauts chose not to walk on the treadmill after landing, perhaps feeling that their coordination was not yet sufficient for the task. Perhaps greater changes would have been detected in these astronauts' gait. In the treadmill studies of neuromuscular activation, the symmetry of activation of the muscles of the 2 lower limbs was not affected by space flight. Few preflight-to-postflight differences occurred in the all-subject average of reduced waveforms for each muscle. However, significant functional increases and decreases were observed after space flight in the normalized mean amplitudes for various muscles around the times of toe off and heel strike. Also, between the preflight and postflight tests, co-contraction of the opposing muscles of the lower leg increased before toe off and decreased before heel strike, while co-contraction of the opposing thigh muscles increased before heel strike. In addition, many statistically significant preflight-to-postflight differences were found in the timing and duration of activation of specific muscles for individual subjects. The temporal relationship between the offset of the gastrocnemius and the onset of activation of the tibialis anterior at toe off was altered after space flight in 8 of the 10 subjects. In half of the subjects, the order of activation of these muscles was actually reversed. Also, the relative amplitude of activation of the tibialis anterior at toe off was reduced after flight. In the normal toe-off process, activity of the gastrocnemius with corresponding inhibition of the tibialis anterior pushes the toes back against the ground. Then, activity of the gastrocnemius ceases and the tibialis anterior is activated to lift the foot so that the toes will clear the ground as the foot swings forward. The changes that were found after space flight might explain the excessive scraping of the feet on the treadmill that was observed in postflight tests. In the studies of spatial orientation while walking the triangular path, distance error was not significantly increased after flight. Astronauts tended to underestimate turns when walking with eyes closed, and the resulting directional error was larger after space flight than before. The astronauts walked the path more slowly after spaceflight, both with eyes open and eyes closed. In the studies of jump landings, closing the eyes did not affect the astronauts' performance, perhaps because they had already judged the height. Some astronauts showed a preflight-to-postflight increase in lower limb compliance, with greater joint flexion and flexion rates. Some showed a decrease in compliance, and some showed no change. In the preflight jumps, after reaching its lowest point, the center of mass moved up and overshot the final rest position. After space flight, astronauts whose compliance had increased had much slower upward responses with little overshoot, while those whose compliance had decreased had faster upward responses with greater overshoot. The simple spring-and-damper model was able to predict the postflight alterations in the motion of the center of gravity by changing leg stiffness only; changes in damping did not appear to play a significant role. These results are important for understanding how astronauts' abilities to manage an emergency egress, or even to walk on another planet, could be impaired after space flight The results show that space flight alters the coordination between vertical trunk movements and compensatory pitch head movements during walking. This alteration may partly account for the oscillopsia that was reported during the postflight treadmill tests. The postflight changes that were observed in the neuromuscular control of heel strike might affect the transmission of the jolt from the heel strike to the head, possibly exacerbating the postflight oscillopsia. Various head movement strategies were observed after flight. Astronauts who reduced the amplitude of their pitch head movements may have been trying to reduce confusing signals from the vestibular organs. It is also possible that the various strategies were not subject-specific but were part of an ongoing process of relearning motor strategies that are appropriate to Earth's gravity. The results indicate that veteran astronauts adapt more quickly upon returning to gravity, suggesting that preflight exposure to conflicting visual and vestibular inputs during locomotion could be used to train astronauts to rapidly reorder their motor control strategies to reduce postflight motor disturbances.
