title: Women Astronaut Health
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: In October 1997, the Longitudinal Study of Astronaut Health (LSAH) reported on some variables concerning astronauts and their first flights. These data, valid through 1996, detailed various laboratory measurements including the mean differences in blood pressure and pulse values for pre- and postflight examinations. In 1996, there were 135 active astronauts: 30 women and 105 men. There were only 6 inactive women and 129 inactive men. The average age for active women astronauts is 39.9 years while the same average for active men is 41.9 years. For inactive corps members, men have a mean age of 50.9 years while women have a mean age of 46.5 years. At first flight, women average 39 years of age. Approximately 59 percent of men and 29 percent of women received a Master's degree as their highest degree earned. Fifty-one percent of women astronauts received a doctoral degree (M.D. or Ph.D.) while 28 percent of the men hold a doctoral degree in medicine, philosophy, or veterinary medicine. Racial makeup for the astronaut corps includes five groups: White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Native American. Eighty-eight percent (30) of female astronauts and 89.2 percent (141) of male astronauts are White. The next largest racial group is Blacks with 9 percent (8) of men and 5 percent (3) of women. From 1978 through 1996, women have been eligible to participate in 82 different missions. Of all flights: Women were crewmembers on 42 of those missions (51%) A woman was a pilot on 1 mission (1.2%) There were at least 2 women on 13 of those missions (15.9%) The purpose of this study was to examine the differences between male and female astronaut physiological parameters.
approach: Blood Pressure: The preflight (L-10) and postflight (R+0) examinations were used to calculate the differences in blood pressures for all astronauts. Pulse: Again, these values were obtained from L-10 and R+0 examinations, with the subjects in the sitting position.
results: Blood pressure: In particular, women had a mean difference in sitting diastolic BP: 10 mmHg for flights of six days or less (N=5) 8.2 mmHg for flights of 7 through 10 days (N=11) 0 mmHg for flights of 11 through 17 days (N=3) The mean differences in sitting systolic BP are: 14 mmHg for flights of six days or less (N=5) 12.7 mmHg for flights of 7 through 10 days (N=11) 14 mmHg for flights of 11 through 17 days (N=3) The mean differences for men were less than the mean differences for women on all flights except those 11 to 17 days in length. For those flights, men had a mean difference of 11.9 and 16.8 mmHg for diastolic and systolic BP, respectively. Sitting Pulse Values for Women: The average mean differences in sitting pulses for women are: 17 beats per minute (bpm) for flights of six days or less (N=4) 11.2 bpm for flights of 7 through 10 days (N=6) 1.3 bpm for flights of 11 though 17 days (N=3) The average mean differences in sitting pulses for men are: 7.7 bpm for flights of six days or less (N=22) 16.2 bpm for flights of 7 through 10 days in length (N=23) 8.0 bpm for flights of 11 through 17 days (N=17) Physiological differences between men and women will continue to be investigated.

title: Center for Research on Cardiac, Vascular, and Acute Effects of Space Radiation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Recent evidence strongly suggests that humans will face increased risks for adverse effects on heart and blood vessels from radiation exposure during space travel; however, these risks are not well defined. The Center for Research on Cardiac and Vascular Effects of Space Radiation comprises teams from four institutions with experts in the fields of space radiation, cardiovascular radiation injury, and modern techniques of molecular analysis. The goal is to characterize the cardiovascular risks of space radiation. Studies involve mouse, rat, and rabbit models of exposure to protons and oxygen ions. Animals were monitored for up to 12 months after radiation exposure, comparable to many years observation in humans. Heart function was measured non-invasively at regular intervals with high-resolution ultrasound. Heart and abdominal aorta were obtained at different time points after irradiation to investigate pathological changes, including cell death, adverse tissue remodeling, and inflammatory cell infiltration. Plasma and urine samples were collected to assess clinical markers of cardiac injury and changes in metabolic profiles using proteomics and metabolomics approaches. We also examine the microvasculature in the heart and retina, since low-dose ionizing radiation may cause changes in the microvasculature that could alter heart and eye function. Mathematical modeling will be used to assess in vivo and ex vivo obtained reconstructions of the microvascular bed in the heart and retina. Lastly, we will test whether gamma-tocotrienol, a safe dietary antioxidant and the strongest natural product radiation protector yet discovered, will reduce the effects of low-dose oxygen ions on heart and blood vessels. Altogether, these studies use innovative methods to characterize acute and degenerative cardiovascular effects of space radiation, and will help develop safe and effective countermeasures to protect humans against these effects.
approach: The Center for Space Radiation Research (CSRR) pursues the following Specific Aims: 1) Define acute effects of low-dose proton irradiation on the hematopoietic system, skin, heart, and retina; 2) Examine acute effects of low-dose protons in combination with modeled microgravity; 3) Evaluate acute effects of protons on the adaptive immune response; 4) Determine effects of heavy ion and proton irradiation on cardiac and vascular function and structure; 5) Identify acute and chronic biomarkers of cardiovascular dysfunction after particle irradiation; 6) Elucidate the role of metabolic and epigenetic changes in the cardiovascular response to radiation; 7) Determine effects of radiation dose and quality on endothelial cell functional phenotype; and 8) Test whether gamma-tocotrienol protects against acute and cardiovascular effects of particle irradiation.
results: This experiment is currently in progress. Results will be available at the conclusion of the study.

title: Effect of Spaceflight on Microbial Gene Expression and Virulence (Microbe)
archive_status: No data from this study was submitted to LSDA. Please contact LSDA if you know of available data.
objectives: Determine the effect of spaceflight on the virulence potential of the pathogenic microorganisms: S. typhimurium, P. aeruginosa, and C. albicans, immediately following their return from spaceflight Determine the effect of spaceflight on cellular morphology of the pathogenic microorganisms: S. typhimurium, P. aeruginosa, and C. albicans, immediately following their return from spaceflight Compare S. typhimurium cultures grown in nutrient limited media to those grown in nutrient rich media to determine the potential effects of nutritional status on changes in gene expression, morphology, and virulence properties during spaceflight.
approach: Three GAPs were used for each of 4 projects: S. typhimurium in rich media; S. typhimurium in minimal media; P. aeruginosa in rich media; C. albicans in rich media. Temperature loggers and radiation area monitors (RAMs) were used to collect the thermal profile and radiation profile experienced by the flight samples, respectively. Synchronous ground controls (12 GAPs) were loaded at the same time as the flight. Asynchronous ground controls were performed at the PI lab post-flight utilizing the Rotating Wall Vessel and the temperature data recorded from the flight experiment temperature logging devices. The FPAs (flight and synchronous) were loaded with the flight reagents (terminators and growth media) and static cultures and installed into the GAPs at approximately launch minus L-5 days. On-orbit, the cultures were activated with growth media on Flight Day 10 and allowed to grow for 24 hours +/- 2 hours. The experiment was terminated with addition of either RNA Later II, for post flight microarray studies, or fresh media for post flight LD50 studies. Postflight, microarray gene expression was performed on the fixed samples. A mouse (465 BALB/c female) LD-50 study was also performed at KSC to assess changes in virulence potential.
results: Confirmed the effects of microgravity observed in the STS-115 Microbe experiments and homed in on the importance of the growth medium for gene expression and virulence of the microbe Samonella during spaceflight. A large number of Hfq-regulated genes were differentially expressed (167). Hfq is known to regulate one third of the 167 differentially expressed genes. Hfq may serve to globally modify bacterial responses to microgravity.

title: Inter Limb Resistance Device Evaluation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The Inter Limb Resistance Device (ILRD) has been tested on the KC-135 and in the Weightless Environment Training Facility (WETF). The ILRD is a safe, simple, compact, low mass exercise harness with an inelelastic cable and pulley system that allows the subject to exercise one limb against the other. The objectives of this experiment were: 1. Expected to minimize vibration of sensitive experiments aboard the spacecraft. 2. Evaluate for ease of set up and stowage, and physical comfort during exercise. 3. Demonstrate ability to provide concentric, eccentric and isometric resistive exercise. 4. Evaluate the subject restraint system used to stabilize the exercising subject. 5. Evaluate the impact on the microgravity environment of the orbiter utilizing an on-board acceleration measurement system, when available.
approach: Heart rate monitor was worn prior to and during each session. Evaluated: setup, ILRD donning and doffing, restraint system. Configured for anti-gravity muscle training, performed general repetitions at high loads, followed by "running" at lower loads. Minor reconfiguration for calf and upper body exercise (press, bicep curl and tricep curl). The ILRD had to be stowed between exercise sessions due to middeck constraints.
results: The Inter-Limb Resistance exercise device performed very well during its first "shake-down" test in the short-duration microgravity on board the KC-135. Three subjects generated peak forces ranging from 640 to 1156 N (144 to 260 lbs) during the leg press (sum of force from both legs). Two subjects performed the calf press and generated peak forces of 702 to 782 N (158 to 176 lbs). The biceps curl exercise produced up to 623 N (140 lbs) for one subject. Forces approaching peak values were sustained throughout the range of motion for all exercises. Subjects successfully donned, reconfigured, and removed the Inter-Limb Resistance device during microgravity tests.

title: Correlation of Disconjugate Eye Torsion with the Time Course of the Space Adaptation Syndrome
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Space motion sickness (SMS) during space flight is very similar to motion sickness on Earth. SMS can be predicted during parabolic flights on Earth by observing characteristic eye movements. By identifying these same characteristic eye movements, particularly rotary eye movements during the course of space flight, researchers hope to obtain information on SMS, which will have a direct impact on Earth-based motion sickness. This study documented the correlation of eye torsional changes with the development and recovery over time of SMS.
approach: Three astronauts underwent preflight, inflight, and postflight testing of spontaneous ocular torsion and ocular counterrolling (OCR) reflexes governed by the gravity-responsive otolith organs in the inner ear. Subject A flew a 30-day space mission during Euromir '94 and was examined with a monocular video-oculography (VOG) system. Subjects B and C were studied with a binocular VOG during the 180-day Euromir '95 mission. VOG is a technique used to examine the function of the human balance system located in the inner ear (vestibular system) and the visuo-oculomotor interactions of the vestibular organ. The subjects’ eye movements were measured, recorded, and evaluated by state-of-the-art video techniques. Preflight and postflight measurements were performed with the subject in a head-upright position. Inflight measurements required only that the subject remain stationary. To record images from both eyes simultaneously during Euromir ‘95, the monocular VOG used during Euromir '94 was augmented by one additional camera and recorder unit. The binocular system videotaped both eyes simultaneously providing 25 synchronized images of each per second. The torsional eye position was derived from surface landmarks of the iris. First, a circular ring segment or arc was selected and defined by its radius from the center of the pupil, the thickness of the ring segment, and the angle swept by the arc. A geometric assumption was made that the visible borders of the pupil were part of a circle or an ellipse. For each line of the video image that passed through the pupil, the threshold for entering and leaving the pupil was determined. If a line passing through the pupil was interrupted by reflections or other artifacts, that line was rejected. The accepted lines were calculated to form a circle. In this manner, reliable pupil center could be determined even though up to 50% of the pupil was not visible. A reference iris profile was calculated and stored in computer memory. Using this reference, subsequent iris profiles could be compared to determine any changes in ocular torsion, e.g. the reference iris profile obtained preflight was compared with other profiles obtained preflight, during flight, and postflight. In the preflight and postflight experiments, the astronauts were strapped into a special chair. An individual bitebar was made and fitted to a mask-headband assembly containing two small video cameras, one in front of each eye. The bitebar was also rigidly attached to the chair. The astronaut’s eyes were adjusted to Earth-horizontal. Once the bitebar-to-mask and bitebar-to-chair attachments were satisfactory, the joints were tightened and sealed in position. The bitebar could fit only one way to the mask and chair. This meant the relation of the mask and its cameras in front of the eyes could be precisely replicated for all other preflight and postflight experiments. In the earth-based studies, subjects were seated in the special chair, the bitebar-mask-head apparatus donned, and the eye position verified to be Earth-horizontal. The subjects maintained their eyes in the primary position by gazing at a target one meter away. The heights of the cameras were adjusted so that the iris images were equidistant from the lower edge of the video monitor. In each of these Earth-based experiments, the eye positions were recorded for two minutes as the subject sat quietly upright. Following the upright position, eye positions were recorded for two minutes with the subject tilted and maintained at a 30º right-ear-down tilt and two minutes with the subject in a 30º left-ear-down tilt. For space-flight experiments, an identical individual bitebar-to-camera apparatus was made for each subject and taken to the Mir Space Station. These masks maintained the same head-to-eye-to-camera relation as the ground experiments. The astronauts were adept at donning the apparatus and making sure the iris images were equidistant from the bottom of the video monitor. A two-minute videotape was made with the head “upright” in six to eight experiments during the six-month space flight. As required, all three subjects had vestibular “deconditioning” training for several weeks before space flight and again toward the end of flight. This consisted of vigorous head rotation in the pitch and yaw modes. During each experimental session in flight, each subject marked a detailed questionnaire of SMS symptoms as being absent, mild, moderate, or severe.
results: Five to six preflight baseline data collections (BDCs) were obtained for each subject. In the upright position while seated quietly, spontaneous torsional eye movements were approximately ±0.75º, consistent with earlier studies of normal subjects. The eyes were mostly conjugate. When held for two minutes in a static tipped position, mean ocular counterrolling (OCR) in the three subjects was –5.94º and +5.54º in response to the 30º right and left tilts, respectively. All inflight and postflight analyses were based on a preflight external reference image enabling comparison of eye positions relative to the preflight baseline. In all three subjects, the torsional position of each eye was substantially changed from its preflight setting. A torsional reset was manifested during the entire inflight and postflight testing period, although each eye position might vary considerably throughout the study. The SMS evaluation forms on two subjects indicated no SMS symptoms during space flight. One had moderate nausea in the Soyuz transport vehicle on the way to Mir and on flight day 4. This subject was symptom-free at all other times. Upon return to Earth, two subjects were grossly ataxic immediately after landing. Seven hours after landing, both subjects could walk slowly with support. Turning caused them to lurch to one side. Both were pale and weak with marked atrophy of the legs. Both were nauseated and had headaches. One subject became nauseated by repeated head rotation, while the other felt too ill to be tested at all. The day after landing (R+1), both could slowly walk independently with no further nausea, even with head rotation maneuvers. After several more days, their overall behavior seemed normal. The leg atrophy was improved by R+10. Postflight testing repeated the preflight protocol with two minutes in each upright position, 30º right and 30º left. In all three subjects, OCR amplitude differed from that observed preflight. Subject B showed increased OCR to both sides of tilt, especially to 30º left, even considering the torsional reset of the eyes in the upright position. Subject C also showed increased OCR to the left and approximately the same OCR to the right as preflight. Subject A had decreased OCR on the day of landing, increasing daily until postflight day 10 (R+10), at which time it exceeded the baseline OCR in both directions of tilt. At day 150, however, this subject’s torsional eye position had returned to its preflight baseline. No tests were performed between day 10 and 150, and therefore the time course of recovery cannot be ascertained. By R+10, subject B’s right eye had approached its preflight baseline; however, with the head in the upright position, the left eye remained about 2.5º torted counterclockwise. Subject C had likewise not returned to his baseline settings by R+10. As two of the three subjects did not have SMS and the third had none or marginal SMS, none of the changes in ocular torsion found during this study can be related to SMS. However, analysis of parabolic flight disconjugacy in two of the present subjects correctly predicted absence of SMS.

title: Renal Stone Risk Assessment During Long Duration Space Flight
research_area: Metabolism and nutrition; Endocrinology; Renal, fluid and electrolyte physiology; Skeletal physiology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Exposure to microgravity alters human physiology. A number of the recognized changes are expected to contribute to an altered urinary environment that in turn influences the potential for renal stone formation. During previous missions, the most obvious changes observed in astronauts were an increased excretion of calcium and a negative calcium balance. Both are thought to be the result of altered bone resorption processes. Other changes included increased urinary phosphate and decreased urinary output, urinary osmolality, and magnesium and citrate concentrations. All of these changes were expected to increase the urinary supersaturation of stone-forming salts and increase the risk for renal stone formation. Data collected during short-term Shuttle flights (4-14 days duration) indicated an increase in the potential for renal stone formation, particularly for calcium oxalate and uric acid stones. Some of the renal stone risk indices also appeared to be influenced by mission duration. Therefore, it was hypothesized that long-term mission durations further increase the potential risk of renal stone formation. To quantify the inflight and postflight risk for renal stone formation, the investigation had three (1) To determine the effects of exposure to microgravity on the potential for renal stone formation. (2) To determine the effect of mission duration on the potential risk for renal stone formation. (3) To determine how long after flight the increased risk exists for renal stone formation.
approach: All three Mir-18 crewmembers participated in this investigation which involved 24-hour urine collections and 48-hour diet monitoring periods. The three crewmembers collected urine voids over a 24-hour period three times during the preflight period (L-148, L-58 and L-34), and following landing on R+0, R+6, R+10 and R+13. Inflight urine samples were collected on Mission Day (MD) 14, MD 93 and MD 110. Inflight, individual urine voids were collected into a urine collection device containing 1 ml lithium chloride as a volume marker. Two 7 ml urine aliquots were drawn into syringe tubes containing 0.05% thymol or 0.1% thimerosal, mixed well and stored at ambient temperatures until return to Earth for analyses. Following the return of the samples, urine volumes were determined from the diluted lithium concentration. Twenty-four-hour urine pools were constructed from the individual voids and samples were analyzed for osmolality, calcium, oxalate, uric acid, citrate, sodium, sulfate, phosphorus, magnesium, potassium and creatinine. Pre- and postflight, the subjects collected 24-hour urine specimens. The pooled urine was stored chilled at approximately 4 degrees Celsius. After total volume and pH were recorded, two 10 ml aliquots were removed for biochemical analysis. The first sample was analyzed for creatinine, magnesium, phosphorus, potassium, sodium and uric acid. The second 10 ml aliquot was acidified with 6M hydrochloric acid (HCl) and analyzed for calcium, magnesium, citrate, oxalate and sulfate. All samples were processed immediately or stored at -20 degrees Celsius until analysis. From the measurements, the relative urinary supersaturation of the stone forming salts were calculated and renal stone risk was estimated. The derived parameters were urinary supersaturation of calcium oxalate, brushite (calcium phosphate), sodium urate, struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) and uric acid saturation. Detailed diet logs were maintained by each crewmember for 24 hours prior to urine collection and during the 24-hour urine collection period to assess the effect of dietary factors on the potential for renal stone formation.
results: The overall quality of the preflight, inflight and postflight urine data were very good. Some of the individual inflight urine samples appeared to have bacterial contamination, which might have an effect on the quality of the assessment of renal stone risk. Postflight, urine samples collected on R+0 and R+1 by one crewmember were not labeled and were lost for analyses. Inflight dietary monitoring was incomplete. Complete dietary data were received from only 2 inflight days out of the 9 inflight monitoring days that were requested. The Bar Code Reader (BCR) was not used as intended and not all dietary items were scanned. Also, a large percentage of dietary items consumed during the monitoring period were from previous missions and were not bar-code labeled. These items were not entered manually into the log book by the crew. Due to the incompleteness of the dietary database, the effects of environmental factors on the potential risk of renal stone formation are difficult to describe. Conclusions from the Mir 18 mission can be summarized as follows: 1. Calcium excretion was increased while urinary output was decreased. Both are believed to be a result of the exposure to microgravity. Both effects increase the risk of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate stone formation. 2. It was difficult to describe the effects of long-duration exposure to microgravity based on the Mir 18 results alone. Data analyses showed that an exaggerated risk existed even during the preflight period. 3. The urinary output was overall very low and returned to preflight levels by R+6. Urinary calcium phosphate (brushite) values returned to preflight levels at R+10 but the risk of calcium oxalate stone formation remained in the high risk range throughout the postflight period. A considerable analyte variation was present between the subjects participating in this investigation making general assumptions on the potential risk of renal stone formation difficult at this time. Mir 18 data sets will be combined with data from future NASA-Mir missions for more complete renal stone risk assessment.

title: Characterization of Microbial Transfer Among Crewmembers During Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Increased risk of infections among crewmembers during space flight results from working and living in a crowded, closed environment with limited capabilities for air revitalization and disinfection. Alterations in the immune response during space flight as well as stress, aerosols, and altered fluid distribution within the body could increase the incidence of infectious disease during long-duration space missions. Staphyloccus aureus has been the target of many epidemiological studies because of its known virulence potential and as a prominent cause of nosocomial infections. This bacterium has also been of interest to NASA's human space flight program. Staphyloccus aureus was chosen as the subject for this study because it is frequently isolated from both crewmembers and the spacecraft environment and has been examined in previous space flight programs, providing a benchmark for the current missions as well as the technology employed. Studies initially conducted during the Apollo Program and Apollo-Soyuz Test Project using bacteriophage typing patterns reported that the transfer of Staphyloccus aureus among crewmembers was a common occurrence. A phage typing experiment was also conducted during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project to study microbial exchange among the U.S. and Russian crewmembers. Further phage typing studies were conducted during the Skylab program, which also included data regarding dissemination of the organism through the spacecraft environment. Data from the Skylab 3 mission suggested two incidences of intercrew transfer.
approach: Isolates of Staphyloccus aureus were collected over a two-year period from nasal, throat, urine, and feces specimens of Space Shuttle flight crewmembers and from surfaces inside the spacecraft. Clinical specimens were collected from crewmembers 10 and 2 days prior to flight, and immediately after landing. The internal surfaces and air of the spacecraft were sampled 30 days and I day before flight, and at landing.
results: Staphyloccus aureus was chosen as the target bacterium to study the spread of microbes in the spacecraft because it is frequently isolated from crewmembers and from the Space Shuttle environment. This 2-year study included 10 Space Shuttle missions ranging from 5 to 16 days in duration, with 5-7 crewmembers per mission. A total of 57 astronauts (45 male and 12 female) participated in the study, and 33 (58%) were culture-positive during one or more sampling periods for Staphyloccus aureus . The 139 isolates collected during the study included 96 Staphyloccus aureus strains isolated from culture-positive subjects, and 43 strains isolated from surfaces inside the Shuttle crewmember compartment. In 37% of the subjects, Staphyloccus aureus was isolated at all three sample collection periods while 21% of the subjects were intermittent carriers, from which the bacteria was isolated during one or two of the three sampling periods. Staphyloccus aureus was not isolated during the pre- or postflight sample collections from 42% of the subjects. Of those harboring the target bacteria, the most common site for isolation was the nose. Isolates were also obtained from throat and urine specimens, however, these comprised only about 25% of the Staphyloccus aureus isolates.

objectives: To determine the effects of microgravity on connectivity of afferent neurons and inner ear hair cells and vestibular nuclei neurons, and characterize changes in innervation patterns of inner ear afferent and efferent neurons.

title: Mental Workload and Performance Experiment
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Whether on Earth or in space, people tend to work more productively in settings designed for efficiency and comfort. Because well-designed accommodations enhance performance and contribute to congenial relationships among coworkers, the living and working areas of spacecraft used during long-term missions assume particular importance. Also, the complexity of future Space Stations require crewmembers to be capable of supervising the on board electronic logistics. It is necessary to design workstations with efficient computer display formats and input devices. To optimize the setting for interactions between astronauts and on board computer control systems were the main objective of the Mental Workload and Performance Experiment (MWPE). The experiment focused on motor and cognitive skills associated with such interactions, and designed to understand the demands placed on the astronaut’s mental and physical capabilities during space flight and particularly while operating graphic input devices such as cursor keys, joysticks, and trackballs.
approach: The natural posture of the human body is different in space than on Earth. Therefore, furnishings that are conducive in 1-g may prove uncomfortable or inefficient in microgravity. The crewmembers of the Spacelab 1 mission had to exert considerable efforts to maintain their positions at a computer workstation that had been engineered for a person standing in a typical Earth position. On board the IML-1 Spacelab, the crewmembers used an anthropometric workstation with an adjustable surface for their daily planning sessions and record keeping. In general, one crewmember performed the daily planning while a second crewmember videotaped the activities using the Closed Circuit Television (CCTV) camera located in the end cap of the Spacelab module. The video-footage provided information about the astronauts’ range of motion and variety of positions while at the workstation. Besides the video-footage, reports from the astronauts and measurements of the location of the adjustable surface provided complementary information. A second part of the investigation was the evaluation of mental function, reaction times, and physical responses of the astronauts during space flight. A portable microcomputer with a display monitor and keyboard were attached to the anthropometric workstation. The subject then followed a performance assessment program displayed on the computer monitor. The MWPE performance assessment test was based on the Fittsberg task, a combination of Fitts’ Law and Sternberg tasks, that combined tests of eye-hand-coordination and short-term memory, respectively. The Fitts’ paradigm was developed to examine the control and accuracy of movement and was used to measure response execution. Subjects were required to manually acquire a target of a certain size and distance away from an initial cursor position as quickly and as accurately as possible. The Sternberg memory search task required the subject to determine if a displayed item was a member of a previously memorized set. Each memory set contained 1 or 4 letters. For each memory set, 8 test stimuli were presented. After a set of 12 memory sets were presented, the subjects were asked to move to the next input device. Three different devices were used: keyboard cursor keys, a two-axis joystick (rate-contol device), and a trackball (position-control device). The microcomputer recorded the speed and accuracy of the movements and the time needed to interpret the instructions. These data were complemented by the crew’s evaluations of the equipment. The four IML-1 astronauts participating in the MWPE experiment performed these activities 2-4 times before, and 4 times during their space flight to determine whether mental and physical performance were influenced by adaptation to microgravity.
results: The MWPE experiment showed a significant increase in movement time for all four subjects (movement time is the time the subject starts to move the cursor until the cursor reaches its target). In other words, a decrease in fine motor control performance was observed in the microgravity environment. To determine whether these changes were caused by the exposure to microgravity, a 7-day ground-based study was conducted under similar conditions. The motor control of the four subjects participating in the ground study did not change. The Sternberg task tested the cognitive performance of the four astronauts while in space. No significant changes could be measured between preflight and inflight test results. Evaluating the different input devices for control strategies, two main results were found: (1) in both up-down and left-right cardinal movement-directions, no differences in the movement times between the used devices were observed, and (2) in the diagonal target directions, a significant increase in movement time was noted for the joystick while the trackball basically did not differ from other conditions.

title: Ability of Polyethylene Glycol Interleukin-2 (PEG-IL2) to Counteract the Effect of Spaceflight on the Rat Immune System
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Cytokines, proteins that serve as messengers to activate immune responses in lymphocytes and macrophages, appear to be altered during spaceflight. Because of this suppression of the immune system in otherwise healthy subjects, spaceflight offers a unique opportunity to study the effects of biological substances without the complications of illnesses normally present in immunosuppressed subjects. Polyethylene Glycol-Interleukin 2 (PEG-IL-2) is an immunological mediator and enhancer developed and manufactured by Chiron Corporation. The purpose of this experiment in conjunction with the Immune 2 experiment was to confirm and define the ability of Polyethylene Glycol-Interleukin 2 (PEG-IL2) to prevent or ameliorate the detrimental effects of space flight on immune responses of rats.
approach: Half of the animals in each group were injected intravenously with PEG-IL-2 two to three hours before transfer to the Animal Enclosure Modules (AEMs). Upon recovery of flight subjects, the following tissues and organs were removed and weighed: brain, heart, kidneys, liver, lungs, trachea, spleen, and thymus. Blood samples were collected and analyzed for blood cell counts and differentials. They were also analyzed for corticosterone concentration with radioimmunoassay. Macrophage (M-CSF) and granulocyte-macrophage stimulating factor (GM-CSF) dependent macrophage colony formation from bone marrow cells was assayed. Lymphocytes were obtained from the spleen and lymph nodes and assayed to determine cell proliferation rates and the secretion of cytokines, M-CSF, IL-6, IFN-g, and TGF-§. Peritoneal macrophages were assayed for secretion of TNFa and IL-6. The femur and tibia were collected and underwent biomechanical testing to calculate strength (N), deflection (mm), and energy (mJ). Bones were then dried and ashed in order to assess mineral content.
results: The results of this experiment are joined with the Immune 2 experiment. There was no significant pattern observed for body weight and organ weight parameters. Additionally, few immunological parameters were consistent across the Immune 1 and Immune 2 experiments, making conclusive observations difficult. Significant changes in bone parameters were observed in Immune 2, but not Immune 1. The inconsistencies between the two experiments prevented any conclusive evidence concerning the effectiveness of the PEG-IL-2 treatment. Several factors may have played a role in these discrepancies. Some of the animals flown were found to have damage to their tails upon recovery (necrosis, loss, and gangrenous tissues). However, compared to the animals in the same group, these changes did not correlate with any of the parameters measured. While there were the expected trends in the Immune 1 experiments, the control animals did not exhibit as many of the flight-related changes as were anticipated. In contrast, the control group in the Immune 2 study did have more dramatic changes associated with spaceflight. These differences in the control groups may have been due to the fact that flight animals in the Immune 2 experiment were exposed to significantly higher ambient temperatures than animals in Immune 1.

title: Leg Plethysmography
research_area: Cardiovascular physiology; Renal, fluid and electrolyte physiology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Signs and symptoms secondary to fluid shifts in weightlessness were among the first physiologic effects noted in the manned space flight program. These effects included puffy faces, nasal congestion, in-flight and postflight weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, and cardiovascular changes. The headward shift of body fluids, both intravascular and extravascular, results from the absence of the 1-g hydrostatic gradient. The purpose of this study was to measure leg volume changes during space flight.
approach: The stocking plethysmograph, first used on STS-5, 7 and 8, continued to be used for determination of direct girth-length measurements. From a series of circumferential measurements, volume was calculated under the assumption that a truncated cone represents a reasonable approximation of a leg volume segment. On these later Shuttle flights, the original leg volume protocol was modified to study the time course of leg volume changes; a sequence of measurements were made as early as possible in flight. Furthermore, leg volumes were obtained pre- and postflight during the routine medical stand tests.
results: Time course of the fluid shift was determined to be exponential with a time constant of 6-8 hours. A second result seen was the relatively small amount of fluid which is pooled in the legs postflight and the disproportionately large signs of orthostatic stress this induced. Either the blood volume remains small or there is a large pooling elsewhere in the body. There was also a suggestion that a blunting of normal heart rate response may have occurred. The volume change and percentage change were all compared with the preflight volume determinations. The landing measurements were made within 1.5 hours of touchdown. The postflight measurements were made during the first week post-landing. It should be noted that the 1-g leg volume measurements for Skylab and ASTP were made with the crewmembers in the supine position, whereas the measurements in the Shuttle program were made with the crewmembers standing. When going from standing to supine, there is a shift of approximately 300ml of blood out of the legs. The in-flight volume changes found in the 11 subjects from the Shuttle program demonstrated a mean volume change of 1026 ml or 11.6% with a range from 1790 ml or 16.9% to 685 ml or 8.3%. The majority of the subjects had a 10% to 12% volume change. This compares with the 12.2% from Skylab and 10.0% from ASTP. The source of this leg volume change is a relatively rapid shift of blood followed by interstitial fluid and probably intercellular fluid, with some tissue loss secondary to muscle atrophy.

title: Expression of Contractile Protein Isoforms in Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Normal function of cardiac and skeletal muscle depends heavily on the regulatory contractile proteins troponin T and troponin I. In both cardiac and skeletal muscle, a change in the expression of isoforms of these two proteins occurs during development. In turn, these isoforms alter the property of muscle myofibrils. Currently, the mechanisms behind the changes in isoform expression are unknown. It is hypothesized that microgravity will alter troponin isoform expression. Using microgravity to alter the expression of these isoforms may help to reveal the systems that alter gene expression and mRNA processing in cardiac and skeletal muscle on Earth. Understanding the basic processes controlling cardiac and skeletal muscle may prove useful in the treatment of heart disease and other medical problems.
approach: Analysis concentrated on cardiac troponin T isoform expression. Hearts were isolated from embryos fixed in space and in ground experiments at ages 7, 10, 14, and 16 days. RNA was purified from individual embryonic hearts for gene expression analysis by reverse transcriptase-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and rapid amplification of cDNA ends (RACE) experiments.
results: Initial experiments using RT-PCR primers based on chicken cardiac troponin T cDNA sequences were unsuccessful. Subsequently, primers based on human cardiac troponin T sequences successfully generated a quail cardiac troponin T cDNA. However, it lacked the 5' sequence encoding the region of alternative splicing. The inclusion or exclusion of this sequence is the basis of the two cardiac troponin T isoforms expressed in the avian heart, and therefore the missing 5' sequence is essential to testing the effects of microgravity on isoform expression and cardiac function. Rapid amplification of the cDNA 5' was used to attempt to generate the region of alternative splicing. This approach was not successful. However, results demonstrate that sufficient RNA can be isolated from individual quail embryonic hearts to successfully perform RT-PCR, supporting future studies of gene regulation in microgravity.

title: Greenhouse III: Developmental Analysis of Seeds Grown on Mir
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Successful plant reproduction during spaceflight has always been difficult. The environment within a spacecraft has many factors that make plant growth problematic. Experiments are limited to specific constraints on both available energy and space. Recent studies have shown that near identical gaseous environments can have drastically different effects on plant growth and reproduction. There appears to be a strong correlation between the degree of ventilation that a plant receives and how successfully it grows. This study focuses on the effects of microgravity upon plant reproduction. Specifically, the study looks at whether microgravity reduces the storage reserves available for reproduction.
approach: The experiment began with the planting of Brassica rapa seeds in the Russian greenhouse's (Svet) two root zone modules. The crew photographed plant development, made observations and physical measurements in the log book, and took video images. Plant samples were collected and fixed twice during the vegetative stages of the growth cycle, on days 13 and 18. To encourage the plants to stop growing vertically, the tops were pinched off on Flight Day 18. The parts removed were fixed with the plants sampled and returned to Earth. During the flowering phase of growth, pollination was performed once daily for 7 days. The plants were harvested 48 days after sowing, then dried and/or fixed. A portion of the seeds were placed on seed strips for subsequent planting, and the remainder were stowed for postflight analysis.
results: During the three growth cycles, seeds formed on Earth had comparable growth and reproductive output. The two growth cycles composed of first generation seeds formed in space produced fewer flower buds and were smaller than reference plants from Earth seeds grown at the same time in the same environment.

title: Impact of Microgravity on the Cell-CelInteractions between a Mutualistic Bacterium and Its Animal Host
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Beneficial microbes play a significant role in the normal development of animal tissues. Through the formation of healthy stable associations between host and symbiont, particularly during post-embryonic development, carefully regulated developmental pathways can be induced. This experimental research plan will examine the impact of microgravity on the normal molecular interactions between host and symbiont. To examine these effects, the model system between the squid Euprymna scolopes and the luminescent bacterium Vibrio fischeri will be used. For over two decades this squid-vibrio model has served as an ideal ecosystem to examine the influences of mutualistic bacteria on animal development. To simulate microgravity, rotating bioreactors called high-aspect-ratio rotating wall vessel bioreactors (HARVs) will be used to provide a low-shear environment for both the host and symbiont, thereby simulating microgravity. The proposed work has several implications for the field of space biology. First, by examining how normal healthy symbioses are initiated and maintained under microgravity conditions, we can begin to determine the sensitivity of these ecosystems to perturbations in the space environment. Secondly, genetic and metabolic responses to gravity in the presence and absence of symbiosis will be assessed, potentially identifying previously unknown triggers or cues associated with post-embryonic animal development.
approach: Specifically, the following is proposed: 1) Examine the mechanism(s) associated with the delay of bacteria-induced immune cell trafficking that occurs in simulated microgravity; 2) Characterize the changes in the transcriptome of the host squid in the presence and absence of symbiotic bacteria exposure under microgravity conditions; 3) Develop a flight-ready microtiter plate for future flight experiments and optimize the conditions needed to initiate and maintain the symbiosis in this new hardware.
results: 1. The symbiotic V. fischeri appear to modulate the host innate immune and oxidative stress response of the host light organ during modeled microgravity conditions. Using RNA-seq we analyzed the transcriptome of the host light organ (i.e., the site of symbiosis) of the squid in the presence (symbiotic) and absence (aposymbiotic) of beneficial V. fischeri under simulated microgravity conditions. At 12 h post inoculation both the symbiotic and aposymbiotic animals exhibited an upregulation of genes associated with hemocyanin, oxidative stress, and the innate immune system. However, by 24 h post inoculation only the aposymbiotic animals exhibited an upregulated stress response, whereas those animals exposed to V. fischeri no longer showed the stress response suggesting that V. fischeri is helping to modulate the host response. Results were published in Casaburi et al., 2017 – See cumulative bibliography for citation; reported in FY2018 report. 2. Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) shedding by V. fischeri is increased under simulated microgravity conditions. Under modeled microgravity conditions V. fischeri releases a statistically higher amount of the virulence factor LPS, known to cause apoptosis and inflammation in both mutualistic and pathogenic microbes. The LPS production is primarily associated with flagellar movement and by knocking out flagellar production and motion the amount of LPS produced under both microgravity and gravity conditions was reduced. However, even with the removal of the flagella, the LPS shedding was still statistically higher in modeled microgravity conditions compared to gravity conditions. We have ascertained that under modeled microgravity the V. fischeri membrane integrity is compromised and is more susceptible to antibiotic treatment. We are examining whether we can further inhibit the differential shedding of LPS under modeled microgravity conditions. 3. Sequencing and closure of the Euprymna scolopes genome revealed two evolutionary mechanisms for symbiotic organ evolution. Using the RNA-seq data generated during this project we generated a reference transcriptome for the host animal and use that as a scaffold to close the genome of E. scolopes. Although this task was not originally part of our project goals the data was invaluable in providing a closed genome for the squid-vibrio research community. Analysis of the genome and reference transcriptome revealed that there are two distinctive evolutionary processes associated with the origin of symbiotic organs in animals. A manuscript is currently in press at PNAS. 4. Modeled microgravity alters the innate immune pathway of host squid. Using the new technique NanoString, we complemented the previously generated transcriptomes by analyzing the differential gene expression along additional time points (0, 2, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 24 h) and have generated a new model of the receptor and signal cascade of the innate immune system. We have also determined that modeled microgravity impacts the expression of the innate immune genes and we have identified key parts of the pathway that are being disrupted. 5. Modeled microgravity does not significantly alter the transcriptome of the symbiont V. fischeri; however, the global regulatory gene hfq is critical to regulate the bacterial stress responses in low shear modeled microgravity (LSMMG). The transcriptome of the bacterial symbiont was examined during both exponential and stationary phase growth and results indicated that modeled microgravity had no significant impact on gene expression at 12 and 24 h. However, when the global regulator gene hfq was deleted from the bacteria, there was a pronounced change in gene expression under LSMMG conditions. There was a dramatic increase in the number of transcripts associated with TCA cycling and stress responses suggesting that the Hfq protein serves as a critical regulator for the bacteria under modeled microgravity conditions. Additional data is available from GeneLab's Data Repository at https://genelab-data.ndc.nasa.gov/genelab/accession/GLDS-119/

title: Reactivation of Latent Viruses During the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Reactivation of latent viruses may pose an important health risk for people living and working in extreme environments, such as space and Antarctica. Risks associated with many infectious agents are reduced by the preventative measures of the health stabilization program before each mission. However, reactivation of latent viruses is unaffected by such actions. A variety of stess factors may cause reactivation of these viruses, such as psychosocial stress, trauma, sunlight, resiratory infection, and fever. Stress-induced changes in immune function under such conditions may also increase the incidence and duration of viral reactivation and shedding. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), a DNA virus that infects more than 90% of the adult population worldwide and is the etiologic agent of infectious mononucleosis, is highly infectious. Normally, primary infection is a self-limiting disease leading to a lifelong persistence of EBV in the B-lymphocytes or epithelial cells of the oropharynx of infected individuals. EBV can be found in saliva after reactivation, which can be triggered by a variety of factors, perhaps including space flight. The physical and psychological stresses associated with the launch and landing of spacecraft, and living and working in the crowded, closed environment in microgravity, may result in viral reactivation and shedding. The limited access to space requires the use of ground-based analogs of space flight. Environmental chambers have been used since the Skylab program (1973-1974) to simulate specific aspects of space flight. In the present study, the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was used to identify EBV DNA in saliva and CMV DNA in urine as a measure of viral shedding in response to 60-day (Phase IIa) and 91-day (Phase III) chamber studies of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) at NASA Johnson Space Center.
approach: Viral shedding and reactivation patterns were studied for eight subjects (five male and three female) participating in the 60-day (Phase IIa) and 91-day (Phase III) chamber studies of the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP) at NASA Johnson Space Center. Saliva samples were collected from the eight subjects before, during, and after chamber isolation. Blood and urine samples were collected once before entry and once after exit. Samples from 11 healthy age-matched adults were collected as controls (ten males and one female). Saliva, urine, and blood samples (one of each) were collected from each of these subjects on day 1, day 7, and day 22 of the tests. This collection schedule closely approximates the pre- and postflight collection schedule of a 12-day Shuttle flight. One-time urine samples were also collected from 30 additional healthy age-matched subjects for CMV analysis. Saliva samples were collected with Salivette kits, which consist of a cotton roll in a polypropylene vial. Subjects placed the roll in their mouth until it became saturated, and then returned the roll to the vial. Saliva samples were centrifuged immediately after collection and stored frozen at -70ºC. All samples collected from a given subject were analyzed simultaneously. Using a polymerase chain reaction assay, saliva samples were processed for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA and urine samples were analyzed for cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA detection. Saliva (2 to 3 ml) and urine (3 ml) specimens were concentrated with a 100-KD filtration unit. DNA was extracted by a nonorganic extraction method, and EBV DNA was detected as described here briefly. The PCR primers were directed at the EBV polymerase accessory protein gene (BMRF1): P1, 5-GTC CAA GAG CCACCACAC CTG and P2, 5-biotin CCC AGA AGT ATA CGT GGT GAC GTA GA. These primers were used at a concentrationof 200 µM with 10 µM deoxynucleic acid triphosphates. PCR was optimized using buffer II with 2.5 mM MgCl 2 . Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) was added to a final concentration of 5%. AmpliGold (2.5 units per 100 µl reaction mixture) was added, and 5 µl of the purified DNA was added to 20 µl of the reaction mixture. The cycle parameters were 95ºC for 9 min, followed by 40 cycles of 94ºC for 15 sec, 61ºC for 15 sec, and 72ºC for 15 sec, with a final extension step at 72ºC for 5 min. CMV DNA was detected using primers that target the major immediate early gene (P1, 5-TGT CCT CCC GCT CCT C and P2, biotin 5-ATG AAG GTC TTT GCC CAG TA). All reactions were carried out using a Perkin-Elmer GenAmp system 9600. An initial denaturation step of 94ºC for 9 min was followed by 40 cycles of 94ºC for 30 sec, 69ºC for 15 sec, 72ºC for 30 sec, 72ºC for 7 min, and a 4ºC hold. The amplified product was analyzed for the presence of EBV or CMV using the Digene Sharp Signal System according to the manufacturer's instructions. EBV and CMV antibody titers from blood samples were determined by indirect immunofluorescence assay. Commercially prepared substrate slides and control sera were used for determining antibody (IgG) titers for viral capsid antigen (VCA) and early antigen (EA) of EBV, CMV, and measles (Bion Enterprises, Park Ridge, IL). Four-fold dilutions of plasma were prepared with phosphate-buffered saline. The endpoint titer was determined as the highest dilution of serum in which immunofluorescent-positive cells could be detected. All specimens were batch analyzed and read blind-coded. The frequency of viral shedding in saliva and viral antibody titers in plasma from chamber study subjects and controls were tested for normality. One-way analysis of variance was performed to study significant differences across different times during the study. The method of generalized estimating equations with a logit link was used to find significant difference between the phases (pre-, in-, and postchamber). The differences between sampling periods were considered significant if P
results: A total of 418 saliva samples were collected from the eight subjects participating in the two chamber studies. Overall, EBV DNA was detected in 35% of the 418 total saliva samples collected from these subjects. The subjects in the 60-day chamber study had EBV DNA in 13% (range 0 to 31%) of their samples, and the subjects in the 91-day study had EBV DNA in 51% (range 33 to 81%) of their samples. During both studies, all but one subject (in the 60-day chamber study) shed EBV. Sixteen urine samples collected from the subjects of both chamber studies before and after the in-chamber phase were analyzed for CMV DNA. Interestingly, not a single sample showed evidence of CMV DNA. The presence of CMV DNA in urine from the control group was also rare (1/81 samples). Viral antibody titers for EBV and CMV measured in samples from all 8 subjects before and after the study were not significantly different. Therefore, the data were pooled for further analysis. No significant differences in EBV VCA, EBV EA, or CMV IgG antibody titers were observed before and after either of the studies. Interestingly, EBV antibody titers did not differ significantly from the controls. However, CMV antibody titers of subjects were greater than those of the control group before and after the study. Our current finding of increased viral reactivation in closed chamber study subjects agrees with our previous Space Shuttle and Antarctic data. These results support and extend our previous observations that latent viral reactivation increases during space flight, which is consistent with a stress-induced decrease in immune function.

title: The Effect of Spaceflight on Cartilage Cell Cycling and Differentiation
research_area: Skeletal physiology; Cell and molecular biology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Although space flight has long been known to induce loss of bone and muscle, the exact mechanism of loss is not understood. This experiment studied the effect of microgravity conditions on the cell differentiation process, which appears to be the physiological event most affected by space flight. Cartilage cells from chick limb buds flown in space were studied to determine the impacts on the differentiated cell, the cell cycle and differentiation process, and cell death.
approach: Mesenchymal cells from chick limb buds were grown for eight days preflight and then placed into WRAIR incubators. The incubators were divided into flight and Ground Control groups, and the flight group was flown for nine days. Cartilage samples were fixed with 70% ethyl alcohol and 2% sucrose at 2, 4, 7, and 9 days of flight. After flight, the samples were collected, divided and analyzed using either flow cytometry or immunocytochemistry.
results: After performing flow cytometry, the flight cells showed significantly higher Cyclin E, PCNA and p27 protein content compared to Ground Controls, which indicates that the flight cells experienced more cell cycle activity. Flight cells metabolized glucose to lactate continuously throughout the flight and possibly at a reduced rate compared to Ground Controls, although this significance is still indeterminate. No significant differences were found when comparing number of cartilage nodules and cell cycling within the nodules in the flight and control groups. In conclusion, this experiment proved indeterminate due to significant variation in the flow cytometry and immunocytochemistry results. However, some of the collected data aided the understanding of how the cycling cells contribute to tissue growth.

title: Otoconial Morphology in Space-Flown Rats
archive_status: No data from this study was submitted to LSDA. Please contact LSDA if you know of available data.
objectives: Weightlessness imposes a new bias against which translational accelerations must be judged. One question to be answered by space flight is whether gravity receptors will show degenerative changes during short- or long-term exposures to microgravity. The ultrastructural study of inner ears obtained from space-flown rats and from age-matched, ground-based controls is a first step in attempting to answer this question. This study was to determine whether the system adjusts to this change in bias induced by exposure to microgravity by undergoing visible alteration or degeneration, or more subtle adaptive processes.
approach: Inner ear tissues were obtained from three rats perfused intravascularly, and inner ears of an additional six rats were fixed. Macular tissues were prepared for ultrastructural study. Otoconial complexes were removed during dehydration and mounted on stubs for study in a scanning electron microscope. Approximately half of the masses were positioned upright and the others with the underside exposed.
results: Otoconia of control and flight rats showed only normal configurations; there were no signs of degeneration in any of the flight specimens. It seems possible that instead of demineralization, a slight increase in otoconial mass occurred. This may be because the loading on the receptor may be tied to the functioning of the system, that is, to a species' requirements for resolving translational acceleratory forces with respect to gravitational attraction. Species differences could account for the fact that an increase in number of utricular otoconia occurred in the space-flown rats, while an increase in their size was observed in a study of space-flown amphibia. Also, in space-flown rats, tiny otoconia appeared to be growing within organic material at the surfaces of already existing otoconia; and in the sacculus, otoconia were achieving more rounded body surfaces than was typical of controls. These observations suggested that in a mature system, it may be easier to grow or spawn new otoconial substance on already existing units rather than to produce otoconia de novo.

title: Commercial Biomedical Testing Module (CBTM)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Commercial Biomedical Testing Module: Effects of Osteoprotegerin on Bone Maintenance in Microgravity (CBTM) provides the capability to use the microgravity environment for evaluation of new pharmaceutical candidates in small mammals. Results may expedite the review of new pharmaceuticals for allowing immediate access to new disease treatments. Osteoporosis is a debilitating disease that afflicts millions of people worldwide. One of the physiological changes experienced by astronauts during spaceflight is the accelerated loss of bone mass due to the lack of gravitational loading on the skeleton. This bone loss experienced by astronauts is similar to osteoporosis in the elderly population. Osteoprotegerin (OPG), a bone metabolism regulator, is being considered by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) as a new treatment for osteoporosis. APPROACH Laboratory mice were treated with either OPG or a placebo before launch. The mice were housed in an Animal Enclosure Module (AEM) designed specifically for spaceflight. This experiment provided a preclinical trial model to determine the effectiveness of OPG in treating bone loss.
results: Mice exposed to microgravity exhibited a 15 - 20 percent decline in femur elastic strength and a 40 - 60 percent decrease in bone formation when compared to the controls. The femur elastic strength decline was caused by three mechanisms: reduced bone formation, increased bone resorption, and inhibition of mineralization. OPG treatment in mice exposed to microgravity nearly reversed the decline in strength and the increase in bone resorption found in untreated mice. Gene expression data is available in the NASA GeneLab Data Repository at https://genelab-data.ndc.nasa.gov/ (accession number GLDS-21, Effects of spaceflight on murine skeletal muscle gene expression).

title: Cardiovascular Conditioning
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The cardiovascular system was the first major body system to show physiologic change following space flight. As a result, it was extensively investigated by various means during the Gemini missions. The purpose of the Cardiovascular Conditioning (M001) experiment was to determine the effectiveness of the pneumatic cuff technique in preventing orthostatic intolerance to a 1-G stress after space flights lasting up to 14-days. Water immersion studies in support of this experiment indicated that pneumatic leg cuffs alone, when inflated to 70 to 75 mm Hg for 2 out of every 6 minutes, provided protection against cardiovascular deconditioning. Four healthy, male subjects were immersed in water up to neck level for six hours on two separate occasions, two days apart. Before and after each period of water immersion, the heart rate of each subject was measured during a tilt table test. Data analysis indicated that the first water immersion period, during which the subjects' did not wear leg cuffs, resulted in cardiovascular deconditioning. This was evidenced by cardioacceleration in excess of that observed during the tilt-table test prior to water immersion. Also, syncope occurred in two of the four subjects. Tilt table responses following the second period of immersion, during which leg cuffs were utilized, revealed that a definite protective effect was achieved. Cardioacceleration was less pronounced, and no syncope occurred. The physiological mechanisms responsible for the observed efficacy of the cuff technique were not completely understood. It was hypothesized that the cuffs prevented thoracic blood volume overload, thus resulting in the Henry-Gauer response with its resultant diuresis and decreased effective circulating blood volumes. It was also postulated that the cuffs induced an intermittent artificial hydrostatic gradient (by increasing venous pressure distal to the cuffs during inflation) across the walls of the leg veins, mimicking the deterioration of normal venomotor reflexes. It was theorized that this action would decrease the pooling of blood in the lower extremities and increase the effective circulating blood volume upon return to a 1-G environment following weightlessness or its simulation.
approach: One astronaut from each of the Gemini 5 (8-day) and Gemini 7 (14-day) missions participated as a test subject, described here as subjects A and B respectively. The remaining astronaut aboard each respective flight acted as a control subject (subjects C and D.) In-flight, the two test subjects wore cuff devices designed to maintain venous pressure in the lower extremities. The experiment equipment consisted of a pneumatic cycling system and a pair of pneumatic cuffs. The cycling system alternately inflated and deflated the cuffs that were form-fitted to the proximal thigh region of the test subjects. The bladder portion of each cuff was positioned on the dorsomedial aspect of each thigh. Upon reaching orbit, the cuffs were automatically pressurized to 80 mm Hg for 2 minutes out of every 6 minutes. The system was capable of continuous operation during flight, but could be switched off for sleep periods if required. The experiment imposed no operational requirement other than activation of the device after reaching orbit and deactivation prior to reentry. The experiment lasted for the first 4 days of the Gemini 5 mission and for the first 13.5 days of the Gemini 7 mission. During the Gemini 5 mission, the cuffs were to operate continuously for the full 8-day mission. After 4 days, however, the pneumatic programmer stopped cycling when the oxygen pressure in the storage vessel dropped below operational levels. Before and after flight, all Gemini Program astronauts, including the subjects of this experiment, were given a series of tilt table tests to measure orthostatic intolerance. Parameters measured included heart rate, blood pressure, pulse pressure, and leg volume. Leg volume was determined by the strain-gage technique. Changes in blood volume, plasma volume, and red cell mass were determined using radioactive isotope (125I, 51Cr) techniques. Body mass was also measured. The tilt table test protocol was as follows: each subject lay supine for 5 minutes. The subject was then elevated into a +70 degree, head-up tilt position for 15 minutes. Leg volume was measured for the duration of the 15-minute tilt. After the tilt was completed, the subject was again supine for 5 minutes. Leg volume was measured for an additional 5 minutes after the tilt was completed. Heart rate and blood pressure were monitored continuously throughout the 25-minute test. All subjects completed three preflight tilt-table tests. The astronauts of Gemini 5 completed 6 post flight tilt table tests, while the astronauts of Gemini 7 completed 4 post flight tilt table tests. Post flight tests for the Gemini 5 astronauts were conducted between 2-104 hours after recovery. The Gemini 7 astronauts were measured between 2-56 hours after recovery.
results: Post flight heart rates: All four Gemini 5 and 7 crewmembers had increased resting heart rates during the first 12 to 24 hours after recovery. Subjects A and C had a twofold greater increase in heart rate than did subjects B and D during the first two post flight tilts. Although subjects B and D had a smaller increase in heart rate during the tilt procedures, subject B had to be returned to the supine position after 12 minutes during the first tilt. This experience on the first tilt procedure may have accounted for his increased heart rate during the second and third tilts. The heart rates of all subjects decreased during succeeding tilts to approximately preflight values. Post flight blood pressure: All four crewmembers had decreased resting systolic blood pressure 2 to 4 hours after recovery. Test subject B and control subject C maintained systolic pressures that were lower than the preflight values throughout the post flight test period. All four crewmembers had a decreased resting diastolic blood pressure during each post flight tilt test except during the first and last tilts of control subject C and during the second tilt of test subject B. Post flight pulse pressure: All four Gemini 5 and Gemini 7 crewmembers had narrowed pulse pressures during the first post flight tilt (compared with the preflight tilt and the post flight resting values). Test subject A and control subject C also had a significant pulse pressure narrowing during the second (8 to 12 hours) post flight tilt. Control subject C maintained a low systolic pressure during the third and forth tilts, whereas the systolic pressure of test subject A returned to normal preflight levels after the second post flight tilt. Test subject B and control subject D had no significant pulse pressure narrowing during the second, third, or fourth post flight tilts. Post flight leg volume changes: Leg volume changes during the post flight tilts indicated that test subjects A and B, who wore the pneumatic cuffs, pooled significantly less blood in their legs than did control subjects C and D. During the first post flight tilt table test, test subject B had signs of vasodepressor syncope. The tilt was interrupted and the subject was returned to the supine position. The episode occurred despite no evidence of increased pooling of blood in the lower extremities. During subsequent tilts, test subject B showed no signs of syncope or of impending syncope. It was significant that this episode of syncope occurred despite the fact that the measured blood volume of both test-subject B and control-subject D was unchanged from preflight values. Researchers concluded it was possible that the syncopal episode was the result of sudden vasodilation. The effects of which were a pooling of blood in the visceral region, a diminished venous return and cardiac output, and a decrease in cerebral blood flow. Blood volume, plasma volume, and red cell mass variation: Subjects' B and D of Gemini 7 sustained a 4 and 15 percent increase respectively in plasma volume during the 14-day mission. Subjects' A and C of Gemini 5 lost 4 and 8 percent respectively of their plasma volume during the 8-day mission. All four subjects lost 7 to 20 percent of their red cell mass. The decrease in red cell mass and the increase in plasma volume of subjects B and D offset each other to result in a net zero percent change in blood volume. The reduction in plasma volume and red cell mass subjects A and C contributed to a 12 and 13 percent decrease in blood volume. These changes in blood volume may have reflected, in part, the extent of hydration of the Gemini 5 subjects, but this was not true for the Gemini 7 subjects. Body mass changes: Test subject A and control subject C sustained a loss in body mass of 8.5 and 7.5 pounds, respectively. Test subject B and control subject D lost 6.5 and 10.0 pounds, respectively. These values were similar to those observed after other missions of shorter duration. Subjects' B and D regained less body weight during the first 24 hours post flight than did subjects A and C (25 percent and 40 percent compared with 50 percent.) Flight conditions that were operative during the Gemini 7 mission were notably different from those that were operative during the Gemini 5 mission. These differences were of sufficient magnitude that a comparison of the experiment results from the two missions was difficult, if not impossible. The Gemini 7 mission was different from previous Gemini missions in that the Gemini 7 astronauts did not wear their suits during an extensive portion of the 14-day flight. Their food and water intake more closely approximated the optimum than it did on previous flights that assured better hydration and fluid electrolyte balance. Also, the Gemini 7 exercise regimen was more rigorous than that used on previous flights. These variables, in addition to the individual variability, precluded any direct comparison of results on the two missions. Further, the pneumatic cuffs were operative during only the first half of the Gemini 5 mission. The post flight physiological responses of subjects B and D were different from, and generally improved in comparison with, those observed for subjects A and C. However, it was difficult to determine which variables were responsible for the observed improvement. Researchers concluded that pneumatic cuffs were not effective in decreasing post flight orthostatic intolerance. This conclusion was not based on the occurrence of syncope during the first tilt of test subject B. It was based on the higher heart rates observed (as compared with the control subject) during subsequent tilts. (Syncope itself is a poor indicator of the extent of cardiovascular deconditioning.) Researchers did conclude, however, that the pneumatic cuffs did lessen the extent of post flight pooling of blood in the legs as determined by the strain-gage technique.
