title: Physiological Variables of EVA Participants--An Update
research_area: Cardiovascular physiology; Pulmonary physiology; Clinical medicine
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The physiological variables of extravehicular activity (EVA) participants were first explored in the October 1998 issue of the LSAH Newsletter. This initial article investigated EVA participants within the Shuttle program, up to January 1998. Between then and December 2001, 26 additional EVAs within 12 missions have been performed. All but three of these EVAs were performed in support of assembly and maintenance of the International Space Station. As this assembly and maintenance process is a continual one, many more EVAs will have to be performed in the future.
approach: The following is an updated look at EVA astronauts, to see if the increased number of participants leads to observations different than previously noted. As before, this analysis compares physiological variables between astronauts who have flown in space (i.e., crewmembers) and those who have performed EVAs. Currently, 312 individuals have been selected into the NASA astronaut corps. Of these, 197 have flown in the Shuttle program through the launch of STS-108 on December 5, 2001. Within the same time period, approximately 109 EVAs have been performed. In analyzing the data, each mission is counted as an individual even for both Shuttle astronauts who have flown and EVA participants. Therefore, one astronaut may count for more than one crewmember, and be in more than one age group. Through December 2001 there have been 536 NASA crewmembers, with 79 EVA participants. Of the Shuttle crewmembers, 519 had available data from the annual examination closest to, and before, their missions. Their gender distribution shows that 86.4% are males. Almost half of these crewmembers were between 38 and 43 years of age, making this age group the largest subset. About 70% of the entire group was younger than 44 years of age. Means of the following variables were measured for the Shuttle crewmembers: age (at time of examination), body mass index (BMI), percentage of body fat, mean VO2 max , and maximum heart rate (MHR). BMI and percentage of body fat provide measures of fatness for the group. BMI, which is more accurate for a group of people than for an individual, is calculated by dividing the weight (in kilograms) by the squared height (in meters). A BMI between 22-26 for both men and women is about standard. Percentage of body fat is an estimation of fatness based on the sum of three skin-fold measurements and age at last birthday. Values of 10%-15% for men, and 20%-25% for women, are considered to be the norm for the general population. VO2 max and MHR are estimations of cardiovascular fitness that are measured during an Exercise Tolerance Test. VO2 max is measured by the volume of oxygen, in milliliters per kilogram of body weight, expired per minute, and is an indicator of an individual's max aerobic capacity. A higher number indicates a higher aerobic capacity. The normative values of VO2 max for men and women in good aerobic condition in the 30-49 years age group are 41 ml/kg/min and 37 ml/kg/min respectively. The MHR is measured in beats per minute, and lower values are more desirable. For individuals in the 38-49 years of age group, the expected MHR is 179.7 beats per minute. Each EVA per mission is accounted for, so that an astronaut is counted for every EVA mission and the age group s/he has achieved. All 79 EVA participants had data available from examinations closest to and before their missions. The majority (70.9%) of the EVA participants were under the age of 44, and 91.1% of them were male. The small number of female participants precludes data analysis of this subset.
results: As expected, the crewmembers, those in the 30-43 year age group, had higher VO2 max and lower MHR values than the previously mentioned norms. All of the parameters varied only slightly between EVA participants and Shuttle crewmembers. The largest age group representation for both EVA participants and crewmembers is in the 38-43 year age group (48.1% and 47.2%, respectively). In comparing the majority of each group's subjects (38-43 year age group), there is very little difference in the BMI, average percentage of body fat, or mean MHR between the two age groups. When these values are compared in terms of aging trend, EVA participants, unlike Shuttle crewmembers, did not show the expected trend of increasing BMI, increasing percentage of body fat, and decreasing VO2 max in progressing from the younger to older age groups. This may mean that EVA participants maintain better overall fitness within the older age group than crewmembers as a whole. However, the small age group subsets of this sample may also affect their mean values. There is little difference in the age makeup between the Shuttle crewmembers and EVA participants. The majority of crewmembers and EVA participants also have very similar fitness levels, as shown in the small difference in the physiological variables values between the two age groups. The difference in aging trend between the two groups may indicate that EVA training facilities maintenance of aerobic fitness for the crewmembers. As the entire astronaut corps ages, and more EVA data accumulate from the maintenance and assembly of the ISS, a more comprehensive analysis can be performed to substantiate this observation.

title: Clinical Biochemistry
research_area: Clinical medicine; Network physiology; Renal, fluid and electrolyte physiology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The Clinical Biochemistry studies performed during the Apollo 7-17 missions were instituted to provide data that would, in concert with medical histories and physical examinations, permit an objective assessment of crew physical status. Since comparable results were not consistently available from the Mercury and Gemini programs, these studies provided investigators with their first documentation of the normal biochemistry of astronauts. The objectives of the biochemical studies were: 1. To provide routine laboratory data for assessment of preflight crew physical status and for postflight comparisons. 2. To detect clinical or pathological abnormalities, which might have required remedial action preflight. 3. To discover, as early as possible, any infectious disease process during the postflight quarantine periods following certain missions. 4. To obtain fundamental medical knowledge relative to man's adjustment to and return from the space flight environment.
approach: Chemical measurements of blood and urine constituents were one portion of a comprehensive medical examination intended to disclose a state of well-being or the presence of occult disease processes. Blood and urine samples were collected pre- and postflight only. Preflight, venous whole blood samples were collected at 30, 15 and 5 days prior to flight. Postflight samples were collected at approximately 2 hours, 1 day, 6 days, and 13 days after landing. Twenty milliliters of blood was drawn during each sampling session. Preflight samples were frozen immediately then transported to the JSC clinical laboratories for analysis. Postflight samples were stabilized and returned to JSC for analysis. For both sets of samples, time critical analyses were performed prior to freezing the samples. Fasting blood samples, with the exception of the sample collected 2 hours after flight, were drawn at approximately the same time each day with the astronaut in the recumbent position. Twenty-four hour urine samples, starting with Apollo 8, were collected at the same time the blood draws were performed. The urine was aliquoted, stabilized, and frozen for transport to JSC for subsequent analysis. Whenever possible, an aliquot of serum was frozen and stored for subsequent or retrospective analysis. The medical history of each crewmember was obtained in order to evaluate the data obtained for this study. Medication history was obtained one month preflight, during flight, and postflight. Exposure to radiation and toxic products (if known) were recorded. Description of pertinent history and physical examination findings were also noted. The crew consumed a conventional diet during preflight and postflight periods and flight food throughout the mission. The approximate dietary intake as well as the amount and times of alcohol consumption were recorded. No restrictions were placed on fluid intake.
results: Biochemical measurements from all the Apollo crewmembers showed no values outside of the normal range established for the astronaut population. However, postflight results showed significant changes over preflight measurements. This comparison described consistent and significant decreases in potassium, magnesium, lactic dehydrogenase (LDH), creatine phosphokinase (CPK), albumin, uric acid, triglycerides and cholesterol. Increases were described in creatinine, total protein, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and glucose. Decreases were measured in the 24-hour urine volume and in the 24-hour excretion of sodium, potassium, chloride, magnesium, and uric acid. Increases were noted in specific gravity and osmolality. Since the preflight diet of the astronauts was not controlled, there was a large deviation in the means that resulted in large standard deviations. Blood Constituents Measurements Postflight decreases in serum potassium, although not significant clinically, were found in 24 of the 33 crewmembers. Based on samples collected during the Apollo 16 and 17 missions, the increase in aldosterone, which occurred during flight, was believed to be partly responsible for the decrease in serum potassium and for the lack of change in serum sodium postflight. A decrease in serum magnesium was interpreted as evidence of a reestablishment of ionic equilibrium, principally in muscle tissue, which occurred while in space. Immediate preflight creatinine and blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels were increased over preflight mean values with return toward preflight levels by one day after recovery. These increases, often associated with pre-renal diversion of water, increased protein catabolism and impaired renal function. Although no evidence of renal impairment was suggested in the chemistry data, it could not be ruled out. Increased protein catabolism or dietary factors probably influenced the creatinine and BUN levels, as well as the state of hydration of the returning crewmembers. Serum Creatine Phosphokinase (CPK) levels was reduced immediately postflight, and mild elevations were evident 24 hours after recovery. This alteration was probably a result of both muscle inactivity incident to weightlessness and increased muscular activity during the first 24-hour postflight interval. The decrease in LDH could not be as readily explained, since this enzyme would be expected to increase with exercise. However, it is likely that preflight LDH levels were atypically elevated due to rigorous physical conditioning by the crew, such that the postflight level reduction in LDH may simply have been a return to normal enzyme balance. Postflight levels of blood glucose were elevated indicating a possible reaction to the stress of reentry. This was supported by increases in epinephrine and steroid levels, which correlated well with the hematologic findings of leukocytosis. For additional results see experiment AP008 Endocrine, Electrolyte, and Fluid Volume Changes Associated with Apollo Missions . However, short-term bed rest is also associated with elevated glucose levels, and raised the possibility that these increased levels seen after the missions were not entirely a result of stress. This may have been a result of diminished uptake of glucose by inactive muscle cells. White blood cell counts reverted to preflight levels within 24 hours postflight. The increase in total protein at recovery, and the subsequent decrease in the days following, portrayed the immediate postflight state of hydration of the individual crewmembers and the redistribution of fluid compartments that occurred throughout the postflight interval. The immunological proteins were elevated also in many of the crewmen, which perhaps contributed to total protein elevation. Urine Constituent Measurements Postflight 24-hour urine collections revealed significant retention of sodium, potassium, and chloride ions associated with reduced total urine volume and hyperosmolality. These findings are consistent with the reestablishment of preflight fluid and electrolyte balance and with hormonal adjustments required for readaptation for the space flight environment. The decrease in urinary uric acid predictably reflects the anabolism that occurs postflight. Although dietary factors cannot be ruled out in uric acid metabolism, by six days postflight the crewmember should have consumed diets sufficient to return those levels to the preflight mean.

title: Endocrine, Electrolyte, and Fluid Volume Changes Associated with Apollo Missions
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The objective of this study was to evaluate the biochemical changes in Apollo crewmembers. The areas studied were balance of fluid and electrolytes, regulation of calcium metabolism, adaptation to the environment, and regulation of metabolic processes. Although these studies, like others of the Apollo program, were designed mainly for crew health maintenance and well-being, the results of these studies provided an idea of the nature and the extent of the endocrine responses by the crewmen who flew the Apollo missions.
approach: The same general protocol described below was used for the Apollo 7-10 and 15-17 missions. It has been reported that deviations from this procedure were necessary during the Apollo 11-14 missions due to the constraints imposed by the lunar quarantine program. The general protocol was as follows: with the crewmembers reclining for 30 minutes, a 45 ml sample of venous blood was drawn 30, 15, and 5 days before flight. Blood samples were also drawn approximately 2 hours, and 1, 7 and 14 days postflight. All preflight blood samples were drawn after a fasting period from midnight to 7:00 a.m., approximately one hour after waking up. Postflight samples were drawn regardless of time of day and food intake. The sample drawn two hours after recovery was taken approximately six hours after the crew's last meal and eight hours after waking up. Pre- and postflight 24-hour urine samples were collected from each crewman on the same days as the blood samples. Additionally, urine samples were collected in flight during the Apollo 16 and 17 missions only. Samples were collected using the Biomedical Urine Sampling System (BUSS), which contained a large 4-liter pooling bag in which the urine was collected. Each pooling bag also contained 10 g of boric acid for stabilizing certain organic constituents. The pooled urine was collected without additive, aliquoted, stabilized with boric acid, and frozen for analysis. One entire 24-hour urine sample was returned for each Apollo 16 crewman. For Apollo 17 collections, a sampling bag was used which could store as much as 120 cc of urine for later analysis. The Apollo 17 collection bags contained 30 ml of lithium chloride. The final lithium concentration was used to estimate total urine volume. Blood samples were analyzed for osmolality, sodium, potassium, chloride, adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), angiotensin I, cortisol, growth hormone (GH), insulin, parathormone, thyroxine, and tri-iodothyronine. The 24-hour urine samples were analyzed for electrolytes, osmolality, volume, aldosterone, cortisol, antidiuretic hormone (ADH), total and fractionated ketosteroids, and amino acids. Prolonged exposure to increased temperature and to the boric acid preservative made the urine samples collected inflight unsuitable for catecholamine or ADH analysis.
results: Apollo crewmen showed an average of 5% decrease in body weight after flight when the mean of the preflight results was compared to the individual postflight values. One-third of this weight was regained within 24 hours after recovery. Significant differences were observed in a 7.3 % decrease in potassium and a 4.5% decrease in magnesium immediately postflight. No significant changes in serum sodium or chloride accompanied these changes. The 24-hour urine electrolyte results exhibited significant decreases in sodium, potassium, chloride and magnesium values. Renin activity, measured as angiotensin I in blood samples, and aldosterone levels, measured in urine, were aids in the understanding of water and electrolyte balance and renal function. Plasma angiotensin I values showed a 488 % increase in the crewmen tested on the day of recovery. This elevation was followed by a significant increase (57%) in urinary aldosterone during the first day following recovery. A postflight 32% decrease in urine volume was detected along with significant increases in osmolality (20%) and ADH (152%). The creatinine clearance results showed no significant change in renal function after flight. A slight but significant increase in blood urea nitrogen (BUN) was found. Urinary calcium, phosphorus, and parathormone (PTH) results reflect normal bone metabolism and seem to reflect normal renal function, as well. Plasma cortisol and ACTH results showed no significant changes, but a mean decrease was found for each hormone. Urinary cortisol demonstrated a 24% increase, whereas the total 17-hydroxycorticosteriod excretion was decreased by 30%. Both catecholamine compounds showed decreases after flight when the data from all crewmen were grouped for analysis. Results of total and fractionated ketosteroid demonstrated a 30% decrease in the total component, which is spread over four fractions: androsterone, etiocholanolone, dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), and 11=OH etiocholanolone. A slight increase was observed in pregnanediol and 11=O etiocholanolone. Glucose showed a 10% increase after flight and insulin showed an increase of 32% after flight. Human growth hormone demonstrated a 304% increase after flight. The postflight increase in thyroxine was statistically significant, whereas slight change was noted in percentage of tri-iodothyronine binding. Variable results were obtained when pre- and postflight levels of six urinary acids were compared. These amino acids were phosphoethanolamine, taurine, glycine, alanine, tyrosine, and ß-alanine. Taurine, however, was consistently elevated after flight by 140%. After considering all of the previously mentioned data, together with the clinical condition of the returning Apollo crewmen, the following hypothesis was proposed to explain the changes: in a weightless environment, there is a tendency for plasma volume to shift from occupying the gravity-dependent extremities to occupying a more even distribution throughout the vascular system. Receptors, possibly in the right atrium, interpret this shift as an increase in vascular volume. This increased volume is counteracted by an increased water loss, followed by a compensatory, adrenal-pituitary-mediated retention of water and sodium and by a continued loss of potassium. Other hormone changes observed are tentatively ascribed to the stresses associated with the condition of the Apollo space flights, to the well known consequences of hypokinesis, and to the metabolic effects of hypocaloric nutritional intake. The crewmembers' in-flight diet of low-residue, high-fat and high-carbohydrate foods may have been the cause of decreased levels of cholesterol, triglycerides and uric acid. However, these values did not return to preflight levels in two weeks after the mission, even though the crew began eating a conventional diet immediately after recovery. This fact suggested possibly that other metabolic consequences were involved. Adrenal steroids have been shown to be elevated during flight which may have accounted for the decrease in the stores of precursor cholesterol, particularly if not replaced by the diet. The decreased cholesterol was in agreement with elevated thyroxine levels, and contributed to the evidence of increased thyroid function during flight.

title: Effective Dose Measurement during EVA
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: One of the many risks of long-duration space flights is the dose burden from cosmic radiation, especially at times of maximum solar activity. At such times, for instance during an extravehicular activity (EVA) when the wall of the spacecraft is not there to protect the astronauts, cosmic radiation poses a potentially serious health threat. Accurate dose measurement as well as the measurements of the ratio of low to high linear energy transfer (LET) dose components will become increasingly important in forthcoming years during the assembly of large orbital stations. Therefore an onboard thermoluminescent dosimeter (TLD) system capable of providing such measurements offers a solution for EVA dosimetry.
approach: The TLD system used during the NASA 4 mission (Pille '96 system), was a modified version of the Pille '95 TLD system used by the European Space Agency (ESA) during the Euromir '95 mission. The difference between the units was that the sensitivity of the reader was enhanced, due to the short duration of most EVAs. Also, the LiF TLD with a linear heating profile was introduced with this system to ensure effective LET measurement using the high temperature region (HTR) method. The TLD system was brought to Mir aboard STS-81 and recorded environmental space radiation measurements until May 6, 1997. The TLD system consisted of a portable TLD reader (Pille '96) and eight individual dosimeters. Seven TLDs were mounted at locations throughout the base block, two of which were used on one occasion to record radiation dose during an EVA. TLDs were removed from their respective locations and analyzed using the TLD reader at eight separate times during the mission. The memory card from the TLD reader was returned to the ground at the end of the mission for further analysis. This experiment was also scheduled to be performed during NASA 5. However, the TLD reader was located in the Spektr module which was damaged on June 25, 1997, and thus became inaccessible. This incident resulted in no data being collected for the NASA 5 mission.
results: The dose rate (10.0 mGy/h) measured by an individual dosimeter on the astronaut was significantly lower than the mean value of the other three dosimeters (15.0 mGy/h) located at the working area and sleeping cabin. Three of the dosimeters (1A, 2A and 3A) were located at the same place as Area Passive Dosimeters (APDs) exposed during the NASA 2 mission (NMA-1, NMA-2 and NMA-3). These results show that the radiation situation remained virtually unchanged. The extra dose due to EVA was compared to the dose measured inside, and showed that the mean ratio, EVA/inside, without any correction is 4.2. Results from the Euromir '95 mission have been used for correcting the effect of higher background radiation inside the space station due to the South Atlantic Anomaly (SAA). The corrected EVA/inside dose rate ratio is 3.15. The glow curves from LiF-TLDs exposed on Mir Space Station show significantly enhanced high temperature TL-emission compared to glowcurves after 137Cs irradiation. According to the calibrations the estimated mean LET value was 7.5 ± 1 keV/mm.

title: Acoustic Noise During the Phase III Chamber Test
research_area: Human factors; Neuroscience; Environmental monitoring; Clinical medicine; Behavior and performance
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: During the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP), four test subjects participated in the 91-day experiment. As part of the acoustic study, they measured sound decibels in different life support areas of the test chamber. The LMLSTP enclosed test chamber was divided into three levels. The first level contained general living quarters with a dining/work table, communications, test and video equipment. The first level also contained a kitchen, bathroom and laundry facilities. The second level contained the mechanical equipment for air revitalization, storage and stationary bicycle. This level was the noisiest, and due to the location of the stairs, the subjects had to pass through this level while traveling between the first and third levels. The third level contained primary living quarters with bedrooms, partial bath and entertainment equipment. This level was the quietest. The goal of the acoustic noise study was to monitor and describe the noise environment of the 20-foot chamber during its extended 91-day operation. Noise levels were measured at multiple locations and subjects performed hearing threshold tests called audiograms at various frequencies before and after the chamber experience. The hearing threshold is the softest sound a person is able to hear. It is not clear what level of hearing threshold shift is cause for concern, but it is certain that larger changes in threshold are more serious. Monitoring acoustic noise in the chamber enabled recommendations to be formulated for hearing protection, if necessary. These measurements also established a baseline measure of the noise environment for comparison with other Earth-bound analog test facilities. In acoustic studies, noise is defined as undesirable sounds in the air in the hearing range of approximately 20 to 20,000 Hz. A certain level of noise can be tolerated over an eight-hour workday without long-term hearing detriment, but this same noise level may not be acceptable if it is continuous over a 24-hour period, such as in the closed environment of a space vehicle. During periods of loud noise, the blood vessels in the ear involuntarily constrict and reduce blood flow to protect the hair cells responsible for hearing. Outer hair cells respond to low intensity sound and become continuously stimulated or "saturated", by loud noise. The inner hair cells remain functional because they respond only to high intensity sounds. A temporary hearing threshold shift may thus occur due to chronic noise. An upward shift of hearing threshold can become permanent, since the outer hair cells that respond to low intensity sound would not have a chance to recover their normal function and would eventually die. Government regulations developed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) set the maximum background noise level that an individual may be exposed to during an eight-hour day at 90 dB. Exposure to levels over 85 dB requires routine monitoring for hearing loss and the institution of hearing conservation programs. The EPA suggests that an eight-hour average noise level over 75 dB presents a reasonable risk for hearing loss.
approach: LMLSTP test subjects collected sound level measurements in various locations throughout the chamber module starting with entry day ceremonies, continuing regularly during the 91-day operation and ending with the welcome home celebrations. In total, 283 sample measurements of acoustic noise were collected from the chamber during the experiment. Noise levels were measured using an audio dosimeter and a more accurate sound level meter to obtain an A-weighted overall sound pressure level measurement at each location. The A-weighting represents the ear sensitivity by combining all frequencies together and averaging them to give a decibel value. Sample measurement locations were determined using two methods. In one method, each subject was asked to subjectively identify the noise sources and noisier locations in the chamber. Following discussion, the subjects jointly decided upon 25 locations to measure noise, including quiet locations that served as controls. The other method of determining measurement locations was the use of predetermined, geographically-spaced areas on each chamber level. Four different heights above the floor were monitored based on locations where a hypothetical fiftieth-percentile person's ear would be located during various activities. Measurements were taken at 10 cm above the surface of the floor to represent a person lying down, at 75 cm above the floor to represent a person sitting on the floor, at 120 cm above the floor to monitor a person sitting in a chair, and at 150 cm above the floor to represent a person standing. The locations were spaced at 30-degree increments about 60 cm from the wall, space permitting, and at the center axis of each level. Locations where the subjects were likely to spend more time were also chosen, such as a computer workstation, bed, stove, table, exercise machine, etc. A measurement was taken within 60 to 100 cm of the middle of any large area not already measured by other methods. Since this was a screening procedure, most data were rounded off to the nearest unit. Noise loudness is measured using sound level meters. Total noise exposure over a period of time is measured with a noise dosimeter. To determine how acoustic noise levels varied throughout a typical 24-hour day for each subject, an Ametek Audio Dosimeter (Model MK-3) was used in the dosimeter mode. An average was determined each minute as loudness equivalent (Leq 1 min) of a 24-hr period. This method produced 1440 samples each day. Data was downloaded to a desktop computer and graphed as noise level versus time, creating a histogram for each selected noise level interval. Each test subject wore the dosimeter over two 24-hour periods. Additionally, one subject wore the dosimeter for approximately one hour before, and one hour after, entering the chamber on the first day and an hour before and after exiting the chamber on the last day. On each of three other days, the dosimeter was placed in a central location in a bedroom, left among equipment on the second level, and attached to the ceiling in the middle of the first level. The exact days that the subjects wore the dosimeter, and the exact days and locations that the dosimeter was placed in a room were up to the subjects' discretion. Investigators wanted to know whether or not the noise levels inside the chamber would affect the threshold hearing levels of the subjects over the course of the 91-day stay in chamber. Hearing tests, called pure-tone air conduction audiometry, were conducted under standard conditions at the health clinic at NASA's Johnson Space Center (JSC) in a sound-insulated booth. A microprocessor-controlled audiometer presented pure tone stimuli to the subject and recorded his or her responses. The subject wore a headset through which the sounds were transmitted to each ear. When the subject heard a sound, he or she pushed a button, and the monitoring computer recorded the response. The computer presented sounds at predetermined frequencies and at incremental amplitudes, getting softer until there was no subject response, and then louder until there was a response, to double-check the person's threshold. Each ear was tested independently starting with frequencies of 1000 cycles per second (Hz). This first measurement at 1000 Hz was a training run. Then, the test was conducted at frequencies of 500 Hz, 1000 Hz, 2000 Hz, 3000 Hz, 4000 Hz, 6000 Hz and 8000 Hz for a total of seven data collection sessions and 42 audiogram measurements per subject. In an audiometry test, the hearing level is quantified based on what the normal ear detects, and a score of zero indicates normal hearing. Scores above zero indicate hearing loss. A 100 dB hearing loss at any frequency is nearly equivalent to complete deafness at that particular frequency tested. The four chamber test subjects were each given three audiograms. The first, conducted at the time of medical examination for eligibility, established a baseline measure. The second audiogram was performed within two hours after the subject left the chamber to determine whether there was any shift in hearing threshold after 91 days in the chamber. The third audiogram occurred between six and fourteen weeks after chamber egress to determine whether the hearing threshold had returned to baseline. It was expected that there would be a hearing threshold shift on egress day, but that no permanent shift would occur.
results: On the first chamber level, the acoustic noise from 105 measurements averaged 63.2 dB(A). The noisiest general area was the airlock, which averaged 63.7 dB(A), and where major noise contributors included exercise machines and ventilation fans. The only measurements that equaled or exceeded 70 dB(A) were from intermittent noise sources. The television was the loudest measured equipment noise source (average 75.2 dB(A)). The second level was much noisier, and the subjects reportedly avoided the area. The average noise level over 94 measurements was 74.6 dB(A). Only two of the samples were measured at less than 70 dB(A). Twelve measurements were in excess of 80 dB(A). On the third level, which was quieter than the others, noise levels were similar to those in a typical single-family residence. The average noise level over 84 measurements was 51.5 dB(A). Measurements in the immediate proximity of the beds averaged 42.4 dB(A). The noisiest area on the third level was in the hallway, averaging 59.8 dB(A), especially near the ladder that led to the noisier second level. Data from the dosimeter attached to a subject for a 24-hour period was consistent with that obtained by the sound level meter. It was possible to discern where the subject was in the chamber by analyzing the readings from the dosimeter. The first level's background noise was measured in the mid-60 dB(A) range, with an occasional spike attributed to human voices during conversation. Periods of time where noise measured above 70 dB(A) represented transitions through, or short visits to, the louder second level. Rest or quiet work on the third level could be assumed from the periods of time that measured 60 dB(A). When the subjects exited the chamber at egress, the dosimeters measured above 90 dB(A) during the first 10 minutes and above 80 dB(A) for most of the first hour. Audiogram measurements of the subjects on the pre-test ranged from 0 to 50 dB. A measure of 0 indicates that the threshold of hearing is the same as that for an average person without hearing loss, while larger numbers indicate hearing loss. Shifts of 5 dB or less are not considered problematic because they are within the range of expected test errors. On egress-day, audiogram measurements were 0 to 50 dB. Post-test measurements were 0 to 45 dB. For two subjects, all measurements were at or below 20 db; for another subject, all were at or below 25 dB. The final subject gave readings at or below 10 dB in one ear, while the other ear measured hearing loss in the 45 to 50 dB range for all three-test administrations. Audiometry data graphs indicate no clear distinction among pre-test, egress day and post-test audiometry measurements. A modified sign test was performed on the data as an indication of the overall tendency of the measured hearing threshold. Arithmetic differences between the egress day and pre-test measures were obtained for each data pair. There was no significant difference between the two measurements for hearing loss or improvement. However, a similar comparison showed that the hearing threshold measured at the post-test was better than either the pre-test or egress day tests. Yet, of the 56 comparisons among the pre-test, egress day and post-test, there were five for which the egress day measurements suggested hearing threshold loss that did not return to pre-test baseline level. Some interesting factors may explain the audiogram results. Upon egress, cheering crowds generated more noise than that found in the living areas of the chamber. This can be observed from the dosimeter readings. The loud celebration noise may have confounded the results of the egress day measures that were taken within two hours after egress. Another confounding factor may have been the subjects' environment during the pre-test baseline measures. During this timeframe, the subjects were involved in the development, assembly and testing of the mechanical equipment for the chamber. All pre-test hearing measurements were taken during the afternoon, after at least a half-day of work in a noisy environment. The subjects were also involved in the operation and maintenance of this equipment during the 91 days of the chamber test. About a week after egress day, the subjects took vacations, and the equipment was turned off. So the post-test measures were obtained after the subjects had been in a different noise environment, and under different stress conditions that were not monitored. After the first data were analyzed and reported to the subjects in the chamber, steps were taken to reduce the noise. Noise insulation barriers were constructed and redundant equipment was turned off. Schedules were changed so that the noisiest equipment was not operated when the subjects were in that area. The results of this study will be used to provide motivation to reduce the noise levels of the air and water revitalization equipment. A continuing benefit for habitation study crews is an increased understanding and awareness of the noise levels in a closed environment.

title: Stability and Precision of Human Performance During a Spaceflight Mission
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The success of long-term space flights with humans depends in part on harmonious individual and group behavior. The development of a technology that can effectively predict and provide behavioral support for individuals during prolonged exposure to confined environments is of primary importance. Performance studies of small groups over the past two decades have demonstrated that the consequence of any single individual's behavior is a critical determinant of both individual and group behavior under conditions of prolonged social and cultural isolation. Computerized procedures have been developed during ground-based studies for engendering and maintaining stable measures of complex human behaviors, including cognitive and psychomotor performances. In studies involving continuous performance monitoring, human participants were able to work productively and energetically over extended time intervals. The stability and sensitivity of the measures generated made it possible to assess both decrements and enhancements of performances affected by such things as sleep deprivation, medications, and other stressful conditions. The sensitivity and utility of these computerized tests allowed crewmember performance to be evaluated during space flight.
approach: Four subjects participated in this study. A computerized task battery was administered preflight, inflight and postflight. The task battery required approximately 20 minutes to complete and consisted of the following components: A 72 item research version of the Profile of Mood States (POMS) questionnaire requiring a 1 (not at all) to 5 (extremely) keypad rating of adjectives associated with eight empirically derived mood scales. An 11 item Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) requiring the use of a computer tracking ball to move an indicator to a location on a line between the labels titled "not at all" (on the left) and "extremely" (on the right). The action was in response to words on the computer display screen representing the subject's feeling at the time of presentation. A Time Estimation Task (timing measure) requiring that repeated presses on the keypad be spaced by a fixed time interval. The action would advance a point counter and increase the monitoring gauge on the computer display screen. A Repeated Acquisition Task (learning measure) requiring that the subjects learn to press four designated keys on the keypad to complete a sequence of 10 responses. Feedback for correct and incorrect responses was provided on the computer display screen. A new order for pressing the four designated keys was learned each time the task was presented. A Number Recognition Task (measure of short-term memory performance) requiring the subject to hold down two keys simultaneously on the key pad, one of which was designated a "yes" key and the other a "no" key. An array of numbers presented on the computer display screen disappeared after a brief exposure and a single test number appeared. If the test number was presented in the previous array, the finger was lifted from the "yes" key and if not, the "no" key finger was lifted. A Digit Symbol Substitution Task (psychomotor performance measure) requiring presses on a 9 digit keypad corresponding to the location of filled squares in signaled boxes in 3x3 patterns of boxes that appeared on the computer display screen. The location of the filled squares and the 3x3 signaled boxes on the computer display screen were changed frequently to prevent memorization of the patterns. daily log was also completed during each phase of the study, which provided information on sleep, diet, exercise and medication usage. In addition, debriefing reports were obtained during postflight interviews conducted with each individual. Performances during the computerized task battery were recorded on separate individualized computer diskettes. The time and duration of each data collection session were recorded along with rating scale responses and the number of correct and incorrect responses to each of the programmed tasks. The number of data collection sessions during each phase of the study varied between subjects. Each subject had 6 or more training sessions followed by 5 or more preflight baseline sessions, 5 or more inflight sessions, and 6 or more postflight sessions.

Results obtained with the self-report mood (POMS) and feelings (VAS) scales reliably reflected changes in selected items during each study phase. POMS and VAS data obtained from individual subjects also showed consistency in the relationship between scale items, reflecting progressive changes inflight. Timing performances for all four subjects, as measured by the Time Estimation Task, remained stable and accurate throughout the study with no evident perturbations during any phase of the investigation. Learning performances as measured by the Repeated Acquisition Task were also found to hold up well throughout the study with no identifiable changes. Within each data collection session, all four subjects rapidly learned the correct 10-response sequence. There was evidence of increased efficiency of the learning performance across preflight, inflight, and postflight phases of the study. Across sessions, the efficiency with which these sequences were learned remained stable in the absence of any conditions that affected learning ability. title: Microgravity Effects on Bone Cell Gene Expression
research_area: Cell and molecular biology; Skeletal physiology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Astronauts on long-term missions suffer continuous calcium loss and degradation of skeletal weight-bearing bone mass. Bone loss has been attributed to a decrease in the rate of bone formation, which is possibly caused by both direct and indirect effects of microgravity. Other effects of microgravity include caphalic fluid shifts, loss of muscle mass, space motion sickness, anemia, reduced immune response, and loss of fluid and electrolytes. Systemic or hormonal changes in body chemistry or the cellular response to a lack of stress due to gravity could contribute to these conditions. These experiments attempt to ascertain the mechanisms which cause these gravity related changes.
approach: About 120,000 to 200,000 cells of an osteoblast cell line that is clonally derived from embryonic mouse calvaria, the MC3T3-E1 line, were plated for flight experiments. These plates were grown in 10% serum containing alpha minimal essential medium (a-MEM) and then the plunger units were held in the shuttle middeck for 17 hours before launch. A modified guanidinium thicyanate method was used to extract the cultured osteoblast cells. Agarose gel electrophoresis was used to identify polymerase chain reaction bands. The bands were then photographed and scanned at 400 dpi (dots per inch) for quantification.
results: Comparison of data from the GR, 0-G, and 1-G cells lead to several conclusions. First, it showed that early RNA induction, in conjunction with sera activated growth, was not affected by microgravity. Second, the data supported the conclusion that microgravity affected early protein translation through the reduction of early protein synthesis. Thirdly, the 0-G cells were shown to have a significant change in cell structure, which may impede the formation of osteoblasts. Overall, the study highlighted the importance of having a 1-G control on board to examine the effect of microgravity on the living cells. Overall, the experiment supports the hypothesis that microgravity affects osteoblast morphology, gene expression, and prostaglandin content.

title: Toxicological Assessment of Airborne Volatile Organic Compounds
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Astronauts living for an extended period of time in a closed environment, such as the Mir Space Station, are continuously exposed to pollutants in respirable air. Pollutants originate from material off-gassing, human metabolism, systems and payload leaks, and utility chemicals. If pollutant concentrations reach high levels, crewmembers may experience health problems and scientific experiments could be confounded. This experiment was designed to sample the Mir Space Station air at various locations and times in order to estimate the effects of airborne pollutants on crew health. The following were objectives of this experiment: Determine if Mir air meets U.S. standards for crew health during long-term exposure to trace contaminants Sample air using several types of hardware to compare similarity of sampling methods Sample Mir Space Station air at multiple locations simultaneously to assess spatial variations in the Mir complex Measure ethylene concentrations to determine if plant growth experiments could be affected. Assess the rate of pollutant mixing after hatch opening between shuttle and Mir.
approach: In-flight air sampling was performed on NASA-Mir 2-7. Instantaneous air samples were obtained using grab sample containers (GSCs), and 24 hour time-averaged air samples were obtained using solid sorbent air samplers (SSASs). Formaldehyde badges were used to measure formaldehyde concentrations throughout Mir. The GSCs and SSASs were tested preflight at the Johnson Space Center (JSC) Toxicology Laboratory to ensure that each sampler was clean and could perform as expected. Formaldehyde badges were tested, reconfigured to fit the NASA flight configuration, and packaged for use during flight. During flight, GSC and SSAS samples were taken approximately every thirty days. After each sampling session, the date, time, and location were recorded. Once during each mission, a spatial variation assessment was performed by sampling multiple modules simultaneously. The formaldehyde badges were worn by the crewmembers and also placed in the individual modules. Upon return to Earth, the GSC samples were analyzed by gas chromatography (GC) and a modified EPA TO-14 gas chromatography/mass spectrometry (GC/MS) method. The GC analysis was used to estimate ethylene concentrations. The SSAS samples were analyzed only via the GC/MS method. The filters were removed from the formaldehyde badges and extracted with formaldehyde-free water. The aqueous extracts were then analyzed for formaldehyde using a chromotropic acid-spectrophotometric method.
results: The air quality on NASA-Mir 2-7 met, and exceeded, U.S. standards for human-rated spacecraft. However, the irritant group was slightly above a toxicity index of 1 during NASA-Mir 2, 6, and 7, and the carbon dioxide toxicity index was above 1 during NASA-Mir 2 and 3. The toxicity index was calculated for each toxicological group by summing the ratios of the measured concentrations to the space maximum allowable concentrations for each contaminant in a toxicological group. The high toxicity index of the irritant group was due in part to high concentrations of formaldehyde. As hypothesized, spatial variations of contaminants were small within the Mir complex for both SSAS and GSC samples. The variations were most likely caused by contaminants localized in the different modules. The rate of pollutant mixing after hatch opening between Shuttle and Mir could not be established because of too few samples. A comparison of the U.S. and Russian air sampling methods showed that the Russian AK-1 sorbent system samplers, on average, measured higher concentrations than did the U.S. samplers. During the course of this experiment, several opportunities arose that allowed scientists to study situations that had previously been unexamined. During NASA-Mir 4, a fire was caused by the solid fuel oxygen generator (SFOG); this presented an opportunity to study the contaminants released into the Mir atmosphere due to the fire, and also assess how well the life support system scrubs contaminants from the air. The life support system worked excellent and brought the pollutants associated with the fire back to baseline concentrations within 32 hours. During NASA-Mir 4 the investigators also had the opportunity to compare the results of the formaldehyde badges to those of the formaldehyde active sampler (FAS). Because of the difficulties involved with collecting inflight formaldehyde samples, conclusive results were not obtained. However, another opportunity arose to compare these two methods during the second phase of the Lunar Mars Life Support Test Project (LMLSTP). The results of this test verified the validity of the badges when compared to other methods. During NASA-Mir 5, all sampling hardware was lost due to the decompression of the Spektr module. The focus of the experiment then changed to analyzing how well the humidity control system would scrub a large concentration of ethylene glycol from the air. It was hypothesized that ethylene glycol present in Mir air due to a leak would be removed quickly. However, ethylene glycol detector tubes were used to measure ethylene concentrations, and it took one month for the concentration to drop below the 180-day SMAC level. Additionally, ethylene concentrations measured by the GSCs during the other NASA-Mir missions were determined to be high enough to affect plant growth experiments. The final unscheduled event occurred during a low temperature catalytic oxidizer (LTCO) burn. Improper operation of the LTCO caused dangerously high levels of carbon monoxide (CO) to be released into the Mir atmosphere. The combustion products analyzer (CPA) recorded high levels of CO, but because the crew appeared to be doing well after the incident, the high levels were thought to have been caused by hydrogen interference. Because this was such a serious toxicological incident, many steps have been taken to prevent a reoccurrence. One step, which will be used on the International Space Station (ISS), is the use of a new CPA that has much less cross sensitivity to hydrogen.

title: Neuroendocrine and Cardiovascular Response to Tilt (Flight Analog)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete.  All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Stand tests are used to assess the effects of prolonged weightlessness on orthostatic tolerance during upright posture. Attempts are made to identify high-risk crewmembers before their current flight and adjust their inflight countermeasures accordingly, such as varying the proportion of aerobic versus resistive exercise and adjusting end-of-mission countermeasures. Postflight data are used to guide rehabilitative measures and optimize performance on future flights. Group data are used to assess the influence of other physical and physiological factors such as countermeasures, mission duration, and heat stress.
approach: Subjects were placed on a tilt table with ECG electrodes applied to the chest and abdomen. An intravenous catheter was placed in a vein in the arm. Blood pressure cuffs were placed on the arm that does not contain the catheter. The subject rested for 20 minutes and then blood was drawn. Continuous measures of heart rate, ECG, arterial pressure, and aortic blood flow were collected for five minutes. The subject was then tilted upright at 80 ° for 30 minutes. A final blood draw took place at the conclusion to compare with that drawn in the supine position. If the subject could not tolerate 30 minutes of upright tilt, the tilt table was placed in the -10 ° head down tilt (HDT) position and blood drawn immediately if the subject stood for longer than seven minutes; otherwise, blood was drawn after one minute.
results: During the artificial gravity (AG) pilot study it was concluded that AG can mitigate some aspects of bed rest-induced cardiovascular deconditioning, including orthostatic intolerance and aerobic power. Mechanisms of improvement were not cardiac-mediated, but likely through improved sympathetic responsiveness to orthostatic stress.

objectives: During bed rest studies, the Case Report Form (CRF) provided a mechanism by which nursing and dietary staff, and other subject monitors, could record subject monitoring data. The information was then shared with each of the experiment teams as necessary.
approach: The CRF was comprised of the following forms: Medical Status and Vitals: a daily record of the subject's vital signs, including blood pressure, respiration rate, pulse, body temperature, and weight. The temperature and ambient humidity of the subject's room were also recorded daily. Height was measured once at the beginning of the pre-test, in-test, and post-test periods. Daily Meal Status: a daily record of the times that breakfast, lunch, and dinner meals were started and completed. Any deviation from the dietary protocol was noted. Stretching Session I and II: a daily record indicating whether two separate stretching sessions were completed during the 24-hour period. Medication Log: a record of all medication given during the campaign, including the dosage, time of administration, medical indication, and outcome. Protocol Deviation Summary: a record of any protocol deviations that might have occurred during the campaign. Symptom Complaint Log: a record of all complaints reported by the subject during the campaign, the measures taken address the issue, and the resolution of the complaint. Urine Collection Log: a record of all urine specimens collected during the campaign, including the weight and specific gravity of each specimen. Water Intake Log: a daily record of water intake by the subject. Fecal Collection Log: a record of the date, time, and weight of each bowel movement. Emesis Log: a record of each emesis episode (if any), for the Artificial Gravity Pilot Study, including the measured weight of the emesis. Test Specific CRF: each bed rest test had a test-specific CRF form to record details about each testing session. Sample Collection CRF: specific details regarding the collection of each blood and saliva specimen was documented. These are the case report forms that were collected and documented during Campaign 11 and Campaign 19. title: Bone Densitometry Assessment (Flight Analog)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete.  All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The objective of this study was to track individual skeletal integrity (bone loss and recovery) particularly with regard to prolonged disuse, experienced by subjects participating in long duration bed rest studies.
approach: Bone Densitometry was performed using a Hologic Discovery whole body densitometer located at the bed rest facility at the University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB). This device employed the technique of Dual-energy X-Ray Absorptiometry (DXA). DXA was capable of distinguishing between hard tissue (bone) and soft tissue. Soft tissue was distinguished further as either lean tissue or fat. Subjects participated in scans of the following regions: whole body, lumbar spine, proximal femurs (hips), calcaneus (heel), and forarm (wrist). This protocol mirrors that of Medical Requirement 035L. The subjects were scanned in triplicate for all the sessions and total time (including setup) was about two hours. Scan analyses was performed using the analysis software provided by Hologic. Due to the lack of load on the skeleton during long duration bed rest, bone mineral density changes may occur in the hips, spine, pelvis and heel. DXA results provided control data for longer duration bed rest studies, complement assessment of markers of bone and calcium metabolism, and allowed assessment of subject body composition. The MR035G testing transitioned during the Campaign 11 (CFT70) Study Protocol and are utilizing the intelligent dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (iDXA) instead of the Hologic DXA hardware. Bone Densitometry was performed using a General Electric Lunar whole-body densitometer located at John Sealy Hospital at UTMB, Galveston. This iDXA device can distinguish between hard tissue (bone) and soft tissue. Soft tissue can be distinguished further as either lean tissue or fat. Subject’s participated in scans of the following regions: whole body, lumbar spine, proximal femurs (hips), and forearm. The subjects were scanned in triplicate for the pre- and in-bed rest sessions; the follow-up tests were conducted at 6-month and 12-month as single scans.
results: This experiment has concluded in ground-based studies sponsored by NASAs Human Adaptation and Countermeasures Division. Bone mineral density changes were consistent with earlier bed rest and spaceflight studies, with statistically significant losses averaging 1% per month in the hip, pelvis, and heel. Recovery data were also consistent with data obtained after spaceflight. Bone biomarker data are described, and support the findings of previous studies. Specifically, the process of normal bone remodeling is uncoupled: increased bone resorption with no concomitant change in bone formation. In conclusion, the Flight Analog Project (FAP) appears to be a valid test bed for skeletal disuse studies, and should provide a useful research platform for evaluating countermeasures to spaceflight-induced bone loss.

title: Bed Rest Standard Measures: Cardiovascular Function
archive_status: Data preservation is complete.  All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The objective of this test was to aid in the proper assessment of hemodynamic parameters, vascular responses, and cardiac size and function. Investigators hypothesized that bed rest changes in cardiac dimensions and function will be similar to those seen after space flight. They expect to see changes in cardiac function which is similar to those seen pre-bedrest.
approach: Hemodynamic assessment was accomplished by the use of continuous, pulsed wave, and color flow Doppler. All four cardiac valves were evaluated for regurgitation. A critical factor on cardiac function is the relaxation component or diastolic function. To address the diastolic function, several traditional echocardiographic measurements and indices were used in addition to more investigational measures. The echocardiography was used to give views necessary to image all valves and chambers of the heart. Electrodes were placed on the subject and ultrasound measurements were made of the heart.
results: Results from the Artificial Gravity Study indicate that artificial gravity can mitigate some aspects of bed rest-induced cardiovascular deconditioning, including orthostatic intolerance and aerobic power. Mechanisms of improvement were not cardiac-mediated, but likely through improved sympathetic responsiveness to orthostatic stress. More information can be found in the publications cited.

title: Cellular Immune Response
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The functional capacity of lymphocytes (phytohemagglutinin (PHA) responsiveness only) was found to be depressed for studies conducted during Apollo missions 7 through 13 and Skylab missions 3 and 4. T-lymphocyte numbers were also suppressed in Skylab. The objective of this study was to examine the effects of space flight on the cellular immune response in Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP) crewmembers.
approach: Samples of heparinized peripheral venous blood (10cc) were obtained preflight and postflight on days L-30 (30 days before liftoff), L-15, L-5, R+0 (day of recovery), R+1 (recovery +1 day), R+8 and R+13. Samples were processed within 1 to 24 hours of collection. Parameters measured for this study included: 1) white blood cell concentrations, 2) lymphocyte numbers, 3) B-lymphocyte and T-lymphocyte distributions in peripheral blood and 4) lymphocyte responsiveness to PHA, pokeweed mitogen (PWM), Concanavalin A (Con A) and influenza virus antigen. Before separation, total leukocyte counts were performed using a hemacytometer and/or a Coulter Counter. Differential counts were determined using slide preparations stained with Wright’s stain. Lymphocytes were separated by Ficoll-Hypaque centrifugation, which uses a special liquid that provides a density gradient. Higher density blood cells are pulled far down into the liquid by centrifugal action, while the more buoyant lymphocytes remain near the center. The supernatant was removed by pipette, and the resulting mononuclear cells were washed three times in minimum essential medium (MEM). B-lymphocyte distributions were determined by calculating the percentage of 200 mononuclear cells with surface immunoglobulins, which were detected by the immunofluorescent antibody technique. The presence of E-rosette-forming lymphocytes (T-cells) was determined using a concentration of one million lymphocytes in 0.25 ml of 0.5% sheep red blood cell (SRBC) suspension. After mixing, the tubes were incubated at 37 degrees Celsius for 5 minutes, and then placed in ice water for 2 hours. Approximately half of the supernatant was removed, and the top cell layer was gently resuspended. Two hundred lymphocytes were counted with 3 or more adhering SRBC’s, which were used as criteria for E-rosetted lymphocytes. Purified lymphocytes (one million cells) in MEM containing 40% fetal calf serum were placed in culture plates. The antigens were diluted in MEM (containing Pen-Strep and L-glutamine) in the following concentrations: 0.01 ml PHA/ml MEM; 0.01 and 0.05 ml PWM/ml MEM; and 25 and 50 micrograms Con A/ml MEM. These diluted antigens were placed in the appropriate wells of the tissue culture plates in 0.1 ml aliquots (in duplicate). The cultures were incubated in a humidified carbon dioxide atmosphere at 37 degrees Celsius (3 days for PHA and 5 days for Con A and PWM). On the day of harvest, samples were treated as described in the following section for influenza virus antigen cultures. An inactivated monovalent type A influenza virus vaccine containing 1600 chick cell agglutinating units/ml of a Hong Kong strain was dialyzed against phosphate-buffered saline and stored at -70 degrees Celsius until used for tests. Separated lymphocytes were added in 0.1 ml aliquots for each influenza antigen dilution, and the cultures were incubated in a humidified carbon dioxide incubator at 37 degrees Celsius for periods of either 2 or 3 days. On the day of harvest, cells were pulsed for 2 hours with 1 microcurie of methyl(tritium)-thymidine, a radioactive marker. Cells were then harvested with an automated harvester onto glass-fiber filter strips and counted in a liquid scintillation counter. Data were expressed as counts per minute (CPM)/one million lymphocytes, and the stimulation index (SI) was calculated by dividing the mean result for stimulated cultures by that for unstimulated cultures. Allantoic fluid was used separately as a control of each crewman’s reactivity to chick embryo proteins.
results: Preflight (L-30) white blood cell (WBC) counts for ASTP and Skylab were 6640±1830 WBC/mm3 and 6013±254 WBC/ mm3, respectively. The ASTP crew had significant increases in WBC numbers noted on R+0 (11,110±4210 WBC/mm3) and R+1 (13,530±610 WBC/mm3). Individual variation in WBC values was noted among the three Skylab crewmembers at R+0 (8980±5560 WBC/mm3), which is reflected in the large standard deviation. However, all values were within clinically normal ranges (7110±2400 WBC/mm3). Less variation overall was noted for total lymphocyte values; however, values at R+0 for ASTP (1950±490 lymphocyte count/mm3) and Skylab 4 (1177±381 lymphocyte count/mm3) were decreased below their previous baseline values (ASTP L-30=2820±480 lymphocyte count/mm3 and Skylab L-30=1940±670 lymphocyte count/mm3). Fluctuations in the individual values of T-lymphocytes, B-lymphocytes and nonreactive lymphocytes of ASTP crewmembers were indicated, but values remain within one standard deviation for normal laboratory values. T-cell values ranged from 1.29 million +/- 490,000 to 2.53 million +/- 440,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=1.59 million +/- 630,000 lymphocytes/ml), B-lymphocytes from 470,000 +/- 20,000 to 710,000 +/- 40,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=510,000 +/- 300,000 lymphocytes/ml) and nonreactive lymphocytes from 120,000 +/- 120,000 to 710,000 +/- 370,000 lymphocytes/ml (normal=850,000 +/- 560,000 lymphocytes/ml). In contrast, highly significant changes were noted in B and T cell distributions of the Skylab 4 crewmen. Results from culture studies show a definite decrease in the ability of lymphocytes to react with PHA at R+0 (SI=20±15) and R+1 (SI=12±8) for all three Apollo astronauts. Baseline SI mean at L-30 was 36±4. By R+8, all were back within normal ranges (SI range=10 to 282). Crewmembers began and remained at low-level SI ranges for Con A (3 to 49) throughout the preflight and postflight periods, except for one subject, who had a strengthened Con A stimulation of 151 at splashdown. Considerable individual variation was noted in the PWM data and no consistent trend was obtained. Variation of antigen stimulation indexes may be expected, due to the rapid exchange of cells between different compartments in the body. The entire Apollo crew responded to influenza virus England strain preflight in cultures, and one of the three astronauts responded postflight to influenza virus Hong Kong strain. Total lack of reactivity may reflect influenza susceptibility. ASTP crewmembers experienced contact with toxic gases upon splashdown. Depressions observed at R+0 were caused by either space flight or gas exposure a few hours prior to sample analysis. Similar depressions in lymphocytic responsiveness were observed in Skylab 3 and 4 data, although both of these missions were of much longer duration than ASTP. However, in comparable missions of similar lengths (i.e., the Apollo series) no changes in lymphocytic responsiveness were reported. The toxic gas exposure was severe enough to create concern for lung inflammation, which resulted in a corticosteroid treatment on R+1. Most cortisone preparations are known to cause a lymphocytic reaction. Consequently, it is likely that the increased immunosuppressions noted by cultural responses on R+1 for all mitogens and on R+8 for Con A were attributable to the steroid therapy.

title: Immunological Assessment of Crewmembers
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The assessment of crew immunocompetence was required for the determination of space flight infectious disease risk. This is of significant importance for longer duration missions and particularly, orbital station environments.
approach: Data was collected from 54 crewmembers during six shuttle flights. White blood cells were collected after removal of the serum for use in the nominal Medical Operations physical. These cells were resuspended in isotonic saline and divided into two aliquots. One sample was used for flow cytometric analysis to determine cellular subpopulations and the other was further processed for functional assay of different immune cells (neutrophils, monocytes, and T-cells).
results: Phenotypic Analysis Flow cytometric analysis indicates that crewmembers exhibited a statistically significant decrease in total T cells with alterations in specific T cell subsets. In addition, a statistically significant increase in B cells as well as variable alterations in circulating monocytes was observed. Neutrophil Functional Testing Neutrophils exhibited a variable effect following space flight in response to a chemotactic factor.

title: Vitamin D Metabolites and Bone Demineralization
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Research data from previous calcium imbalance studies have shown that exposure to microgravity during space flight may cause bone mineral loss, increased plasma calcium, increased urinary calcium excretion, and an overall negative calcium balance. The objective of this experiment was to determine whether plasma levels of vitamin D metabolites, and parathyroid hormone (PTH) were altered in the crew of the 8 day Spacelab 2 mission. Significant changes in these hormones during space flight may indicate that the calcium homeostatic mechanism is adversely affected by exposure to microgravity. The calcium homeostatic mechanism operates through the integration of intestinal calcium absorption, calcium deposition and resorption from bone, and calcium excretion. The mechanism is regulated by the interaction of several hormonal factors, including PTH, calcitonin, and vitamin D. Vitamin D plays a key role because one of its metabolites, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (1,25(OH)2D), regulates intestinal calcium absorption and, in conjunction with PTH, induces bone mineral resorption to maintain normal blood calcium levels. An increase in circulating levels of these two hormones could be responsible for initiating changes in the calcium homeostatic mechanism by activating bone remodeling sites and by regulating calcium transport in the intestine, kidneys, and in bone. Long term space flight may cause hormonal imbalances in this mechanism which can lead to detrimental effects such as bone demineralization and kidney stone formation.

One sample was collected early in the mission while the other was collected toward the end of the mission. The blue team collected their early samples at 18 hours into the mission while the red team collected samples at 31 hours. The late samples were collected at 6 days, 19 hours and 7 days, 7 hours for the blue and red teams, respectively. Two tubes of blood were taken during each sample session; one tube was used for the vitamin D metabolite analysis while the other tube was used for measurements of PTH, albumin, calcium, and phosphorus. The volume collected for all samples was 25 ml and each sample yielded 4 to 5 ml of plasma. The vitamin D metabolite analysis included measurements for 24,25(OH)2D, 25 OHD, and 1,25(OH)2D.

title: Collecting Mir Source and Reclaimed Waters for Postflight Analysis
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: In this investigation, the water on the Mir space station was analyzed in detail to study the effectiveness of the Mir purification system. Potable water, water used to maintain hygiene, and water that accumulates from humidity condensate were analyzed to confirm that any potentially harmful contaminants were maintained at acceptably safe levels. The information gathered by this research supported the development and evaluation of water purification units, water quality standards, and in-flight water sampling hardware for the International Space Station. The experiment objectives were to: Characterize the chemical composition of Mir recycled water, Russian ground-supplied water prior to launch and on orbit, and the Mir humidity condensate to support development and testing of the water recycling and monitoring systems for the ISS. Determine and compare the chemical composition of Mir and Space Shuttle condensate. Determine whether the potable water on board Mir meets the Joint U.S./Russian water quality specifications for ISS. This experiment has flown under the NASA Human Life Sciences Discipline during the Mir 18/NASA 1, Mir 19, Mir 20/STS-74, and Mir 21/NASA 2/STS-79 missions. In addition, this activity was performed under the Space Medicine Program during the Mir 22/NASA 3/STS-81, Mir 23/NASA 4/STS-84, Mir 23/NASA 5/STS-86, Mir 24/NASA 6/STS-89 and the Mir 25/NASA 7/STS-91 missions. Shuttle flights were used to return items and resupply the experiment.
approach: Recycled and stored water samples were collected periodically during each mission using U.S. developed water sampling hardware. In addition, raw unprocessed humidity condensate was collected using Russian-supplied hardware, while partially processed condensate was collected using U.S. supplied hardware. The partially processed condensate samples were collected as a result of ethylene glycol leaks on board the Mir, to assess the ability of the water processor system to remove this contaminant.
results: In general, the recycled and stored water supplied to the Mir Space Station met NASA, Russian Space Agency (RSA), and/or U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) standards. Exceptions were found to include total organic carbon (TOC) and turbidity in the recycled water which routinely exceeded NASA standards. The TOC in some cases, exceeded Russian standards as well. Other parameters such as ethylene glycol, barium, nickel, chloroform, phenol, and dioctyl phthatate occasionally exceeded NASA, RSA or EPA standards. All but the TOC violations were transient. The humidity condensate exhibited steadily increasing levels of ethylene glycol throughout the missions. This is believed to reflect the increased levels of ethylene glycol in the Mir atmosphere following coolant loop leaks and maintenance activities. In one case, the presence of ethylene glycol in a condensate sample alerted the ground and crew to the presence of a previously undetected coolant loop leak. The chemical quality of the recycled and stored water, as determined through post-flight analysis met performance and potability requirements. The analysis of samples has provided important data for assessing the potability of recycled water. In addition, these data will be instrumental in developing appropriate water quality monitoring standards for ISS.
