title: Alterations in Postural Equilibrium Control Associated with Long Duration Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The sensorimotor systems of humans have evolved phylogenetically and ontogenetically to optimize body movements and posture control in the terrestrial gravitational field. The central nervous system (CNS) has developed neurosensory systems that monitor and process sensory inputs from visual, vestibular, somatosensory, and proprioceptive receptors to assess the biomechanical state of the body (spatial orientation), and neuromotor systems that create, select, and employ motor command strategies and synergies to adjust the biomechanical state toward the desired equilibrium point. Adaptation to microgravity alters neurosensory systems by eliminating, reinterpreting, or modifying the weighting of sensory information used to assess spatial orientation in response to the sudden loss of tonic gravitational otolith stimulation. Adaptation to microgravity also alters neuromotor systems by modifying the repertoire of motor command strategies and synergies used for movement control in response to the sudden redistribution of forces along the body, reductions in the biomechanical support reactions, and alteration of relationships between motor command and body movement. These inflight sensorimotor adaptations disrupt postflight postural equilibrium control. The long-term objective of this experiment was to determine the role of central adaptive mechanisms in reorganizing postural equilibrium control in humans subjected to long-duration space flight. Ultimately, these data, when coupled with similar data obtained from short-duration missions, will lead to development of return-to-duty criteria for returning crewmembers, to development effective countermeasures to the untoward effects of sensorimotor adaptation to space flight, and to improving our understanding of the adaptive processes required to compensate for clinical deficits in sensory-motor function. Hypotheses: (1) The effectiveness of reflexive (open loop) responses to stability-threatening external disturbances, which is known to be reduced after space flight, presumably because of inflight neuromotor adaptation, will be further reduced by concomitant neurosensory adaptation. (2) The effectiveness of the closed loop control of quiet stance, which is known to be reduced after space flight, presumably because of inflight neurosensory adaptation, will be further reduced by concomitant neuromotor adaptation, and the magnitude and recovery time course of this ataxia will increase with mission duration because of the increased time for sensory-motor adaptation to microgravity.
approach: The Equilibrium investigation used two test paradigms: (1) neuromotor control tests and (2) neurosensory control tests. Only pre- and postflight data collection sessions were scheduled. NeuroMotor Control Tests: Graded perturbations were used to challenge the posture control system by suddenly moving the center of mass close to the backward limit of stability. Two types of perturbations were used: support surface translations and chest pushes. Base-of-support perturbations were administered at two displacement levels by automatically translating the posture platform force plate (support surface) in the forward direction using a computer-controlled DC motor. The lower displacement level (1.25 cm over 250 msec) was used to assess response thresholds, while the higher displacement, level (5.70 cm over 400 msec) was used to assess the subject's ability to scale the motor response appropriately. Data from the eyes open support surface translation trials can be compared directly to the large existing set of U.S. postflight data currently being collected. Chest pushes were administered manually at two force levels by one of the investigators using a push stick with integral force transducer. The lower force level (2-5 Kg peak) was used to assess response thresholds, while the higher force level (10-20 Kg peak) was used to assess the subject's ability to scale the motor response appropriately. Data from the eyes open chest push trials can be compared directly to the large existing set of Russian postflight data collected by the Institute of Biomedical Problems (IBMP) group. Changes in the roles of sensory inputs in selecting and issuing motor commands can be inferred from the data collected during the reduced sensory input trials. The role of vision can be inferred from comparisons between eyes-closed trials and eyes-open trials, and the combined roles of ankle proprioception and plantar somatosensation can be inferred from comparisons between trials with the subject standing directly on the force platform and trials with the subject standing on thick (10 cm) foam rubber atop the force platform. The primary dependent measures in this experimental paradigm are derived from electromyographic (EMG) activity observed in the anti-gravity muscles of the leg and trunk. In particular, latencies of the initial EMG responses are used to assess the subject's ability to detect the perturbation and to select and issue a motor response. EMG sequencing, strength, and duration, coupled with biomechanical measurements of segmental and center of mass body movements are used to assess the strategy, synergy, and scaling of the motor response. Times to recovery of biomechanical equilibrium are used to assess the effectiveness of the motor response, and total integrated EMG activity is used to assess the efficiency of the response. Neurosensory Control Tests: Eliminating vision, decorrelating ankle proprioceptive inputs from Earth-vertical, and/or decorrelating visual inputs from Earth-vertical challenged the posture control system. These conditions altered the set of accurate sensory inputs available to the CNS for detection of sway errors and development of compensatory closed loop motor output adjustments. Sets of six sensory organization tests were administered automatically using a modified clinical dynamic posturography system. To decorrelate the ankle proprioceptive and visual inputs from Earth-vertical, the pitch orientations of the support surface and visual surround with respect to the subject's ankle joint were servo-controlled to follow the subject's center of mass sway. This process, which is referred to as sway referencing, eliminated changes in ankle angle and visual flow during low frequency body sway. The six sensory organization test (SOT) conditions used were: SOT 1. Eyes open - this is a control condition; all available sensory feedback systems are intact; tests the overall effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system; SOT 2. Eyes closed - tests the effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system without visual feedback; SOT 3. Sway-referenced vision - tests the effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system with inaccurate visual feedback; examines how well the system resolves visual-proprioceptive and/or visual-vestibular conflicts; SOT 4. Sway-referenced support surface - tests the effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system with inaccurate proprioceptive feedback; examines how well the system resolves proprioceptive-visual and/or proprioceptive-vestibular conflicts; SOT 5. Sway-referenced support surface with eyes closed - tests the effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system with inaccurate proprioceptive feedback and absent visual feedback; only vestibular feedback is accurate; examines how well the system resolves proprioceptive-vestibular conflicts and/or how well the system controls posture with only vestibular feedback; SOT 6. Sway-referenced support surface with sway-referenced vision - tests the effectiveness of the closed loop posture control system with inaccurate visual and proprioceptive feedback; only vestibular feedback is accurate; examines how well the system resolves simultaneous visual-vestibular and proprioceptive-vestibular conflicts and/or how well the system controls posture with only vestibular feedback. During each test session, three trials of each of the six sensory organization test conditions were presented to the subject. Each trial lasted for 20 seconds, and the order of presentation of the 18 trials was randomized. The primary dependent measures in this experimental paradigm are derived from biomechanical measurements of segmental and center of mass body movements. In particular, peak-to-peak sway amplitudes, equilibrium scores, and center of pressure (COP) under each condition were used to determine the degree to which the posture control system used visual, vestibular, and proprioceptive feedback to maintain closed loop control of postural equilibrium. Protocol for Pre- and Postflight Studies: Upon arrival at the test facility for each test session, the subject completed a pretest questionnaire designed to identify any uncontrolled factors that could potentially influence the test results. The subject's height was then measured (first pre- and postflight sessions only). Before posture testing, the subject donned a loose-fitting pair of 'gym' shorts to facilitate EMG electrode placement and joint position monitoring. The skin surface at each EMG electrode site was then prepared for electrode placement by scrubbing the region with an abrasive skin cleanser (Omni-Prep). Once each site was prepared, a pre-gelled, disposable, silver/silver chloride surface electrode was applied. The impedance between each electrode and a single ground reference electrode was then measured. The following EMG electrode sites were used: tibialis anterior, soleus, quadriceps (primarily rectus femoris), hamstrings (primarily biceps femoris), paraspinals (at approximately the L-4 level), abdominals (lateral to the midline, just below the umbilicus). Before the subject stepped onto the posture platform, the operator powered-up the EquiTest system and zeroed any sensor offsets. The subject then donned a safety harness and mounted the platform. Next, the operator fastened the safety harness to the safety bar that loops over the platform, positioned the subject on the platform, and attached the body segment position measuring devices (sway bars) and breast plate. The subject then donned a set of headphones used to provide a masking noise input that would eliminate external auditory cues from the posture platform and environment, and the operator adjusted the video camera for a clear field of view. Each test session began with the neuro-sensory control tests, during which the subject attempted to maintain upright postural equilibrium control under the following sensory conditions: (1) Eyes Open, Fixed Support Surface (2) Eyes Closed, Fixed Support Surface (3) Sway-referenced Vision, Fixed Support Surface (4) Eyes Open, Sway-referenced Support Surface (5) Eyes Closed, Sway-referenced Support Surface (6) Sway-referenced Vision, Sway-referenced Support Surface Each of these conditions was repeated three times during the test in randomized order for 18 trials. The duration of each trial was 20 seconds, and the time between trials was less than 5 seconds. The motor control tests followed immediately. During the sensory tests, the subject attempted to recover upright postural equilibrium control as quickly as possible after the following postural perturbations: (a) Small amplitude chest pushes (2-5 Kg) (b) Large amplitude chest pushes (10-20 Kg) (c) Small amplitude support surface forward translations (1.2 cm during 250 msec) (d) Large amplitude support surface forward translations (5.7 cm during 400 msec) Each of these conditions was repeated twice under each of the following sensory feedback conditions: (a) Eyes Open (b) Eyes Closed (c) Eyes Open, standing on thick (10 cm) foam rubber (d) Eyes Closed, standing on thick (10 cm) foam rubber The 16 trials without foam were presented first in randomized order. The 16 trials with foam were presented immediately after, also in randomized order (except for R+1 and R+5 when time constraints did not allow for "foam" trials). The duration of each trial was approximately 6-10 seconds, and the time between trials was less than 5 seconds. Chest pushes were applied manually by one of the investigators using a pushing device with integral force transducer. Support surface translations were applied automatically under computer control using the EquiTest system. Throughout the test period, the operator controlled the execution of the test protocols at the EquiTest system computer rack, while standing near enough to the platform to steady the subject when the subject lost balance. The operator depressed a foot switch to execute the test procedures. When the EquiTest system detected that the subject had lost balance, it automatically interrupted the test procedure and waited for operator's command to abort or continue the test. The overall testing equipment utilized during this experiment included safety harness, hip/shoulder sway bars w/potentiometers, overhead camera, white noise generator, calibrated subject push stick, subject breastplate, dual-axis rate sensors, and a VCR. Others to be described in more detail include the dynamic posturography system, camcorder/tripod, macintosh data acquisition system, and an EMG monitoring system.
results: Overall, the test procedures worked quite well. The motor control procedure was somewhat tedious at times and should probably be shortened for future experiments. In addition, the custom computer interface software was sensitive at times to the speed with which the operator selected test trials. It occasionally selected the wrong test, distorted or lost the real-time center of pressure display, or "locked up" the two experiment control computers. This software should be improved before using the system for future experiments. Mir 18 Balance control deficits following long-duration space flight appear to be far more profound than those following short-duration space flight: two of the three Mir 18 subjects were too ataxic to attempt the balance control testing on R+0, while only 4 of 45 short-duration crewmembers were that severely affected. The nature of postflight balance disturbances appears to be the same following long- and short-duration space flight missions: returning crewmembers are unable to adequately use vestibular system inputs immediately after flight. Neuromotor disturbances persist for a much longer period following long-duration flight than following short-duration flight. Furthermore, they appear to be affected by changes in available sensory information. Complete recovery is substantially delayed following long-duration missions; the slow phase of the recovery process appeared to progress much more slowly than with short-duration subjects. Mir 19 Two Mir 19 crewmembers participated in this experiment, partially fulfilling the postflight data collection requirements. Balance control performances on R+1 were among the lowest ever recorded. Balance control deficits appear to be far more profound, but similar in some aspects to those observed after 5-15 day Shuttle missions: (1) Contribution from vestibular system information is decreased early after flight (2) Reliance on visual system information is highly increased early after flight (3) Head-on-trunk locking strategy has emerged early after flight Complete recovery is substantially delayed following long-duration missions; the slow phase of the recovery process appeared to progress much more slowly than with short-duration subjects. New motor control strategies (co-contraction strategies) seem to emerge early after flight and persist for many days. These strategies were previously unobserved in the short-duration subjects, but, following reanalysis, appear in some subjects. The new strategies may reflect structural changes in the brain stem or the spinal cord. Further study of this observation is warranted. The primary goal of these investigations was to extend the understanding of the central adaptive mechanisms responsible for the appearance and amelioration of postflight postural ataxia. Building on the substantial neuromotor information base that the Russian IBMP group has amassed from primarily long-duration missions, and the similarly substantial neurosensory information base that the U.S. investigators have amassed from primarily short-duration missions, a set of combined studies on the joint US/Russian Shuttle-Mir Science Program was planned. To that end, a joint protocol was developed; employing key elements of both the standard IBMP test procedures and standard JSC test procedures, to which crewmembers were subjected before and after flight. Results from the Mir 18 and 19 subjects have been quantitatively disappointing because so much early postflight data were lost. The limited data obtained have allowed the investigators to begin making direct comparisons of the independent techniques used in the two space programs, but are not likely to be sufficient to lead to new insights into how data from the Russian and U.S. information bases can be combined.

title: Pre- and Postflight Cardiac Assessment
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Space flight causes adaptive changes in cardiovascular function, and many astronauts have suffered postflight orthostatic tachycardia. However, previously available data about these changes have been inadequate and inconsistent. The objective of this study was to collect normative data about the effects of space flight on the volume, mass and function of the heart, and about the orthostatic response of the cardiovascular system.
approach: The heart rate and blood pressure of 32 astronauts were recorded while they were lying supine and then standing, before and after space flights of 4 to 5 days. At the same times, echocardiograms were recorded by 2-dimensional M-mode echocardiography. The total peripheral resistance index (TPRI), left ventricular end diastolic volume index (EDVI), left ventricular end systolic volume index (ESVI), left ventricular stroke volume index (SVI), myocardial mass index and ejection fraction were calculated, and the mean velocity of circumferential shortening of the myocardial fibers was estimated.
results: The heart rate was greater on landing day than before the flight, and the EDVI and SVI in the supine position were less. (The mean EDVI was 11% less and the mean SVI was 17% less.) The mean EDVI, ESVI and SVI in the standing position were also less on landing day, but these changes were not statistically significant. Space flight caused no significant changes in the supine ESVI, the ejection fraction, the thickness of the left ventricular wall or the mass or contractility of the heart muscle. Before the flight, the TPRI increased significantly when astronauts stood up after lying supine. This orthostatic response was reduced on landing day, so that the TPRI failed to change significantly when the astronauts stood up, while the heart rate increased. The changes resolved within 7 to 10 days of landing. These results indicated that temporary changes in cardiovascular function may be expected even after short spaceflights of only 4 to 5 days. These changes included a decrease in the left ventricular end diastolic volume and stroke volume, with a compensatory increase in heart rate, as well as loss or reduction of the normal orthostatic response that maintains the blood pressure during postural changes.

title: In vivo Testing Confirms a Blunting of the Human Cell-Mediated Immune Mechanism During Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Changes in cellular immune potential during or following space flight have been reported in both the U.S. and Russian space programs. These changes were usually discovered using in vitro testing performed after flight, with various findings related to alterations in cellular responses. Direct in-flight, in vivo testing was used in this study to demonstrate the cell-mediated immune (CMI) system response during space flight.
approach: The delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) response of 10 Space Shuttle astronauts to 7 common recall antigens was measured using the Multitest CMI test system to administer antigens of tetanus, diphtheria, Streptococcus , Proteus , old tuberculin, Candida , and Trichophyton to the forearm after 2, 4, or 8 days of flight. This approach was used because DTH accompanies many manifestations of CMI and because skin reactions have often provided a model for the elucidation of effector mechanisms in CMI. Readings were conducted 48 hours after antigen administration. Data were evaluated in three ways: (a) the number of positive responses of the 7 possible, (b) the individual mean diameter (mm) of the positive response, and (c) the total sum, in mm, of all the positive reactions (reaction score).
results: The mean number of reactions was reduced from 4.5 before flight to 3.0 during flight, and the mean reaction score was reduced from 21.4 mm before flight to 13.7 mm during flight. The data suggest the CMI system was still being degraded by space flight conditions on day 4 of flight, and between day 5 and day 10 the depression maximized and the system began to stabilize at the new level.

title: Protein Metabolism During Long Term Space Flights
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The human body responds to stressful situations in many ways, one of which is an increase in protein production. Previous studies indicate that the whole body protein synthesis rate increases during short-term space flight. As a result of these observations, it was hypothesized that space flight is associated with an initial metabolic stress response. The initial stress deteriorates within the first few weeks during a long-term stay in Earth orbit and the return to preflight protein metabolism status takes several weeks after landing. The objectives of the experiment were: 1. To determine the duration of the metabolic stress response associated with space flight. 2. To determine how long it takes for protein metabolism to return to its preflight state after a long duration mission.
approach: The whole body protein synthesis rate was measured four times preflight, periodically every three to four weeks inflight and four times postflight spaced between R+1 and R+72 (days after landing). The 15N-glycine method was used to determine the protein synthesis rates. This method required the oral intake of the amino acid glycine, marked with the stable 15N isotope of nitrogen. The ingested labeled protein is absorbed into the body's protein metabolism. Data on how the labeled protein is metabolized in the human body was gathered by collecting urine samples, measuring body weight, and having the test subjects maintain dietary logs for 24 hours prior to and during the day of the protein synthesis determinations. Each data session started with the collection of a urine sample, which later was used to determine the background 15N. Immediately after the urine sample was collected, the astronaut swallowed a capsule containing 1.0 gram of labeled N-glycine (15N), and the weight of the test subject was measured. During the next 24 hours small samples of urine were collected from each urine void and the volume of each void was measured. Also, over the entire 24 hours, food and fluid intake, exercise, and medication intake was monitored. Additionally, at ten hours after the intake of the 15N, a urine void was collected and a saliva sample was taken. The urine and saliva samples were frozen at - 20 degrees Celsius in the freezer until analysis.
results: NASA 2/Mir 21: During the NASA 2 mission, no inflight data was obtained for the first 120 days of the mission. Determinations of the protein synthesis rate took place on Mission Day (MD) 120, MD 157, and MD 177 for one astronaut, and on MD 149 and MD 186 for the other two astronauts. Postflight tests were performed at R+1, R+6, R+14, R+32, R+40, and R+70 for one astronaut, on R+2, R+7, R+14 and R+72 for the second astronaut; no postflight data was obtained for the third participating crewmember. The preliminary results from this mission indicated that the protein synthesis rate was reduced by about 31% after more than 4 months of space flight. The data also suggested that whole body protein synthesis declined with time in space. NASA 3/Mir 22: During the NASA 3/Mir 22 mission, no early and middle inflight data was obtained. The first protein measurements were taken on MD 120. The data indicated that the protein synthesis rate was significantly reduced after 4 months of space flight. Combined with the data collected during the NASA 2/Mir 21 missions, which increased the data set to n=6 subjects, the results reach statistical significance. The combined data indicated that after 3 plus months in space the whole body protein synthesis rate is reduced by 53%. The bedrest model predicts 15-20%, so the flight reduction is remarkable. It suggests that during periods with no tension on muscles a dramatic reduction of protein turnover takes place. The postflight data shows considerable scatter in the data with no consistent pattern.

title: Canal and Otolith Integration Studies (COIS)
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Determining the position of our bodies, relative to the environment, is a complex function requiring the brain to integrate information from virtually every sensory system, including the eyes and inner ear, as well as receptors in our muscles and joints. The absence of gravity causes adaptive changes in the sensorimotor and perceptual systems, and some of these changes are fundamental. The adaptive mechanisms of the sensorimotor and perceptual systems rely on adjustments in control strategies. Thus, the first aim of the Canal and Otolith Integration Studies (COIS) was a better understanding of the changes in the strategies of oculomotor performance (eye movement), particularly those that rely on spatial orientation. This was tested by systematically evaluating changes in the different classes of eye movements, including the vestibulo-ocular reflex, smooth pursuit and saccades. Changes in eye movements reflect disruptions in the coordination process. The second aim of the study was to test the hypothesis that the absence of an orientational extrinsic gravity vector would result in a change in oculomotor and perceptual responses such that the subjects would begin to use intrinsic coordinates to orient themselves. This hypothesis was tested by evaluating changes in cross-coupling of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) and optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) response axes and by evaluating changes in spatial reorientation performance.
approach: The COIS experiment was composed of three different protocols: Voluntary Head Shakes (VHS), Smooth Pursuit Tracking and Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN). The VHS and Smooth Pursuit Tracking protocols were always performed at the same time (first VHS, then Smooth Pursuit Tracking), while the OKN protocol was not necessarily performed on the same day. During the VHS and Smooth Pursuit Tracking protocols, the subjects were seated and the lower body and trunk restrained. The subject wore a vest called the Instrumented Vest Assembly (IVA), which contained amplifiers and data recorders (called the Superpocket Assembly) and provided the connections to the peripheral hardware. The peripheral hardware included an electrooculograph (EOG) to monitor eye movements, a triaxial rate sensor to record head movements, the Luminous Target Display (LTD) and the Electronic Light Occlusion Goggles (ELOG). The LTD provided a cruciform array of Light-Emitting Diodes (LEDs) and was used as a visual target. The ELOG goggles occluded vision under normal conditions and were translucent when a 30-volt DC electrical current was applied. The VHS protocol included two test conditions, both featuring voluntary head shakes at two different frequencies, 0.33 and 1.0 Hertz (Hz), in both the horizontal (yaw) and vertical (pitch) planes. Instructions were given to the subjects via a prerecorded audio tape that played a modulated tone. The subject was asked to move the head so that during the lowest tone the head was at the far right and at the highest tone it was at the far left. During the first test condition, the subjects performed the head shakes using the central light of the LTD as their visual target. During the second test condition, the subject's vision was occluded using the ELOG goggles. The subject was asked to move their head according to the auditory cues and use an imaginary target to fixate gaze. Smooth Pursuit Tracking required the subjects to track a moving target in two ways. In the first type of tracking, the head was held stationary, and the target was pursued with eyes only. In the second type of tracking, both the eyes and head were allowed to move. Two frequencies, 0.33 and 1.0 Hz, were used for both the horizontal (yaw) and vertical (pitch) planes. The diodes of the LTD functioned as targets, providing a peak amplitude of 25 degrees. During the Optokinetic Nystagmus (OKN) protocol, the subjects wore the Optokinetic Stimulus (OKS) goggles. The head-mounted OKS goggles provided the stimuli to provoke optokinetic nystagmus by means of a pattern of red and black 4-degree-wide stripes viewed through a Fresnel lens. The stripe pattern could be moved at a constant velocity of a maximum of 40 degrees per second in the horizontal, vertical or 45 degrees oblique direction. The optokinetic stimulus was maintained in one direction for 20 seconds, followed by 10 seconds in darkness, during which optokinetic after-nystagmus was observed. This was followed by 5 seconds with a stationary display to visually suppress any remaining after-nystagmus before providing 20 seconds of OKS in the opposite direction, followed again by 10 seconds of darkness. During the initial darkness period, eye movements (EOG) were recorded with the subject looking straight ahead to quantify any spontaneous and/or positional nystagmus that might be present. In space, the subjects were free-floating during the OKN trials to avoid external orientation cues. For pre- and postflight testing, the gravitational effects on the OKN were inferred by evaluating the horizontal-to-vertical cross-coupling effects with either visual stimulus by tilting the subject's head by 30 degrees with respect to the spatial vertical. Crewmembers participated as test subjects and operators for COIS, obtaining measurements before, during and after flight. Three preflight data collection sessions were used as a baseline with which to compare inflight and postflight data. Space flight data collection occurred four times for each subject -- two times early and two times late during the mission. Postflight data collection occurred on landing day (R+0), and continued on R+1, R+2, R+4 and R+8.
results: The responses to self-induced, sinusoidal head rotations further indicates that VOR gain and phase are modified as is gaze. These modifications in the VOR system are the direct result of the vestibular system to aid in the stabilization of the retinal image. This in tum sets-up conditions which are ideal for retinal lip and possible degradations in visual performance. Although the test used in this experiment was simple to implement, some training was necessary before the crewmembers could perform the necessary head oscillations correctly. Once learned, the procedures were performed perfectly. The horizontal BOG data obtained when vision was occluded, there was a significant drop in VHS response gain during the flight phase of the experiment associated with the 1.0 Hz frequency. Flight Day 2 (FD-2, approximately 30 hours into the mission) shows an immediate drop in the 1.0 Hz response gain from the preflight levels. Gain remained below preflight levels when vision was absent throughout the flight, showing a slight increase on day 16 of the mission. Immediately following the flight (R+O), gain immediately dropped again.to the inflight levels measured prior to FD-16. Following R+O, gain measurements increase to the approximate levels observed during the preflight testing.

title: Viral Reactivation
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Seven or more herpesviruses commonly establish infections in humans. Herpes simplex type-1 (HSV-1), herpes simplex type-2 (HSV-2), cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), varicella-zoster virus (VZV), human herpesvirus-6 (HHV-6) and human herpesvirus-7 (HHV-7) are some examples of the double stranded DNA viruses that may establish a life-long latent infection in a host organism. Latent viruses are subject to intermittent reactivation. For example, replication of the reactivated herpesvirus genome may give rise to both infectious and noninfectious (defective) virus particles. Since one or more of the herpesviruses infects nearly 100% of the adult population, they are prime candidates for studying the effects of space flight on latent viral reactivation in astronauts. Latent virus reactivation may be an important threat to crew health during extended space missions where crewmembers live and work in a closed environment for 3 months or more. Exposure to infectious agents such as bacteria, fungi, viruses and parasites can be controlled by preflight quarantine as opposed to latent virus reactivation, an infection that originates inside the host organism. The establishment of viral latency and the subsequent reactivation are not well understood, but changes in the immune system are known to increase the incidence and duration of viral reactivation and shedding. Increasing scientific data indicates that the physical and psychological stressors associated with space flight cause alterations in the human immune response. Therefore, the objectives of this experiment were to evaluate the effects of long-duration habitation in space on latent virus reactivation, indicative of perturbations to the intricate host-parasite relationships. In this experiment, scientists tested the hypothesis that stressors associated with space flight will alter the host-parasite relationship in crewmembers inhabiting the Mir space station during extended stays, increasing both the incidence and the duration of herpesvirus reactivation and shedding.
approach: The approach to this experiment was to assess viral reactivation by the collection of serum and saliva samples. The original plan for sample collection included both the Mir 18 and 19 crew. The inflight and postflight sampling sessions on Mir 18 were not completed due to a cancellation of this experiment. Preflight saliva samples were obtained, but no blood samples were collected. However, contingency saliva sampling was performed on one crewmember during the flight. Preflight, inflight, and postflight saliva samples were collected from two crewmembers of the Mir 19 mission. Detection of the herpesvirus reactivation and shedding was conducted by saliva sample collection, DNA extraction from saliva, Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) amplification of herpesvirus DNA, and analysis of PCR products by gel electrophoresis. DNA extraction from saliva Saliva was collected and transferred to microcentrifuge tubes for extraction. DNA was extracted using a modification of the RNAzol method. Genomic/viral DNA was isolated simultaneously by adding 0.75 ml of Tris-saturated phenol (pH 6.6) RNAzol solution to 250 microliters saliva and briefly vortexing. After incubating on ice for 15 minutes, the tubes were centrifuged for 15 minutes at 12,000 x g and stored at -20 degrees Celsius overnight. The tubes were then centrifuged for 30 minutes at 16,000 x g and the supernatant removed. The DNA was then washed once with 7% ethanol and resuspended in 20 microliters DEPC-treated water. The suitability of extraction was evaluated by gel electrophoresis without nucleic acid quantitation. PCR Amplification of Herpesvirus DNA The oligonucleotide primers selected for this investigation amplified a highly conserved region of the DNA polymerase gene from the herpesvirus group. These primers allowed amplification of DNA to be directed to selected nucleotide fragments of the DNA polymerase genes for HSV-1, HSV-2, CMV and EBV . DNA was amplified in a total volume of 25 ml or a reaction mixture consisting of 50 mM KCl, 10mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.3), 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.01% gelatin, 5% dimethylsulfoxide, 200 micromolar deoxynucleoside triphosphates, 20 pmol of each oligonucleotide primer, 0.625 U Taq polymerase, and 2 ml purified DNA solution. The reactions were performed in an automated thermocycler. The cycle, repeated 40 times, consisted of 15 seconds of denaturation at 96 degrees Celsius, 15 seconds of annealing at 60 degrees Celsius, and 15 seconds of elongation at 72 degrees Celsius. All samples were run with simultaneous positive control and negative (reagent) control. Measures to control contamination included the use of latex gloves, aerosol-resistant pipette tips, and two separate laboratories for preamplification and postamplification procedures. Analysis of PCR Products Ten microliters of the reaction mixture was run on a 2% Nusieve GTG agarose gel containing 1 microgram of ethidium bromide per ml in 1x TBE buffer. The gels were then placed under UV light for visualization of the amplified products and photographed.
results: The cancellation of this experiment on Mir 18 resulted in a limited sample collection. Inflight and postflight samples were not collected from the Mir 18 crewmembers. Preflight samples were collected from three crewmembers and five inflight samples were collected from one crewmember as contingency samples. Therefore, the only samples analyzed were those collected from the crewmember that participated in the inflight collection. The samples collected from the other crewmembers are archived for future analysis. All of the preflight samples were negative for the presence of herpesvirus DNA. However, two of the five inflight samples were positive for the presence of herpesvirus DNA. Since these data were very limited, no conclusions were made concerning the effects of microgravity on the host-parasite relationship. However, the methodology and sample handling logistics were successful. Two cosmonauts, both backup crewmembers for Mir 18, participated in the viral reactivation study on the Mir 19 mission. Thus, the preflight saliva specimens collected to establish baseline shedding patterns were collected prior to the Mir 18 mission. Saliva specimens were collected before, during, and after the flight. The samples were analyzed for the presence of Herpes simplex type-1 (HSV 1) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). All specimens were negative for HSV 1. Unfortunately, preflight saliva specimens were insufficient in number and frequency to establish a sound baseline for either crewmember. However, preflight shedding of EBV in the saliva was detected in over half of the total specimens. EBV DNA were detected in the saliva of crewmember A before, during, and after the flight. At least six episodes of shedding of EBV were observed during the mission. Inflight saliva specimens were collected beginning at about FD 25 and ending on FD 75. Shedding was also observed on R+14 and R+24. Crewmember B shedded EBV much less frequently during the mission than crewmember A. EBV DNA was observed in saliva from crewmember B on only two occasions during the mission. The conclusions made from this experiment were: (1) PCR methodology was capable of detecting latent viral DNA in saliva specimens collected and stored on the ground and on Mir, (2) neither crewmember appeared to be shedding HSV 1, (3) both crewmembers shed EBV before, during and after the mission, (4) shedding patterns of EBV of the two crewmembers were highly different during the inflight phase, (5) the technical feasibility of the approach was clearly demonstrated. The low number of subjects prevented any major conclusions from being drawn related to host-parasite relationships during space flight.

title: Microgravity, Sleep/Wake Immune Functions (SWIF) in Humans
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: This experiment was designed to study changes in the immune system coincident with sleep physiology during extended space flight and relate any found changes to preflight and postflight conditions. In particular, researchers wanted to determine if there are any long-term adverse effects of microgravity on the immune system that can be related to the sleep-wake cycle. Such disturbances in neuroendocrine system and immune system functions might have an impact on the risk for ill health, especially infectious disease. The study would contribute to our understanding of the role of the immune system in the sleeping-waking brain especially during and following spaceflight microgravity conditions. In addition to the theoretical and space flight importance, there are important clinical implications to psychiatric and medical disorders. The associations of stress and depression with altered immune functions have been reported in medical literature. Stress, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep deregulation, and reduced slow wave sleep are related to major depressive disorders. Specifically, natural killer cell (NK cell) activity is reduced in sleep disturbed depressed patients. Furthermore, altered non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep physiology and immune function changes have been described in fibrositis/fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome that shares features of unrefreshing or non-restorative sleep, diffuse myalgia, multiple tender points, fatigue and depression. The outcome of the research would have important implications on the contributions of disordered sleep and immune functions for the pathogenesis of these illnesses.
approach: This investigation was conducted for the first time as part of the NASA-Mir Increment 4 mission. Three crewmembers completed measurements preflight, inflight and postflight. For each phase of the flight, the experiment was divided into segments called measurement "blocks". The inflight measurement blocks were scheduled early in the mission (mission day 37-49), in the middle (MD 79-91) and at the end (MD 110-122) of the mission. Preflight baseline data collection was performed once. Readaptation data was collected during two sessions postflight. The experiment protocols were repeated on the NASA 5/Mir 24 mission with two additional crewmembers. During the preflight and postflight phases of the experiment, subjects answered questions before and after sleep periods on sleepiness, fatigue, pain and mood as well as performance. These questions were the main focus of a separate sleep study performed simultaneously with this investigation (see: "Human Circadian Rhythms and Sleep in Space" by Timothy H. Monk, Ph.D.) In addition to the questionnaires, preflight baseline blood collection (BDC) involved 25 blood samples collected over a 24-hour wake/sleep cycle. Five daytime samples of 4-ml of blood were taken at 0800, 1000, 1200, 1400 and 1600 hours. A catheter was inserted before 2200 hours to allow for frequent blood sampling during sleep. Starting again at 2200 until 0700 half-hourly and again at 0800 hours, twenty 3-ml blood samples were taken in sterile, heparinized, pyrogen-free tubes connected to a 4-meter line and manifold located outside the bedroom. Samples were transported immediately to the laboratory for analysis. A total of 80 ml for each subject was collected. The following immunologic assays were carried out: natural killer cells and T-cell subsets were stained and sorted using the two-color immunofluorescence technique with flow cytometry; plasma cortisol and human growth hormone (hGH) were determined by radioimmunoassay (RIA); plasma IL-1ß, IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1ra) and IL-2 and IL-2r concentrations were determined using enzyme-linked-immunosorbent-assay (ELISA). Cytokine biological activities were determined by reactions with D10 and CTLL cell lines; natural killer cell activity was tested by Chronium-51 release assay; IL-1ß mRNA from peripheral blood monocyte cells was studied by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (Rt-PCR). Plasma obtained from subjects was stored at -70 degrees C until use. During flight, pre- and post sleep questionnaires were also completed. Blood samples were drawn on days 4 and 5 of the second and third blocks. Samples were drawn in the early afternoon (approximately 1400 hours) and prior to sleep. For each blood sample collection, two 3-milliliter (ml) blood samples were taken. One 3 ml sample was taken in a 5 ml plasma separator tube for centrifugation and storage at -20° C. One milliliter of the second 3 ml sample was injected into each of three 7 ml tubes prefilled with a cryopreservative. The procedure was repeated on the second day. Eight samples each of 6 mls for a total of 48 ml blood was collected from each subject in flight. Blood samples obtained during the mission were used to examine natural killer cells and plasma for lymphokines and endocrine substances. Immunologic and endocrine assays were carried out on samples returned to principal investigator. Also on days 4 and 5 of the second and third blocks, subjects attached electroencephalography (EEG) electrodes and donned a Medilog Sleep Research Recorder (MSRR) skull cap prior to sleep. This piece of hardware was used to make standard sleep-wake physiologic assessments. The Medilog recorder was donned within two hours of sleep and removed within two hours after awakening. Data were recorded on magnetic tape and stored for return to Earth. After flight, sleep tape recordings were scored without subject identification by a trained observer using standard criteria on a Medilog replay unit located at the principal investigator’s laboratory. Brain wave frequencies recorded on the MSRR tapes were analyzed to assess the relationship of brain waves delta (slow wave) sleep activity to immune functions. The method allowed for an objective, quantifiable, and reliable method for analyzing sleep EEG frequencies during sleep. Blood analyses and MSRR data were compared to test that changes in sleep, particularly between wakefulness and slow wave sleep, are indices of causal mechanisms that produce changes in the immune system.
results: Immunologic and endocrine assays were carried out on blood samples collected preflight, inflight, and postflight to examine the relationship between sleep activity to immune functions. Preflight baseline data collection from all crewmembers were compared to a group of healthy male volunteers to determine if sleep/wake age-related immune and endocrine functions were present in the middle-aged male crewmembers during baseline conditions before flight on Mir versus young healthy males. Middle-aged crewmembers in preflight baseline conditions differed from young healthy males in the timing of the diurnal pattern of natural killer cell cytotoxicity, hGH and cortisol. They also secreted less hGH and more cortisol over a 24-hour period. These hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenocortical (HPA) axis endocrine differences in healthy middle-aged men were similar to those seen in healthy older men. While the dynamic structure of natural killer cell cytotoxicity differed, there was no overall mean difference from young males.

title: Pre- and Postflight Measurement of Cardiorespiratory Responses to Submaximal Exercise
research_area: Cardiovascular physiology; Muscle physiology; Clinical medicine; Exercise physiology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: It is known that regular aerobic exercise can maintain aerobic capacity during bed rest. Therefore, aerobic exercise might also be able counteract the deconditioning effects of microgravity on aerobic exercise capacity. The objectives of this study were to document the degree of aerobic deconditioning after space flight and to investigate the use of aerobic exercise during flight to reduce the severity of postflight deconditioning.
approach: The study included 39 astronauts (35 men and 4 women) from missions lasting 8 to 16 days. The astronauts performed exercise tests on an upright cycle ergometer at increasing rates of work until they reached 85% of their age-predicted maximum heart rates. A monitor recorded the heart rate every 15 seconds during the tests. Aerobic capacity was defined as the peak oxygen consumption during the tests, which was measured with a Q-Plex system. The Q-Plex system is a computer driven device for cardiac, respiratory, and rehabilitation stress test (similar to an EKG stress monitor). The composition of exhaled air was analyzed either with a mass spectrometer preflight or with zirconium oxide and infrared sensors postflight. Oxygen consumption during the last minute of exercise was used as the index of cardiovascular performance. Results from tests performed 10 days before launch were compared to results from landing day. The astronauts exercised on a cycle ergometer during flight. No specific exercise protocol was required. Heart rates were recorded every 15 seconds during exercise. The frequency and duration of in-flight exercise sessions was noted, and the intensity of the exercise was quantified as the percentage of age-predicted maximum heart rate achieved during a session.
results: Lower work rates were achieved on landing day because the target heart rates were reached sooner, ending the tests. The rate of oxygen consumption that corresponded to a given heart rate was lower after the flight than before. At 85% of predicted maximum heart rate, the decrement in oxygen consumption was nine percent for astronauts who exercised during flight for more than 20 minutes at least three times a week at more than 70% of their predicted maximum heart rate. The decrement was greater for astronauts who exercised less often or at lower intensities. It was 15% for astronauts who exercised more than three times a week but achieved lower heart rates, and 23% for astronauts who exercised less frequently. The decrease in oxygen consumption did not correlate with flight duration. Because the exercise tests were performed upright, both exercise deconditioning and orthostatic deconditioning would have contributed to the higher heart rates during exercise. In this way the tests were similar to an emergency egress from the Shuttle. The results showed that in-flight exercise can help to maintain postflight aerobic capacity and that the intensity of exercise is important. On the basis of this and other studies (see DSOs 476, 608, and 618), it was recommended that space crews exercise for more than 20 minutes at least three times a week at work rates that elicit 70% of maximum heart rates, but that the maximum heart rates should be determined in preflight maximum exercise tests rather than estimated by age.

title: Sleeping Short
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: For various reasons, astronauts typically "sleep short" in space, seldom getting the 8 hours intended by the time line schedule. For some, this may not present a problem, because they are naturally short sleepers who can get by with 5 1/2 hours of sleep, for example, without any consequent daytime sleepiness. For others, sleeping short inevitably leads to impairments in mood, alertness, and ability to perform at full capacity. This project comprises a detailed investigation of "sleeping short" using ground-based studies of healthy men and women (20y-59y). This study sought to address three critical questions: 1. Which countermeasure or combination of behavioral and physiological countermeasures will optimally mitigate specific performance problems associated with sleep loss and circadian disturbances during a Mars mission? 2. What individual biological and behavioral characteristics will best predict successful adaptation to long-term space flight of sleep and circadian physiology and the neurobehavioral performance functions they regulate? 3. What are the best methods for monitoring the status of sleep and circadian functioning and for assessing the effects of sleep loss and circadian dysrhythmia that are also portable and non-intrusive in the spaceflight environment? It has three aims which coincide broadly with the three years of proposed research. In Year 01, we will develop a questionnaire/diary instrument (the "Sleep Length Index" - SLI) designed to identify those who are naturally short sleepers who can thrive on less than 6 hours of sleep (as opposed to those who restrict their sleep inadvisably and suffer from daytime sleepiness). Year 02 will be concerned with determining the sleep and circadian rhythm, mood and performance differences between short sleepers (as identified by the SLI) and age and gender matched controls. The study will use an enhanced laboratory version of the 72-hour measurement block we have used in previous bedrest and astronaut studies. Year 03 will test the efficacy of Modafinil as a countermeasure when medium sleepers are required to "sleep short." The drug will be tested in a double blind placebo controlled cross-over design, during a week of severe (40%) sleep restriction in the laboratory, involving detailed sleep, circadian, rhythm, mood, and performance measures. The project seeks not only to provide findings of operational benefit to NASA, but also to provide tools and information of general benefit for those of us on the ground who have to restrict the time available for sleep because of occupational and/or care giving commitments. This experiment sought to provide questionnaire and diary instruments designed to assess habitual sleep need, and to assess the circadian regularity of human behaviors. It also had the aim of testing a particular pharmacological countermeasure (Modafinil) to reduced sleep amounts. In particular, the experiment involved a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of Modafinil as a countermeasure to five consecutive nights where sleep was restricted by 60% (i.e. to 40% of habitual durations). The 3 specific aims are: development of questionnaire instruments to assess habitual sleep need and timing, to identify “naturally short sleepers”, assessing the personality and circadian characteristics, also the evaluation of the consequences of unmet sleep need (thus identifying short sleepers who were sleeping short unwisely); continued development and testing of an easily administered diary instrument to assess circadian regularity in human behavior (the 5-item Social Rhythm Metric SRM-5); and a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of Modafinil as a countermeasure to 5 consecutive nights where sleep was restricted by 60% (i.e. to 40% of habitual durations).
approach: Aim 1a: Identifying and characterizing naturally short sleepers While most people require more than 6 hours of sleep to feel well rested, there appears to be a group of people who can function well on between 3 and 6 hours of sleep. The aims of the present study were: 1) to compare 12 naturally short (3.0h-6.0h) sleepers recruited by a media publicity campaign with age and gender matched medium length (7h-8.5h) sleepers on various measures; 2) to determine the prevalence of naturally short sleepers in a volunteer sample of 71 University alumni; and 3) to examine the distribution of the various measures from the alumni study, and the position of the 12 naturally short sleepers identified in #1 on these distributions, determining the extent, if any, to which they were outliers. Measurement instruments included diaries and questionnaires to assess sleep duration and timing, as well as questionnaire assessments of sleep pathology, morningness-eveningness, extroversion, neuroticism, pathological daytime sleepiness, perceived competence, optimism, depressive symptoms, exercise, and work habits. Aim 1b: Development of a questionnaire instrument to assess sleep duration and timing The initial proposal called for a development of a Sleep Length Index (SLI). However, rather than limiting ourselves to sleep length only, we felt it better to develop an instrument yielding measures of both timing and duration of the habitual sleep episodes. This resulted in the development of the Sleep Timing Questionnaire (STQ). The objective was to develop a single-administration instrument yielding equivalent measures of sleep to those obtained from a formal (2-week) sleep diary. Test-retest reliability was examined in 40 subjects who were given the STQ on 2 occasions separated by less than one year. Convergent validity was measured both by comparing STQ derived measures with objective measures derived from wrist actigraphy, and by comparing STQ derived measures with other subjective measures derived from a detailed 2-week sleep diary in 2 non-overlapping samples. Correlations of STQ measures with age and morningness-eveningness (chronotype) were also examined. Most subjects were healthy volunteers; some subjects were patients (enrolled in research protocols). Aim 1c: Consequences of sleeping short unwisely In order to provide baseline data for various research studies at the University of Pittsburgh over a 10-year period, 266 healthy subjects meeting certain criteria each completed a 14-night sleep diary. For each night, the diary allowed the subjective measurement of bedtime, wake time, Time In Bed (TIB), sleep efficiency, number of minutes of Wake After Sleep Onset (WASO), alertness upon awakening, and percentage of mornings needing an alarm (or a person functioning as one). Weeknight versus weekend night differences in TIB (TIBdiff), weekday alertness, and reliance on alarms were examined as possible indicators of sleep debt. Additionally, general descriptive data were tabulated. Aim 2: Continuing and testing a brief diary device to evaluate daily lifestyle regularity A brief diary instrument to quantify daily lifestyle regularity (SRM-5) is developed and compared to a much longer version of the instrument (SRM-17). Three studies are described. In Study 1, SRM-17 scores (2 weeks) were collected from a total of 293 healthy control subjects (both genders) aged between 19 and 92 years. Five items--(1) Get out of bed, (2) First contact with another person, (3) Start work, housework or volunteer activities, (4) Have dinner, and (5) Go to bed--were then selected from the 17 items and SRM-5 scores calculated as if these 5 items were the only ones collected. Comparisons were made with SRM-17 scores from the same subject-weeks, looking at correlations between the 2 SRM measures, and the effects of age and gender on lifestyle regularity as measured by the 2 instruments. In Study 2 this process was repeated in a group of 27 subjects who were in remission from unipolar depression after treatment with psychotherapy and who completed SRM-17 for at least 20 successive weeks. SRM-5 and SRM-17 scores were then correlated within an individual using time as the random variable, allowing an indication of how successful SRM-5 was in tracking changes in lifestyle regularity (within an individual) over time. In Study 3 a SRM-5 diary instrument was administered to 101 healthy control subjects (both genders, aged 20 – 59 years) for 2 successive weeks to obtain normative measures and to test for correlations with age and morningness. Aim 3: A controlled trial of Modafinil as a countermeasure to sleep restriction This study was a small-sample (10 subjects) double-blind placebo controlled study of Modafinil as a countermeasure to 5 consecutive nights of partial sleep restriction (to 40% of habitual time in bed). The study was a within-subjects cross-over design in which subjects experienced both drug and placebo conditions in 2 week-long sessions, separated from each other by 2 weeks. Each session involved the subject living in a time isolation apartment with no time cues or knowledge of clock time. The routine was specified by technicians who informed the subject when to get up, go to bed, take meals, etc. All sleeps were polysomnographically recorded, rectal temperature measured continuously, evening salivary samples collected (to detect the timing of the Dim Light Melatonin Onset - DLMO), and a battery of mood, alertness and performance measures (5 times per day) taken on each day of the study. On the final day of the study (before the recovery sleep) a Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT) was given to assess daytime sleepiness under drug and placebo conditions. Bedtime and wake time on the first night (of each week) were at the subject’s habitual times. On nights 2 through 6, bedtimes were made later and wake times earlier (by equal amounts) until time in bed (TIB) was at 40% of baseline levels (a 60% reduction). A placebo pill was taken at breakfast on the first morning (after the full night of sleep) and a pill (either placebo or drug depending on condition) at breakfast on the mornings following nights 2 through 6. The first 2 subjects also took a pill at lunchtime. The dose of Modafinil at each administration was 200mg. In all cases, between 100% and 150% of habitual TIB was made available for sleep on night 7 (the recovery night). With the exception of drug versus placebo, the procedure was identical for the two sessions for a given subject. One subject terminated the study early for family reasons, thus data analysis is proceeding using nine subjects (6f, 3m, age 21-58 years).
results: Aim 1a: Identifying and characterizing naturally short sleepers Few measures showed reliable differences between naturally short sleepers and controls except the obvious ones related to sleep duration. There was, however, some evidence for subclinical hypomanic symptoms in naturally short sleepers. The prevalence of naturally short sleepers in a volunteer alumni sample was about 3% after shift work, daytime sleepiness, psychopathology and sleep disorders had been excluded. Aim 1b: Development of a questionnaire instrument to assess sleep duration and timing Test-retest reliability for the STQ was demonstrated for estimates of bedtime (r=0.705, p 75 minutes with those with a TIBdiff <30 minutes), the group with more “catch up sleep” on weekends had shorter weeknight TIB durations (by about 24 minutes) and relied more on an alarm for weekday waking (by about 22%), indicating the possible utility of these variables as sleep debt indices. Aim 2: Continuing and testing a brief diary device to evaluate daily lifestyle regularity Measures of lifestyle regularity from SRM-5 correlated quite well (about 0.8) with those from SRM-17 both between subjects, and within-subjects over time. As a detector of irregularity as defined by SRM-17, the SRM-5 instrument showed acceptable values of kappa (0.69), sensitivity (74%) and specificity (95%). There were, however, differences in mean level, with SRM-5 scores being about 0.9 units (about one standard deviation) above SRM-17 scores from the same subject-weeks. SRM-5 scores also deviated more from a Gaussian distribution than did SRM-17 ones. In a study with a sample size of 101, the new SRM-5 instrument yielded scores with a mean of 4.11 and a standard deviation of 1.13. Correlations between lifestyle regularity and age, and between lifestyle regularity and morningness appeared similar whether 5-item or 17-item SRM measures were used. When a gender difference in lifestyle regularity appeared, it was detected by both SRM-5 and SRM-17 measures. Aim 3: A controlled trial of Modafinil as a countermeasure to sleep restriction The tenth subject was only completed at the end of September, and data analysis is ongoing, so the final results of this study cannot yet be reported.

title: Intraocular Pressure
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Intraocular pressure (IOP) has been shown to be an objective and quantitative measure of fluid shifts toward the head in the 10-degree head-down tilt bed rest model of microgravity. However, insufficient numbers of measurements have been made in microgravity to correlate bed rest changes with changes that occur in weightlessness. A study by Mader and Meehan (Mader et al., 1990) has quantified IOP changes that occurred with a 10-degree whole body head-down tilt over 48 hours. An immediate rise in IOP was documented upon assuming the head-down position. For the next 48 hours, variations in IOP were observed. Upon resuming the sitting position, there was a significant drop in IOP below the initial sitting values. The results of this study support the theory that distension of the retinal veins is a mechanism for the sudden changes in IOP that occur with changes in position. Assuming that head-down tilt is a valid model for fluid shifts in microgravity, the results from this study predict a similar sustained IOP increase in microgravity and a corresponding temporary drop in IOP (to below preflight values) upon return to Earth. Significant increases in IOP could result in visual impairment affecting crew performance and operations. This study was designed to test the following hypothesis: Intraocular pressures will rise immediately upon entering microgravity due to fluid shifts toward the head, and will drop to below preflight levels upon return to 1-G. The objectives of this study were: 1. To establish a database of changes in intraocular pressures that can be used to evaluate crew health, 2. To validate 10-degree head-down tilt bed rest as a model for fluid shifts toward the head in microgravity, 3. To facilitate the interpretation of data by providing a quantitative measure of microgravity induced fluid shifts toward the head, 4. To validate the hand-held tonometer as an effective tool for diagnostic and scientific data collection that can be used in on orbit investigations.
approach: A series of measurements were taken (on one eye only) preflight at Launch-6 (L-6) weeks, L-4 weeks, and L-10 days (dates are approximate) using the Tono-Pen (a clinical instrument commonly used by non-physicians in an ophthalmologist's office for measuring IOP). All preflight measurements were taken with the subject in the seated position. During flight, measurements were taken as soon as possible on orbit, post-sleep on flight day (FD) 2 and on the final flight day post sleep. Additional measurements were desired on orbit (pre- and post sleep), but were optional. Postflight measurements were taken at return (R)+0 and during the postflight physical on R+3. One drop of the short-activity topical anesthetic (proparacaine 0.5 percent) was instilled into the left eye and the subject instructed to look straight ahead. During flight, the drop of proparacaine was brought into contact with the lower conjunctival fornice to be absorbed onto the cornea by capillary action. The operator performed the following steps: 1. Replaced the tonometer tip cover. 2. Instilled one drop of proparacaine into left eye. 3. Gently tapped the cornea 3-6 times until a beep is heard. 4. Recorded the data displayed on the Tono-Pen LCD screen. 5. Repeated the procedure 5 times. Measurements were taken in the subject's left eye at each data collection point (in prior studies, there have been no significant differences between the measurements taken in 2 healthy eyes of an individual). The data collection sessions were approximately 5 minutes per subject; however, 15 minutes was scheduled to allow for the effects of the proparacaine to abate (the anesthetic deadens the eye for approximately 15 minutes). Neither the anesthetic nor the pressure measurement with the Tono-Pen caused discomfort to the eye when used properly.
results: Acceptable data was acquired from 9 subjects on missions STS-31, 32, 34, 41, 52 and 53. Sufficient data was not collected on STS-33, 44, and 50. There was a mean increase in intraocular pressure during the first two days of space flight. This increase of approximately 20 percent above baseline values decreased during the remainder of the flight but was elevated above baselines on landing day.

title: Exercise Response
research_area: Cardiovascular physiology; Clinical medicine; Exercise physiology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The success of the Apollo program overall, and the lunar landing missions specifically, was dependent upon the ability of the astronauts to engage in long and strenuous hours of extravehicular activity (EVA). Although it was expected that reduced gravity would make some tasks less difficult, it was noted that reduced suit mobility and the complexity of the mission timeline indicated that metabolic activity would exceed resting levels for extended periods of time. Because the type and extent of physiological dysfunction that could result from habitability in a zero-G environment had not yet been established, appropriate physiological tests were performed within Apollo program constraints to ascertain whether the physiological response of the crewmen to exercise was altered as a result of space flight. The objective of this investigation, performed during the Apollo 7-11 and 14-17 missions, was to evaluate the physiological response to exercise pre- and postflight in order to assure the success of lunar surface extravehicular activity (EVA).
approach: A bicycle ergometer and graded stress protocol were used to conduct the exercise stress tests. Heart rate (beats per minute) was used in determining stress levels. The bicycle ergometer was the only device capable of enabling quantitation of the work level. The graded exercise test permitted a progressive evaluation of physiological control system response and provided a better understanding of safe stress limits. By maintaining the same heart rate levels before and after flight, the same relative cardiovascular stresses were imposed. The tests were conducted 30, 14 and 4 days before flight, on recovery day (R+0), and 24 and 36 hours postflight. The same equipment was utilized before and after flight to conduct the stress tests. The protocol was comprised of exercise levels at heart rates of 120 ( for 6 minutes), 140 ( for 3 minutes), and 160 ( for 3 minutes). Samples of expired gas were obtained at appropriate times during each test. The Apollo 9 and 10 crewmen were also evaluated at stress level of 180 beats per minute (bpm). During each test, workload, heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory gas exchange (oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide production, and minute volume) were measured every minute. For Apollo 15 to 17, cardiac output measurements were obtained by single-breath technique. Arteriovenous oxygen differences were calculated from the measured oxygen consumption and cardiac output.
results: Each preflight test was treated separately and a mean value was computed for each mission with the crewman serving as his own control. A preflight mean and variance estimate for all crewmen was then computed and a similar statistic was computed for the separate postflight examinations. Statistical evaluations were made by means of standard t-test criteria. The test protocols were divided into three basic categories: pre-stress, exercise stress, and post-stress. Pre-stress Data: Heart rate was increased on R+0 by an average of 16 beats per minute for the sitting heart rate but was not significantly elevated by the second test (R+1). A slight increase was detected in minute volume on R+0 and R+1, and in the resting respiratory gas exchange ratio on R+1. Exercise Stress Data: There were several significant changes noted during this period. The relationship between heart rate and oxygen consumption (O2 pulse) was significantly altered at all heart rate levels postflight, whether elevated on an absolute basis (liters per minute) or corrected for body weight (liters per minute per kilogram). There were no significant changes in the oxygen required for a given workload immediately after flight, although a small increase was noted during the R+1 examination. Both the systolic and diastolic blood pressures attained at a given heart rate level were significantly decreased immediately after flight but returned to normal by R+1. There were no significant changes in the relationship between blood pressure and levels of oxygen consumption or cardiac output. The interrelationships of respiratory parameters (O2 consumption per minute volume and O2 consumption per CO2 production) indicated no significant changes immediately after flight. Results of the R+1 examination indicated that minute volume increased minimally. A statistically significant decrease of large magnitude (36 percent) was noted after flight in the cardiac output at a heart rate of 160 beats per minute. This variable had returned to preflight levels by the time of the R+1 examination. Post-stress Data: None of the measured variables changed significantly after the flight. Based upon the above physiological responses to exercise measured after space flight, it can be assumed that there was no significant change in mechanical or respiratory efficiency. There was a decrease in stroke volume which could have been caused by changes in the circulating blood volume and/ or redistribution of blood volume to the lower extremities. Heart rate was elevated for the same oxygen consumption. When coupled with a reduced stroke volume, increased heart rate maintained the same cardiac output/ oxygen consumption relationship.
