title: Effects of Circadian Rhythms on Decompression Outcome
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Decompression sickness (DCS) can occur when the dissolved gases in blood and tissues exceed the ambient pressure of an individual following a pressure reduction. Astronauts performing space walks (extravehicular activity, EVA) are subjected to significant pressure decreases as they decompress from the space shuttle/station cabin pressure of 14.7 pounds per square inch absolute (psia) to that of the space suit at 4.3 psia. Decompression also occurs with deep-sea divers upon returning from the higher pressures beneath the ocean to surface pressure. DCS symptoms range from mild joint pain to severe neurological injury or even circulatory collapse. Most symptoms are attributed to the formation of gas bubbles in various tissues and venous blood. These bubbles may react with blood cells (platelets and neutrophils) and vascular endothelial membranes, causing an inflammatory-like response. The response is caused by mediator release (arachidonic acid metabolites) and other cellular injurious agents. These mediators can result in endothelial cell injury, vasoconstriction, alterations in vessel wall permeability, and tissue edema formation. In this project, researchers examined the effects of the body’s endogenous circadian rhythms on the physiological consequences of decompression-induced venous bubble formation. Specific indices of inflammation and lung injury have been previously reported with DCS, even with mild to moderate levels of decompression. Based on these observations, the research team studied the effect of the circadian rhythms on the tolerance to decompression exposure and the underlying 24-hour bioperiodic dependencies. The overall objectives were to evaluate the quantitative evaluation of the physiological stress of decompression at different circadian times and to relate this to rhythms in cellular and biochemical variations over the 24-hour span. The measurement of these responses was hoped to elucidate some of the less understood risks associated with decompression illness, leading directly to operationally useful procedures. The study included had five specific hypotheses: Changes in decompression-induced neutrophil and platelet counts are circadian rhythm dependent. The severity of decompression-induced changes in inflammatory mediators (leukotrienes and thromboxanes) correlates with specific stages of known circadian rhythms. The severity of DCS symptoms and lung injury correlate with circadian rhythms. Decompression-induced variables in Hypotheses 1-3 above are the result of venous bubble formation and blood interactions. Pharmacological inhibition of decompression-induced symptoms and inflammatory mediators is dose-responsive as a result of circadian rhythm dependencies.
approach: Circadian Rhythm Studies: Twelve groups of 12 adult male Sprague-Dawley rats (440 ± 35 gm) were studied in this series of experiments (n=144). For a minimum of 14 days, the rodents were acclimated to a 12-hour light/12-hour dark schedule and then selected for decompression exposure in reference to hours after lights on (HALO). The protocol called for the rats to be exposed to conditions that induce DCS at 6 different times, (i.e. at 4-hour intervals throughout a 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycle). Data were collected at HALO 2, 6, 10, 14, 18 and 22. The animals were placed in the compression chamber and allowed 5 minutes to acclimate. If testing occurred in the animals’ dark cycle, the study was conducted in darkness with the decompression chamber covered to maintain the lighting conditions. The decompression exposures were selected to cause moderate to significant venous bubble formation in greater than 90% of the animals. Previous studies have demonstrated the utility of this model for decompression evaluation. The symptomology, however, was far less than usually reported with rodent experimentation where death or recovery endpoints were selected. The purpose of this study required less severe symptomology for outcome evaluation. For decompression, the rats of 6 randomly selected groups (experimental) were placed in the decompression chamber, compressed to 683 kPa over 11 minutes (60 minutes exposure), then decompressed over 9.5 minutes back to ambient pressure, followed by a 60-minute observation period. The remaining 6 groups (controls) remained at atmospheric pressure for 60 minutes. Symptom scores were based on a normalized relative severity scale (minor = 1, to more severe (including death) = 4)). At 60 minutes post decompression, the rats were anesthetized (halothane) for sample collection (urine, pleural fluid and arterial blood for differential cell counts, protein and mediator analysis) and pulmonary edema measurement. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was collected for protein, cell and eicosanoid analysis using enzyme immunoassays (EIA) and correlated as to the circadian staging. Concentrations of thromboxane B 2 (TXB 2 ), 11-dehydrothromboxane B 2 (11-DH-TXB 2 ) and leukotriene E 4 (LTE 4 ) in the biological samples were determined by enzyme immunoassay. Plasma nitric oxide was analyzed using chemiluminescence. Pulmonary edema was determined using a blood-corrected wet/dry weight ratio method. Statistical evaluation consisted of analysis for time effect by analysis of variance (ANOVA) and cosinor using a single (24-hour) or multiple (24 + 12-hour) component cosine model. Pharmacological Intervention Studies: Another aspect of this study was the investigation of the effects of inflammatory inhibitors to these mediators in decompression-exposed rats. Results of the decompression studies identified the extent of risk of DCS that is dependent on circadian rhythms or specific inflammatory mediators. From such data, the 2 biological times (with reference to circadian rhythms in risk) - one corresponding to the greatest and the second to the least susceptibility - were selected to conduct dose-response investigations of drug effect both on overt variables and on the release of inflammatory mediators (eicosanoids). Three agents were studied. The first was aspirin for determining the role of cyclo-oxygenase products of arachidonic acid metabolism, namely thromboxane A 2 and its stable byproduct TXB . The second was zileuton, produced by Abbott labs, which is specific to the 5-lipoxygenase pathway of arachidonic acid metabolic products, namely the leukotrienes. Zileuton actually blocks the 5-lipoxygenase enzyme rather than act as a leukotriene receptor antagonist. By selecting the appropriate cyclooxygenase and 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors above, and evaluating their dose response effects at different time points, it is anticipated that circadian rhythm dependent patterns will emerge and thereby enable a better assessment of risk and intervention possibilities with DCS. ß-agonist actions were studied with isoproterenol. Each drug was administered, either subcutaneously or by gavage, to the rats (468 ± 29 gm) prior to compression. Post decompression analysis is described above. Data were analyzed by ANOVA with Fisher’s post-hoc comparison for differences between means (p < 0.05 statistically significant).
results: DCS-induced venous bubbles can lead to obstruction of blood vessels, alteration in vessel wall permeability and vasoconstriction. Apart from the mechanical obstruction induced by the bubbles, these effects are partially caused by biochemical processes such as release of arachidonic acid metabolites, including thromboxanes and leukotrienes, resulting from bubble-activated neutrophils and endothelial cell injury. Significant circadian rhythm dependencies in the tolerance to DCS were evident in most of the parameters studied. This was most apparent in measured variables comparing HALO 2 and 12 time points. Clear circadian rhythm dependencies were found in the inflammatory mediator levels and in the extravascular lung-water ratio levels post decompression. These observations concur with other studies examining the circadian rhythm-dependencies of inflammatory-like reactions to various different stresses. Pharmacological intervention on the effects of inflammatory-like responses to DCS showed reductions. However, the hemodynamic and mechanical effects of the intravascular bubbles may also require specific intervention. Investigators concluded that DCS risk is affected by the circadian time structure and should be taken into consideration for properly assessing the underlying mechanisms of DCS, as well as the efficiency of preventive and intervention strategies.

title: Staged Decompression with an Argon-Oxygen (ARGOX) Breathing Mixture to 3.5 PSIA
research_area: Clinical medicine; Hyper- and hypobaric physiology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Long-term NASA goals include permanent occupation of the International Space Station (ISS) and missions to both the moon and Mars. One of the critical issues to be addressed for reaching these goals is the definition of an optimum pressure for extravehicular activity (EVA) suits. Currently, a 4.3 psia (pounds per square inch absolute) pressure suit is used for space shuttle EVAs in zero gravity. This suit, in combination with current preoxygenation schedules, is effective for decompression sickness (DCS) prevention. However, at 4.3 psia, the astronauts experience hand and arm fatigue due to the 'stiffness' of the suit. Also, due to the gravitational forces that exist on the moon and Mars, the current suit will be too heavy for planetary EVA. The trade-off for the advantage of a space suit with a lower pressure will be an increase in preoxygenation time. The first objective of this study was to test a decompression schedule for DCS prevention for a 3.5 psia EVA suit. In addition to the need for a lower pressure EVA suit, potential changes in the breathing gas composition needed to be evaluated. The Martian atmosphere has argon as a constituent, which will appear in the breathing mixture unless costly and heavy systems are provided to separate it from the nitrogen. The second objective of this study was to determine the DCS implications of breathing a 38% oxygen and 62% argon mixture (ARGOX) during decompression prior to EVA. The hypothesis was that breathing the ARGOX during denitrogenation at 7.3 psia for a maximum of 4 hours would not increase the risk of DCS during exposure to 3.5 psia, as compared with an identical exposure with 100% oxygen breathing. No attempt was made to define an operational preoxygenation schedule, nor to determine an operationally acceptable level of DCS risk. The data obtained from this experiment provides a crucial starting point, from which future experiments can be designed to determine an operationally specific preoxygenation schedule for a 3.5 psia pressure suit.
approach: Forty (40) subjects completed three hypobaric exposures each. Exposure A was a 5-hour preoxygenation routine (including ascent time) for exposure to 3.5 psia. Exposure B was a 5-hour preoxygenation routine (including ascent times) for exposure to 3.5 psia, utilizing a 7.3 psia stage. Finally, Exposure C was a 5-hour preoxygenation routine (including ascent times) for exposure to 3.5 psia, utilizing a 7.3 psia stage with an ARGOX breathing mixture. For exposures B and C the subject was decompressed to 7.3 psia and remained at that level for 4 hours. For this time period, the probability of DCS was expected to be extremely low. After this 4-hour stage, the subject was decompressed to the final pressure of 3.5 psia and remained there for 3 hours. During the 3.5 psia portion of the exposure, the subjects performed simulated EVA exercise. Exercise took place during the first 10 minutes of preoxygenation and consisted of dual-cycle ergometry performed at approximately 75% of each subject's maximal oxygen uptake. The 10 minutes of supine exercise was estimated to be equivalent to 60 minutes of supine resting preoxygenation. To simulate microgravity, subjects were supine on a gurney for the entire experiment session. All ascents were at 1,000 ft/min. Precordial echo-imaging for venous gas emboli (VGE) was accomplished at approximately 15-min intervals throughout the exposures using a Hewlett Packard SONOS 1000 echo-imaging System. The VGE were graded using a modified 4-grade Spencer Scale, where Grade 1 was infrequent VGE and Grade 4 VGE was of sufficient magnitude to overwhelm heart sounds. Grades 3 and 4 were classified as severe VGE (SVGE). The grading system was used as an indication of relative severity of exposure. Subjects were continuously monitored for symptoms, including self-reported mild symptoms of joint pain or any other DCS symptoms. The experiments were terminated with the completion of the 3 hour exposure to 3.5 psia or the occurrence of signs or symptoms of DCS. Thus, for any given subject, total exposure to 3.5 psia ranged from 3 hours maximum to a low of 0 hours (if the subject developed DCS during the staged decompression).
results: All statistical tests were performed at a confidence level of 95%. McNemar's tests for correlated proportions were used to compare the overall DCS, SVGE, and VGE incidence rates among the three profiles. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, with associated log-rank tests, was used to compare DCS, SVGE, and VGE incidence curves among the three profiles. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used to compare the maximum VGE of the three profiles. Of the 40 subjects, 13 (33%) developed DCS in profile A, 22 (55%) in profile B, and 31 (78%) in profile C. The difference in DCS incidence between profiles A and B was not statistically significant (McNemar's test), but was significantly different between profiles A and C, and B and C. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis tests showed significant differences between all three profiles, when compared to one another. 13 (33%) of the 40 subjects developed VGE in profile A, 18 (45%) in B, and 29 (73%) in C. Overall VGE incidence was significantly different (McNemar's test and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis) between profiles A and C, and B and C. SVGE (grade 3-4) were observed in 8 subjects (20%) in profile A, 13 subjects (33%) in profile B, and 23 subjects (58%) in profile C. Statistical analysis of SVGE showed the same pattern of statistically significant incidence as was shown for VGE. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test showed that profile C had the highest maximal VGE score and profile B had the second highest. In profile A, the subjects remained at ground-level for preoxygenation before being decompressed to 3.5 psia and, therefore, did not develop any VGE or DCS during that time. In profile B, two subjects developed VGE during preoxygenation at the stage decompression pressure of 7.3 psia. In profile B, two subjects also developed DCS at the stage decompression pressure, before the scheduled 3.5 psia was reached. One subject developed DCS during the 17 min ascent from the stage pressue. In profile C, six subjects developed VGE during ARGOX breathing at the stage decompression pressure of 7.3 psia. Three of these subjects also developed SVGE at the staged decompression pressure. Three subjects developed DCS during the ascent from the stage pressure before the scheduled 3.5 psia pressure was reached. Of the three, one developed VGE at the stage and SVGE during the ascent from the stage. This study showed that the staged decompression pressure of 7.3 psia during oxygen breathing for 4 hours did not protect against DCS at 3.5 psia compared with similarly long preoxygenation period at ground-level pressure. The overall incidence of DCS and SVGE tended to be higher, the incidence curve of DCS was steeper, and the maximal VGE scores were higher. The fact that 2 subjects developed VGE and three subjects presented with DCS before that final scheduled decompression to 3.5 psia was completed indicates that the staged decompression pressure of 7.3 psia likely allows development of some nitrogen bubbles in the tissues. If the staged decompression pressure had been higher (lower altitude), the increased risk of DCS and higher incidence of VGE may have been reduced. The results of this study suggest that if using 100% oxygen breathing, reduction of risk of DCS can be achieved by either using a higher stage decompression pressure, or by not using a staged decompression at all. A breathing mixture of ARGOX during the staged decompression has the advantage of using an inert oxygen diluent obtained directly from the Martian atmosphere, and being acceptably fire-safe. However, the results of this study indicate that it also results in a higher incidence of VGE and an increased risk of DCS compared with 100% oxygen breathing during stage decompression.

title: Assessment of Humoral Immune Function During Long-Duration Space Flight
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Since the late 1960s, the immune system has been studied by United States and Russian space scientists. Depressed immune cell function has been confirmed in-flight by reduced responses to in vivo delayed-type hypersensitivity tests. Changes in cell-mediated immune function have been consistently documented. However, the effect of space flight on the humoral immune system has not been thoroughly assessed during flight. Therefore, the goal of this experiment was to test whether space flight has an adverse affect on humoral immune function similar to that observed with the cell-mediated immune system. It was expected, based on the decrease in other immune system functions, that the ability to mount an antibody response to new or recall antigens would be depressed during space flight. It was hypothesized that the specific antibody titers following immunization during flight would be significantly lower than the titers obtained from a ground-based control group. The objectives of this experiment were to (1) determine the effects of long duration space flight on baseline levels of immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgD, IgE and IgM) in serum (2) assess the ability to produce appropriate antibodies in response to a specific antigenic challenge during space flight and (3) determine secretory immune function by measuring salivary IgA and lysozyme levels in response to immunization during space flight.
approach: An in-flight vaccination with specific antigens (23 pneumococcal polysaccharide antigens) was used to test the ability to mount an antibody response in vivo . These antigens produce well-characterized antibody responses in normal, healthy individuals. Blood and saliva samples were collected prior to flight and immediately before in-flight immunization to determine the baseline values of the specific pneumococcal antibodies. Vaccination took place during the late flight period. Additional saliva and serum samples were scheduled to be taken 7, 14 and 21 days after the in-flight immunization to measure the magnitude of antibody production. It should be noted that in-flight immunization was performed on two out of three subjects scheduled to receive antigen injections. In addition, the post flight sample collection schedule was significantly modified due to crewmember and medical requirements. The final post flight sample collection was delayed for two crewmembers. The result was that samples were not collected on immunization+21 days (3 weeks after immunization). Samples were collected at 4 weeks after immunization for the two crewmembers, therefore, the peak antibody response was missed. Antibodies to the immunization antigens were measured by Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) in the serum and saliva samples. The degree of response was compared to those obtained from a ground-based control group which were age- and sex-matched volunteer subjects.
results: The three crewmembers all exhibited minor shifts in the levels of isotype specific antibodies between the preflight and in-flight pre-immunization period. In general, these variations did not appear to be highly significant, and they suggest the serum antibody levels were not altered directly by space flight. The immunized crewmembers did respond to the vaccine, indicated by the increase of antigen-specific antibody titers. However, the magnitude of response may be altered for some isotypes in some individuals. The degree of the response was not particularly robust in one crewmember. It was found that antibody titers of two of the four isotypes doubled the pre-immunization levels but did not reach 200 nanograms antibody-nitrogen/ml for one crewmember. Incidentally, a positive response is a two-fold increase over the baseline level and a post-immunization titer above 300 nanograms antibody-nitrogen/ml. However, since the data set is very small, this data may suggest a decreased response to the vaccine in this crewmember, or it could be a function of individual variability since some of the isotype levels were adequate. General immunoglobulin levels did not change significantly during or after flight in any of the crewmembers.

title: Orthostatic Function During Entry, Landing and Egress
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Several cardiovascular parameters were measured during entry, landing, and egress in order to develop and assess countermeasures designed to improve orthostatic tolerance upon return to Earth.
approach: Heart rate and rhythm, blood pressure, cardiac output and peripheral resistance were monitored during entry and landing of the Shuttle, and during crewmember egress from the Shuttle.
results: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure increased during space flight and were highest when gravity reached its peak during entry and at touchdown. Systolic blood pressure decreased significantly when the astronauts first stood up from their seats after landing. Heart rate increased at the time of peak gravity during entry and at touchdown, and it rose even higher when the astronauts first stood up. The increase in heart rate varied, but was generally substantial.

title: Vestibular Modulation of Autonomic Responses to Orthostasis
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Orthostatic intolerance and related functional impairment remain a common problem for astronauts upon return from space. Despite considerable effort to develop countermeasures for this problem, a fundamental question remains unanswered: What is the cause of orthostatic intolerance? Post flight symptoms vary widely and include both vestibular and orthostatic intolerance manifestations. The role of vestibular disturbances in orthostatic intolerance is unknown. Although it is known that vestibular signals project to the vasomotor centers of the brainstem in cats, there has been no prospective study of vestibular system effects on blood pressure control during orthostasis or on orthostatic tolerance in humans. Most fundamental, it remains unknown whether otolith inputs play an important role in the cardiovascular adjustments to the upright position in humans. The altered vestibular function after space flight may influence orthostatic tolerance indirectly (producing intolerable symptoms requiring recumbent posture) and/or directly (by affecting autonomic responses to orthostasis). Post flight vestibular disturbances are complex and probably include some involvement of otolith inputs, semicircular canal inputs and related inputs. The purpose of this study was three-fold: 1) to determine the otolith contribution to the cardiovascular adjustments to the upright position; 2) to determine whether altering otolith or semicircular canal inputs affect blood pressure regulation during orthostasis; 3) to determine whether altering otolith or semicircular canal inputs affect orthostatic tolerance. The specific aims of the study were as follows: 1. To determine the role of otolith input in mediating the cardiovascular adjustments to the upright position. 2. To determine how otolith orientation affects the occurrence of pre-syncopal symptoms during an orthostatic stress. 3. To determine the effect of semicircular canal stimulation (with caloric testing) on the cardiovascular adjustments to orthostasis. 4. To determine the effect of semicircular canal stimulation (with caloric testing) on orthostatic tolerance.
approach: Study 1 : This study was performed to address specific aim 1. The response to seven perturbations involving combinations of head-up tilt (0, 30 and 60 degree) and neck position to affect otolith orientation. (30 degree flexion or extension) were obtained in random order. Study 2 : This study addressed specific aim 2 by assessing the heart rate, arterial pressure, sympathetic nerve activity, heart rate and blood pressure variances, respiration, responses to sustained orthostasis (30 degree head-up tilt plus lower body negative pressure at 10, 20 and 30 mmHg) with and without otolith input (0 degrees versus 60 degrees otolith orientation). Study 3 : This study addressed specific aims 3 and 4 by assessing the heart rate, arterial pressure, SNA. heart rate and blood pressure variances, responses to graded orthostasis (lower body negative pressure at -30, -40, -50 and -60 mmHg) with and without semicircular canal stimulation (caloric ear canal irrigation).
results: Study 1 : Within the first 20 seconds of tilt, arterial pressure increased most obviously in the 0 to 1 Gz otolith condition. Thoracic impedance tended to increase more in otolith-constant conditions. But no dependent variable differed significantly between tilt conditions, and no significant time x tilt interactions emerged. Study 2 : There was a trend for greater increases in heart rate, but not for differences in arterial pressure or vascular resistance during the graded orthostasis. In addition, changes in low frequency and high frequency spectral power trended toward significance,, but did not achieve significance. In some subjects, this effect suggests that autonomic control was modestly affected by the otolith stimulus during graded orthostasis. Study 3 : Significant nystagmus was provoked by the caloric stimulus in each subject with insignificant effects on baseline heart rate, mean arterial pressure, or sympathetic nerve activity consistent with previous pilot data and previous findings. The cold caloric stimulation performed during LBNP resulted in similar changes as the thermoneutral stimulus in heart rate and blood pressure suggesting that there was not a significant effect of semicircular canal stimulation.

title: Operational Psychology Countermeasures During the Lunar-Mars Life Support Test Project
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: A number of psychological activities were conducted to ensure successful operations and protect crewmember well-being, including individual crewmember selection, crew composition, training and preparation family inclusion, educational briefings, in-mission tracking, operational interventions, and post mission repatriation. The Lunar Mars Life Support Test was a ground-based study based in a chamber facility, which included four different phases, Phase I, II, IIA, and III. This study describes these activities, the rationale behind their design, the similarities and differences to techniques utilized for space flight, and considerations related to designing psychological countermeasures for confined environments. In addition to testing physical and engineering systems, the chamber study series, functioned as an effective test bed for developing operational concepts and countermeasures for extended space missions. The study tested human crews in four tests, or phases, whose objective was to ultimately produce equipment and processes that could be incorporated into a variety of lunar, Martian, and low-Earth orbit stations and vehicles. The four tests were termed Phase I (15 days, one person), Phase II (30 days, four persons), Phase IIa (60 days, four persons), and Phase III (91 days, four persons). The crewmembers performed a number of technical and research tasks in the areas of engineering, station maintenance, medicine, and life science. In addition, they had exercise, housekeeping, media events, educational outreach, and other duties related to the conduct of high-profile confinement missions. A number of psychological activities and countermeasures were conducted to ensure successful completion of the phases and to protect the crewmembers' psychological health and well-being. These operational activities, including crew selection, training and preparation, family inclusion, control room team management, in-mission tracking, management consultation, in-mission interventions, post mission debriefings. The psychological countermeasures were implemented specifically and solely to assure that the objectives of the tests, including psychological health and readiness objectives, would be achieved. The team that designed and provided the psychological countermeasures had previous experience doing so for missions in other ground-based, underwater, and space environments. The purpose of this study was to give an overview of the psychological countermeasures designed for the closed-loop living environment as well as some of the operational considerations that steered their implementation.
approach: Phase I, the 15-day, one-person test was the first to be conducted. The test duration was similar to that of a Space Shuttle mission. Several beneficial factors where taken in account for during phase I such as: Basic psychological requirements had been applied to accommodate fundamental psychological needs inside the chamber. Tasks were straightforward and meaningful. The participant was a NASA engineer who had been highly involved in the development of the regenerative life support systems being tested. The outside control team was small and was composed of friends and colleagues of the participant inside the chamber. The duration of the test was short. The participant possessed the necessary personality characteristics and motivational set needed to cope with the solo conditions of the test. The only measures taken for this phase by the psychological team were basic requirements, selection, and monitoring. In Phase I, selection consisted of a review of the participant's ability to fulfill the mission. Monitoring was accomplished through informal visits to the chamber and control team to see that things were proceeding well. The human accommodations incorporated into this first test were rudimentary but sufficient for the duration The Phase II test was a four-person, 30-day test. The second phase was located in a larger chamber, and added additional hardware maintenance tasks to the internal workload, and gradually extending the duration. There was not only the matter of learning to structure and manage the activities of the confined participants, but also the job of learning how to staff and structure the activities of the outside control room (CR) and their relationship to the inside team. In an early planning meeting between project management and the psychology team, several decisions were made that would affect not only the course of Phase II but subsequent phases as well. These decisions addressed programmatic design issues of a psychological nature that, in the past, had direct effects on the success of other confinement tests and analogous missions. Among the key decisions were: To promote a shift from a "mentality" to a "mission mentality". The addition of a few medical and life science objectives resulted in a more diverse set of test objectives to be carried out. Education outreach objectives were increased over Phase I, and methods similar to those used in space missions were utilized. Hence, instead of "subjects", the participants would be called "crewmembers" and comprise a cohesive "crew". Distinct job roles for each of the crewmembers would be identified and a crew "commander" would be formally designated. Together, the crew, the control room (CR) personnel, and project management were tasked with carrying out the ground-based "mission". The establishment of a crew identity and mission mentality was especially important to the psychology team. Crew psychological health, well-being, and productivity are greatly facilitated by the motivation and focus that is derived from a mission context. This is particularly helpful when mission durations lengthen, and a greater burden is placed on individual and team coping strategies. In addition, the mission model offers a template from which the organization can draw a number of solutions to issues such as control room staffing schedules, management of human research data, and so forth. To use the early, relatively brief phases to create a cadre of experienced crewmembers for later, more difficult phases and follow-on programs. It was anticipated that the later phases would be considerably longer and that programs, which followed LMLSTP, might be far more complex and psychologically challenging. It was recommended that the organization pursue a "farm club" approach with respect to crew selection; the objective being to expose as many engineers as possible to the briefer confinements before tackling the tougher missions. This would result in a local group that was operationally and psychologically experienced from which to draw crewmembers. The farm club approach requires that the early phases not be overly difficult and that they be an explicit part of building a potential crewmember pool for later projects. To compose crews that are diverse in gender and experience but which represent all of the essential technical skills needed inside the chamber. There are no magic numbers that comprise the "best" crew size or the "best" gender mix. The principal driver for these issues is ensuring that you have the necessary technical skills and minimum number of people inside the chamber to most effectively achieve the mission objectives. A mixed gender crew was recommended. The psychological countermeasures for Phase II were increased over those for Phase I, but were still at a relatively low level due to the brief duration. The development of the mission context was the single most effective and far-reaching psychological act. After that, psychological selection activities had the greatest impact. In all types of missions (e.g., space, military, polar, ground studies, etc.), many diverse factors influence who is actually assigned to a mission, and psychological information is only one part of the overall selection process. However, within that part, individuals are sought who are psychologically suited for the target mission and who work well together as a team. In general, the determination of individual suitability and team compatibility for long-duration missions is a systematic, multi-stage process that involves psychological testing, structured screening interviews, structured reference interviews, skill-based training and selection exercises, sociometric ratings, formal briefings, individual strategy sessions, and other techniques. The specific techniques are chosen and adapted according to the characteristics of the target mission. Similarly, the psychological training and preparation of the individual crewmembers, the crew, the CR personnel, and the crew families varies according to the demands that the target mission is expected to place on them. In mission monitoring and support procedures, as well as post mission repatriation and tracking activities, also must be tailored to the individual mission. For Phase II, selection and compatibility were determined by an abbreviated version of psychological testing and through a structured interview, which was a combination of two screening ("select-out") and suitability ("select-in") interviews used for selecting astronauts for extended missions. The select-out testing and interview process addressed the clinical psychological fitness of potential candidates, and the select-in testing and interview process addressed the psychological suitability of each candidate for the target mission. The criteria were scaled to a level appropriate for a ground-based test bed of 30 days' duration. Training and preparation consisted of two crew briefings and an individual planning session with each crewmember, in which lessons learned from previous similar missions were passed along, potential issues were identified, and personal and team strategies were created and reviewed. As in preparation for space missions, the lessons, issues, and strategies that were covered were divided into three categories, specifically those that applied to: 1) the individual crewmember, including family issues; 2) the crew as a whole, including leadership; and 3) the wider organization, including management and control room relations. Phase IIa, the next mission, extended the duration for a four-person crew to 60 days. The increased psychological demand inherent in this phase necessitated a slightly greater set of countermeasures. A more stringent version of the selecting testing and interviewing process was applied to the individual candidates, and significantly more effort was expended on assembling a compatible crew. Additionally, activities were added in the areas of preparation of CR personnel and family members. The issues facing CR personnel were significant, because the organization had little experience maintaining a rested external team over an extended period of time. The psychological team passed along CR lessons learned from other environments and promoted three general themes: 1) further inclusion of the CR group as an integral part of the team and acknowledgment of their contribution, 2) mutual understanding of the daily issues facing the crew and the CR groups and strategies for managing that interface, and 3) a reasonable work-rest schedule for individuals in the CR. The organization as a whole was very eager to pursue these themes, because there was a vital, preexisting team spirit and a high tendency toward inclusion in general. During the mission, both of the groups made it clear that they valued the other's continuing efforts. Similar to the Phase II experience, one of the principal lessons learned from Phase IIa was that the definition of the work roles and responsibilities of key people inside and outside of the chamber must be made clear and specific to an extraordinary degree. This somewhat mitigates the misunderstandings and erroneous assumptions that naturally arise between two interdependent groups that are physically and visually separated. Disconnects and miscommunications of intention between crews and their control rooms can lead to a "we-they" phenomenon that is a classical occurrence in a variety of venues (polar, space, military, etc.). This did not occur in Phase IIa, because both groups consciously worked to lessen the issue. Beginning with Phase IIa and continuing into Phase III, the crewmembers' families or significant others were brought together before the mission and during the mission for psychological information about the mission, and to create an environment of mutual support between them. In Phase IIa, these informal gatherings occurred over lunch. Inclusion of family members is a powerful crew support method for many reasons, in addition to being a source of strength for the crewmembers' families. Phase III study took place over a 90 day duration. In addition to increased length, the project included a large number of science experiments or technology demonstration projects from the life sciences. With the scientific, hardware maintenance, and education outreach tasks, there would be plenty of opportunity for meaningful work. However, the duration and complexity of the test bed were not trivial, and that warranted the application of more extensive psychological countermeasures. Selection was more stringent; the criteria were in line with the increased demand on the individual to adapt effectively and to function well as part of a confined team. Individual selection activities were extended to include structured interviews of character references and more extensive reviews of each candidate's history in past work teams. It was essential that the applicant possess the skills to maintain a cohesive crew while still enabling diversity of opinion. The initial process of testing, interviewing, and history review resulted in eight candidates remaining, from which four would be assigned as prime crewmembers and four as back up crewmembers. Activities were devised that served both psychological training and selection needs. Within the group of eight individuals, some had worked together in NASA for years and knew each other very well; some came from outside organizations and were unknown to most of the group. Some had been crewmembers in previous chamber missions, and some had no experience with either confinement or operational environments. The objectives at this stage were to: Identify a set of four people, who would work well together as a prime crew, Prepare all eight individuals to work together in the event that back up crewmembers were rotated in during the mission, Provide a means for the eight to get to know each other in problem-solving situations and under conditions of mild stress, and Begin to integrate the new people into the NASA group that was fielding the mission. An outdoor challenge course was used to accomplish these selection and team building objectives. An initial series of low-level, physical problem-solving situations was presented to the eight as a group, and the team worked these out as they saw fit. In a subsequent series of high-level traverses and climbs, the group split into pairs and triads to resolve the challenges. Membership in the pairs was rotated, so that people would have a chance to work with each other in a smaller unit. Each situation was debriefed by the group and the psychological team for lessons learned that might apply to the actual Phase III mission, and general information regarding teamwork styles for extended missions was passed along. The most significant benefit of this training was the familiarization and integration of the eight team members with one another. Following this preparation, the eight team members completed a sociometric form in which each of them gave their input regarding who they would select to be with them on the upcoming mission. This was an opportunity for the crewmembers to express their social preferences and to have their input factored into the crew assembly process. The psychological team combined this input with their own to develop recommendations for crew composition. Ultimately, of the four prime crewmembers that were assigned, two were NASA engineers who were crewmembers on previous enclosed system study missions, and two others were scientists with no previous confinement or mission experience. The early integration and sociometric activities would later prove to be a good investment when a prime crewmember had to be swapped out for a back up just prior to mission start. Another aspect of the study was to provide sufficient preparation of the crewmembers, their families, the control room, and project management. In some cases, researchers only provided encouragement and assistance to key people to prepare themselves for the mission, as was the case with meetings to further define job roles and responsibilities and a training workshop for CR personnel. In other cases, researchers provided direct training. This included more lessons learned briefings for the prime and back up crewmembers, individual planning sessions to discuss potential situations that might arise and to review strategies for dealing with them, information and integration meetings with the families, a training briefing for project management, and a five-day experiential training course on confined team operations for the prime crew. The Confined Team Operations training was designed to prepare the prime crew in precisely the following areas: 1) confined living and working, 2) integration and organization as a team, and 3) actual mission operations experience. A working underwater station with a topside control and logistics facility was the setting for the weeklong training. The crew was provided with a schedule, scientific and station maintenance goals, and crew organization goals that were comparable to those expected on the three-month mission. In addition, the design incorporated a condensation of a number of scenarios and conditions that had arisen on previous enclosed system study missions, or on analogous missions of three months' duration, which had the possibility of arising during their upcoming mission. The prime crew was provided with a blend of didactic, discussion, and hands-on experience regarding living and working in confined settings, leadership and follower, personal adaptation, safety, scheduling and rescheduling, time management, team norms, managing a relationship with the control center, contingency planning, conducting interviews with the media, analogue lessons learned, and other topics related to the upcoming mission. In addition, the designated commander had an opportunity to establish the leadership style that he would use, the entire crew had an opportunity to sort out their roles, and the experienced crewmembers brought the others up to speed on all aspects of the organization, procedures, and points-of-contact among other things. Approximately one month prior to the start of the Phase III mission, the psychological team held individual meetings with the prime and back up crewmembers to review their readiness for the mission, and to jointly identify any issues that needed to be handled. For the back up crewmembers, the main issue was certainly one of psychological readiness, because it is very typical for back up crewmembers, once prime crew assignments are made, to shift their attention to the demands of their daily jobs rather than the demands of the impending mission. The back up crew has a higher probability of being on the outside of the chamber during the mission than on the inside, and it is not easy for a back up crewmember to maintain a state of mental preparedness for something he or she is not likely to do. Consequently, the individual meetings were, in part, designed to relight the process of mental preparation in the back up crewmember. Approximately two weeks prior to the mission tart, the prime crew commander had to be removed from the crew for medical reasons. A back up crewmember was rotated in, and a commander was assigned from the remaining prime crew. The tracking of the crew's psychological health and well-being was accomplished through regular visits to the chamber at various times during the workweek and on weekends. Of particular interest were aspects of the ongoing mission such as individual workload, technical concerns including failed equipment, the development of threats to the mission completion, or to crew health and well-being, the amount and quality of sleep, significant news from home or work, mood and humor, any significant mission events, and crew cohesion. Contacts were made with the Control Room (CR) team, managers, principal investigators, family members, and crewmembers. Contact with the crew was through two-way video meetings, telephone calls, and electronic mail. Family lunches also were held periodically during the mission. The psychological team served as a sounding board and information resource for all of these groups.
results: The Advanced Human Life Support Enclosed System Study series was successful from both a technical and psychological point of view. The mission goals were attained, the crewmembers look back on their experience with a sense of satisfaction and accomplishment, no significant mission management difficulties were encountered, and a step or two was taken forward on the road to the Moon and Mars. Early on, the project management recognized the importance of the human factor in the overall success of the series and was willing to invest in the pre-mission psychological activity necessary to ensure positive results. Psychological countermeasures are a key aspect of any long-duration, human-rated test bed. They are most effective when they are specifically designed for the demands of the target mission, and address the crewmembers, but their families, key external personnel, and the wider organizational system that is fielding the test. Countermeasures act to increase the probability that the goals of the test will be met, and they do so by preventing difficulties and promoting performance readiness. There is a direct, inverse relationship between the level of effort invested in the human aspects and the number of difficulties that arise during a confinement mission. Any report from other such missions of difficulties with individual participants, within teams, between cultures, between external control personnel and internal participants, between participants and project managers, etc. can only be understood in light of the type, extent and quality of the interventions applied to prevent such problems. More often than not, when such problems occur, they can be traced back to the organization(s) that are fielding the mission and are responsible for implementing operational psychology countermeasures. How much effort should be invested? The answer to this depends upon how much difficulty and risk, and what kinds of difficulty and risk the organization is willing to accept.

title: Haughton Mars Walkback
archive_status: No data from this study was submitted to LSDA. Please contact LSDA if you know of available data.
objectives: Results of previous research showed that six male astronauts were able to ambulate 10 km on a level treadmill while wearing a prototype extravehicular activity (EVA) suit in simulated lunar gravity. However, the effects of lunar terrain, topography, and real-time navigational requirements on ambulation performance are unknown. This study characterized the effect of lunar-like terrain and navigation on maximal oxygen consumption (VO2) and distance traveled during an unsuited 10 km (straight-line distance) ambulatory return in earth gravity.
approach: Three subjects completed simulated returns under two different conditions. The first condition was navigation over lunar-like terrain at Haughton Crater, Canada (10KNAV). For 10KNAV, unsuited subjects began at a location 10 km from the finish point and were instructed to return at a rapid but sustainable pace using a global positioning system receiver for navigation and tracking speed and grade. Three separate starting points, each 10 km from the finish point, were defined and subjects completed each route once. The second condition was a single unsuited trial on a treadmill (10KTM) that reproduced the grade and speed from one of their 10KNAV trials. VO2 was measured during all conditions.
results: 10KNAV was completed with an average time of 126.5 ± 28.7 minutes and VO2 of 27.8 ± 5.1 mL/kg/min. Straight line distance between starting and ending points was 9.91 ± 0.22 km and actual distance traveled was 10.61 ± 0.61 km. Comparison between 10KNAV and 10KTM indicated that lunar like terrain increased VO2 by 9.8 ± 3.8 mL/kg/min, a 56% increase.

title: Gene Expression Patterns Predictive of Radiation-Enhanced Colon Tumorigenesis: Diet as a Countermeasure
research_area: Cell and molecular biology; Radiation biology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: There is currently no reliable, non-invasive method to determine the response to radiation exposure and development of colon cancer throughout the disease process. One potential method to monitor changes in colonocyte gene expression that occur during the various stages of the disease is through global transcriptional profiling using exfoliated colonocyte mRNA. This proof of principle project has as its main goal the modification of existing protocols in order to improve the effectiveness of polyA isolation from feces in preparation for analysis of gene expression using microarray techniques. Specific Aims 1. The first aim was to optimize polyA isolation and sample handling steps prior to array hybridization in order to develop a protocol that could reliably be used to measure gene expression from exfoliated colonocytes. 2. The second aim was to establish normalization procedures capable of handling the problem of sample degradation that occurs in fecal samples.
approach: Weanling Sprague-Dawley rats (n = 60) were provided one of two diets that contained either the combination of fish oil and pectin, or the combination of corn oil and cellulose. Half of the rats were exposed to 1 Gy of 1 GeV/nucleon Fe ions at Brookhaven National Laboratory 3 weeks after starting the experimental diets. All rats received injections of a colon-specific carcinogen (azoxymethane, AOM) on days corresponding to 10 and 17 after irradiation. Fecal samples were collected 7, 14 and 28 weeks after the last AOM injection. Fecal pellets were collected soon after defecation, stored in RNA protection buffer and frozen (-80 Celsius) until processed.
results: Modifications to the isolation and processing procedures for fecal polyA samples has resulted in highly improved quality and quantity of polyA that can be used for micorarray analysis of gene expression. We have developed a two-stage normalization procedure to process the data generated from the partially degraded RNA that is capable of handling this type of data, yet can be computed in a reasonable amount of time. Analysis of the data indicates there are strong effects of radiation on gene expression documented throughout this model of colon carcinogenesis, and that the effects can be tracked using a non-invasive procedure.

title: Digital Echocardiography in Manned Space Flight: Remote Diagnosis and Quantitative Analysis
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: An echocardiogram uses high frequency sound waves called ultrasound to create a moving picture of the heart. Using Doppler ultrasound, it provides information on blood flow across the heart valves. Average echocardiograms contain approximately 30 loops and 10 still images. Each loop is a series of frames from a single cardiac cycle; although, multiple cycles can apply if clinically required. The objective of this experiment was to enhance the design and analysis of real-time transmission of ultrasound images from crewmembers on board the International Space Station (ISS) and exploration missions. Four specific aims were evaluated in this ground-based study, each consisting of several projects. The four specific aims of the investigation were : To develop infrastructure for digital acquisition, storage, and transmission of echocardiograms both on Earth and by satellite; To test existing and new digital compression algorithms for impact on clinical interpretation and quantitative content; To validate new quantitative approaches to assess cardiovascular mechanics in microgravity; and To refine the acquisition, segmentation, display, and analysis of three-dimensional echocardiograms. Due to the complexity of this experiment, each of the four specific aims was accomplished through one or more individual research projects that often overlapped. Specific details of the individual projects can be found in the investigator's final report. The first specific aim tested ultrasound operations. The ultrasound system will be used by highly trained crewmembers on the ISS. Sufficient ability is needed to perform examinations in case of a medical emergency. To prepare for such a contingency, this study investigated whether novice operators can perform diagnostic ultrasound. The second specific aim tested existing and new digital compression algorithms for impact on clinical interpretation and quantitative content. A Virtual Collaborative Clinic was designed to combine sophisticated imaging with high-performance networks and provide advanced medical technology access to underserved communities. The goal was to provide physicians and scientists with a network where information needed to perform operations in virtual space could be shared. In addition, remote hospitals would be able to access knowledge and techniques of larger institutions, and the technology could be extended into space, servicing astronauts. The use of Video Home System (VHS) and Moving Pictures Experts Group (MPEG) formats were also studied. The third specific aim was relevant to cardiology diagnostic methods on Earth and the ISS. Five projects supported this specific aim. One project assessed ventricular function using Doppler tissue imaging, a new methodology able to assess heart function. In contrast to Doppler imaging, Doppler tissue imaging records the velocity of heart muscle motion rather than blood flow. Another project dealt with shortened early transmitral filling deceleration time, which has been associated with increased filling pressure and reduced survival in patients with heart disease and increased left ventricular stiffness. Another project characterized pulmonary venous inertance. In defining the physical components of cardiac fluid dynamics, the inertial component of pulmonary venous flow was determined to interpret clinical recordings of flow in lung veins. Another project consisted of bed rest studies. The impact of three-dimensional ultrasound imaging for human cardiovascular physiology and pathology was investigated through the fourth specific aim to validate a new real-time echocardiographic method for future use on the ISS. Three-dimensional ultrasound has advantages over current two-dimensional ultrasound that includes imaging speed of the entire heart without special training. Heart chamber size, volume, and muscle mass can be determined without geometrical assumptions. Obtaining blood flow velocity in three-dimensional space may provide knowledge on the change in blood flow distribution under microgravity. One project of the fourth specific aim was to validate three-dimensional ultrasound with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Another project involved the structure and motion of the mitral annulus, a fibrous ring surrounding the mitral valve between the left atrium and left ventricle of the heart. Software was developed to obtain segmentation of the mitral annulus using commercial three-dimensional echocardiographic review software. Another project evaluated outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a condition of excessive thickening of the heart muscle with some misalignment of the cells. Again, three-dimensional and two-dimensional techniques were compared. Another project involved volumetric changes with simulated microgravity. In addition to four projects involving human studies, several animal studies were employed in the fourth specific aim to address the accuracy of left ventricular volume measurements and flow quantification using three-dimensional echocardiography. The projects involved aortic regurgitation, flow quantification using real-time three-dimensional color Doppler, left atrium volume quantification and non-invasive assessment of left atrium function, and quantification of left ventricular mass.
approach: Specific Aim #1 To develop the infrastructure for digital acquisition, storage, and transmission of echocardiograms, ultrasound images were evaluated using the ISS video system developed by the Human Research Facility Project at the Johnson Space Center. A design and analysis test of real-time ultrasound data transmission from the ISS evaluated the impact of reducing transmission rate on image quality. Images were tested at rates from 60 fields per second down to 1.875 fields per second. Another project leading to the first specific aim was to develop the infrastructure to review and analyze digital echocardiographic data collected in various locations. The hypothesis that novice operators could perform diagnostic ultrasound was tested using five employees of the Cleveland Clinic Foundation who were untrained in the use of the ultrasound. Each test subject received four hours of training before attempting ultrasound examinations. All operators performed exams on normal subjects and patients with defined pathology. Specific Aim #2 Several projects supported the second specific aim. The Haughton Mars Project Testbed involved a blinded review of echocardiographic data. A 45-minute delay in the transmission mimicked the scenario of communication from Mars. As part of the test, five pathological cases were forwarded to the Haughton Mars Project for retransmission along with normal echocardiograms. Another project was transmission of echocardiographic data across the NASA Research and Education Network (NREN). A sonographer and a cardiologist looked at cell loss and cell error ratios. For the echocardiographic image compression project, six reviewers performed blinded measurements from still frame images selected from twenty echocardiographic studies simultaneously acquired in VHS and MPEG formats. A virtual hospital project also supported the second specific aim. A demonstration showed feasibility for high bandwidth telemedicine between remote clinics and tertiary care hospitals. One activity was real-time transmission of three-dimensional echocardiograms. Doctors received and rotated three-dimensional high-resolution color stereo medical images online at desktops and collaborated with remote colleagues for consultation, diagnosis, and treatment planning including surgical simulation. High-performance networks connected participating Virtual Collaborative Clinic sites with the application server. Specific Aim #3 To address specific aim three, bed rest studies were conducted using fourteen days of 4 degree head-down tilt with three subsequent recovery days. Exercise echocardiographic data pre- and post-bed rest, Doppler tissue imaging, and color M-mode flow propagation were studied on five subjects. Left ventricular volumes, cardiac output, and brachial reactivity were measured to discover changes in intravascular tone. In another collaboration, combined echocardiographic indices were applied for the assessment of left ventricular filling pressures in healthy volunteers on bed rest. Specific Aim #4 A total of eight hundred thirteen patients with a variety of heart diseases underwent three-dimensional studies to address the fourth specific aim of refining the acquisition, segmentation, display, and analysis of three-dimensional echocardiograms. In almost all subjects, the data were acquired without any geometrical assumptions. To validate real-time three-dimensional echocardiography with MRI, a total of thirty-four patients were evaluated with the three-dimensional method in the operating room or the echocardiographic laboratory. Thirteen of twenty-eight patients with heart disease and six subjects with normal left ventricular function were evaluated by three-dimensional echocardiography and MRI for left ventricular volumes and ejection fractions. The human studies that involved volumetric changes with simulated microgravity used a tilting bed system to mimic microgravity in ten normal subjects. The stroke work of the left ventricle was evaluated as was ejection fraction and left ventricular volume.
results: The test of real-time transmission of ultrasound data from the ISS using the communications simulator showed that for cardiac ultrasound, optimal results were obtained at field rates of 80 or above, and rates as low as 15 per second provided useful information. For abdominal examinations, lower frame-rates were acceptable; although, rates of at least 15 fields per second were necessary for meaningful real-time guidance to the data. For strictly diagnostic purposes, frame-rates below 7.5 fields per second were acceptable for non-moving structures. Researchers concluded that if this protocol could be used on board the ISS, then ground guidance of ultrasonic acquisition would be possible during a medical event involving crew members that do not have expert training in ultrasound. The hypothesis that novice operators can perform diagnostic ultrasound studies was confirmed with preliminary analysis that demonstrated excellent capability for general imaging by the novice operators. However, acceptable image acquisition using cardiac ultrasound was achieved only when guided in real time by an expert sonographer. The blinded review of echocardiographic data in support of the second specific aim revealed excellent image quality, especially for abdominal structures, with adequate image quality on cardiac structures. All key pathological features were successfully identified, even after retransmission. The examination was promising for future use of portable ultrasound in exploration class missions. When echocardiogram data was played over the NREN, cell loss and cell error ratios of 10 -5 showed performance was nominal with image quality far superior to videotape. When the cell loss and cell error ratios rose to 10 -3 , the system froze, but this represented an extreme degree of network noise. When echocardiographic studies were simultaneously acquired in VHS and MPEG formats, there was excellent agreement between the two. Quantitative off-line measurements from MPEG digitized echocardiograms were feasible and comparable to those obtained from VHS. Analysis of the third specific aim showed that transmitral and intraventricular pressure differences could be estimated noninvasively in canines and humans. The importance of inertial contributions was demonstrated. Further results showed that in adults with heart disease, a transmitral filling deceleration time provided an accurate estimate of left ventricular operating stiffness and supported its application as an index in the evaluation of diastolic function. In a separate project, pulmonary venous flow was primarily governed by inertial forces with little convection or viscous effects. The bed rest study project showed that combined echocardiographic indices, which were previously validated with acutely ill heart disease patients, could be used to assess left ventricular filling pressures in healthy subjects. These results apply to assessment of crew health and response to space flight. The results that involved validation with MRI showed that real-time three-dimensional echocardiography was feasible in patients with heart disease and could provide a fast low-cost alternative to MRI for evaluating cardiac function. Three-dimensional techniques were also superior to two-dimensional ones when outflow obstruction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was evaluated. When cardiac function was studied in simulated microgravity, stroke work of the left ventricle was different from normal gravity. The animal studies supporting the fourth specific aim showed several results. Left ventricular stroke volume and stroke work increased proportionally with the amount of aortic regurgitant volume quantitatively and reflected the additional energy consumption needed by volume overload in aortic regurgitation. Techniques were also shown to estimate the peak blood flow rate and demonstrate better understanding of blood flow phenomena and quantification. A three-dimensional technique was used to estimate left atrium volumes; although, it showed some underestimation relative to MRI. This same technique provided an excellent means to determine left ventricular mass as compared to conventional two-dimensional and other methods.

title: Apollo Flight Crew Vestibular Assessment
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The United States manned space flight program addressed the potential problems that could arise during flight due to vestibular disturbances, particularly motion sickness. Concern was expressed because of the highly unusual microgravity environment encountered during space flight. Interestingly, astronauts from the early Mercury and Gemini programs reported no significant vestibular problems. However, the Apollo program presented several significant changes from previous programs, including increases in the size of the spacecraft's interior and differences in the activities being performed during the mission. Due to the larger habitable volume of the Apollo Command Module (CM), as compared to the Mercury and Gemini modules, crewmen were able to move about freely within the spacecraft. In addition, inflight docking procedures allowed the crewmen to move back and forth between the Lunar Module (LM) and the Command Module. It was also noted that crewmen would make the transition from zero-g (0-G) to the one sixth-G environment on the lunar surface and then back to 0-G numerous times during the six Apollo lunar-landing missions. With these changes, particularly the greater mobility permitted by the larger volume of the CM and the LM, the potential for the first serious vestibular problems became evident. Therefore, a set of qualitative assessment procedures was developed for the Apollo series of missions in order to document the vestibular disturbances experienced by the astronauts. Opportunities for inflight quantitative monitoring of the vestibular system were severely limited because of the principal mission objectives and the technical nature of the tasks that were performed on each mission. The objective of the vestibular investigations performed during the Apollo program was to obtain definitive information regarding the effects of microgravity on the vestibular system while using primarily qualitative data collection procedures.
approach: Qualitative assessment procedures: The qualitative information used in the study was gathered from a variety of sources. An attempt was made to compile detailed information on the history of the astronauts' motion sickness experiences. These histories indicated whether an individual astronaut had ever experienced motion sickness in automobiles, boats, during 0-G parabolic flight, or during spacecraft egress exercises. In addition, heavy emphasis was placed on subjective reporting by astronauts regarding the type and magnitude of vestibular disturbances experienced during and following their missions. The inflight subjective reports documented whether the astronauts experienced stomach awareness, nausea, vomiting, or illusions while performing tumbling exercises. Special preflight and postflight laboratory measurements: To accomplish a comprehensive evaluation of vestibular function, two types of pre- and postflight tests were performed on the Apollo 16 and 17 astronauts. Postural equilibrium tests were selected as a means of providing an assessment of a behavioral skill that is sensitive to altered vestibular inputs resulting from prolonged exposure to weightlessness. The second test, caloric irrigation, complemented the tests of balance by monitoring changes in semicircular canal activity as a possible cause of postflight equilibrium disturbances. For the postural equilibrium test, each astronaut was fitted with military-type shoes to rule out differences in footwear as a variable in subject comparisons. Duration of time was the parameter designated as the performance measure of the balancing tasks. The subject was instructed to stand on the prescribed support with eyes open and his feet in a tandem heel-to-toe arrangement and then to fold his arms and maintain his balance. Timing began when the subject folded his arms. In the second series of tests, the time measurement was initiated after the subject attained a balanced position and closed his eyes. Rails of four widths (1.90, 3.17, 4.45, and 5.72 cm) and the floor provided the foot support for the standing subject. A strip of tape 10.16 cm wide and 68.5 cm long served as a foot-guide alignment for the floor portion of the test. The caloric irrigation test required electrodes for recording nystagmic eye movements. The silver chloride electrodes (Beckman) were placed at the outer canthus of each eye and the reference electrode was placed in the center of the forehead. A Tracor RN-243 electronystagmograph system was used throughout the caloric test to record potential changes across the cornea and the retina. Eye movement calibration and all subsequent caloric testing were done in a dark room. Electronystagmographic calibration of eye movements in degrees per centimeter was obtained with the subject sitting in an upright position and fixating on two alternately flashing red lights placed at a distance from the center of eye rotation, providing a separation of 20 degrees of arc. The subject was then reclined in a Tracor torsion swing chair so that his head was approximately 60 degrees from upright. Baseline measurements were taken for 40 seconds to determine the presence of spontaneous nystagmus. Two separate water baths were maintained at temperatures that ensured irrigating temperatures of 35.5 degrees Celsius (C) and 34.0 degrees C. Calorization of each subject proceeded according to the following schedule: right ear (RE), 35.5 degrees C; left ear (LE), 35.5 degrees C; RE, 34.0 degrees C; and LE, 34.0 degrees C. In each case, approximately 160 ml of water was directed onto the tympanic membrane for a period of 40 seconds. To maintain mental alertness, the subject silently solved arithmetic problems during the response period. Following irrigation of each ear at 35.5 degrees C and a period of continuous recording that indicated the disappearance of all nystagmic response, an additional period (140 seconds) of rest was started; this rest period was increased to 260 seconds following the 34.0 degree C irrigation. After all caloric testing, eye movement calibrations again were made in accordance with the pretest procedure. Nystagmus parameters measured during the caloric irrigation test included direction of eye movement, lag time, average velocity, maximum velocity, maximum frequency, duration of nystagmus, and right-left asymmetry. Lag time is defined as the time between the onset of irrigation and the first measurable nystagmus. Maximum velocity was obtained by selecting the 10-second time frame of a given record that contained the greatest preponderance of high-velocity, slow-phase nystagmus, and by calculating the average slow-phase velocity value for that time frame. Maximum frequency was obtained by a similar calculation. The duration of nystagmus was the interval between onset and complete cessation of nystagmus. Right-left asymmetry was a measurement which compared right and left ear nystagmus responses and documented which ear elicited the greater response. Preflight data were collected on the Apollo 16 prime and backup astronauts 30 days before launch (L-30). Postflight data were collected on all three prime astronauts three days following recovery; two of the three crewmen were tested again four days later. Preflight data on the Apollo 17 prime and backup crewmen were collected at L-30 and at L-15. No postflight data were collected on the Apollo 17 crewmen.
results: Motion sickness (MS) history and inflight MS: The results of the MS history examination indicated that twenty-seven of the thirty-three Apollo crewmen had a positive MS history. However, only nine of those twenty-seven crewmen experienced inflight MS symptoms. Of the six crewmen who had a negative MS history, only two experienced MS symptoms during flight. Therefore, the total number of Apollo astronauts who experienced inflight MS symptoms was eleven. Severity of inflight symptoms: The total number of occurrences of mild MS (stomach awareness) was six. Moderate MS symptoms (stomach awareness, nausea) occurred only twice throughout the entire series of Apollo missions. However, severe MS symptoms (stomach awareness, nausea, vomiting) occurred three times. Previous space flight experience: Of the thirty-three Apollo crewmen, fifteen were classified as inexperienced astronauts (first space flight). Six of the fifteen inexperienced crewmen experienced MS symptoms during flight. Of the eighteen veteran crewmen (one or more space flights), only five experienced inflight MS symptoms. Special pre- and postflight laboratory measurements: Postflight data were not collected on the Apollo 17 crew. Therefore, a complete data analysis was completed only for the Apollo 16 crew. Preflight results for the postural equilibrium test indicated that all three crewmen were within the range of performance typically exhibited by young, healthy, pilot-type subjects. Postflight results indicated that during the first and second test periods, 3 (denoted as R+3) and 7 (denoted as R+7) days after landing, respectively, postural equilibrium with eyes open was nearly identical to preflight performance in all crewmen. However, at R+3, the Commander (CDR) and the Command Module Pilot (CMP) showed a marked decrease during the eyes-closed test. When these two individuals were tested again at R+7, there was a definite improvement in postural stability with eyes closed compared to their R+3 results. The preflight results for the caloric irrigation test indicated that all Apollo 16 crewmen possessed normally functioning vestibular canals. The nystagmus produced was always in the expected direction. Spontaneous nystagmus was present in all three crewmen, but no meaningful trends were observed. All of the crewmen exhibited an asymmetry in right and left ear nystagmus responses which generally remained unchanged through the R+7 test date.
