title: Studies of Mechanisms Underlying Orthostatic Intolerance using Ambulatory Monitoring, Baroreflex Testing, and the Valsalva Maneuver
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Over the last three decades, symptoms of altered cardiovascular function ranging from orthostatic tachycardia on landing day to serious cardiac rhythm disturbances have been associated with short duration space flight. However, there is a lack of understanding about the effects of long duration space flight on cardiovascular function. It was hypothesized that: (1) after flight, autonomic responses to changes in arterial pressure (supine and standing) will be compromised; (2) carotid baroreceptor-cardiac reflex (baroreflex) function will decrease steadily during the first four weeks of flight and then remain stable; this decrease in function will relate to postflight orthostatic intolerance; (3) blood pressure (BP), heart rate (HR), and their variabilities will be decreased throughout the flight, and the reduced variabilities will relate to reductions in carotid baroreflex function and postflight orthostatic intolerance; (4) changes in heart rate and arterial responses during Valsalva maneuvers will reflect inflight loss of autonomic function. The primary objective of this experiment was to assess cardiovascular function before, at regular intervals during, and after long duration space flight by performing a standard battery of tests. The second objective was to characterize the integrated responses of arterial pressure reflex control systems to standing before and after long duration space flight. The third objective was to relate inflight changes in the integrated responses of arterial pressure reflex control systems before and after long duration space flight. The last objective of this experiment was to determine the importance of changes in blood volume to postflight decrements in orthostatic tolerance.
approach: There were four functional objectives in this experiment: 24 hour ECG and Blood Pressure Monitoring, Carotid Baroreflex, Valsalva Maneuver, and Stand Test. For the 24-hour period prior to carotid baroreflex measurements, HR, BP, and cardiac rhythm disturbances were recorded during normal routines in the ground and in flight. Holter monitors recorded the electrocardiogram continuously and blood pressure monitors recorded auscultative BP automatically every 20 minutes while awake and every 30 minutes while asleep. After the flight, a Holter analysis system automatically generated reports, which included average heart rate and incidence of atrial and ventricular dysrhythmias. All reports were verified by at least one board certified cardiologist. Blood pressure results were also verified. For the carotid baroreflex, carotid barorecptors were stimulated with a stereotyped series of pressure changes applied to a neck chamber. Pressure was raised initially to about +40 mmHg, reduced to about -60 mmHg, and then raised back to +40 mmHg in 20 mmHg, R-wave triggered steps. R-R interval responses were plotted as functions of carotid distending pressure. Baroreflex responses were reduced to the following set of parameters for analysis: range of R-R interval responses, maximum slope of the stimulus-response relation, and operational point. The operational point is a measure of the amount of buffering capacity below baseline systolic pressure. The crewmembers performed two 15 second Valsalva maneuvers at 30 mmHg expired pressure after the baroreflex measurements were completed. Two minutes separated each Valsalva maneuver. Before, during, and after each stimulus, the electrocardiogram, beat-to-beat finger blood pressure, and Valsalva straining pressure were recorded. Controlled frequency breathing was performed before and after each Valsalva maneuver. Valsalva responses were divided into four phases for analysis: Phase I, the initial blood pressure and R-R interval rise immediately after the onset of straining Phase II, the early blood pressure and R-R interval fall and partial recovery during straining Phase III, the sudden and brief blood pressure and R-R interval reduction immediately after the release of straining Phase IV, the blood pressure and R-R interval overshoot of recovery. Stand tests were performed preflight and postflight after Valsalva maneuvers were completed. For stand tests, crewmembers were instrumented for electrocardiogram, manual blood pressure, beat-to-beat finger blood pressure, and transcranial Doppler. An intravenous catheter was inserted into an antecubital vein. Following a 20-minute supine rest period, plasma volume was determined using carbon monoxide rebreathing. A blood sample was drawn for plasma norepinephrine and plasma epinephrine levels. Then, 2-D and M-mode echocardiography were used to determine aortic cross-sectional diameter and aortic flow was measured with continuous-wave Doppler ultrasound. Middle cerebral artery flow was measured with transcranial Doppler ultrasound. Measurements continued while subjects remained supine for six additional minutes. Crewmembers were then assisted to a standing position by three investigators. The finger with the continuous arterial pressure device was held at heart level by a system of Velcro straps. Crewmembers then remained standing without support for 10 minutes. A final blood sample was drawn at the end of the standing period. All data were recorded on digital tape and on paper.
results: A number of preflight, inflight, and postflight anomalies occurred during the experiment. Data were lost due to equipment failure, subject compliance, and crew support personnel interference. Due to these various anomalies, some data collections were compromised. Nonetheless, this experiment has yielded important information about cardiac function during long duration space flight. Findings from this investigation are very similar to those reported from short duration space flight investigations and indicate that most autonomic cardiovascular adaptations occur within the first days of space flight, possibly the result of decreased sympathoexcitation. These changes persist for at least four months in flight. However, the occurrence of a significant event of ventricular tachycardia during the mid-portion of the flight does not preclude the possiblity that long duration space flight increases the likelihood of malignant dysrhythmias.

title: EVA Walkback Test
archive_status: No data from this study was submitted to LSDA. Please contact LSDA if you know of available data.
objectives: As lunar exploration vehicle and extravehicular activity (EVA) suit requirements mature it’s important to determine whether one or two surface rovers will be required to enable safe and efficient human exploration of the moon (1/6-g) and Mars (3/8-g). The increased mass, volume, and cost associated with the launch and transport of two rovers to the lunar surface could be considerable and might not be necessary if it is possible for the crewmembers to walk back to a habitat in response to a failed rover. As a starting point, it was assumed that 10 km would be the maximum EVA excursion distance from a habitat based on anticipated lunar surface operational concepts and results from the Apollo program. A multi-disciplinary team was assembled from the Constellation Program’s EVA Systems Project Office in collaboration with Johnson Space Center’s (JSC’s) Space Life Sciences Directorate Human Research Facility’s EVA Physiology, Systems and Performance (EPSP) Project to investigate the feasibility of performing a suited 10 km ambulation, (henceforth referred to as “walkback”) independent of whether the subject walked, jogged, loped, or ran. This study was designed not only to determine the feasibility of a 10 km walkback, but also to collect human performance data relevant to optimizing space suit design for the targeted operational environment. The basic approach involved performing suited tests with unsuited controls with the goal that specific physiologic and biomechanical parameters of the suit could be understood across a range of gravity levels and ambulation speeds.
approach: All subjects were recruited from a pool of personnel who typically perform EVA-suited studies for the Engineering Directorate and from the group of astronauts selected to support exploration EVA studies. Suit fit checks in the Mark III Advanced Space Suit Technology Demonstrator EVA Suit (MKIII) were performed on a range of subjects, and only those who had good suit fit were selected for inclusion in this study due to the projected length of the 10 km test and potential medical safety issues. From the candidates, six male astronaut subjects participated in the data collection phases of the study, including the 10 km portion. Two backup subjects including one female performed only the maximal oxygen consumption (VO2pk) test. At the time of the test, no available female astronauts properly fit in the MKIII suit.
results: All subjects completed the 10 km walkback in less than two hours and completed the test with little difficulty working at about 50% of their aerobic exercise capacity. Preliminary analysis indicated that the metabolic cost of the suit was significant compared to unsuited controls. Weight-matched unsuited trials provided an initial estimate accounting for the metabolic cost of the suit due to the increased weight of the suit. But additional factors such as inertial mass, center of gravity (CG) alterations, pressure-volume work, and suit kinematic constraints could not be isolated. Additional tests will be needed to evaluate these other suit related factors. Results of this study clearly indicated that crewmembers in the MKIII suit may perform well on the moon but may not perform well on Mars due to the increased gravity. In the lunar trials, the suited metabolic rates were all submaximal, whereas in the Mars-suited trials, subjects rapidly approached near maximal physiologic effort while brisk walking.

title: Effects of Simulated Microgravity on the Anesthetic Properties of Propofol
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Despite careful health screening by NASA, astronauts adapted to microgravity are likely to require the administration of anesthesia for a variety of surgical conditions not only in the highly autonomous environments of space habitation or Mars-type missions but also for immediate surgical care after evacuation from low orbital missions. Little-to-no information is available regarding the most appropriate anesthetic technique in microgravity. Physiologic adaptation to weightlessness (e.g., changes in blood and plasma volume, fraction of cardiac output directed to brain, autonomic nervous system activity) can be expected to markedly alter the in vivo behavior and characteristics of anesthetics/hypnotics. Such an altered/increased effect may underlie the anesthetic complications encountered in the two rhesus monkeys aboard Bion 11 that were anesthetized for minor surgery on post-flight day one. On the other hand, data from medication use during space flight indicates normal efficacy of bezodiazepines and even a decrease in the self-reported incidence of sedation caused by promethazine. Total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) is probably the ideal cost-effective method of rendering subjects insensitive to pain during surgery under microgravity conditions. Unlike volatile agents, which require vaporization and waste gas scavenging, TIVA is a light, compact and self-contained (closed) system that interfaces the patient. It consists of a small programmable syringe pump, which holds a syringe containing an intravenous (IV) anesthetic, which in turn, is attached to tubing that allows drug to be directly infused from the syringe into the vein of a patient. Among the TIVA agents in use today, propofol (2, 6-diisopropylphenol) is the best single suitable agent for use in space. Propofol has several key properties that make it a desirable anesthetic in a space environment: 1) rapid induction of and emergence from anesthesia, 2) ability to adjust the dose to achieve anesthetic states ranging from conscious sedation to general anesthesia 3) lack of drug accumulation in the body, even during long procedures, 4) significant anti-emetic properties, and 5) a simple and reliable means for assessing the depth of anesthesia/hypnosis, the bispectral index (BIS), derived from the electrical activity of the brain The hypotheses for this study are: !(1) Adaptation to microgravity increases the hypnotic/anesthetic effect of propofol by changing its pharmacokinetics (PK), but not pharmacodynamics (PD). (2) Adaptation to microgravity does not change the recovery of cognitive function after propofol anesthesia. This study will determine the effect of microgravity on the following characteristics of propofol anesthesia: 1) onset and offset kinetics, 2) dosing requirements for sedation and anesthesia, 3) PK/PD/metabolism, and 4) recovery of neuro-cognitive function in the postoperative period 5) occurrence of delayed postoperative cognitive dysfunction.
approach: Twenty volunteers were enrolled to receive propofol anesthesia, ten volunteers for each of the two groups.
results: Of the 20 volunteers in the propofol groups, 18 completed the study without complications. Two anesthetics in Group II were stopped, one because of persistent coughing – likely a residual from a respiratory tract infection - and one because of regurgitation without aspiration – most likely caused by inadequate anesthesia. Independent review of all anesthetics by a panel of 4 anesthesiologists as part of Data Safety Monitoring oversight did agree with the investigators that no unexpected novel safety concerns were raised by the study anesthetics. Antiorthostatic bed rest led to hemoconcentration and typical mild symptoms of back pain or a sensation of fullness of the head/ headache. For both propofol groups the anesthetic effect of propofol was similar in normal gravity and simulated microgravity. The clinical assessment by the modified observer’s assessment of alertness/sedation scale was corroborated by BIS monitoring. As intended, subjects in group II underwent clinically equivalent anesthetics in normo- and simulated microgravity. Consistent with the expected hemoconcentration, but unexpected from the clinical course, these anesthetics resulted in propofol plasma concentrations for up to 60 minutes after the anesthetic that were higher in simulated microgravity than in normogravity (p<0.05, repeated measures ANOVA). While propofol impaired aspects of cognitive function early after the anesthetic, the recovery was the same for normal and simulated microgravity. There was no evidence of delayed postoperative cognitive dysfunction. The results suggest only a minor impact of the adaptation to weightlessness on the pharmacodynamic/pharmacokinetic profile of propofol. There are important limitations to the study. First, adaptation to microgravity was only brief, i.e. simulated by 48 hours of antiorthostatic bed rest. While this duration is sufficient to cause the changes in blood volume and blood flow characteristic of microgravity, and thereby simulates microgravity-induced changes in distribution and elimination of drugs, it falls short of reproducing the clinical scenario of anesthesia care after a medical evacuation from ISS or autonomous care on a long-term mission. Second, anesthesia was studied in the absence of surgery and surgical disease. Both alter the neuro-humeral milieu and may profoundly influence the patient’s response to an anesthetic.

title: Physical Fitness Evaluation Oxygen Uptake Measurement
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The Periodic Fitness Evaluation with Oxygen Uptake Measurement (PFE-OUM) was performed to demonstrate the capability of crewmembers to perform periodic fitness evaluations (PFE) with continuous oxygen consumption measurements within 14 days after arrival on ISS, and once monthly during routine PFEs. Once the capability of the pulmonary function system (PFS) is verified to then perform PFEs, crewmembers will be able to integrate their monthly PFE with oxygen consumption measurements to fulfill the requirement for cardiovascular fitness evaluations during long-duration space flight. This experiment was a collaborative effort between the European Space Agency (ESA) and NASA. A medical requirement performed on the International Space Station Medical Operations called for the performance of a Periodic Fitness Evaluation (PFE) on board the International Space Station (ISS) with oxygen consumption measurements, referred to as OUM. A measurement of aerobic capacity (VO 2 max) reflected the maximum rate that oxygen can be taken up and utilized by the body during exercise. The magnitude of VO 2 max depends on the capacity of the lungs to exchange oxygen between the air and blood in lung capillaries, the capacity of the cardiovascular system to transport oxygen to the muscles, and the muscles' capacity to use oxygen. The highest rate of oxygen uptake and use reflects the upper limit in the ability of the body to supply energy via aerobic metabolism to the active muscles during strenuous exercise and the ability to carry out weight-bearing tasks. Currently, the crew aerobic capacity on-board is only estimated using heart rate and work load while the crew goes through a set exercise protocol. It was assumed that the oxygen consumption per given work load was equivalent to the pre-flight measurements. The validity of this assumption has not been verified with in-flight data. This investigation provided the necessary hardware to measure oxygen uptake with the crewmember breathing through a mouthpiece in the performance of the routine PFE evaluations.
approach: Crewmembers routinely performed a ground-based exercise test using metabolic gas analysis before and after space flight. During these tests, OUMs were made and used to estimate the crewmember's aerobic capacity. Measurements of aerobic capacity allowed exercise physiologists and flight doctors to assess crew health and fitness and accurately prescribe exercise countermeasures for use on-board the ISS. While performing this test, the crewmember's heart rate and blood pressure were recorded using the Blood Pressure/Electrocardiograph (BP/ECG). Heart rate data along with the prescribed cycle ergometer workloads, allowed ground personnel to estimate changes in crewmember aerobic capacity by comparing the heart rate response to increases in workload performed during pre-flight evaluations. There were several limitations to this approach. First, a method does not currently exist to verify that the cycle ergometer was correctly calibrated or maintaining calibration over time on orbit. Second, due to the fact that the cycle ergometer aboard the ISS is vibration isolated, which lead to instability between the exercising subject and the cycle, the metabolic cost associated with exercising on the cycle may differ than that measured during cycle ergometer tests performed on the ground. These factors may lead to misinterpretation of the crewmember's changes in aerobic fitness during long-duration space flight. At the time of this experiment, OUMs had not been possible during the PFE because hardware capable of measuring oxygen uptake had not been available aboard the ISS. Now, the NASA/ESA Pulmonary Function System (PFS) provided the ability to perform the required OUMs. This evaluation was performed in two phases. The first phase was used to assess the feasibility of making OUMs during the PFE. The data provided investigators the necessary information to determine if the PFS was able to accurately perform OUMs aboard the ISS within the current crew timelines designated for the PFE. The second phase of this evaluation was used to compare the current methods of estimating ISS crewmember's aerobic fitness with the more direct method of performing OUMs. The data collected during this phase along with data collected during phase one was analyzed using the current method of estimating changes in aerobic fitness (i.e., workload and heart rate observations alone) and direct analysis of the heart rate data in association with OUMs. Preflight, crewmembers performed their required medical testing, Cycle Ergometry (MR080L), using nominal metabolic gas analysis hardware. The testing included a maximum cycle ergometry test at approximately 270 days prior to flight and (L-270 days) and a submaximal cycle test at approximately 30-45 days before flight. Post-flight, the crewmember performed the nominal submaximal cycle test 5-7 days following landing and again at 30 days post-flight as part of the medical testing using the nominal metabolic gas analysis hardware. Crewmembers performed the same submaximal cycle exercise test post-flight as performed pre-flight. The PFS hardware measured the O2 and CO2 concentrations using the Photoacoustic Analyzer Module (PAM) and the ambient humidity, temperature and pressure. During the exercise test, the subject inhaled cabin air and expired through a mouthpiece, and the nostrils were occluded with a nose clip. The fractions of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the expired air was measured by the PFS and used to calculate oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide production and metabolic rate. Blood pressure was measured at designated time intervals throughout the protocol, while ECG was recorded continuously via the BP/ECG. The initial in-flight PFE-OUM session was performed at mission day 14 and then every 30 days after throughout the mission. The NASA/ESA Pulmonary Function System (PFS) was one of the major components of the HRF Rack 2 and was launched to International Space Station (ISS) aboard STS-114 in July 2005. The PFS was a facility class research hardware consisting of: The Photoacoustic Analyzer Module (PAM) developed by ESA. The Pulmonary Function Module (PFM) developed by ESA. The Gas Analyzer System for Metabolic Analysis Physiology (GASMAP) developed by NASA. The Gas Delivery System (GDS) developed by NASA All hardware pertaining to the OUM activity was stored in the HRF Rack 2 and was checked out during Increment 12. Initial use of the system on-board the ISS was performed by an ESA augmentation crewmember in July 2006 during Increment 13. The PAM determined the concentration of seven respired gas components that also contained significant concentrations of nitrogen and water vapor utilizing two photoacoustic analyzers and the oxygen analyzer mixture. The PFM, when operated together with either the Gas Analyzer System for Metabolic Analysis Physiology (GASMAP) or PAM plus the GDS, formed a respiratory facility capable of a wide range of respiratory and cardiovascular measurements including, breath-by-breath measurements, diffusing capacity of the lung, expiratory reserve volume, forced expired spirometry, functional residual capacity, cardiac output, alveolar ventilation, volume of pulmonary capillary blood, and numerous other specialized tests of pulmonary function. It consisted of the Respiratory Valve Unit with associated flow-meters, a re-breathing bag and an electronics unit. The GDS provided special gas mixtures needed for the calibration of the GASMAP and PAM and for the performance of such physiological tests as re-breathing and washout measurements. The GDS supported five canisters of gas mixtures which were permanently presented on-orbit and supported re-supply of these gases.
results: This experiment has concluded on the ISS as a collaborative effort between the ESA and NASA agency. Eight subjects completed two peak cycle ergometer tests and exercise stage through 250 Watts (W). Therefore, the planned comparisons of the dependent variables were conducted at 100, 150, 200 and 250 W. The oxygen consumption (VO2) did not differ between devices at 100, 200 and 250 W; however, a statistically significant difference between the devices was observed at the 150 W stage. At this stage, the percent difference in VO2 between the two devices was 5.4%. In addition, the peak VO2 of the subjects demonstrated a non-significant difference of 3.8% between the two devices, also within the ranges reported in the literature of day-to-day variation in VO2PK. No differences were seen in expired pulmonary ventilation (VE), even though the systems compute pulmonary ventilation using differing methods. Both the PFS and ParvoMedics use a differential pressure pneumotach to measure flow; however, the PFS measures flow on the inspiratory side, while the ParvoMedics measures flow on the expiratory side. Additional information can be found in the NASA Technical Report NASA/TP-2007-214756.

title: Promoting Sensorimotor Response Generalizability
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The goal of this study is to develop an inflight treadmill training protocol that enhances adaptive generalization of locomotor function to facilitate rapid and robust recovery of functional mobility after long-duration space flight. Specifically, the investigator hopes to determine whether subjects exposed to a special inflight treadmill protocol will have greater proficiency in reassembling an appropriate, full-body postflight locomotor response. Will they recover locomotor function sooner than subjects not exposed to the inflight treadmill protocol? Data from this experiment are planned to be used to develop a countermeasure system.
approach: Locomotor function were assessed before and after space flight using two tests of gait function. Test 1: The Integrated Treadmill Locomotion Test characterizes alterations in the integrated function of multiple sensorimotor subsystems. This test required subjects to walk on a motorized treadmill while researchers assessed changes in dynamic postural stability, head-trunk coordination, visual acuity and lower limb coordination strategies. Subjects walked at 6.4 km/h on a motorized treadmill while performing a visual task consisting of identifying the position of the gap in the letter "C" that is presented centrally on a laptop computer positioned 4 meters in front at eye level. Each trial lasted approximately 30 seconds and was repeated four times. Subjects also walked at 6.4 km/h on the treadmill while performing the same visual task described above, but in this case, with the letter "C" presented centrally on a micro-display positioned 50 centimeters in front at eye level. Each of these trials lasted approximately 30 seconds and were repeated four times. While subjects were walking on the treadmill and performing the visual task, 3-dimensional full-body motion data were acquired using a video-based motion analysis system; gait cycle timing was measured using foot switches placed in the shoes and dynamic visual acuity was assessed by the visual task described above. Test 2: The Functional Mobility Test provides a corresponding assessment of the functional and operational changes in locomotor function by testing a subject's ability to negotiate an obstacle course placed over a medium-density foam floor. Subjects walked at a preferred pace through an obstacle course set up on a base of 10 cm thick medium density foam. The foam provided an unstable surface that increases the challenge of the test. The 6.0 m x 4.0 m course consists of several pylons and obstacles made of foam. Subjects were instructed to walk through the course as fast as possible without touching any of the objects on the course. This task was repeated three times in the clockwise direction and 3 times in the counterclockwise direction. The dependent measures are time to complete the course and the number of obstacles touched or knocked down.
results: Test 1: Integrated Treadmill Locomotion Test Results showed that subjects exhibited postflight changes in head-trunk coordination, toe clearance and gait cycle timing during treadmill locomotion. Dynamic visual acuity was decreased postflight, followed by an improvement in performance during the postflight recovery period. An analysis of the relationship between inflight treadmill usage characteristics and postflight functional mobility performance revealed that subjects who exercised on the iRED with greater body loading had enhanced postflight (R+1) functional mobility performance. Test 2: Functional Mobility Test Results indicate that adaptation to space flight led to a 62% increase in time to traverse the obstacle course on one day after return, and recovery of function took an average of 11 days after return. In conclusion, recovery of functional mobility after long-duration space flight is composed of two distinct but interrelated motor learning processes: 1) rapid on-line strategic change characterized by immediate onset after landing and 2) slower adaptive change requiring days to complete after landing. Postflight (R+1) changes in gaze control produced decreases in dynamic visual acuity (DVA) during walking. For some subjects, the decrement was greater than the mean acuity decrement seen in a population of vestibularly-impaired patients (collected using a similar protocol). The population mean showed a consistent improvement in DVA performance during the two-week postflight recovery period. Post-flight neurological exams conducted by flight surgeons have rated gaze and ocular symptoms from mild to severe in over 50% of returning Shuttle astronauts. These observations are consistent with the decrements in visual acuity during locomotion described in this report. Future work should focus on the addition of a “field” test of dynamic visual acuity that could be incorporated in the postflight examinations. This research should focus on the development of a portable system that will provide passive body motion (i.e. seated subject on a motion base) while subjects perform tests of visual performance. Astronauts should be tested as soon as possible after landing to assess the early effects of gaze dysfunction related to sensorimotor adaptation. This will allow a better determination of the potential impacts of changes in visual acuity on landing performance. This research led to conduct of ground-based studies focusing on developing adaptability training programs that include both gait and manual control training. In addition this research is investigating the retention capabilities of adaptability training, allowing this type of training to be conducted preflight and therefore reduce the requirement for an inflight training component, thus saving inflight crewtime and upmass hardware requirements. It will be useful to examine the relationship between other in-flight exercise modalities (cycle ergometer, upper body resistive exercise) and post-flight functional mobility performance to determine if a relationship exists. The current in-flight exercise data set includes only average data from US crewmembers over the entire duration of the mission. The exercise prescriptions to US crewmembers are graded over the duration of mission with the intensity (especially loading) and duration increased towards the end of the mission. Hence, the above analysis may be overly conservative in its estimates and should be extended with data over separate in-flight periods to confirm the relationships observed in the present study. Results obtained from this research helped motivate the design of the Functional Task Test, a pre/postflight battery of tests used to assess performance of astronauts on functional tasks that are representative of critical mission tasks for lunar and Mars operations. The Functional Task Test will allow better definition of the linkage between physiological change and functional performance including across several physiological systems (sensorimotor, cardiovascular, muscle performance).

title: Results of Pulmonary Function Tests
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Pulmonary function has been studied in detail following exposure to hypoxic and hyperoxic environments at normal gravity, but few studies have dealt with normoxic environments at zero gravity. Previous space flight history has shown no major changes in pulmonary function when evaluated postflight. During the first and second Skylab missions only a functional screening test on vital capacity was performed. Due to substantial decreases in cardiac output following these two missions, a more thorough pulmonary function screening effort was undertaken for Skylab 4 and the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project (ASTP). The objectives of this study were to document changes in pulmonary physiology and postflight adaptability and to determine the effect of body fluid redistribution on lung mechanics.
approach: Pulmonary function tests were performed to evaluate the mechanical properties of the lung by studying lung volumes and capacities. All three crewmen were tested in conjunction with other medical evaluations on L-45 (45 days preflight), L-30 and L-15, R+0 (day of recovery) and R+1 (1 day postflight), R+2, R+5, R+13 and R+29. The hardware was similar to the Skylab 4 pulmonary function test equipment, except the metabolic analyzer's analog computer was substituted with a PDP-8e digital computer system. This improved the system's flexibility and computational accuracy. It also allowed the volume of nitrogen washout to be computed.
results: Due to hardware malfunction on L-45, data were not obtained, and only two data sets were used for preflight means (L-30 and L-15). The Apollo atmosphere was 258 torr oxygen, but varied from 165 torr to 200 torr during Apollo-Soyuz docking and subsequent activities. Further complications ensued following exposure to nitrogen tetroxide fumes during reentry. Therapy was administered by breathing 100% oxygen at 760 torr for 15 to 20 minutes aboard the recovery vessel. All crewmen complained of chest tightness, retrosternal burning sensation, inability to inhale deeply and nonproductive cough. Pulmonary function tests were conducted on each crewmember on R+0, and no significant changes were observed when compared to preflight means. However, ventilatory equivalent (V A /RV) showed a 30% increase, which indicated poor ventilation during residual volume (RV) determinations. Nitrogen tetroxide exposure was anticipated to cause significant pulmonary difficulty within the first 24 to 36 hours after landing. Thus, any physiological changes associated with space flight were probably concealed by responses to nitrogen tetroxide exposure. Twenty-four hours later, symptoms worsened for all crewmen. Because of discomfort associated with deep inspiration and breath holding, satisfactory data could not be obtained on R+1 and R+2. Blood gas analysis indicated mild respiratory alkalosis with hyperventilation and hypoxia. The only significant finding, on R+2, was a decrease in the single-breath carbon monoxide diffusing capacity (DLCO SB ). These findings agreed with the observed radiograph abnormalities that revealed the presence of diffuse nodular-type infiltrates throughout both lung fields. This decrease in DLCO SB persisted until testing on R+13. R+29 data showed pulmonary function parameters, including DLCO SB and repeat blood gas determinations (breathing room air and 100% oxygen), were within normal limits. On R+0, Crewman A showed decreased RV, total lung capacity (TLC) and forced vital capacity (FVC), which remained below preflight values on all remaining tests. This indicated that nitrogen washout at the RV position did not start during postflight determinations. FVC, TLC and maximum expiratory flow rate (MEFR) were decreased on R+29. Crewman B demonstrated increased RV, closing volume (CV), and FVC on R+0. At R+29, the CV remained increased whereas FVC was slightly reduced relative to preflight. On R+0, Crewman C showed slightly reduced maximum midexpiratory flow rate (MMFR). R+29 increases were observed in VC and FVC. In conclusion, the weightless environment appeared to have no significant impact on either respiratory mechanics or lung structure. Although, as reported by Tripler Army Hospital, R+1 data did show nitrogen tetroxide exposure caused pulmonary difficulty, which resulted in decreased pulmonary function. Overall, no disturbing decreases or significant changes, which could be attributed to space flight, were observed when compared to preflight means.

title: In-flight Assessment of Renal Stone Risk
research_area: Skeletal physiology; Renal, fluid and electrolyte physiology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Physiological changes that occur in microgravity include changes in urine volume and composition that could contribute to the formation of kidney stones. An earlier study showed that spaceflight increases urinary concentrations of calcium and tends to increase concentrations of phosphate, probably as a result of bone demineralization. Also, earlier studies showed decreases on landing day in the concentration of citrate, which is an inhibitor of the formation of stones that contain calcium, and in urinary pH. A decrease in pH decreases the solubility of uric acid, which can form crystals that act as a nucleus for the formation of other stones. The objectives of this study were to make a preliminary assessment of spaceflight-induced changes in a profile of risk factors for kidney stones and of the influence of diet on these risk factors.
approach: Six male astronauts were studied before, during and after Shuttle missions lasting 11 to 16 days. Urine was collected during six 24-hour periods that occurred more than 10 days before launch, within 10 days of launch, on flight days 3 and 4, within 4 days of landing, on landing day, and 7 to 10 days after landing. In-flight samples were stored at room temperature in tubes containing an antiseptic. Samples collected before and after a flight were refrigerated, but the same antiseptics were added to certain aliquots to serve as controls for the in-flight samples. The urine samples were analyzed for pH and for the concentrations of potential stone-forming solutes. The degree of supersaturation was calculated for various salts, and the risk of stone formation was assessed relative to the risk in a normal population. Before and after the flights, the astronauts kept handwritten logs of food and fluid consumption for 48-hour periods beginning 24 hours before the urine collections began. During flights, intake of food and fluid was tracked with a barcode scanning system.
results: Urine volume was less for the in-flight collections than for the preflight collections (the mean volume fell from 1.7 liters before the flight to 0.8 liters early in the flight), although the difference was not statistically significant. Urine pH dropped significantly on landing day. Urinary calcium levels increased late in the flight and were significantly greater on landing day than before the flight. Urinary potassium levels were significantly lower during the flight than before the flight, and citrate levels were also lower, although the change was not statistically significant. Relative supersaturation ratios indicated a high risk for formation of calcium oxalate, calcium phosphate, struvite (ammonio-magnesium phosphate), sodium urate and uric acid stones early in the flight. The risk of calcium oxalate stones remained high throughout the flight. Dietary intakes of fluid, energy, protein, potassium, phosphorus and magnesium were all significantly reduced during the flight. The results of this preliminary study showed that astronauts (at least male astronauts) are at risk of forming kidney stones because of reductions in urine output and changes in chemical composition of the urine during spaceflight. These changes may include decreases in pH and in the concentration of citrate, as well as an increase in the concentration of calcium. Learning how to minimize the risk of forming renal stones before or after spaceflights will require additional studies of larger numbers of astronauts. A preliminary recommendation was made that astronauts drink 2.5 liters of water daily to dilute the urinary concentration of stone-forming salts.

title: Red Blood Cell Mass and Survival
research_area: Hematology; Metabolism and nutrition; Cardiovascular physiology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Studies of red blood cell (RBC) mass during short-term, 9-day space flight revealed a rapid decrease in total blood volume of about 12% within the first 24 hours of the mission. The associated decrease in plasma volume resulted in an increase in packed cell volume (central body hematocrit) compared to 1-G. Erythropoietin release and serum erythropoietin levels were also decreased during the flight. Measurements using labeled RBC revealed that the labeled circulating cells were not diluted by newly produced cells and that the RBC mass declined by 9% during the 9-day mission. The decline is concomitant with normal survival of circulating red blood cells (loss of 0.83% per day). As a result of this study, investigators surmised that (a) the release of newly produced RBCs from bone marrow into the blood stream stopped immediately after the subjects entered microgravity and that (b) a change of this magnitude could only result from nearly complete cessation of the release of red blood cells into the blood stream caused by the decrease in erythropoietin levels. The decline in erythropoietin release and serum erythropoietin levels are probably a consequence of increased oxyhemoglobin delivery to the kidney (assumed unchanged total renal blood flow) because of the decrease in plasma volume and increase in hematocrit. During this short-term flight, the subjects displayed a production rate of new RBCs similar to that present at 1-g, but far fewer of these cells ever appeared in the blood stream. Moreover, at the time of launch, the bone marrow in these crewmembers contained nearly mature cell precursors that should have been released within the next three days. Retaining and perhaps destroying the RBCs within the bone marrow can only explain this discordance. Intramedullary destruction of RBCs is a recognized phenomenon and has been termed "ineffective erythropoiesis"; it is known to occur in several disease states such as different types of anemia. The aim of this study was to prove the ineffective erythropoiesis hypothesis during a long-duration mission, based on the observations of the 9-day Shuttle flight. The previous study suggested that the immediate down-regulation of red cell production during space flight was caused by ineffective erythropoiesis, resulting from decreased erythropoietin levels in the blood stream.
approach: To estimate red blood cell mass and survival, a stable chromium isotope (50 Cr) was used as a tracer to label red blood cells (RBCs). Twenty milliliters (ml) of venous blood were drawn from the subject by venipuncture. The autologous RBCs were tagged with 50 Cr isotopes and the labeled cells were reinfused into the subject. A blood sample was taken about 20 minutes later and the initial dilution of labeled red blood cells was used to calculate red blood cell mass (RBCM). During the next four weeks, subsequent blood samples were drawn; counts of labeled RBCs from these blood samples were used to calculate RBC life span. Dosages of 50 Cr labeled RBCs were given 35 days before launch and landing day. Two more scheduled sessions (launch day and sixteen days after landing) were not performed. Each 50 Cr session was followed by two or three blood draws over the next few weeks. In addition to RBC mass and survival measurements, the blood samples were used to determine the levels of all major hormones and substances involved in the both the production and destruction of red blood cells in the bone marrow: erythropoietin, haptoglobin, ferritin and iron. Overall, a total of 3 preflight, 9 inflight and 8 postflight blood samples were collected for this experiment. To validate this method, two assumptions were made: (1) the 50 Cr labeled red blood cells were not diluted upon entry into microgravity, and (2) the immediate destruction of nearly mature RBCs in the bone marrow should be reflected by a sudden rise in urobilinogen concentration. To measure urobilinogen concentration in urine, the subject swallowed a capsule containing the stable, non-radioactive nitrogen isotope 15N. Over the next few hours following the ingestion, urine was collected void-by-void to determine the ratio between 15N-labeled- and total urobilinoids. Logs of food, fluid, and medication intake, as well as exercise regimen, were kept by the astronauts during the testing period.
results: The results of this experiment were compromised because no labeled red blood cells could be administered to the crewmembers shortly before launch. The last 50 Cr dosage given to the subjects was 35 days prior to launch. Also, urine samples were destroyed by the failure of the EuroMir Freezer. In consequence, urobilinogen and urobilinoid measurements were not performed. The collected data revealed that the erythropoietin serum concentrations were decreased in all three subjects compared to preflight levels. Hematocrit was also lower during and after the space flight. During their mission, the subjects consumed an average of 13.5 mg iron per day. The indices of iron storage and availability were increased during and after flight. Serum ferritin was greater during flight (average > 100 ng/mL) than before flight. Serum iron was increased in two subjects (average 20% greater than preflight) and unchanged in the third subject. Total iron binding capacity was lowered by an average of 10% during flight and was still below preflight levels 9 days after landing (R+9). On landing day (R+0), red blood cell mass (RBCM) was decreased by 17% compared to preflight baseline values, while serum ferritin concentrations were elevated. Serum erythropoietin was decreased in 2 of the 3 subjects on landing day, and elevated (80% greater than preflight) in all three subjects nine days later (R+9). All other indicators of iron status were unchanged. During additional measurements at R+3 months, the serum ferritin concentrations were below preflight level in all three subjects. Overall, investigators concluded that the subjects' RBC mass and survival adaptation to a microgravity environment resulted in a state of anemia. The anemia can be used as a model to better understand the mechanisms of erythropoiesis during space flight.

title: Carotid Baroreflex Function during Prolonged Exercise
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: Astronauts are often required to work (exercise) at moderate to high intensities for extended periods while performing extra-vehicular activities (EVA). Although the physiologic responses associated with prolonged exercise have been documented, the mechanisms involved in blood pressure regulation under these conditions have not been fully elucidated. An understanding of this issue is pertinent to the ability of humans to perform work in microgravity and complies with the emphasis of NASA's Space and Physiology and Countermeasures Program. Prolonged exercise and a constant workload is known to result in a progressive decrease in mean arterial pressure (MAP) concomitant with a decrease in stroke volume and a compensatory increase in heart rate (HR). The continuous decrease in MAP during exercise, which is related to the thermoregulatory redistribution of circulating blood volume to the cutaneous circulation, raises the question as to whether there is a loss of baroreflex regulation of arterial blood pressure. The researchers proposed that with prolongation of the exercise to 60 minutes, progressive increases in central command reflect a progressive upward resetting of the carotid baroreflex (CBR) such that the operating point of the CBR is shifted to a pressure below the threshold of the reflex rendering it ineffectual in correcting the downward drift in MAP. In order to test this hypothesis, several experiments were designed to uncouple the global hemodynamic response to prolonged exercise from the central command mediated response via continuous maintenance of cardiac filling volume by intravenous infusion of a dextran solution and whole body surface cooling to counteract thermoregulatory cutaneous vasodilation. As the type of work (exercise) performed by the astronauts is inherently arm and upper-body dependent, the researchers also examined the physiologic responses to prolonged leg cycling and arm ergometry exercise in the supine positions with and without lower body negative pressure (-10 torr) to mimic spaceflight-related decreases in cardiac filling volumes.
approach: Experiment 1 Subjects performed two 1-hour bouts of leg cycling exercise with 1) no intervention and 2) continuous infusion of a dextran solution to maintain central venous pressure constant at the 10-min pressure. Leg (L) exercise alone was performed at 50 and 75% VO 2max , and L exercise combined with arm (A) exercise (L + A) was performed at 75 and 100% VO 2max . title: Sleep and Vestibular Adaptation

objectives: This experiment was designed to study the effects of space flight on both sensorimotor (especially vestibular) and cognitive functions (especially orientation.) Optimal human performance depends upon integrated sensorimotor and cognitive functions both of which are known to be exquisitely sensitive to loss of sleep. The main objective of this study was to investigate variations in sleep and dreaming over an extended period of space flight, with special attention to changes in sleep and dreaming associated with the vestibular adaptation that occurs with adaptation to microgravity, and readaptation to 1-G conditions. To achieve this, a sleep monitoring system was tested that could accurately identify periods of wake, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep on-board the Mir space station.
approach: Five crewmembers completed measurements relating to the protocol before, during and after space flight. The inflight measurement blocks were scheduled early in the mission (mission day 37-49), in the middle (MD 79-91) and at the end (MD 110-122) of the mission. This investigation was conducted for the first time as part of the NASA 4 and Russian Mir 23 missions with three crewmembers participating. The experiment protocols were repeated on the Mir 24 mission with two additional crewmembers. It consisted of a simple athletic headband into which a head movement sensor had been sewn, along with a self-adhesive eyelid movement sensor that attached to the surface of the upper eyelid. The sensors were connected by two cables to a wallet-sized recording unit called the Night Headband Monitor (NHM). Subjects wore the NHM in a supplied arm band or attached the unit to a nearby wall with Velcro. The NHM analyzed data from the sensors and could store up to 30 nights before transfer to a computer. Usually, data from the NHM was uploaded to a laptop computer daily and subsequently stored on disk. Data was stored as one-minute counts of the number of 250 ms epochs during which eye or head movement was detected. Because the head movement sensor originally designed for the Night Headband utilized a gravity-dependent mercury switch, the sensor was redesigned as an inertial switch. The inertial switch had appropriate sensitivity in microgravity; no head movements were detected during quiet rest, but gentle rotations of the head were adequate to produce clear head movement signals. title: Autonomic Mechanisms During Prolonged Weightlessness
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The microgravity environment present during low-earth orbit (LEO) spaceflight may contribute to changes in autonomic cardiovascular regulation experienced by long-duration spaceflight crewmembers when they return to Earth's gravity. Theses changes manifest themselves as increased heart rates when standing, decline in arterial blood pressure, and even frank syncope. Several factors likely contribute to these changes, blood volume reductions, impaired baroreceptor-cardiac reflex responses, and inadequate increases in total peripheral resistance during standing. This experiment explored the probability that the disordered arterial baroreflex malfunction, documented during weightlessness or after simulated or actual weightlessness, is part of and a contributor to a broad range of autonomic abnormalities. The researchers developed this experiment using the following hypotheses as a guide: Vagal baroreflex impairment progresses during long-duration space missions, and plateaus to reach some asymptotic limit. Weightlessness impairs aortic as well as carotid baroreceptor reflexes, and that therefore, the baroreflex malfunction that develops in space may be due to central nervous system factors, rather than local changes in the wall of carotid arteries. Progressive impairment of integrated vagal baroreflexes in astronauts is expressed in reduced levels of vagal-cardiac nerve traffic, as reflected in fluctuations of R-R intervals during rigorously-controlled breathing. The progressive reduction of minimum R-R interval during baroreflex testing observed in previous space flight missions reflected increased sympathetic-cardiac neural activity. Diminished vagal-cardiac nerve traffic is associated with a reduced prevalence of atrial, and an increased prevalence of ventricular dysrhythmias in space. Low-frequency diastolic pressure power reflects quantitatively, levels of efferent human muscle sympathetic nerve activity. Reductions of baroreflex gain are related directly and significantly to impairment of vasoconstrictor responses to lower body negative pressure in space. Hypocapnia leads to a greater reduction of R-R interval power at respiratory frequencies, and carotid baroreceptor-cardiac reflex gain in space than on Earth. The researchers used the data obtained from this experiment to determine the adaptive changes that occurred in the autonomic nervous system of the flight subjects and to obtain insight into the various mechanisms that caused the observed integrated autonomic output.
approach: The design of this experiment was built around a battery of tests that activated different afferent nerve fibers, evoking different patterns of neural and cardiovascular responses through both separate and common mechanisms. These tests included: Controlled frequency breathing - a predetermined breathing protocol carried out using the Medikro Laptop Computer as an instructional guide. Valsalva’s Maneuver - performed by attempting to forcibly exhale with the nose closed and the mouth blowing into a pressurized breathing apparatus in order to increase blood pressure. Isometric Handgrip Exercise> - required the subject to sustain a muscular contraction, using a handgrip balloon assembly, to raise arterial blood pressure. Cold Pressor Test - involved rapid, sustained, severe cooling of a crewmember’s hand using the Cold Glove Assembly in order to elicit an increase in the subject's blood pressure and heart rate. Graded Lower Body Negative Pressure - provided a controlled, measured orthostatic stress to the cardiovascular system using the Chibis Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) Device.
results: The data obtained from this experiment showed a decrease in RR-interval standard deviations for all subjects and a decrease in respiratory frequency RR-interval spectral power for two subjects while in microgravity. RR-interval spectral power was decreased and systolic pressure spectral power was increased in all subjects two weeks after returning to Earth. The data also showed that while in microgravity the transfer function between systolic blood pressures and RR-intervals was reduced. The transfer function showed a further reduction the day after the subjects returned to Earth, and had not returned to preflight levels by 14 days after landing. These results suggested that long-duration spaceflight decreased vagal-cardiac control (reduced R-R interval oscillations at a given respiratory frequency) and baroreflex gain (reduced systolic to R-R interval transfer function magnitude), and that after returning to Earth, the effects of weightlessness may persist for at least 2 weeks. This experiment did not come to any conclusions about the cause of the decreased vagal-cardiac nerve traffic; however, the well documented reduction of blood volume that occurs while in microgravity is a probable explanation. The researchers attempted to document the time-course of in-flight adaptations, however, they were unable to adequately record directional trends. It is not yet clear whether changes in autonomic cardiovascular regulation progress or stabilize as a function of the duration of exposure to microgravity. Although the data obtained from this experiment was limited, the researchers hope the information obtained from this experiment can help to guide future research onboard the International Space Station.

title: Pre- and Postflight Echocardiography
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The headward fluid shift of space flight involves the redistribution of body fluids from the legs and abdomen into the thorax and head. This fluid shift is believed to initiate the cardiovascular readaptation syndrome (CRAS) of responses to space flight factors by stimulating arterial and cardiopulmonary sensors. The physiological responses to this stimulation include the reduction of plasma volume through increased urination, decreased thirst, and perhaps even vomiting, and the resetting of cardiovascular reflexes controlling arteriolar tone, venous capacity, and vascular responsiveness to postflight orthostatic stress. A complete understanding of CRAS will require the thorough documentation of the fluid shift and its effects. This understanding can be provided in part by the use of ultrasound echocardiography to determine the dimensions of cardiac and major vascular structures and to measure their normal functioning. Cardiac ultrasound measurements on the crew of the 84 day Skylab flight revealed a significant decrease in left ventricular volume which persisted for over a week postflight. Subsequent measurements on STS crewmembers confirmed that the loss of volume occurs during flights as short as a week or less, and may require a week or more to be completely reversed postflight. The large contribution of individual variability, due to such factors as age and physical fitness, was documented in those data. This study was proposed to continue the data collection, and to include, for the first time, measurements made while the subjects were standing upright. This additional data would have revealed the effects of space flight on the cardiovascular system's response to gravitational stress. The aim of DSO 465 was the determination of cardiovascular adaptations to space flight factors based on the echocardiographic measurement of cardiac functioning in the supine and standing positions.
approach: Cardiac images were made using an ATL/ADR 4000 S/LC real-time two-dimensional ultrasound imaging system. Images were made with the subject resting on a couch or cot in the left lateral decubitus position and during passive standing with his back flat against a wall and his feet nine inches out from the wall with his heels six inches apart. The sector-scanning end-fire transducer was positioned to acquire para-sternal long-axis, para-sternal short-axis and apical four-chamber views. A two-dimensional view was used to select appropriate scan lines for M-mode images at the aortic root for aortic and left atrial dimensions and at the level of the maximum excursion of the mitral valve for left ventricular dimensions. Ventricular dimensions were measured at end-diastole and end-systole; other dimensions were measured at end-systole. Data were collected on a tota1 of two crewmembers preflight, according to the following schedule : Crewman A: L-38, -33, -31, -30, -13, -10 and -9 days Crewman B: L-13, -12, -10 and -9 days Postflight data were not collected immediately after landing on these crewmembers because a late in-flight change in landing site to NASA-Dryden Research Facility in California left inadequate time to transport the equipment and operator from the planned landing site, NASA Kennedy Space Center in Florida. Uncertainties in the crewmembers’ schedule for returning to NASA-Johnson Space Center prohibited data collection on the days after landing.
results: The late change in landing site precluded postflight data collection. Therefore, DSO 465 produced no results. DSO 465 was supplemented by DSO 466. Please refer to DSO 466 for results.

title: In-Flight LBNP: Countermeasure to Reduce Post-Space Flight Orthostatic Intolerance
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are privacy-protected. Data is available via data request.
objectives: Space flight is known to cause a shift in fluid away from the lower body and a resultant decrease in body fluid. Hypovolemia might contribute to the orthostatic intolerance that is common after space flight. However, countermeasures like oral fluid and salt loading or the use of an anti-gravity suit have not succeeded in preventing postflight orthostatic intolerance. It may be that orthostatic intolerance could be counteracted by the ingestion of isotonic saline while negative pressure is applied to the legs and abdomen to allow the plasma volume to increase. The objective of this study was to evaluate this lower body negative pressure (LBNP) and fluid loading countermeasure for use in flight.
approach: Thirteen astronauts were studied before and during space flights of 7 to 14 days. Two months or more before a flight, the astronauts' tolerance of LBNP was checked by applying LBNP in steps of 10 millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) until the astronaut showed signs of presyncope (impending fainting). Orthostatic tolerance was assessed independently of gravity in LBNP ramp tests, in which blood pressure and heart rate were monitored while the astronauts spent five minutes at each 10-mm Hg drop of pressure down to -40 to -60 mm Hg. Ramp tests were carried out before the flight as well as during the flight at three-day intervals before, and one or two days after, the LBNP countermeasure protocol, which was called a "soak." A stepwise decompression (ramp) to -50 mm Hg was followed by 3.5 hours at 30 mm Hg below ambient pressure. During the first hour at -30 mm Hg, the astronauts ingested one liter of water or artificially sweetened fruit drink and eight grams of sodium chloride to provide isotonic saline. The effect of the soak treatment was evaluated by comparing heart rate and blood pressure responses to ramp tests before and after the treatment. A LBNP chamber that could be collapsed and stowed was used aboard the Shuttle. Negative pressure was provided by connecting it to a vacuum source (the Waste Collection System or the Spacelab Vacuum Vent).
results: Evaluable data were obtained from only four astronauts. The heart rate at maximum LBNP increased significantly between preflight and early in-flight ramp tests. Decreased heart rate responses to LBNP one day after the in-flight soak indicated that it provided a protective effect. The systolic and diastolic blood pressures during maximum LBNP were not significantly different from preflight levels during any of the ramp tests or soaks. These results showed that the combination of LBNP with ingestion of isotonic saline may be an effective countermeasure against postflight orthostatic intolerance. Results also suggested that orthostatic tolerance was lost after only 10 days or less in space, and that treatments may be beneficial even during flights of short-duration. However, the countermeasure is impractical for use during Shuttle missions because one treatment of one astronaut takes approximately five hours.

title: Gene Expression Profile Analysis as a Prognostic Indicator of Normal Tissue Response to Simulated Space Radiations
research_area: Cell and molecular biology; Radiation biology
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: This project was funded as a pilot project to determine the feasibility of using gene expression profiles to characterize the response of human cells to exposure to particulate radiations such as those encountered in the space flight environment. The investigators proposed to use microarray technology to examine the gene expression patterns of a bank of well-characterized human fibroblast cell cultures. These fibroblast cultures were derived from breast or head and neck cancer patients who exhibited normal, minimal, or severe normal tissue reactions following low LET radiation exposure via radiotherapy. Furthermore, determination of SF2 values from fibroblasts cultured from these individuals was predictive of risk for severe late reactions. The investigators hypothesized that by determining the expression of thousands of genes they could identify gene expression patterns that reflect how normal tissues respond to high Z and energy (HZE) particles, that is, that there are molecular signatures for HZE exposures. They also hypothesized that individuals who are intrinsically radiosensitive may elicit a unique response. The objectives of this study were to 1) determine molecular profiles (gene expression patterns} for normal human skin fibroblasts that have been exposed to heavy particles of increasing LET; 2) determine if there are unique, or signature, expression patterns that define exposure to a particular HZE particle
approach: In the last decade we have collected fibroblasts from head and neck and breast cancer patients. We have developed fibroblast lines from 100 patients. A significant number of the patients have had adverse reactions to radiotherapy with documented late normal tissue reactions scored according to the RTOG/EORTC scoring system. Late effects documented include skin fibrosis, subcutaneous fibrosis, skin retraction, and soft tissue and bone necrosis. For all of these primary cultures, fibroblast SF2 values were obtained. Interestingly, SF2 ranking appears as a continuous variation which is best approximated by a normal distribution of phenotype, which can be explained by multiple interacting Mendelian factors, that is, a genetic basis for differences in SF2. Because this was a pilot project the investigators limited themselves to 5 cell lines, all having a normal response to radiation exposure.
results: Statistical analysis revealed 45 genes that met the investigators cutoff criteria of 1.5X fold, false discovery rate of 0.05. Two major signaling pathways were identified by gene ontology analysis, and they include genes associated with DNA repair, replication, recombination, and cell growth and death. BAD and BID, and CIOE are unregulated, while BCl-2 is comparatively down-regulated. This opens the door for predicting radioresponse without having to irradiate. More data are needed on other radiosensitive cells lines to validate this supposition.

title: Human Cerebral Cortex Plasticity in Response to Long-term Bedrest as an Analog to Microgravity
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. Privacy-protected datasets are available via data request. Remaining datasets are publicly available.
objectives: This investigation assesses the effects of weightlessness on the central nervous system and specifically the sensorimotor system by inducing cortical reorganization through altered cortical excitability. The measures of cortical excitability will be evaluated for correlation with measures of lower limb functional recovery.
approach: Transcranial magnetic stimulation was used to evaluate motor cortex plasticity through the acquisition of recruitment curves. The location for application of the magnetic stimulation was determined by functional and structural brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Data collected from these control subjects included resting motor threshold, paired pulse sequences and cortical silent periods, The compound motor action potential and Hoffman reflex (H-reflex) response were collected as measures of peripheral stimulation.
results: Significant leg RC slope decreases were observed on post-bed rest day 1 (P1) (t(2805) = -4.14, P < 0.0001), P2 (t(2805) = -6.59, P < 0.0001), P3 (t(2805) = -6.15, P < 0.0001), P5 (t(2805) = -7.93, P <0.0001), P8 (t(2805) = -3.30, P = 0.001), and P12 (t(2805)= -3.33, P = 0.0009), suggesting a group decrease in corticospinal excitability in the immediate post-bed rest period with recovery approaching baseline over the following 2 wk. Significant effects were observed for hand RC slopes only for P2 (t(2916) = 1.97, P = 0.049), P3 (t(2916) = -2.12, P = 0.034), and P12 (t(2916) = -2.19, P = 0.029); no significant effects were observed for days P0 (t(2916) = -1.32, ns), P1 (t(2916) = 1.00, ns), P5 (t(2916) = -0.21, ns), or P8 (t(2916) = -0.27, ns). fMRI showed no change in activation for the hand but an increase in activation post-bed rest for the leg. On an individual basis, a more heterogeneous response was found which showed a potential association with performance on FMT. Results of this research include a better understanding of the cortical plasticity associated with leg disuse and may lead to applications in patient and astronaut rehabilitation.

title: Biochemistry of 3-D Tissue Engineering in the BTS
archive_status: Data preservation is complete. All datasets are publicly available.
objectives: The long term goal of this study was to use the microgravity environment, either simulated in Rotating Wall Vessel (RWV) Bioreactors or during space flight, to generated functional neuroendocrine 3-D constructs which may be useful as clinical replacement tissue in treating neurodegenerative diseases, such as Parkinson’s. Previous ground-based studies have shown that neural crest-derived PC12 pheochromocytoma cells, a well-established model for studying neuroendocrine differentiation undergo tissue-like assembly and neuroendocrine differentiation when cultured in RWV Bioreactors. Investigator’s hypothesized that simulated microgravity conditions in RWVs facilitate the formation of differentiated 3-D constructs of PC12 cells and that “true” microgravity during space flight might enhance /accelerate phenomena observed in RWVs. The specific objectives of this mission (Bio 3-D on board STS86/MIR) were: 1. To use PC12 pheochromocytoma cells for optimizing the experimental design for long-term cell culture in space under suboptimal “minimal cell culture conditions” which accommodate the technical restraints/existing equipment on board MIR. - lack of conventional Acell culture facility - minimal maintenance - limited post-experimental preservation ( no cryogenic freezers, restricted choice of fixatives) 2. To test whether under these conditions cultured PC12 cells/cell assemblies can be passaged serially. 3. To evaluate the assembly and differentiation of PC12 cell aggregates using biochemical, morphological, immunological and molecular biological techniques.
approach: a) Cell Culture: 1. Inoculate 5 x 104 PC12 cells/ml into Tissue Culture Bags (3 samples/time point) _ Weekly sampling of Avital signs@ (glucose, pH, pO2, pCO2. HCO3- , electrolytes) 2. Passage at regular intervals (approximately every 14) _ remove 1/5, break up visible aggregates and inoculate into new bag _ fix 4/5 (using OmnifixTM ) b) Sample Analysis: 1. During Flight: Macroscopic and microscopic observation/photography 2. Post Flight: B Morphology: SEM, TEM, light microscopy B Immunohistochemistry: Junctional Contacts, Adrenergic Differentiation B Gene Expression by RT-PCR
results: The aim of this mission was to use PC12 cells as one of the cell types, previously proven to respond to the RWV culture conditions and to test the feasibility of long-term culture and repeated (5 to 6 times) passaging at ca.14 day intervals. Given the constraints on board Mir, both the cell culture conditions, and the long-term (up to 4 months) sample preservation/storage conditions were far from ideal. There were several major constraints on board Mir which impacted on the experimental set up for cell culture and sample retrieval/preservation: 1. The cells were maintained in 35 ml cell culture bags in an environment (inside the BSTC.), which provided for temperature control in an ambient gaseous environment (i.e. was not a regular CO2 incubator); 2. No maintenance, besides periodic measurements of Avital signs@, i.e. dissolved gases (O2, CO2,-COOH3) and pH was feasible, viz., depleted nutrients could not be replaced, neither could pH or glucose be adjusted; 3. No cryogenic freezer for sample storage was available; and 4. Due to safety considerations on board MIR, no cross-linking fixatives, such as formaldehyde, could be used.
